Shell environment variables take precedence over .env . A benchmark run is five commands: harness2-setup lab , harness2-check --bench lab , the refinement run harness2 --bench lab --k 1 --mode parallel --only-domains antitrust-competition --max-tasks 1 , then harness2-judge and harness2-report with the same arguments. Judging and reporting must use the same benchmark, executor, subset, --k , --mode and seed as the refinement run. --dry-run previews task selection without model calls, and --substrate cx switches from the default OpenCode executor to Codex. Repeat the same command to resume, and use a new HARNESS2_RUNS_DIR when you change models or task selection. The honest trade-offs Recursion is paid for in executions. One Propose, Probe, Compose step at --k 2 in my demo costs seven executions of the same task instead of one (the baseline, four probes, two compositions), and those executions are free only because there is no model behind them. Upstream, every probe is model calls on a real task: the docs say model-backed runs incur API costs and advise starting with a small task selection, and --k multiplies that bill. Scaling the recursion budget brings further gains, so the budget is a money dial, not a quality dial. Selection without ground truth is selection on the evidence you thought to collect. My loop rejected a useless subagent because none of its six evidence values moved. If I had been collecting step counts as evidence, the same edit would have scored a point for adding a delegation step and gone into the refined harness. A contrastive loop will happily adopt an edit that changes behavior without improving it, and the only defense is picking evidence that is hard to game, like read plus declared equaling the row count. The security note in the upstream README deserves its own paragraph. Executor network access is unrestricted, and Codex runs with its sandbox disabled. Public benchmark rubrics may be accessible online, so an executor with open web access can read the grading criteria it is being graded against. The docs tell you to configure network restrictions before evaluation. If you skip that step, your gains measure the executor's search skills. And the whole approach assumes the harness is where your problem lives. If your agent fails because the model cannot do the task, eight editable components will not save it. Harness² keeps weights fixed by design, which is the right call when the harness is the bottleneck and the wrong tool when it is not. What I keep from it is smaller than the framework: probe your harness edits by running the same task twice and diffing the behavior, and write down the evidence that justified every edit you kept. My demo does that in a few hundred lines of standard library Python. Which part of your own agent harness has never been probed, only reviewed?
items.summary_html:
A harness I wrote by hand read two rows out of seven and reported a confident total. No error, no warning, just five hours billed where ten and three quarters belonged, and five rows that never appeared in the output. The prompt was fine. The model was fine. The system around the model was the thing that was broken, and nothing in my loop was looking at it.

Code: github.com/javaAndScriptDeveloper/harness2-how-to

🤖 Run this with an AI agent

The repo carries an AGENTS.md with the same how-to written for an agent to execute. Hand your agent this prompt:

Clone https://github.com/javaAndScriptDeveloper/harness2-how-to and follow AGENTS.md to run the example and show me the output.
What Harness² actually optimizes

Google Research published harness2 with a definition worth copying into your own notes: a harness is the system around a model that enables it to act as an agent, meaning prompts, tools, memory, skills, orchestration and more. Harnessing is the process of optimizing that system.

Harness² connects two levels of recursion while keeping model weights fixed. Task-level recursion refines the execution harness for the current task through a contrastive Propose, Probe, Compose step: propose edits, probe their effects on the same task, and compose a refined harness from behavioral contrasts between executions, without ground-truth feedback. Harnessing-level recursion updates a persistent improvement harness with adopted harnesses and evidence-supported lessons from each task, which guides refinement on the next one.

The published results: across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single Harness² step improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, with gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB's partial pass rate. Increasing the task-level recursion budget brings further gains.

The part that made me build a demo is the phrase "without ground-truth feedback". Every eval loop I have shipped needs a label to score against. This one scores by comparing executions of the same task against each other.

What you build in this tutorial

The repo above is a small standalone implementation of that loop in plain Python, standard library only, no model credentials and no network. It is not the Google Research package. I wrote it to make the mechanics visible, the way you would reimplement a consensus algorithm to understand it before running the real one. Instructions for the real package are further down.

The task is a timesheet. Seven rows, written the way people write them, and one instruction:

# instruction: report billed hours per project and account for every row you cannot read
2026-10-19 | aiden | api-migration | 2h
2026-10-19 | aiden | api-migration | 90m
2026-10-20 | bo | api-migration | 1.5 h
2026-10-20 | bo | onboarding | 45m
2026-10-21 | cyd | onboarding | 2 hours
2026-10-21 | cyd | api-migration | 3h
2026-10-22 | cyd | api-migration |

The base harness names two tools and says nothing about a row the executor cannot read. So the first execution reads 2h and 3h, bills five hours to one project, and silently drops the rest.

The eight components as plain data

Harness² exposes eight editable components around the model: system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts and plugins. They control context construction, the tool interface, delegation and behavior inside the tool loop.

Keeping all eight as data is what makes an edit cheap and a probe trivial:

COMPONENTS = (
    "system_prompt",
    "guardrails",
    "memory",
    "tool_guidance",
    "subagents",
    "skills",
    "scripts",
    "plugins",
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Harness:
    system_prompt: str
    guardrails: tuple = ()
    memory: tuple = ()
    tool_guidance: tuple = ()
    subagents: tuple = ()
    skills: tuple = ()
    scripts: tuple = ()
    plugins: tuple = ()

    def with_edit(self, edit):
        if edit.component == "system_prompt":
            return replace(self, system_prompt=edit.value)
        current = getattr(self, edit.component)
        if edit.value in current:
            return self
        return replace(self, **{edit.component: current + (edit.value,)})

An edit is a name, a component, a value, a scope (general or domain-specific) and a rationale. The executor reads the harness and changes what it does: skills.duration_normalizer swaps the duration parser, guardrails.row_accounting makes the deliverable list every row that was not read, scripts.reconcile_rows runs a row count check inside the execution, subagents.unit_checker delegates a second look at parsed durations.

Probe and contrast, with no answer key

A probe executes the same task under the edited harness. The contrast is the set of evidence keys where that execution behaved differently from the baseline execution:

def contrast(baseline, candidate):
    before, after = baseline.evidence(), candidate.evidence()
    return {key: (before[key], after[key]) for key in before if before[key] != after[key]}

The evidence is six values the run produces about itself: rows read, rows declared unreadable, projects reported, total hours, whether read plus declared equals the row count, and whether the self-check ran and passed. Not one of them needs a correct answer to exist. That is the whole trick, and it is also the limit, which I come back to below.

Composition ranks the surviving edits by how much they changed, builds refined harnesses out of the top ones, executes each, and adopts the strongest by a rule that puts accounting first:

def rank_key(execution):
    return (
        execution.reconciliation == "pass",
        execution.rows_read,
        execution.self_check == "pass",
    )

Reading more rows while hiding the rest never wins.

Run it

Python 3.12, nothing to install:

python3 selftest.py

selftest: 10 checks passed

Then parallel recursion with k = 2, which probes two general and two domain-specific candidates and produces two compositions:

python3 run_parallel.py

harness2 mini demo
mode: parallel
k: 2
task: timesheet-billing (7 rows)
instruction: report billed hours per project and account for every row you cannot read
prior lessons applied: 0
base: rows_read=2 declared=0 projects=1 hours_total=5.0 reconciliation=fail self_check=off
probes:
  guardrails.row_accounting [general] score=2 declared 0 -> 5, reconciliation fail -> pass
  scripts.reconcile_rows [general] score=1 self_check off -> fail
  skills.duration_normalizer [domain] score=3 rows_read 2 -> 6, projects 1 -> 2, hours_total 5.0 -> 10.75
  subagents.unit_checker [domain] score=0 no behavioral contrast
compositions:
  1 edit: rows_read=6 declared=0 projects=2 hours_total=10.75 reconciliation=fail self_check=off
  3 edits: rows_read=6 declared=1 projects=2 hours_total=10.75 reconciliation=pass self_check=pass
adopted: guardrails.row_accounting, scripts.reconcile_rows, skills.duration_normalizer
rejected: subagents.unit_checker (no behavioral contrast)
refined: rows_read=6 declared=1 projects=2 hours_total=10.75 reconciliation=pass self_check=pass
lessons in improvement harness: 3
files: adopted_harness.json, probes.json, billing_summary.txt

Three things in that output are the point of the whole exercise.

The narrow composition, one edit, reads six rows and still fails reconciliation. Better parsing alone produced a nicer wrong answer. The wide composition reads six rows, declares the seventh, and passes.

subagents.unit_checker is rejected. Its probe added a delegation step to the trace and changed no evidence at all, so the composition dropped it. An edit that looks reasonable in review and does nothing in execution is exactly what a contrastive probe is for.

The deliverable now names what it could not do:

Billing summary for timesheet-billing
api-migration=8.0h
onboarding=2.75h
total=10.75h
rows_read=6
needs_review=1
needs_review_1=2026-10-22 | cyd | api-migration |
Sequential mode and the improvement harness

Parallel recursion explores wider, sequential recursion refines deeper. The sequential run does the same work in two successive steps, each probing against the harness the previous step adopted:

python3 run_sequential.py

The middle of its summary:

steps:
  step 1 probed: guardrails.row_accounting score=2, skills.duration_normalizer score=3
  step 1 adopted: guardrails.row_accounting, skills.duration_normalizer
  step 2 probed: scripts.reconcile_rows score=1, subagents.unit_checker score=0
  step 2 adopted: scripts.reconcile_rows

The same summary reports prior lessons applied: 3, because the parallel run left an improvement harness behind at runs/improvement_harness.json. That file is harnessing-level recursion in miniature, and one of its three lessons looks like this:

{
  "edit": "skills.duration_normalizer",
  "component": "skills",
  "rationale": "read 90m, 1.5 h and 2 hours, not only 2h",
  "evidence": "rows_read 2 -> 6, projects 1 -> 2, hours_total 5.0 -> 10.75",
  "tasks": ["timesheet-billing"],
  "adoptions": 1
}

A lesson carries the evidence that earned it. The next task proposes lesson-backed edits before the rest of the pool, so the second run reaches the same harness with half the probes.

Two of the assertions that hold this honest, and that run in CI on every push:

grep -q reconciliation=pass runs/parallel/summary.txt
grep -q api-migration=8.0h runs/parallel/billing_summary.txt
Running the real Harness²

items.title: PHP2Shell: Your Code Was Fine, The Engine Was Not
items.summary: Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product. Imagine you do everything right. You validate your inputs. You use prepared statements. You escape your output. You have a linter, a code review process, and a slightly smug Slack channel called #security-wins. Then someone sends your server one weird HTTP request, and it runs their code instead of yours. Not because of anything you wrote. Because of something PHP did while cleaning up after itself. On October 21, 2026, the PHP project shipped a security release for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 . The internet has already nicknamed the pair PHP2Shell , which is a great name and a terrible Wednesday. Let's walk through what actually broke, why it is a bigger deal than "yet another CVE", and also where the scary headlines are a little ahead of the facts. Why this one is different PHP is not a niche language. W3Techs says 69.3% of websites whose server-side language it can identify run PHP . WordPress, Laravel, Drupal, Magento, that one invoice portal from 2014 that nobody dares touch. Most PHP vulnerabilities live in an application or a plugin. You patch the plugin, you move on. These two live in the engine . The engine is the thing underneath your code. It is the C program that parses your PHP, allocates your memory, and tears down after every request. You can write the most boring, correct PHP of your life, and the floor below it can still have a hole in it. [DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER] the stack, bottom to top: the web server (Apache or nginx), the SAPI (mod_php or PHP-FPM), the PHP engine, then your application code on top. Highlight the engine layer in red with the caption "both bugs live here, below everything you wrote". Show that an attacker's request has to pass through the engine before your code even sees it. Both bugs are about the same unglamorous thing: memory management around a request that goes wrong. To see why, you need to know how PHP spends its life. PHP's life is one request long PHP's model is famously "shared nothing". A request comes in, PHP sets up a fresh little world for it, runs your script, then throws the whole world away. The worker process survives, but the request's state is supposed to die with the request. That is why PHP is so forgiving. Leak some memory in a script? Nobody cares, the request ends and the memory gets reclaimed. Here is the happy path: flowchart LR A([Request arrives]):::start --> B[Request startup build per-request state]:::engine B --> C[Run your script]:::app C --> D[Request shutdown cleanup and free]:::engine D --> E([Worker waits for the next request]):::start E --> A classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a classDef engine fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a classDef app fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a Notice that the purple boxes, startup and shutdown, are the engine's job. Your code only owns the teal one in the middle. Both vulnerabilities are about what happens when something goes wrong between those purple boxes, and the engine's cleanup code assumes a state that no longer holds. PHP has a hard ceiling on how much memory one request may use, memory_limit . Hit it, and PHP gives up on the request on the spot. "Gives up on the spot" is where the trouble starts. Bug 1: cleaning up a house that was never built CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory one. Here is the scenario, paraphrasing the PHP Foundation's write-up and Rapid7's analysis . PHP is in the middle of request startup. It is building that per-request state, piece by piece. A memory allocation fails. PHP abandons the request abruptly. But the state is only half built. Some fields are set, some are whatever bytes happened to be sitting in that memory. Then the cleanup code runs, and it does what cleanup code does: it trusts the state it is handed. It follows pointers that were never initialized. It frees things that were never allocated. It treats garbage as a structure. The mental model I like: a demolition crew is sent to tear down a building. The building was never finished, and the blueprint is a napkin with random scribbles on it. The crew follows the napkin anyway, and demolishes whatever the scribbles point at. Here is the shape of the bug as a deliberately simplified sketch. This is not PHP's real source, just the pattern: // simplified illustration of the bug class, not actual PHP code int request_startup ( request * r ) { r -> headers = alloc_table (); // ok r -> uploads = alloc_table (); // out of memory! bail out... if ( ! r -> uploads ) return FAILURE ; r -> hooks = alloc_table (); // never reached, r->hooks is junk return SUCCESS ; } void request_shutdown ( request * r ) { free_table ( r -> headers ); free_table ( r -> uploads ); free_table ( r -> hooks ); // frees a pointer nobody ever set } The mistake is not in either function alone. It is in the assumption that shutdown only ever runs on a fully started request. Now here is the part that makes this one nasty. How do you make a server run out of memory on purpose? You do not need to hack anything, you just ask nicely and badly. Rapid7 notes that crafted multipart requests can exhaust memory even when their overall size looks like it fits inside the configured limits. And on Apache with mod_php , the demonstrated attack happens before any of your application code runs. That is the whole reason the "zero authentication" line is true. There is no login to bypass. Your code never got the chance to say no. Memory corruption you can trigger with a request, in a place your app cannot guard, is how you end up with "9.2 critical" in a headline. Bug 2: the ghost of requests past CVE-2026-109619, the stale state one. Same family, different flavour. Remember that a worker process handles request after request. Some bookkeeping state is global to the worker, and is supposed to be reset between requests. Now picture this sequence: sequenceDiagram participant A as Request A participant W as PHP worker participant B as Request B A->>W: runs, global state points at memory M W->>W: fatal error interrupts cleanup W-->>W: M is freed, but the pointer to M is not cleared B->>W: arrives on the same worker W->>W: reads the old pointer before init resets it Note over W: use-after-free: B is reading memory it does not own A fatal error, like running out of memory or a timeout, can interrupt the cleanup in the middle. The memory gets freed, but a pointer to it survives. The next request lands on the same worker, and something reads that pointer before normal initialization has a chance to wipe it. That is a classic use-after-free . The name is the best part, because the thing you are using after it is free is not free at all, it is very expensive. Think of a hotel room that was demolished but the key card still opens the door. Whoever is standing there next gets to decide what is inside. Rapid7 describes two concrete paths to reach it. One is the PHP 8.5 fatal error backtrace feature, which is on by default and was confirmed on mod_php . The other is a session upload progress path that works on PHP-FPM, and needs an application operation to leave state behind first. Note the pattern. Neither bug is about a missing bounds check in some parser. They are both about error paths . The happy path of PHP has been tested for decades. The path where a request dies at the worst possible moment is the one that gets less love. So can anyone hack 70% of the internet? Short answer: no, and it is worth being precise, because the headline version of this story sells more than it delivers. What is solid: Both bugs are real and rated 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). Both can lead to code execution as the web worker's user, with no authentication. RCE was demonstrated by researchers , against real setups, not just crashes. mod_php is the highest risk. Rapid7 notes that for the OOM bug, mod_php runs cleanup even when startup failed. PHP-FPM kills the worker when startup fails , which blocks that specific sequence. What is more nuanced: "Any PHP server" is too strong. Rapid7 reviewed multiple public proof of concepts, and each one works only for a specific combination of OS, PHP version and web server. None is broadly reliable yet. The attack complexity is rated High. Memory corruption exploits are fiddly. That is a speed bump, not a wall. Reports of exploitation are mixed. watchTowr says it has seen exploitation in the wild through its honeypots , while Rapid7 has seen attempts but not confirmed in-the-wild compromise. Whichever way that lands, Rapid7 also warns that a more portable technique could show up quickly. And the exposed surface is not small. Palo Alto's Unit 42 brief cites telemetry that counts over 22 million potentially vulnerable internet-facing instances. That is a vendor number, so season to taste, but it is the right order of magnitude for "a lot". If I had to summarize it: not the end of the web, but also not a drill. The part that is actually uncomfortable Here is the story behind the patch, and it is the most human part of the whole thing. flowchart LR A[2024 Quarkslab audit, first signs of the OOM issue]:::early --> B[Fix stalls competing patches, each with trade-offs]:::slow B --> C[Aug 2026 Calif, OpenAI and Wiz report it, RCE shown]:::report C --> D[Oct 20 CVE IDs leak 2 days early]:::bad D --> E[Oct 21 Chainguard images break the embargo]:::bad E --> F[Oct 21, 14:00 UTC patched releases ship]:::good classDef early fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a classDef slow fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a classDef report fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a Per the PHP Foundation , an external audit by Quarkslab back in 2024 led a core developer to spot the first signs of the OOM problem while fixing something else. No exploit path was known at the time. Then the fix stalled. Competing patches each had a cost: breaking compatibility, opening new denial of service angles, or touching lots of third-party extensions. The Foundation's own words are refreshingly blunt: the delay was "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources." Then in August 2026 the bug was reported again, with a working unconditional RCE. The CVE IDs leaked online before the release. The embargo then cracked a second time when a vendor published images that already contained the fix. I find this oddly reassuring and deeply annoying at the same time. Reassuring, because an open source project wrote that sentence about itself in public, and is changing its process: majority decisions, an ecosystem security team, more staff. Annoying, because "everyone who maintains critical infrastructure is under-resourced" is not a new lesson, and PHP is carrying a very large share of the web on it. The AI angle, and where I would push back A lot of the commentary around this release points at one thing: AI changes who can exploit this. The argument goes like this. Turning a subtle memory corruption bug into a working attack used to need rare skills. Now somebody with a laptop and an open-weights model can point an agent at the internet, hand it the advisory and say "go find the ones that are still vulnerable". I think the direction is right and the details are overstated. What is right: the cost of going from advisory to attempt is falling fast. The patch itself is a diff. A diff tells a model exactly where to look. And scanning is cheap when the scanner does not get tired. What is overstated: the hard part of this bug is not finding targets, it is the exploit reliability. Rapid7 says the public PoCs are fragile. Memory corruption is a craft, and models are not magic yet at crafting heap layouts for your particular distro. And there is a side of the story that gets less airtime: the defenders have the same tools. The Foundation says it used AI-assisted scanning and validation as part of its security work, with the line that "a person makes every call and works on every patch." So the realistic summary is not "attackers got superpowers". It is this: The window between "patch published" and "someone is trying it on your server" is shrinking. Your patching speed is now a security control, not an IT chore. What to do about it Boring answer first: update. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. If you are on 8.1 or older, there are no routine upstream releases. Rapid7 notes limited source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, so lean on your distribution or an LTS vendor, or finally take the upgrade you have been postponing since 2022. Two gotchas people will trip on: A patched package on disk is not a patched process in memory. Running workers keep the old code until they restart. Qualys specifically calls this out , so restart or gracefully reload your PHP services after upgrading. Containers do not save you from stale base images. If your image was built last week, it is still carrying last week's PHP. Quick check: php -v # compare against 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35 # then make sure the running workers are the new ones sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm # or: apachectl graceful If you truly cannot patch yet, the advisories list temporary mitigations. They reduce exposure, they do not fix it: ; php.ini or FPM pool config, NOT ini_set() or .user.ini (too late for these) session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 ; closes the known session path fatal_error_backtraces = 0 ; PHP 8.5 only post_max_size = 8M ; and cap multipart size at the frontend too You will see memory_limit=-1 suggested too, and here is where I have to confess the Roll Safe meme is doing real work: It genuinely appears in the advisory guidance, set administratively so apps cannot override it. But Rapid7 is clear that an allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path, so it narrows the window and does not close it. Also, a server with no memory limit has its own personality. items.summary_html:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

Imagine you do everything right.

You validate your inputs. You use prepared statements. You escape your output. You have a linter, a code review process, and a slightly smug Slack channel called #security-wins.

Then someone sends your server one weird HTTP request, and it runs their code instead of yours.

Not because of anything you wrote.

Because of something PHP did while cleaning up after itself.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project shipped a security release for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The internet has already nicknamed the pair PHP2Shell, which is a great name and a terrible Wednesday.

Let's walk through what actually broke, why it is a bigger deal than "yet another CVE", and also where the scary headlines are a little ahead of the facts.

Why this one is different

PHP is not a niche language. W3Techs says 69.3% of websites whose server-side language it can identify run PHP.

WordPress, Laravel, Drupal, Magento, that one invoice portal from 2014 that nobody dares touch.

Most PHP vulnerabilities live in an application or a plugin. You patch the plugin, you move on.

These two live in the engine.

The engine is the thing underneath your code. It is the C program that parses your PHP, allocates your memory, and tears down after every request.

You can write the most boring, correct PHP of your life, and the floor below it can still have a hole in it.

[DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER] the stack, bottom to top: the web server (Apache or nginx), the SAPI (mod_php or PHP-FPM), the PHP engine, then your application code on top. Highlight the engine layer in red with the caption "both bugs live here, below everything you wrote". Show that an attacker's request has to pass through the engine before your code even sees it.

Both bugs are about the same unglamorous thing: memory management around a request that goes wrong.

To see why, you need to know how PHP spends its life.

PHP's life is one request long

PHP's model is famously "shared nothing".

A request comes in, PHP sets up a fresh little world for it, runs your script, then throws the whole world away.

The worker process survives, but the request's state is supposed to die with the request.

That is why PHP is so forgiving. Leak some memory in a script? Nobody cares, the request ends and the memory gets reclaimed.

Here is the happy path:

flowchart LR
    A([Request arrives]):::start --> B[Request startup
build per-request state]:::engine
    B --> C[Run your script]:::app
    C --> D[Request shutdown
cleanup and free]:::engine
    D --> E([Worker waits for the next request]):::start
    E --> A

    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef engine fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef app fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Notice that the purple boxes, startup and shutdown, are the engine's job.

Your code only owns the teal one in the middle.

Both vulnerabilities are about what happens when something goes wrong between those purple boxes, and the engine's cleanup code assumes a state that no longer holds.

PHP has a hard ceiling on how much memory one request may use, memory_limit. Hit it, and PHP gives up on the request on the spot.

"Gives up on the spot" is where the trouble starts.

Bug 1: cleaning up a house that was never built

CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory one.

Here is the scenario, paraphrasing the PHP Foundation's write-up and Rapid7's analysis.

PHP is in the middle of request startup. It is building that per-request state, piece by piece.

A memory allocation fails. PHP abandons the request abruptly.

But the state is only half built. Some fields are set, some are whatever bytes happened to be sitting in that memory.

Then the cleanup code runs, and it does what cleanup code does: it trusts the state it is handed.

It follows pointers that were never initialized. It frees things that were never allocated. It treats garbage as a structure.

The mental model I like: a demolition crew is sent to tear down a building.

The building was never finished, and the blueprint is a napkin with random scribbles on it.

The crew follows the napkin anyway, and demolishes whatever the scribbles point at.

Here is the shape of the bug as a deliberately simplified sketch. This is not PHP's real source, just the pattern:

// simplified illustration of the bug class, not actual PHP code
int request_startup(request *r) {
    r->headers = alloc_table();     // ok
    r->uploads = alloc_table();     // out of memory! bail out...
    if (!r->uploads) return FAILURE;
    r->hooks   = alloc_table();     // never reached, r->hooks is junk
    return SUCCESS;
}

void request_shutdown(request *r) {
    free_table(r->headers);
    free_table(r->uploads);
    free_table(r->hooks);           // frees a pointer nobody ever set
}

The mistake is not in either function alone. It is in the assumption that shutdown only ever runs on a fully started request.

Now here is the part that makes this one nasty.

How do you make a server run out of memory on purpose? You do not need to hack anything, you just ask nicely and badly.

Rapid7 notes that crafted multipart requests can exhaust memory even when their overall size looks like it fits inside the configured limits.

And on Apache with mod_php, the demonstrated attack happens before any of your application code runs.

That is the whole reason the "zero authentication" line is true. There is no login to bypass. Your code never got the chance to say no.

Memory corruption you can trigger with a request, in a place your app cannot guard, is how you end up with "9.2 critical" in a headline.

Bug 2: the ghost of requests past

CVE-2026-109619, the stale state one.

Same family, different flavour.

Remember that a worker process handles request after request. Some bookkeeping state is global to the worker, and is supposed to be reset between requests.

Now picture this sequence:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Request A
    participant W as PHP worker
    participant B as Request B
    A->>W: runs, global state points at memory M
    W->>W: fatal error interrupts cleanup
    W-->>W: M is freed, but the pointer to M is not cleared
    B->>W: arrives on the same worker
    W->>W: reads the old pointer before init resets it
    Note over W: use-after-free: B is reading memory it does not own

A fatal error, like running out of memory or a timeout, can interrupt the cleanup in the middle.

The memory gets freed, but a pointer to it survives. The next request lands on the same worker, and something reads that pointer before normal initialization has a chance to wipe it.

That is a classic use-after-free. The name is the best part, because the thing you are using after it is free is not free at all, it is very expensive.

Think of a hotel room that was demolished but the key card still opens the door.

Whoever is standing there next gets to decide what is inside.

Rapid7 describes two concrete paths to reach it.

One is the PHP 8.5 fatal error backtrace feature, which is on by default and was confirmed on mod_php. The other is a session upload progress path that works on PHP-FPM, and needs an application operation to leave state behind first.

Note the pattern. Neither bug is about a missing bounds check in some parser. They are both about error paths.

The happy path of PHP has been tested for decades. The path where a request dies at the worst possible moment is the one that gets less love.

So can anyone hack 70% of the internet?

Short answer: no, and it is worth being precise, because the headline version of this story sells more than it delivers.

What is solid:

Both bugs are real and rated 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). Both can lead to code execution as the web worker's user, with no authentication.

RCE was demonstrated by researchers, against real setups, not just crashes.

mod_php is the highest risk. Rapid7 notes that for the OOM bug, mod_php runs cleanup even when startup failed. PHP-FPM kills the worker when startup fails, which blocks that specific sequence.

What is more nuanced:

"Any PHP server" is too strong. Rapid7 reviewed multiple public proof of concepts, and each one works only for a specific combination of OS, PHP version and web server. None is broadly reliable yet.

The attack complexity is rated High. Memory corruption exploits are fiddly. That is a speed bump, not a wall.

Reports of exploitation are mixed. watchTowr says it has seen exploitation in the wild through its honeypots, while Rapid7 has seen attempts but not confirmed in-the-wild compromise.

Whichever way that lands, Rapid7 also warns that a more portable technique could show up quickly.

And the exposed surface is not small. Palo Alto's Unit 42 brief cites telemetry that counts over 22 million potentially vulnerable internet-facing instances. That is a vendor number, so season to taste, but it is the right order of magnitude for "a lot".

If I had to summarize it: not the end of the web, but also not a drill.

The part that is actually uncomfortable

Here is the story behind the patch, and it is the most human part of the whole thing.

flowchart LR
    A[2024
Quarkslab audit,
first signs of the OOM issue]:::early --> B[Fix stalls
competing patches,
each with trade-offs]:::slow
    B --> C[Aug 2026
Calif, OpenAI and Wiz
report it, RCE shown]:::report
    C --> D[Oct 20
CVE IDs leak
2 days early]:::bad
    D --> E[Oct 21
Chainguard images
break the embargo]:::bad
    E --> F[Oct 21, 14:00 UTC
patched releases ship]:::good

    classDef early fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef slow fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef report fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Per the PHP Foundation, an external audit by Quarkslab back in 2024 led a core developer to spot the first signs of the OOM problem while fixing something else.

No exploit path was known at the time.

Then the fix stalled. Competing patches each had a cost: breaking compatibility, opening new denial of service angles, or touching lots of third-party extensions.

The Foundation's own words are refreshingly blunt: the delay was "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."

Then in August 2026 the bug was reported again, with a working unconditional RCE. The CVE IDs leaked online before the release. The embargo then cracked a second time when a vendor published images that already contained the fix.

I find this oddly reassuring and deeply annoying at the same time.

Reassuring, because an open source project wrote that sentence about itself in public, and is changing its process: majority decisions, an ecosystem security team, more staff.

Annoying, because "everyone who maintains critical infrastructure is under-resourced" is not a new lesson, and PHP is carrying a very large share of the web on it.

The AI angle, and where I would push back

A lot of the commentary around this release points at one thing: AI changes who can exploit this.

The argument goes like this. Turning a subtle memory corruption bug into a working attack used to need rare skills. Now somebody with a laptop and an open-weights model can point an agent at the internet, hand it the advisory and say "go find the ones that are still vulnerable".

I think the direction is right and the details are overstated.

What is right: the cost of going from advisory to attempt is falling fast. The patch itself is a diff. A diff tells a model exactly where to look. And scanning is cheap when the scanner does not get tired.

What is overstated: the hard part of this bug is not finding targets, it is the exploit reliability. Rapid7 says the public PoCs are fragile. Memory corruption is a craft, and models are not magic yet at crafting heap layouts for your particular distro.

And there is a side of the story that gets less airtime: the defenders have the same tools.

The Foundation says it used AI-assisted scanning and validation as part of its security work, with the line that "a person makes every call and works on every patch."

So the realistic summary is not "attackers got superpowers". It is this:

The window between "patch published" and "someone is trying it on your server" is shrinking.

Your patching speed is now a security control, not an IT chore.

What to do about it

Boring answer first: update.

The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

If you are on 8.1 or older, there are no routine upstream releases. Rapid7 notes limited source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, so lean on your distribution or an LTS vendor, or finally take the upgrade you have been postponing since 2022.

Two gotchas people will trip on:

A patched package on disk is not a patched process in memory. Running workers keep the old code until they restart. Qualys specifically calls this out, so restart or gracefully reload your PHP services after upgrading.

Containers do not save you from stale base images. If your image was built last week, it is still carrying last week's PHP.

Quick check:

php -v                       # compare against 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35

# then make sure the running workers are the new ones
sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm     # or: apachectl graceful

If you truly cannot patch yet, the advisories list temporary mitigations. They reduce exposure, they do not fix it:

; php.ini or FPM pool config, NOT ini_set() or .user.ini (too late for these)
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0   ; closes the known session path
fatal_error_backtraces = 0            ; PHP 8.5 only
post_max_size = 8M                    ; and cap multipart size at the frontend too

You will see memory_limit=-1 suggested too, and here is where I have to confess the Roll Safe meme is doing real work:

It genuinely appears in the advisory guidance, set administratively so apps cannot override it. But Rapid7 is clear that an allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path, so it narrows the window and does not close it.

Also, a server with no memory limit has its own personality. It is called "an outage".

And two things not to reach for. Rapid7 warns that RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA can themselves trigger the vulnerable allocation failure path, and container or cgroup memory limits are an incomplete answer and can kill the whole worker pool.

Do not hide the evidence either. Silencing errors with display_errors or @ does not prevent stale state from being read, and a quiet log is not proof you are fine.

Here is the whole decision as a flowchart, for the person who has a patch window and a manager:

flowchart TD
    A([Do you run PHP on a web server?]):::start --> B{Is it on 8.2.35, 8.3.36,
8.4.27 or 8.5.12 or newer?}:::decision
    B -- yes --> C{Did you restart or reload
workers after upgrading?}:::decision
    C -- yes --> D([You are patched. Go touch grass.]):::good
    C -- no --> E[Restart workers now]:::action
    B -- no --> F{Is it 8.1 or older?}:::decision
    F -- yes --> G[Distro or LTS backport,
or plan the upgrade]:::action
    F -- no --> H[Upgrade to a fixed release]:::action
    G --> I[Apply interim mitigations
until it lands]:::warn
    H --> E

    classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef action fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef warn fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a
The thing worth taking away

The patch is the urgent lesson. The durable one is quieter.

Your security posture includes layers you did not write and never read.

Your code can be perfect and the runtime under it can still ship a bug that was first noticed two years ago.

That is not a reason to panic about PHP specifically. Every runtime has error paths nobody loves, and the next bug of this kind will be in a different one.

It is a reason to treat runtime and base image updates as first class work, to know which version is actually running in production, and to keep the gap between "advisory" and "deployed" as small as you can.

Cleanup code, it turns out, is also code.

Maybe even the code most worth reviewing.


Your team's attention is limited, and the deluge of AI-generated code is making it harder to keep production secure and reliable without slowing you down.

I'm building LiveReview, a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems.

Instead of presenting every diff with equal emphasis, LiveReview scores each change by blast radius — how far its impact reaches through your call graph — so you can focus attention where it actually matters.

I pointed hb judge at the moderation step in my own product's image feature. This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

enki-harness: a free, MIT-licensed test harness for AI filters that refuses to flatter you.

You wrote a safety filter, you wrote its tests, it passes. That proves less than you think: the person who wrote the code wrote the tests, so the tests only check the cases you already thought of.

enki-harness builds the harness for you and adds the parts you'd skip:

  • Twins: for every case it must catch, a near-identical innocent case it must not flag
  • Controls: dumb stand-ins (always-allow, always-block) that must fail, or the harness itself is broken
  • Rules off: switches each rule off, alone and in pairs, to find dead rules and rules that cancel each other out
  • Attacker slice: written by a different generator than your cases (leet, spacing, stretching)
  • Falsifier: you write down what result would prove you wrong before it runs, and it's timestamped

No score until every gate is green. Rows first, the number last.

This week I added add-on #1: hb judge, for when the filter isn't code but an AI model. It sends every case to the model several times and reports flag rates, not one lucky answer.

Demo

Video plus a one-click Windows install: https://enkilabs.co.uk/harness/

The prompts it screens are fixed sentences we wrote ourselves, all describing ordinary adult portraits, with no user text anywhere. Run each one several times and the screen still flagged them at random, about 1 time in 40: a different sentence each time, never the same one twice in a row. Every flag was a false alarm turning away a real user.

With an open-weight model I could run it hundreds of times locally for free, see the rows, and prove the noise was the model, not my wording. Against a closed API, each of those checks costs money and you're guessing.

The Lazy Payoff

It saved me from the "obvious" fix. I was about to spend an evening rewording prompts to dodge the filter. The runs showed the plain cartoon style, already live and working, gets flagged just as often, so rewording would never have fixed it. That screen was only ever judging our own text, so we removed it from that one feature. The checks that actually protect people still run, on the finished image.

Two lessons now built into the add-on:

  • A warm-up call: my first run voided itself because the local model was still loading when the must-pass control ran. The harness refused to score it, which is exactly what it should do.
  • Progress output: a 400-call run that prints nothing looks hung. Now it prints a count every 25 calls.

Then vs. Now (Escalated): Then: Trezor disclosed on August 13, 2026 that a breach at its shipping partner ShipMonk exposed customer names, addresses, phone numbers and emails. Now: Some Trezor customers have received postal letters urging them to 'migrate their wallets' via QR codes that redirect to phishing sites built to steal seed phrases, and the breach's scope has grown to roughly 81,000 customers. Trezor initially reported on August 13, 2026 that a breach at its shipping partner ShipMonk exposed the names, shipping addresses, phone numbers and email addresses of 13,689 customers (11,742 with full exposure, 1,947 with partial exposure), raising concerns about physical-mail and "wrench" attacks on crypto users. In early September, Trezor said the impact had grown to roughly 81,000 customers after older U.S. order records that ShipMonk was supposed to have deleted were also found exposed. By September 9, victims were reporting postal letters with QR codes linking to phishing sites designed to capture seed phrases, a clear escalation of the threat vector. Root Cause and Lessons The Trezor incident stems from a data breach at third-party shipping provider ShipMonk, which exposed customer names, home addresses, phone numbers and email addresses; Trezor says its own systems, devices, private keys and wallet backups were not compromised. Attackers leveraged the exposed addresses to send physical letters that appear to come from Trezor, advising recipients to "migrate their wallets." Each letter contains a QR code that routes through an io-qr.cc redirector to a "qr-trezor" lookalike domain registered on September 3, unrelated to the official site. Scanning the code leads victims to a page that prompts for their seed phrase, resulting in wallet drainage. Hardware security keys protect account logins, but they offer no protection here: anyone who obtains a seed phrase can restore the wallet without any second factor. The only defense is never entering a seed phrase on any website or device other than the hardware wallet itself, and treating unsolicited mail claiming to be from Trezor as hostile. Nvidia's CMP VRAM hack is rooted in firmware that disables memory stacks on GA100 silicon to create lower-spec SKUs. The CMP Unlocker tool, built on Jon Pry's research into defeating stack protection in Nvidia's Falcon security coprocessor, re-enables the hidden stacks entirely in software, with no physical modification, expanding memory capacity dramatically. Results vary, since some of the locked memory may have been disabled because it is defective. This underscores the importance of hardened secure coprocessors and firmware verification to prevent unauthorized hardware modifications. BlindLock's approach stores passwords, notes and 2FA codes inside ordinary-looking PNG images, encrypted in two layers (AES-256-GCM and XChaCha20-Poly1305) and bound to the device's TPM or Secure Enclave. Its crypto feature, WalletLink, is not yet available and would only read public balances and addresses, not hold keys or assets. Users should still keep BlindLock's encrypted backup file and twelve recovery words offline and separate, since a copied image alone cannot restore access on a new device, and the security model assumes the device remains uncompromised. The ShipMonk breach shows how a logistics partner that holds no crypto and touches no private keys can still become the weak link for a crypto firm. Notification emails indicated attackers exploited a vulnerability in the Metabase analytics platform, and ShipMonk also failed to delete older Trezor customer records as required by contract, which widened the exposure. Organizations should enforce strict data-retention and deletion audits for vendors, minimize the customer data shared with third parties, enforce strict email authentication, and train staff to verify unexpected requests. Keep one backup somewhere else. A copy of critical data with a second provider means one compromised account or one regional outage cannot take everything down with it. items.title: I built a SaaS that turns messy company data into dashboards, cited AI answers and a secure API
items.summary: Six months ago I kept hearing the same thing from small business owners: "My data is everywhere, and I can't answer a simple question about it." Sales in Shopify. Payments in Stripe. Costs in Excel. Forecasts in Google Sheets. And no analyst on the payroll. So I built DataShowing — and I want to share the three design decisions that made it trustworthy enough for real company data. The problem with "just ask the AI" Everyone is bolting AI onto products right now. But when the data is company data, a free-form AI is a liability: It can hallucinate numbers that don't exist. It can leak data across tenants if your isolation is sloppy. Nobody can audit what it actually read. So I inverted the model: the AI never generates facts, it only formulates queries. Every number you see in an answer comes from a real row in your database, and every answer links back to the exact query that produced it. Decision 1: Row-level security at the database layer Multi-tenancy is usually done in application code: WHERE tenant_id = ? . One forgotten filter and you have a breach. DataShowing enforces isolation with Postgres row-level security policies . Even a bug in my application code cannot read another tenant's rows, because the database itself refuses. The AI runs under the same read-only role — it physically cannot write, delete, or cross tenants. Decision 2: The AI is read-only and cited The analyst endpoint ( POST /v1/ai/analyze ) takes a question like "What was my best-selling product in September and why?" and: Generates a SQL query (never executed directly — it goes through a validator). Executes it with a read-only, RLS-scoped role. Returns the answer with the query, the rows used and a confidence note . If the data doesn't support an answer, it says "I don't have data for that" instead of inventing a KPI. That single behavior is what makes founders actually trust the tool. Decision 3: Everything is an API Dashboards are for humans. But half of my users wanted their numbers in their own apps, Slack bots or weekly email reports. So every dataset is exposed through a versioned REST API with scoped keys: curl https://datashowing.com/v1/datasets/42/profile \ -H "x-api-key: $DS_API_KEY " Versioned means when I change a response shape, v1 keeps working. Your integrations never break because I shipped a feature. The stack (boring on purpose) TanStack Start + React on the frontend. Postgres with RLS for every tenant boundary. CSV, Excel, Shopify, WooCommerce, Google Sheets and Stripe connectors for ingestion. A read-only analyst layer on top of the same database your dashboards use — one source of truth. Pricing that a solo founder can expense Starter at €2.99 , Business at €5.99 (no VAT, UK company). No sales call, no "contact us". You connect your data and you have a dashboard in ten minutes. What I'm learning from building in public The unsexy truth: the hard part was not the AI. It was making the ingestion boring and predictable — deduplicating rows, normalizing currencies, handling timezone chaos in Stripe exports. Garbage in, garbage dashboard out is the real law of analytics. I'm documenting the whole journey — distribution, SEO, what works and what flops. If you're building something similar, I'd love to compare notes in the comments. Try it free: datashowing.com — feedback is more valuable than money right now. Posted by the founder. I read every comment.
items.summary_html:
Six months ago I kept hearing the same thing from small business owners: "My data is everywhere, and I can't answer a simple question about it."

Sales in Shopify. Payments in Stripe. Costs in Excel. Forecasts in Google Sheets. And no analyst on the payroll.

So I built DataShowing — and I want to share the three design decisions that made it trustworthy enough for real company data.

The problem with "just ask the AI"

Everyone is bolting AI onto products right now. But when the data is company data, a free-form AI is a liability:

  • It can hallucinate numbers that don't exist.
  • It can leak data across tenants if your isolation is sloppy.
  • Nobody can audit what it actually read.

So I inverted the model: the AI never generates facts, it only formulates queries. Every number you see in an answer comes from a real row in your database, and every answer links back to the exact query that produced it.

Decision 1: Row-level security at the database layer

Multi-tenancy is usually done in application code: WHERE tenant_id = ?. One forgotten filter and you have a breach.

DataShowing enforces isolation with Postgres row-level security policies. Even a bug in my application code cannot read another tenant's rows, because the database itself refuses. The AI runs under the same read-only role — it physically cannot write, delete, or cross tenants.

Decision 2: The AI is read-only and cited

The analyst endpoint (POST /v1/ai/analyze) takes a question like "What was my best-selling product in September and why?" and:

  1. Generates a SQL query (never executed directly — it goes through a validator).
  2. Executes it with a read-only, RLS-scoped role.
  3. Returns the answer with the query, the rows used and a confidence note.

If the data doesn't support an answer, it says "I don't have data for that" instead of inventing a KPI. That single behavior is what makes founders actually trust the tool.

Decision 3: Everything is an API

Dashboards are for humans. But half of my users wanted their numbers in their own apps, Slack bots or weekly email reports. So every dataset is exposed through a versioned REST API with scoped keys:

curl https://datashowing.com/v1/datasets/42/profile \
  -H "x-api-key: $DS_API_KEY"

Versioned means when I change a response shape, v1 keeps working. Your integrations never break because I shipped a feature.

The stack (boring on purpose)
  • TanStack Start + React on the frontend.
  • Postgres with RLS for every tenant boundary.
  • CSV, Excel, Shopify, WooCommerce, Google Sheets and Stripe connectors for ingestion.
  • A read-only analyst layer on top of the same database your dashboards use — one source of truth.
Pricing that a solo founder can expense

Starter at €2.99, Business at €5.99 (no VAT, UK company). No sales call, no "contact us". You connect your data and you have a dashboard in ten minutes.

What I'm learning from building in public

The unsexy truth: the hard part was not the AI. It was making the ingestion boring and predictable — deduplicating rows, normalizing currencies, handling timezone chaos in Stripe exports. Garbage in, garbage dashboard out is the real law of analytics.

I'm documenting the whole journey — distribution, SEO, what works and what flops. If you're building something similar, I'd love to compare notes in the comments.

Try it free: datashowing.com — feedback is more valuable than money right now.

Posted by the founder. I read every comment.

items.title: Kevin O'Leary's data center company pushes back on the 'bragawatt' label
items.summary: Kevin O'Leary. Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images O'Leary Digital's CEO says a Wall Street firm's analysis misses work happening before construction. Paul Palandjian, the CEO, said the company's two campuses will generate their own electricity. He outlined land deals, permitting, and early funding, saying delivery should be judged in phases. Kevin O'Leary 's data center company has a message for analysts who doubt its enormous AI ambitions: You're not seeing the whole picture. Paul Palandjian , CEO of O'Leary Digital , pushed back on a Bernstein Research assessment that put the firm near the bottom of the data center industry's credibility rankings. In an emailed response to Business Insider, he detailed land agreements, water applications and licensing, engineering work, and funding that he said the analysis overlooks. "Scrutiny during this cycle is fair," Palandjian wrote. He added, "A score built from announced-capacity data ranks every pre-construction project low on construction progress by definition, and it cannot see confidential work." His response gets at a central question in the AI building boom: How much weight should investors give the work that happens before data center construction begins? Paul Palandjian, CEO of O'Leary Digital. Paul Palandjian/O'Leary Digital Bernstein examined thousands of data center projects using data from the tracking firm Aterio, assessing factors such as construction progress, electricity availability, and industry experience. Its analysis concluded that only about 35% of announced data center capacity in the US will get built. O'Leary Digital received a credibility score of 0.35 out of 5. Bernstein estimated that 489 megawatts of its announced 15-gigawatt pipeline would materialize, roughly 3%. The analysts grouped it with ambitious newcomers described as "bragawatts." Palandjian said the 15-gigawatt figure represents the full build-out of two campuses in Utah and Alberta over several years. "We would rather be judged on milestones than on a model," he wrote. Data center power without the queue Palandjian's clearest distinction concerns electricity, one of the biggest obstacles facing data center developers. "We are not in an interconnection queue," he wrote, referring to the waiting lists for connections to the electricity grid. Instead, both campuses are designed to generate all their electricity on-site, he said, with direct access to natural gas pipelines and supplies. That's what the industry calls " behind the meter ": producing power at the facility rather than relying on an electricity utility to supply it from the grid. Data center land, water, and early money In Utah, Palandjian said the Military Installation Development Authority had approved and executed a 30-year development agreement naming O'Leary Digital as master developer of the project area. About 11,000 acres are under binding agreements, he said. Master planning, ground studies, and laser-based land surveying have finished at both sites, and the company filed an engineered Utah water application in late September, he added. In Alberta, about 13,000 acres are under a binding agreement, and a water license for 6 million cubic meters a year has been granted, Palandjian said. He also said that both sites are away from densely populated residential communities. On money, Palandjian said his firm has capital for both pre-development and advancing the project toward key milestones. He did not specify a funding amount or say the entire build-out was financed. He said that the engineering, power, and construction firms working with the company, and the global banks advising it, provide evidence of its ability to deliver. "With that team, every critical part of the project is being worked through, gaps are identified early, and we are closing them to raise our probability of success," he wrote. Palandjian said that while O'Leary Digital is young, its team has decades of experience in real estate, power, and infrastructure. Bernstein's skepticism does not mean every newcomer will fail. "It's not that all of these guys are sort of terrible and not going to deliver, but we just have lower confidence because we don't know them," analyst Madison Rezaei said. With Palandjian's update, now we know a bit more. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: RAG vs. AI Agents: Choosing the Right Approach for Enterprise Automation
items.summary: Enterprise automation is moving beyond predefined rules and simple chatbots. Businesses increasingly want AI systems that can understand internal information, answer complex questions, and help complete tasks across multiple applications. Two approaches gaining attention are retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents. Although they can work together, they solve different problems. RAG helps large language models generate answers using relevant information retrieved from documents, databases, and other knowledge sources. AI agents go a step further by using models to plan tasks, select tools, and take actions toward a defined goal. One focuses primarily on grounding responses in useful information, while the other focuses on carrying out workflows. Choosing between them depends on the business problem, the reliability of available data, the level of autonomy required, and the risks associated with automated decisions. Understanding these differences helps organizations build practical AI solutions without adding unnecessary complexity. 1. What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)? Retrieval-augmented generation combines a language model with a retrieval system that searches for relevant information before generating an answer. Rather than relying only on information learned during training, the model receives additional context from an organization’s own knowledge sources. A typical RAG system connects documents, internal knowledge bases, databases, and search indexes. When an employee asks a question, the system retrieves relevant information and provides it to the language model, which uses that context to formulate a response. For example, an IT employee might ask how to resolve a recurring application error. A RAG-based assistant can search internal troubleshooting guides, technical documentation, and previous incident reports before suggesting a solution. RAG is particularly useful when answers depend on company-specific information that changes frequently. When documents are updated and the retrieval index is refreshed, the system can use the latest available content without requiring the language model to be retrained. However, RAG does not automatically guarantee accurate answers. Poor document quality, irrelevant search results, missing information, and incorrect access permissions can still lead to unreliable responses. Effective implementations require well-maintained knowledge sources, appropriate retrieval methods, and regular evaluation. Microsoft’s RAG solution design and evaluation guide explains how retrieval quality, document processing, and evaluation influence the performance of these applications. 2. What Are AI Agents? AI agents are systems that use language models to pursue defined goals by selecting tools, processing information, and taking actions. Depending on their design, they may break a task into smaller steps, evaluate results, and adjust their approach when circumstances change. Unlike a basic question-answering application, an agent can interact with business applications through approved APIs, functions, and other tools. Consider an employee requesting a software access change. An AI agent could identify the relevant access policy, check the employee’s request details, prepare the required approval request, and track its status through connected systems. Sensitive actions would still require the appropriate authorization and, where necessary, human approval. This makes AI agents useful for workflows involving multiple systems and decisions. Examples include customer support, IT operations, invoice processing, and employee onboarding. Nevertheless, greater autonomy introduces additional challenges. Organizations should therefore define what an agent can access, which actions it may perform, when it must request approval, and when it should stop and escalate a task. 3. RAG provides access to relevant knowledge, while an agent manages a process that may involve retrieval, reasoning, and action. The key distinction is not that RAG is simple and agents are always advanced. A carefully designed RAG application can be technically sophisticated, and an agent can perform a straightforward task. The right choice depends on the workflow, not the technology’s perceived complexity. 4. When Should Enterprises Choose RAG? A human representative can review the answer before sending it when the situation requires judgment. A RAG application can retrieve relevant policy sections and explain how they relate to a question. Access controls are essential here. The retrieval system must respect document-level permissions so employees cannot obtain confidential information simply by asking the AI assistant for it. In these situations, the objective is primarily to locate, interpret, and communicate information. Introducing autonomous actions may add complexity without providing enough additional value. 5. Resolving the issue may require checking the order management system, reviewing delivery information, applying company policies, and creating a support ticket. More advanced implementations could execute predefined remediation steps after validating the required conditions. In these situations, AI agents for business operations can work alongside Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to connect internal knowledge with business processes. This combination helps organizations automate multi-step workflows while keeping actions aligned with business rules and approval requirements. Consider an IT service desk handling a request to install approved software. The employee submits a request through a service portal. The agent retrieves the relevant software and access policies through RAG. It checks the request details against the applicable requirements. It prepares an approval request or routes the case to the correct team. After the required authorization, it invokes an approved tool to carry out the permitted action. It records the outcome and communicates the status to the employee. RAG provides the relevant policy information, while the agent coordinates the workflow and uses connected tools. This combined approach is useful when a task requires information gathering, interpretation, and execution. However, it should not be adopted automatically. If a single retrieval step answers the question effectively, a standard RAG implementation may be less expensive and easier to maintain. 7. Before implementation, identify authoritative data sources, remove outdated documents where appropriate, define ownership, and establish processes for updating information. For structured business records, verify that APIs and database queries return consistent results. Evaluate existing systems and integration requirements Enterprise information may reside in ERP, CRM, IT service management, document management, and custom legacy applications. Determine how these systems expose information and which actions can be performed through supported interfaces. Start with read-only access where possible. Introduce write permissions only after the workflow has been tested and the necessary authorization controls are in place. Establish security and governance controls The National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Generative AI Risk Management Profile guides identifying and managing risks associated with generative AI. In practice, enterprises should apply least-privilege access, protect sensitive data, validate tool inputs, log important operations, and define escalation procedures. They should also consider prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded in retrieved content attempt to manipulate a model or agent. For agents, additional controls should limit the actions available to the system, require approval for sensitive operations, and provide a way to stop or reverse supported actions. Measure performance against business outcomes A convincing demonstration is not enough to establish that an AI solution is ready for production. Teams should evaluate the system against realistic tasks and compare its performance with the existing process. For RAG, useful metrics include retrieval relevance, factual accuracy, source support, and whether the answer correctly acknowledges missing information. For agents, teams should also measure successful task completion, incorrect tool calls, unauthorized action attempts, escalation rates, and the time required to complete a workflow. Choose RAG when users primarily need answers, summaries, or explanations based on internal documents and data. Choose an AI agent when the system must coordinate several steps or interact with business applications to complete a task. Combine RAG and agents when the workflow needs grounded knowledge retrieval alongside planning, tool selection, and controlled execution. A useful implementation strategy is to start with the simplest architecture that meets the requirement. Build a RAG application first if the immediate need is reliable information access. Add agent capabilities when testing reveals that dynamic tool selection or multi-step execution provides a meaningful benefit. Conclusion RAG and AI agents serve complementary purposes in enterprise automation. RAG helps language models produce answers grounded in relevant organizational information, while AI agents can coordinate tools and actions to complete multi-step workflows. The right approach depends on the business problem, the quality of available data, the integration effort, and the risks associated with automation. Organizations that need dependable knowledge access can often begin with RAG. Those seeking to automate connected business processes may benefit from agents, while more complex workflows can combine both. The most effective strategy is to begin with a clearly defined use case, establish measurable success criteria, and introduce autonomy gradually. With reliable data, appropriate permissions, human oversight, and continuous evaluation, enterprises can build AI systems that solve practical problems without adding unnecessary operational risk.
