Up until recently, it was a great time to be the founder of a neolab, the lavishly funded, research-first AI startups founded by top talent who defected from the likes of OpenAI or Google DeepMind. We reported last month that Jeff Dean, Google's former chief scientist, is seeking a valuation as high as $50 billion for his new AI science startup. OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever's Safe Superintelligence is worth $32 billion. Another OpenAI alum, Mira Murati, is raising a round for Thinking Machines Lab at a valuation of around $40 billion. But lately, in conversations with multiple VCs around Silicon Valley, there is a growing divide about whether neolabs can make the economics work with their multibillion-dollar price tags and formidable competition from frontier labs. One VC at a top firm, who asked that I not use his name, told me neolabs are the most hotly debated type of investment right now. "Some would say you shouldn't invest in any, and others would say this is basically all you should be investing in because software's dead, and you either have to own models or hardware, and even if you enter at a billion, the company could be worth a trillion," he said. Business Insider; Randy Yeip When I recently asked Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy at Business Insider's Growth Mode conference which sector he thought was most overhyped, he immediately cited neolabs, which was noteworthy, given that Menlo invested in some of them . Murphy pointed to an example from his time as an early board advisor at Google, which he said did so well because it "was like a match thrown into a bonfire." "The opposite thing you want to do is start a match with a bonfire," Murphy told me. "That's the risk of what's going on now with companies raising such large rounds." Another Menlo partner, Deedy Das, posted last month about the "difficult game" of making neolab math work. Das seemed a bit taken aback by the reaction to his post and later texted me: "Like all startups, many will fail, some will work." Picking which ones will work is why VCs get paid the big bucks. Neolabs are a power-law bet taken to an extreme, Radical Ventures' Aaron Rosenberg told me. Investors know most will likely burn enormous sums on compute and talent without ever becoming profitable. But the rare winner could become a foundational AI company worth hundreds of billions or more. "We're confident that the best neolabs will attract ongoing support," Rosenberg said. "Talent continues to transition out of the incumbents and academia into founder roles, and we see no signs of that slowing." Like Radical, New Enterprise Associates wrote a bullish view in June . One of the authors, Andrew Schoen, told me his views have not changed. "There are neolabs I know of that are finalizing billion-plus-dollar rounds of equity financing, and those processes are moving very smoothly and quickly," he said. The Buzz Menlo Ventures' partners Shawn Carolan, Matt Murphy, and Venky Ganesan. Will Mackie Productions Katie here. Many of tech's biggest names gathered at the Ritz-Carlton in San Francisco on Saturday, at a black-tie event in the name of Menlo Ventures' 50th anniversary. Hollywood titan turned venture capitalist Jeffrey Katzenberg of Dreamworks fame asked the audience to join a prayer "for the blockbuster IPO of Anthropic," a joking reference to Menlo's early investment in the company. I also spotted Morgan Stanley's storied technology banker Michael Grimes, who is undoubtedly holding his own AI IPO prayers. Other attendees included an array of public company and startup CEOs, including those from Snowflake, Zscaler, Legora, and OpenRouter. As Menlo partner Venky Ganesan quipped, there was more AUM (assets under management) in the room than in many countries, given the attendees' net worth and the investment capital they manage. Menlo isn't the first venture firm to host a splashy anniversary party; Index Ventures recently went big for its 30th anniversary . A person at a rival venture shop expressed disappointment that their firm doesn't host such celebrations. Menlo's night ended with concerts from two super confidential Grammy Award winners trying to rake in those AI bucks! Around the Cap Table We reported this week that Fireworks AI is seeking fresh funding at a valuation of between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after its last blockbuster round was closed. "You Can See Everything" has everyone talking . Ben thought it was absolute genius, if a bit long. It will make this year's Oscars race exciting. See it in theaters before the experience is lessened by spoilers. Our colleague Rya Jetha explored the excitement and pitfalls of investing in robotics startups. Like neolabs, robotics companies are commanding big valuations with little to show for it, yet. Foursquare's $0 acquisition ended with no payout for employees or investors, according to founder Dennis Crowley . Post of The Week There are only 130 US tech companies, public or private, valued at $10B or more (decacorns). That’s roughly 20 to 30 new companies per decade, for the last five decades. This year alone, with a quarter to go, there have been 42 decacorns minted privately. Either this is the most… — Rory O'Driscoll (@rodriscoll) October 21, 2026 The VC Insider team Ben Bergman, chief correspondent, in Los Angeles. Katie Roof, editor at large, in San Francisco. Pranav Dixit, senior technology editor, in San Francisco. Leena Rao, executive editor, in Los Angeles. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI Code Review: Which Changes Still Need a Human?
items.summary: Anthropic’s review process makes the approval decision depend on the change, its author, and the path back. AI-made graphic of a CI permission change requiring human review. More agent-written pull requests make merge policy more important. I would tie human approval to the change’s risk, the author’s eligibility, and the path back if the patch fails. Anthropic’s October 15 account of code review on the Claude Code team gives a concrete example of that approach. Anthropic says Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code’s own code. That figure measures code written. It does not measure how many pull requests merge without human approval. The team describes separate approval requirements for changes at different risk levels. Separate the finding from the approval An automated reviewer can identify a possible bug, point to the relevant lines, and ask the author to address it. A passing test can show that a particular check succeeded. Someone still has to decide whether that evidence is enough for this change to merge. Anthropic’s public Code Review documentation says the product posts findings and a check run. It does not approve or block a pull request on its own. The October engineering account describes an additional policy used in Anthropic’s repositories: automated bug and security reviews produce findings that must be resolved, while the number of required human approvals varies with risk. A team adopting the product would need to set its own merge rules. Claude Code Review Workflow from Anthropic This distinction matters when a review comes back clean. The result tells me what the reviewer reported about the code it examined. I would also want the test output, the scope of the change, and an account of what those checks could miss. A green review cannot answer whether the team meant to change this behavior in the first place. Classify the change before counting reviewers Anthropic’s published risk table gives low-risk changes, such as documentation and copy, a path with no required human approval after automated review and security checks pass. Ordinary product changes and certain sensitive areas require one person. Its highest-risk code and a small set of designated paths require two. A second classifier can still require another person when the assigned risk tier would otherwise allow a lighter path. For an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent can count as one of the required human reviewers. The agent itself cannot count toward a human-review slot. The lighter paths have another condition: they apply only to authors on the repository’s trusted list. Anthropic says other authors need a second person’s approval. It also says owner-designated sensitive paths and CI workflow files always need a person, even if a classifier assigns a lighter tier. Those conditions are part of the policy; the three-row table alone would give a team an incomplete rule. If I were setting this policy for a repository, I would begin by listing changes whose failure could expose data, interrupt releases, alter authentication, or make recovery difficult. The list should reflect that repository’s actual paths and deployment process. I would then decide who can approve each category and what checks must pass. The author’s familiarity with an agent does not tell me what the resulting patch can do. A harmless-looking patch can touch a sensitive path A help-page correction and a CI workflow permission change can each fit in one line. The help text needs to be accurate and appear in the right place. The workflow change may let a job write where it previously could only read. I would send the CI change to a person responsible for that workflow and make the new permission and its reason visible in the review. Anthropic’s policy also requires a person for CI workflow files. The two changes take roughly the same space in a diff, but their failure costs are different. Tie approval to the reviewed commit An approval can go stale when another commit lands. An agent might push a fix for an automated finding after a person has approved the pull request. That person reviewed the earlier version; the fix may alter the behavior they signed off on. Anthropic says an approval in its process covers a specific commit and must be given again when a later change cannot be vouched for. I would record which commit received the required human approval, rerun relevant checks after a change, and ask for fresh approval when the reviewed behavior may have changed. AI-generated flowchart tracing code changes to a human-review decision. Make failure ownership part of the decision A lighter approval path transfers more work to the checks before merge and to the people who watch the change after release. Before I would allow one, I’d want three names or roles on the pull request: who notices a bad outcome, who can stop further rollout, and who restores the affected service. “Revert the PR” is only a useful instruction when a revert actually restores the previous behavior. Anthropic describes merge checks, staged releases, flags, on-call response, and reverts as parts of its process. Its account also says the person who directed an agent-written change remains accountable for the outcome. Those practices explain why its approval table should be read alongside its release and recovery process. A feature flag might quickly disable a new interface. It cannot necessarily undo a destructive data migration that has already rewritten records. For a migration, I would ask for a tested recovery route and a person who can execute it before reducing the approval requirement. I would keep human approval when the effect on existing data or the path back is unclear. The same reasoning applies to a change that is easy to deploy but hard to detect when it fails. If no one can describe the signal that would reveal a regression, a promised fast rollback offers little comfort. Start with a policy you can evaluate I would pilot any lighter rule in one repository and one bounded class of changes, with the existing approval rule as the starting point. For each pull request, record its proposed tier, changed paths, author eligibility, checks, reviewer findings, approval, and reviewed commit. Then record how long it waited for a person and how many review rounds it took. The outcome measures matter as much as the time saved. Track reverts and incidents, and examine any missed risk: was the change classified too lightly, did a check lack the right context, or did the team fail to notice the problem after release? An agent and reviewer repeatedly editing the same patch should also count as a cost, even if the pull request eventually passes. Anthropic reports its own improvement in pull request volume and revert share, but those figures describe its repositories and process. They do not predict a pilot’s result elsewhere. I would loosen the rule only after the team has observed enough of its own changes to judge both review time and failures. If the sample is small or recovery has not been exercised, keep collecting evidence. Anthropic’s Human Approval Requirements by Risk I would retain human approval wherever the consequences or reversibility remain unclear. A well-defined, lower-risk category can earn a lighter path when its checks, owners, and observed outcomes support that decision. That is a policy a team can revise as it learns; the presence of an AI reviewer alone is no reason to change who may approve a merge. AI Code Review: Which Changes Still Need a Human? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0
items.summary:
Gradium has open-sourced Phonon , a family of small text-to-speech models built to run on the device. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Developers get natural speech with no cloud call, no GPU and no per-character bill. TL;DR Size: 31M parameters (excluding the audio tokenizer), 64.5 MB q8 GGUF, 24 kHz mono output. Phonon 40m: 40M, 74.6 MB. Runs on: CPUs, phones, Raspberry Pi 5, browsers (WASM, WebGPU) and NVIDIA GPUs. No GPU required. Performance: top English Elo among open models Gradium tested; about 7 ms to first audio on CPU. Best: 1.70% WER on a 500-sentence hard set, versus 3.50% for Kokoro (Gradium’s eval). Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%). What is Gradium Phonon? Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. The family has three models : Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0. Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0. Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0. How does Phonon work? Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. Phonon 40m uses 9 layers at the same width. Both are distilled from a larger Phonon teacher. Training ran on an NVIDIA H100 cluster with NCCL and CUDA Graphs. The work builds on Kyutai’s Continuous Audio Language Models research and Pocket TTS. Phonon Explainer

Where Phonon 31m leads

  • 1.70% hard-set WER vs 3.50% for Kokoro
  • 6.9 ms to first audio on a MacBook Air M5 CPU
  • 3.7x real time on a Raspberry Pi 5
  • Apache 2.0 weights, tokenizer and voices

Where it falls short

  • 0.51% Seed-TTS WER, behind Kokoro at 0.45%
  • English only at 31M; 40m models are CC BY-NC
  • Prosody resets between sentences on long text
  • All benchmarks are run by Gradium
Sources: gradium.ai/blog, huggingface.co/gradium · self-reported numbersBuilt by Marktechpost
" style="width:100%;height:600px;border:0;display:block;background:transparent;" loading="lazy" scrolling="no"> How does Phonon perform on benchmarks? Gradium ran blind pairwise listening tests with 1,189 raters and 17,270 votes. In US English, Phonon 40m scored 2117 Elo and Phonon 31m scored 2098. Kokoro scored 2043, NeuTTS 2034 and Magpie 1939. Accuracy was tested on a public hard-sentence set . It holds 500 sentences per language, full of phone numbers, emails and postal codes. Phonon 31m scored 1.70% WER against 3.50% for Kokoro and 8.71% for NeuTTS Nano. Built-in text normalization drives much of that gap. On the easier Seed-TTS set, the gap closes. Phonon 31m scored 0.51% LLM WER, while Kokoro scored 0.45%. How fast is Phonon on a CPU? On a MacBook Air M5 CPU with 4 threads, Phonon 31m reaches first audio in 6.9 ms. It runs 29.9x faster than real time. Kokoro takes 517 ms, because it does not stream. With Arm KleidiAI and Apple Accelerate, Phonon 31m reaches 46.7x real time. On a Raspberry Pi 5, Phonon 31m starts in 38 ms and runs 3.7x faster than real time. Gradium says Kokoro needs 7 seconds to start there. On Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, Phonon starts in 7.5 ms at 24x real time. On an NVIDIA L40S, CUDA reaches first speech in 5 ms. An AMD EPYC 7413 CPU takes 43 ms, per the press release . items.summary_html:
Gradium has open-sourced Phonon, a family of small text-to-speech models built to run on the device. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Developers get natural speech with no cloud call, no GPU and no per-character bill.

TL;DR
  • Size: 31M parameters (excluding the audio tokenizer), 64.5 MB q8 GGUF, 24 kHz mono output. Phonon 40m: 40M, 74.6 MB.
  • Runs on: CPUs, phones, Raspberry Pi 5, browsers (WASM, WebGPU) and NVIDIA GPUs. No GPU required.
  • Performance: top English Elo among open models Gradium tested; about 7 ms to first audio on CPU.
  • Best: 1.70% WER on a 500-sentence hard set, versus 3.50% for Kokoro (Gradium’s eval).
  • Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%).
What is Gradium Phonon?

Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium, a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers.

The family has three models:

  • Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0.
  • Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0.
  • Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0.
How does Phonon work?

Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion.

The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop.

Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. Phonon 40m uses 9 layers at the same width. Both are distilled from a larger Phonon teacher. Training ran on an NVIDIA H100 cluster with NCCL and CUDA Graphs.

The work builds on Kyutai’s Continuous Audio Language Models research and Pocket TTS.

How does Phonon perform on benchmarks?

Gradium ran blind pairwise listening tests with 1,189 raters and 17,270 votes. In US English, Phonon 40m scored 2117 Elo and Phonon 31m scored 2098. Kokoro scored 2043, NeuTTS 2034 and Magpie 1939.

Accuracy was tested on a public hard-sentence set. It holds 500 sentences per language, full of phone numbers, emails and postal codes. Phonon 31m scored 1.70% WER against 3.50% for Kokoro and 8.71% for NeuTTS Nano.

Built-in text normalization drives much of that gap.

On the easier Seed-TTS set, the gap closes. Phonon 31m scored 0.51% LLM WER, while Kokoro scored 0.45%.

How fast is Phonon on a CPU?

On a MacBook Air M5 CPU with 4 threads, Phonon 31m reaches first audio in 6.9 ms. It runs 29.9x faster than real time. Kokoro takes 517 ms, because it does not stream. With Arm KleidiAI and Apple Accelerate, Phonon 31m reaches 46.7x real time.

On a Raspberry Pi 5, Phonon 31m starts in 38 ms and runs 3.7x faster than real time. Gradium says Kokoro needs 7 seconds to start there.

On Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, Phonon starts in 7.5 ms at 24x real time. On an NVIDIA L40S, CUDA reaches first speech in 5 ms. An AMD EPYC 7413 CPU takes 43 ms, per the press release.

How can developers deploy Phonon?

The runtime is MIT or Apache-2.0 licensed. It covers Rust, Python (pip install ptts), Swift, C, C++ and the browser via phonon-tts. It also ships an OpenAI-compatible server and a WebSocket server.

Phonon loads in Transformers, MLX-Audio, Ollama and LM Studio. Voice cloning and voice design run in Gradium Studio, then the voice runs locally.

Key Takeaways
  • Phonon 31m is a 31M, 64.5 MB English TTS model under Apache 2.0.
  • It reports 1.70% WER on hard text, against 3.50% for Kokoro.
  • First audio arrives in 6.9 ms on a MacBook Air M5 CPU.
  • It runs 3.7x faster than real time on a Raspberry Pi 5.
  • Multilingual 40m models exist, but under a non-commercial license.

Check out the technical blog, model card, GitHub runtime and hard-sentence dataset. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says mathematicians have already gone from 'we're cooked' to accepting AI
items.summary: Sam Altman says mathematicians are coming around after OpenAI upended mathematics. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and mathematicians have a complicated relationship. OpenAI has taken credit for solving hundreds of math problems, irking many mathematicians. At a recent talk at Stanford, Altman said mathematicians have already gone from anger to acceptance. Like someone in mourning, Sam Altman said mathematicians went through phases after OpenAI began its blitz into the field. First, there was disbelief. Then, there was pain. "The day one reaction was like, 'We're cooked, and our field is over,'" OpenAI's CEO said. "'We're telling our grad students to switch majors.'" After that, there was anger. "The day three reaction was maybe like: 'It's horrible that OpenAI did this,'" Altman said at a recent talk at Stanford, before hundreds of students jittery about the viability of their future careers. Come day five, though, in Altman's telling, mathematicians began to come around to what he described as AI's now-inalienable role in the study of numbers and proofs. "We've now seen a lot of people say, actually, I'm going to have a different but hopefully better kind of career as a mathematician," Altman said. Altman's buoyant assessment contrasts sharply with what some in the math community have described as an existential transformation. After OpenAI abruptly broke into the field's prerogatives in September, announcing its models had solved the Navier-Stokes equations — a famously challenging math puzzle that stumped the industry's brightest since the 19th Century — preeminent mathematicians erupted in fury. A pair of academics, one at New York University and another at Anthropic, accused OpenAI of using data from their chat logs to help crack the problem. Mathematicians also complained that while an AI model might have solved the problem, it didn't show its work, leaving them with the less celebratory task of verifying it. And in the wake of all that controversy, there was more controversy. A group of undergrads at Caltech, wary of how rapidly AI was disrupting their field and wanting to stay relevant, advertised a "mathathon" where participants were encouraged to use AI to solve long-standing problems. OpenAI dropped out of sponsoring the event after more than 700 academics signed an open letter denouncing the competition for promoting AI "slop." (Organizers have since made adjustments to the rules, and the competition is set for November.) More recently, Terence Tao, a math prodigy at UCLA who earned his doctorate at 20, said math's "romantic era" is over, as top academics like him adjust to a workflow that involves verifying AI's work rather than solving problems individually. "Some things are being lost," Tao said after OpenAI this month said it solved over 700 more problems. Meanwhile, Altman, sitting on the opposite side of the debate, has adopted the optimism of the disrupter. "I don't think there's going to be like a job apocalypse," Altman said of AI causing companies to restructure their workforces . In the field of math, however, Altman said the disruptions came more quickly than in other disciplines and industries. "That was the fastest that I think we've all gotten to watch a field go through this cycle," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: There Are Signs of Serious Trouble in the Data Center Industry
items.summary: Ever since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, a torrent of money has flowed into building out data centers to power the AI boom. The efforts reached a fever pitch the day after Donald Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, when a bevy of AI luminaries including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Softbank founder Masayoshi Son crowded into the Oval Office to announce a $500 billion private investment in data centers. But as the public has grown jittery about the impacts of AI on society and the job market — and story after story has landed about the downsides of hosting data centers in local communities — the buildout has emerged as a major political flashpoint and a key issue in the looming midterms. The data industry’s headwinds aren’t just political, either. As the Financial Times reports , serious cracks are forming at the financial and logistical level, especially as serious AI revenue remains elusive. Numbers cited by the paper are eye-popping. Drawing on data from regulatory intelligence outfit RegLayer, the FT reports that 47 large data center projects have already fallen through this year. Analysts at the equity research firm Bernstein only believe that about 35 percent of planned facilities are feasible. All those canceled projects are due to a lot of factors, including local communities mobilizing against them , but it’s also macroeconomic. The buildout is taking place during a period of high interest rates and shaky bond markets, and people involved with the effort told the paper that the situation is “threatening their ambitions.” Some of the plans were shaky to begin with. The FT reports that top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have pushed so hard for the developments, believing them to be key to their success, that they’ve swallowed outsized costs and deemphasized due diligence. Investors are taking notice: stock in CoreWeave, a cloud provider closely linked to the AI data center industry, has fallen by more than 27 percent over the past month. The really big question, though, is what happens to all these data center projects if the bottom starts to fall out of the AI industry financially, a situation that many economists have warned is a possibility over the past few years. For now, things are still chugging along — albeit much more slowly than anticipated. “People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore,” one unnamed executive told the FT . “It’s much harder today to finance a data center.” More on data centers: Residents Reject $10,000 Each to Let a Data Center Set Up in Their Town

Ever since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, a torrent of money has flowed into building out data centers to power the AI boom.

The efforts reached a fever pitch the day after Donald Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, when a bevy of AI luminaries including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Softbank founder Masayoshi Son crowded into the Oval Office to announce a $500 billion private investment in data centers.

But as the public has grown jittery about the impacts of AI on society and the job market — and story after story has landed about the downsides of hosting data centers in local communities — the buildout has emerged as a major political flashpoint and a key issue in the looming midterms.

The data industry’s headwinds aren’t just political, either. As the Financial Times reports, serious cracks are forming at the financial and logistical level, especially as serious AI revenue remains elusive.

Numbers cited by the paper are eye-popping. Drawing on data from regulatory intelligence outfit RegLayer, the FT reports that 47 large data center projects have already fallen through this year. Analysts at the equity research firm Bernstein only believe that about 35 percent of planned facilities are feasible.

All those canceled projects are due to a lot of factors, including local communities mobilizing against them, but it’s also macroeconomic. The buildout is taking place during a period of high interest rates and shaky bond markets, and people involved with the effort told the paper that the situation is “threatening their ambitions.”

Some of the plans were shaky to begin with. The FT reports that top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have pushed so hard for the developments, believing them to be key to their success, that they’ve swallowed outsized costs and deemphasized due diligence. Investors are taking notice: stock in CoreWeave, a cloud provider closely linked to the AI data center industry, has fallen by more than 27 percent over the past month.

The really big question, though, is what happens to all these data center projects if the bottom starts to fall out of the AI industry financially, a situation that many economists have warned is a possibility over the past few years. For now, things are still chugging along — albeit much more slowly than anticipated.

“People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore,” one unnamed executive told the FT. “It’s much harder today to finance a data center.”

More on data centers: Residents Reject $10,000 Each to Let a Data Center Set Up in Their Town

items.title: Cohere Releases Rerank 5 With Passage-Level Context Focus and Calibrated Scores
items.summary: Cohere AI has released Rerank 5 , a new reranker family in Pro and Fast tiers. Cohere Rerank 5 is a retrieval model that reorders search results before they reach an LLM. It adds 2 developer features: Context Focus, which returns relevant passages inside each document, and calibrated relevance scores. For RAG and agent builders, the message is simple. Send fewer, better tokens to the LLM. TL;DR Size: Parameter count not disclosed. 32K token context window. Two tiers: rerank-v5.0-pro and rerank-v5.0-fast . Runs on: Hosted API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, or private VPC and on-prem. Cohere benchmarks speed on a single NVIDIA A100. No open weights or quantized builds. Performance: Pro ranks first on 39 of 46 composite datasets in Cohere’s own evaluation. Best: Pro scores 82.2 on BRIGHT (RCP-nDCG@10), 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3. Worst: Pro median latency is 11.7 s per 96-document request, versus 4.1 s for Fast. What is new in Cohere Rerank 5? Rerank 5 ships as two models. Pro targets ranking quality on reasoning-heavy queries and long, domain-specific documents. Fast targets low latency and high throughput for agents running many searches. Both models support over 100 languages and a 32K context window. They also rerank semi-structured data such as JSON, tables and YAML records. Upgrading needs no re-indexing. Developers change the model parameter and keep their existing keyword, vector or hybrid search. How does Context Focus work? Context Focus is an optional feature, off by default. A single Rerank call returns document scores plus scored character spans. Each span carries start and end offsets into the original text. Developers set it through the relevant_spans field, with a threshold and max_spans value. Cohere tested it on 30 QA datasets . Removing half the retrieved text kept 96% of answer quality. Removing three quarters kept 87%. Cohere says teams can push to 10x less context at some quality cost. In a search-agent test across 17 datasets, BM25 alone scored 46% accuracy. Adding Rerank 5 Pro raised it to 49%. Context Focus at the default 0.1 threshold cut tokens per task by 19% and reached 57%. At 0.4, tokens fell 34% and accuracy hit 58%. Versus BM25 alone, the full stack used 35% fewer tokens. On 6 deep-search benchmarks, tokens fell 41% and accuracy rose from 39% to 52%. What do calibrated relevance scores change? Rerank 5 scores read as probabilities. A score of 0.7 means a 70% chance the document is useful. Cohere team measured expected calibration error (ECE) against blind human graders and NIST TREC-DL assessors. Rerank 5 scores about 0.06 on both. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 0.234 and 0.307. Rerank 4 Pro scores 0.384 and 0.309. In practice, dev teams can filter by threshold instead of a fixed top-k. An agent can also detect when nothing relevant came back. How does Rerank 5 perform on benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Cohere using RCP-nDCG@10 , a Cohere-developed variant of nDCG. Cohere ran the competitor models itself. Pro leads all four main benchmarks. It scores 92.2 on ViDoRe V3 , 90.4 on BEIR , 82.2 on BRIGHT and 87.3 on nanoMTEB. BRIGHT shows the largest jump: 12.4 points over Rerank 4 Pro. Fast beats Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Rerank 4 Pro on all 4. It ties Voyage AI Rerank 3 on ViDoRe V3 at 90.6. It trails it on BEIR, 88.1 versus 88.6. On parsed PDFs, averaged over 47 datasets, Pro scores 89.9 and Fast 88.5. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 88.4. Pro ranks first on 14 of 19 non-English languages in Cohere’s internal suite. && How does Rerank 5 compare with competing rerankers? Feature Cohere Rerank 5 Pro Cohere Rerank 5 Fast Voyage AI rerank-3 Voyage AI rerank-3-lite Qwen3-Reranker-8B Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed 8B Context window 32K 32K 32,000 32,000 32K Languages 100+ 100+ Not disclosed Not disclosed 100+ License / access Proprietary API, VPC, on-prem Proprietary API, VPC, on-prem Proprietary API Proprietary API Apache 2.0 open weights API price per 1M tokens $0.05 $0.02 $0.05 $0.02 Self-hosted Passage extraction Context Focus Context Focus Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed BRIGHT* 82.2 77.5 76.4 69.4 69.8 ViDoRe V3* 92.2 90.6 90.6 87.9 85.1 BEIR* 90.4 88.1 88.6 86.1 83.8 nanoMTEB* 87.3 85.1 83.9 80.7 82.1 ECE, human judges* (lower is better) 0.058 0.058 0.234 0.226 Not disclosed *Scores are RCP-nDCG@10 or ECE from Cohere’s Rerank 5 post , measured by Cohere. items.summary_html:
Cohere AI has released Rerank 5, a new reranker family in Pro and Fast tiers. Cohere Rerank 5 is a retrieval model that reorders search results before they reach an LLM. It adds 2 developer features: Context Focus, which returns relevant passages inside each document, and calibrated relevance scores. For RAG and agent builders, the message is simple. Send fewer, better tokens to the LLM.

TL;DR
  • Size: Parameter count not disclosed. 32K token context window. Two tiers: rerank-v5.0-pro and rerank-v5.0-fast.
  • Runs on: Hosted API, Model Vault, Microsoft Foundry, Amazon SageMaker, or private VPC and on-prem. Cohere benchmarks speed on a single NVIDIA A100. No open weights or quantized builds.
  • Performance: Pro ranks first on 39 of 46 composite datasets in Cohere’s own evaluation.
  • Best: Pro scores 82.2 on BRIGHT (RCP-nDCG@10), 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3.
  • Worst: Pro median latency is 11.7 s per 96-document request, versus 4.1 s for Fast.
What is new in Cohere Rerank 5?

Rerank 5 ships as two models. Pro targets ranking quality on reasoning-heavy queries and long, domain-specific documents. Fast targets low latency and high throughput for agents running many searches.

Both models support over 100 languages and a 32K context window. They also rerank semi-structured data such as JSON, tables and YAML records. Upgrading needs no re-indexing. Developers change the model parameter and keep their existing keyword, vector or hybrid search.

How does Context Focus work?

Context Focus is an optional feature, off by default. A single Rerank call returns document scores plus scored character spans. Each span carries start and end offsets into the original text. Developers set it through the relevant_spans field, with a threshold and max_spans value.

Cohere tested it on 30 QA datasets. Removing half the retrieved text kept 96% of answer quality. Removing three quarters kept 87%. Cohere says teams can push to 10x less context at some quality cost.

In a search-agent test across 17 datasets, BM25 alone scored 46% accuracy. Adding Rerank 5 Pro raised it to 49%. Context Focus at the default 0.1 threshold cut tokens per task by 19% and reached 57%. At 0.4, tokens fell 34% and accuracy hit 58%. Versus BM25 alone, the full stack used 35% fewer tokens. On 6 deep-search benchmarks, tokens fell 41% and accuracy rose from 39% to 52%.

What do calibrated relevance scores change?

Rerank 5 scores read as probabilities. A score of 0.7 means a 70% chance the document is useful.

Cohere team measured expected calibration error (ECE) against blind human graders and NIST TREC-DL assessors. Rerank 5 scores about 0.06 on both. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 0.234 and 0.307. Rerank 4 Pro scores 0.384 and 0.309. In practice, dev teams can filter by threshold instead of a fixed top-k. An agent can also detect when nothing relevant came back.

How does Rerank 5 perform on benchmarks?

All scores below are self-reported by Cohere using RCP-nDCG@10, a Cohere-developed variant of nDCG. Cohere ran the competitor models itself.

Pro leads all four main benchmarks. It scores 92.2 on ViDoRe V3, 90.4 on BEIR, 82.2 on BRIGHT and 87.3 on nanoMTEB. BRIGHT shows the largest jump: 12.4 points over Rerank 4 Pro.

Fast beats Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Rerank 4 Pro on all 4. It ties Voyage AI Rerank 3 on ViDoRe V3 at 90.6. It trails it on BEIR, 88.1 versus 88.6.

On parsed PDFs, averaged over 47 datasets, Pro scores 89.9 and Fast 88.5. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 88.4. Pro ranks first on 14 of 19 non-English languages in Cohere’s internal suite.

Key Takeaways
  • Rerank 5 ships in Pro ($0.05) and Fast ($0.02) per 1M tokens, both with 32K context.
  • Pro scores 82.2 on BRIGHT, 5.8 points above Voyage AI Rerank 3.
  • Context Focus returns scored passages in 1 call, cutting agent tokens 35% to 41%.
  • Calibrated scores reach about 0.06 ECE, so 1 threshold works across domains.
  • All benchmarks are self-reported on Cohere’s RCP-nDCG@10 metric.

items.title: Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift
items.summary: Ramp spent months testing managed agent APIs, open-source frameworks, and third-party platforms before concluding it would be better off building its own. The result is Laminar, an internal agent harness that took six weeks to reach a first version and now powers every agentic product at the fintech company. “We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house.” “We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house,” Sam Kronick , the Ramp engineer behind the platform, writes in the company’s engineering blog . In Tuesday’s post, Ramp detailed how Laminar brings agent execution, sandboxing, observability, and asynchronous workflows under a single platform. The architecture caught the attention of LangChain CEO Harrison Chase , who praised several design choices in his X post , while pointing to similar work underway in LangChain’s Deep Agents . Ramp and LangChain are approaching the problem from different directions, but both point to a bigger shift in agent infrastructure . As harnesses take on more responsibility, enterprises have to decide how much of that infrastructure they want to build and maintain themselves. Why Ramp built in-house Ramp didn’t want to be locked into one model provider. It needed the flexibility to switch models based on cost, speed, and performance, along with better visibility into how its agents behaved. Engineers were already digging through traces to find unnecessary tool calls, bloated context, and errors, but existing observability tools made that harder than it needed to be. So Ramp built its own debugging interface into Laminar. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes. Chase agreed with Ramp’s priorities, particularly model independence and observability, both of which LangChain has emphasized in its own work. And, there were other parts of Laminar’s architecture that caught his attention. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes. Sessions split from sandboxes Laminar runs everything from customer service agents to Ramp Inspect , the company’s cloud coding agent, and Glass, which handles longer-running, collaborative work. Supporting these products requires a harness that can manage persistent sessions, human approvals, and work across environments. Chase highlights Kronick’s observation that a production harness does far more than run a simple execution loop. “ +100 to this ,” he writes, pointing to LangChain’s investment in Deep Agents. Ramp keeps agent sessions separate from the sandboxes where code runs. Conversation history and execution state are stored independently, allowing sandboxes to spin up and shut down without disrupting a session. Chase sees the sandbox-as-a-tool approach as a growing trend, noting that Deep Agents uses a similar design. It also keeps credentials and orchestration outside the sandbox, an important consideration as developers work to isolate agents running untrusted code . Async agents by default Laminar lets agents keep working without waiting for every step to finish. Chase describes non-blocking asynchronous agents as the future and says LangChain is developing similar functionality for Deep Agents. Ramp’s Connectors Service also caught his attention. It centralizes authentication, credentials, access controls, and tool execution behind a shared API. Chase says LangChain is exploring comparable features for managed Deep Agents. Centralizing those functions also gives platform teams a consistent place to manage access and credential handling rather than implementing them separately for every agent. The harness is also where teams can trim inference costs, and LangChain has made that case directly. In an October 1 engineering post , it describes moving model selection into the harness of Open SWE , its open-source coding agent. A router examines the initial request and assigns one of three models based on expected task complexity, sending the simplest work to GLM-5.3-Flash, intermediate tasks to GPT-5.6 Sol, and the most demanding requests to GPT-6 Astra. Routing trims inference costs Across 973 agent threads, the router cut median LLM costs from $2.61 to $0.94 per thread, a 64 percent drop compared with using GPT-6 Astra for every task. The savings didn’t come with a measurable hit to performance. Merged pull request rates were 29.2 percent for routed threads and 27.3 percent for the control group, a difference that wasn’t statistically significant. Ninety percent of requests went to the two less expensive model tiers. LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway , where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. The harness already knows which prompts, tools, and domain context are involved, giving it more information to make that choice. LangChain uses model-selection middleware to pick a model at the start of each thread. The results don’t tell us whether building a custom harness is cheaper than using an existing framework. Ramp wasn’t part of the experiment. But they do show how much companies can save by making smarter model choices at the harness level, especially when their agents handle tasks with very different demands. The harness ownership dilemma Ramp’s decision also shows how coding agents have changed infrastructure costs. Kronick says agents generated all of Laminar’s initial code, with experienced engineers guiding the architecture and implementation. But building the first version in six weeks is one thing. Maintaining it is another. Ramp still needs engineers to handle incidents, update the platform, and support its product teams. The company also hasn’t published operating-cost comparisons or benchmarks against competing platforms, which makes it difficult to judge whether building in-house is cheaper. LangChain offers another option. Rather than building a harness from scratch, companies can use frameworks that handle much of the underlying infrastructure, an approach other vendors are also taking as they open-source their own harnesses .

Rather than trust the leaderboard, we rebuild it from the verdicts Datalab released for 27 parsers, after feeding the scorer a hand-made page to see which mistakes flip a verdict. We then measure ranking certainty, slice it by document type, test whether the two models the card names as helping build tests behave differently on tests a model corrected, and run Tesseract and Indra OCR ourselves on a 50-page sample. The two models named on the card fall less far than the others on tests a model corrected, which we report as a flag rather than proof. In this tutorial, we implement OmniParseBench, Datalab’s open benchmark for document parsers, which grades a parser’s output with 16,288 small pass-or-fail tests across 2,937 pages, from scanned forms and handwriting to arXiv math and dense tables. Rather than trust the leaderboard, we rebuild it from the verdicts Datalab released for 27 parsers, after feeding the scorer a hand-made page to see which mistakes flip a verdict. We then measure ranking certainty, slice it by document type, test whether the two models the card names as helping build tests behave differently on tests a model corrected, and run Tesseract and Indra OCR ourselves on a 50-page sample. Along the way, we find that the top two parsers are statistically tied, the leader changes on most slices, and one launch figure doesn’t match the released files.

RESULTS = {}          # step -> one-line result, for the summary table

CURRENT = ["1"]
 
 
def banner(title):
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)
 
 
def section(name):
    def wrap(fn):
        def run(*a, **kw):
            CURRENT[0] = name.split(".")[0]
            banner(name)
            t0 = time.time()
            try:
                out = fn(*a, **kw)
                RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok"
                return out
            except Exception as e:
                RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
                print(f"\n[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                traceback.print_exc(limit=3)
                return None
            finally:
                print(f"\n[{time.time() - t0:.1f} s]")
        return run
    return wrap
 
 
def claim(text, held):
    CLAIMS.append((CURRENT[0], text, bool(held)))
    return held

Before trusting a score, we want to see what a verdict means, so we write a gold file by hand with thirteen tests on an invented page and grade predictions with unit_tests.score, the function the benchmark itself uses. A base prediction passes everything, and each variant changes one thing. The headline is the mean of the text, tables and layout pass rates with unsupported tests left out, so a parser that cannot return layout blocks, such as Tesseract, gets no headline at all. def per_document(df, systems, groups):
    """For each system: an array (documents x groups x [passes, scored tests]); `groups` maps a name to a row mask."""
    docs = {d: i for i, d in enumerate(sorted(df.document.unique()))}
    s = df[df.result != "unsupported"]
    out = {}
    for name in systems:
        g = s[s.system == name]
        arr = np.zeros((len(docs), len(groups), 2))
        for k, mask in enumerate(groups.values()):
            sel = g[mask(g)]
            d = sel.document.map(docs).to_numpy()
            arr[:, k, 0] = np.bincount(d, weights=(sel.result == "pass").to_numpy(), minlength=len(docs))
            arr[:, k, 1] = np.bincount(d, minlength=len(docs))
        out[name] = arr
    return out, len(docs)
 
 
def resample(n_docs, B, seed):
    """B bootstrap resamples of the documents, each as a count per document."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return np.stack([np.bincount(rng.integers(0, n_docs, n_docs), minlength=n_docs) for _ in range(B)]).astype(float)
 
 
@section("5. How sure is the order at the top? A document-level bootstrap")
def bootstrap_step():
    top = list(TABLE.headline.nlargest(6).index)
    families = {f: (lambda g, f=f: g.family == f) for f in ("text", "tables", "layout")}
    arrs, n_docs = per_document(VERDICTS[VERDICTS.system.isin(top)], top, families)
    W = resample(n_docs, 2000, seed=20261022)
    head = {}
    for s in top:
        tot = np.tensordot(W, arrs[s], axes=([1], [0]))            # resamples x families x [passes, tests]
        head[s] = 100 * (tot[..., 0] / tot[..., 1]).mean(axis=1)
    point = {s: 100 * (arrs[s].sum(0)[:, 0] / arrs[s].sum(0)[:, 1]).mean() for s in top}
    print(f"2,000 resamples of {n_docs:,} documents; a document's tests stay together\n")
    print(f"{'parser':22s} {'headline':>9s}  {'95% interval':>15s}   {'gap to ' + top[0]:>26s}  {'resamples where it leads':>24s}")
    leader = np.argmax(np.stack([head[x] for x in top]), axis=0)
    for s in top:
        lo, hi = np.percentile(head[s], [2.5, 97.5])
        d = head[top[0]] - head[s]
        gap = "" if s == top[0] else f"{point[top[0]] - point[s]:+.2f} [{np.percentile(d, 2.5):+.2f}, {np.percentile(d, 97.5):+.2f}]"
        print(f"{s:22s} {point[s]:9.2f}  {lo:6.2f} - {hi:6.2f}   {gap:>26s}  {100 * np.mean(leader == top.index(s)):23.1f}%")
    d = head[top[0]] - head[top[1]]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(d, [2.5, 97.5])
    claim(f"{top[0]} and {top[1]} cannot be told apart (the 95% interval of their gap includes zero)", lo < 0 < hi)
    return f"{top[0]} vs {top[1]}: {point[top[0]] - point[top[1]]:+.2f} points, 95% interval [{lo:+.2f}, {hi:+.2f}]"

def slice_headline(df):
    """Per system: family pass rates on a slice of tests and their mean, as the benchmark's headline is built."""
    s = df[df.result != "unsupported"]
    fam = s.groupby(["system", "family"]).result.apply(lambda r: 100 * (r == "pass").mean()).unstack()
    return fam.mean(axis=1), fam

def predict_pages(run, pages, alive=lambda: True):
    """Predict every page the run still lacks. A failed call is recorded, not raised, so we count failures ourselves."""
    t0, n, failed = time.time(), 0, []
    for p in pages:
        if not alive():
            raise RuntimeError(f"{run.provider}: the server stopped after {n} pages")
        if need := benchmark.needs(run, p):
            got = harness.predict(run.provider, p.doc_path, need, timeout=900, **run.options)
            benchmark.record(run, p.page_id, got)
            n += 1
            if any(c.get("failure") for c in got["calls"]):
                failed.append(f"{p.page_id}: {got['errors']}")
    if failed:
        print(f"{len(failed)} of {n} pages failed, e.g. {failed[0][:160]}")
        if 2 * len(failed) >= n:
            raise RuntimeError(f"{run.provider} failed on {len(failed)} of {n} pages")
    return n, (time.time() - t0) / max(n, 1)

    run = benchmark.Run("tesseract", {}, WORK / "runs" / "tesseract")
    benchmark.prepare(run, str(DATA), 900)
    n, per_page = predict_pages(run, SAMPLE)
    s = benchmark.grade(run, SAMPLE, say=lambda *_: None)
    fam = s["families"]
    print(f"\nTesseract: {n} pages read, {per_page:.1f} s per page")
    for k, v in fam.items():
        print(f"   {k:7s} " + ("unsupported (no blocks output)" if v["score"] is None else f"{100 * v['score']:5.1f}% of {v['tests']} tests"))
    print(f"   headline {'none' if s['headline'] is None else round(100 * s['headline'], 1)} (a family it cannot produce leaves no headline)")
    return f"Tesseract on 50 pages: text {100 * fam['text']['score']:.1f}%, tables {100 * fam['tables']['score']:.1f}%, {per_page:.1f} s/page"
 
 
tesseract_step()

Rebuilding a leaderboard from published verdicts is one thing; producing verdicts ourselves is another. data.select picks a fixed 50-page sample spread over all 22 suites, and we download only those pages. The loop is the benchmark’s own: needs lists the outputs a page still lacks, harness. predict runs the parser; record saves the prediction and grades the folder, so an interrupted run can resume. On Ubuntu we also link Tesseract’s script models into the layout the adapter expects. Tesseract passes 30.4% of the sample’s text tests against 17.6% on the full set, a gap that depends on which pages were sampled.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
def agreement(folder, published):
    """Our verdicts against the published ones for the same tests, where both scored the test."""
    ours = pd.read_json(folder / "scores.jsonl", lines=True)[["test_id", "result", "why"]]
    pub = VERDICTS[VERDICTS.system == published][["test_id", "result"]]
    m = ours.merge(pub, on="test_id", suffixes=("_ours", "_pub"))
    m = m[(m.result_ours != "unsupported") & (m.result_pub != "unsupported")]
    return m, int((m.result_ours == m.result_pub).sum()), len(m)
 
 
@section("9. Indra OCR on the same pages, served on the CPU from the package's own server code")
def indra_step():
    if sys.version_info < (3, 12):
        raise RuntimeError("the Indra pins (numpy 2.5.4) need Python 3.12 or newer")
    venv = WORK / "indra-venv"
    py = venv / "bin" / "python"
    if not py.exists():
        uv = shutil.which("uv") or str(Path(sys.executable).parent / "uv")
        subprocess.run([uv, "venv", "-q", "--python", sys.executable, str(venv)], check=True)
        subprocess.run([uv, "pip", "install", "-q", "--python", str(py)] + INDRA, check=True)
    server = Path(harness.__file__).parent / "providers" / "oss" / "indra" / "server.py"
    # server.py counts cores with os.sched_getaffinity, which macOS lacks; on Linux the shim changes nothing
    launcher = WORK / "indra_launch.py"
    launcher.write_text("import os, runpy, sys\n"
                        "if not hasattr(os, 'sched_getaffinity'):\n"
                        "    os.sched_getaffinity = lambda pid: set(range(os.cpu_count()))\n"
                        "sys.argv = ['server.py', '--port', '8001', '--workers', '2']\n"
                        f"runpy.run_path({str(server)!r}, run_name='__main__')\n")
    log = open(WORK / "indra_server.log", "w")
    proc = subprocess.Popen([str(py), str(launcher)], stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    t0 = time.time()
    while True:
        try:
            urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8001/health", timeout=2)
            break
        except Exception:
            if proc.poll() is not None or time.time() - t0 > 600:
                proc.terminate()
                raise RuntimeError("the Indra server did not start; see " + log.name)
            time.sleep(2)
    print(f"server up in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s: {INDRA[0]}, 2 worker processes")
    try:
        run = benchmark.Run("indra-ocr", {"base_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8001"}, WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr")
        benchmark.prepare(run, str(DATA), 900)
        n, per_page = predict_pages(run, SAMPLE, alive=lambda: proc.poll() is None)
        s = benchmark.grade(run, SAMPLE, say=lambda *_: None)
    finally:
        proc.terminate()
    fam = {k: 100 * v["score"] for k, v in s["families"].items()}
    print(f"Indra OCR: {n} pages, {per_page:.2f} s per page; text {fam['text']:.1f}%, tables {fam['tables']:.1f}%, "
          f"layout {fam['layout']:.1f}%; headline on these pages {100 * s['headline']:.1f}\n")
    ids = {p.page_id for p in SAMPLE}
    fmt = lambda x: "none" if x is None else f"{100 * x:.1f}"
    print(f"{'on the 50 pages':22s} {'headline':>9s} {'text':>6s} {'tables':>7s} {'layout':>7s}")
    for name, folder in (("Tesseract", WORK / "runs" / "tesseract"), ("Indra OCR", WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr")):
        pub = unit_tests.summarize(VERDICTS[(VERDICTS.system == name) & VERDICTS.page_id.isin(ids)][COLS].to_dict("records"))
        ours = unit_tests.summarize(benchmark.read_scores(benchmark.Run(name, {}, folder)))
        for who, x in (("ours", ours), ("published", pub)):
            f = x["families"]
            print(f"{name + ', ' + who:22s} {fmt(x['headline']):>9s} " + " ".join(f"{fmt(f[k]['score']) if k in f else 'none':>6s}"
                                                                         for k in ("text", "tables", "layout")))
    print()
    for name, folder in (("Tesseract", WORK / "runs" / "tesseract"), ("Indra OCR", WORK / "runs" / "indra-ocr")):
        m, same, total = agreement(folder, name)
        diff = m[m.result_ours != m.result_pub]
        print(f"{name:10s} our verdicts equal the published ones on {same} of {total} tests ({100 * same / total:.1f}%); "
              f"of the {len(diff)} that differ, {(diff.result_ours == 'pass').sum()} pass only for us and "
              f"{(diff.result_ours == 'fail').sum()} only in the published run")
        if len(diff):
            by_page = diff.test_id.map(TESTS.set_index("test_id").page_id).value_counts()
            print("           differing tests by type:", {k: int(v) for k, v in diff.test_id.map(TESTS.set_index("test_id").test_type).value_counts().items()},
                  f"| on {len(by_page)} pages, {by_page.iloc[0]} of them on {by_page.index[0]}")
        claim(f"{name}: our verdicts equal the published ones on at least 95% of the sample's tests", same >= 0.95 * total)
    return f"Indra OCR on 50 pages: headline {100 * s['headline']:.1f} (text {fam['text']:.1f}, tables {fam['tables']:.1f}, layout {fam['layout']:.1f}), {per_page:.2f} s/page"
 
 
indra_step()

Indra OCR is an open CPU model, and the package ships the HTTP server its adapter talks to, so we install the versions pinned in that server’s Dockerfile into a separate environment and start it in the background. Against the published verdicts on the same pages, Tesseract agrees on every scored test, so its sample score matches the published one. Indra agrees on 203 of 221, and all of its table differences sit on one page, which accounts for the whole gap between its published tables score of 36.1 and our 69.4. One page moving a family that far is the clearest argument for resampling documents.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
@section("10. Bring your own parser: grade a PDF text-layer baseline with the same code")
def byo_step():
    import pypdfium2 as pdfium
 
    def text_layer(path):
        if path.suffix.lower() != ".pdf":
            return ""                                    # an image has no text layer to read
        doc = pdfium.PdfDocument(str(path))
        try:
            return "
" + html.escape(doc[0].get_textpage().get_text_range()) + "
"
        finally:
            doc.close()
 
    out = WORK / "runs" / "text-layer"
    (out / "predictions").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for p in SAMPLE:
        (out / "predictions" / f"{p.page_id}.json").write_text(json.dumps({"html": text_layer(p.doc_path)}))
    s = benchmark.grade(benchmark.Run("text-layer", {}, out), SAMPLE, say=lambda *_: None, settings={"unsupported": ["blocks"]})
    kind = {p.page_id: "PDF" if p.doc_path.suffix == ".pdf" else "image" for p in SAMPLE}
    print(f"{'parser on the same 50 pages':28s} {'text: PDF':>10s} {'images':>8s} {'all':>6s} {'tables':>8s}")
    for name in ("text-layer", "tesseract", "indra-ocr"):
        sc = pd.read_json(WORK / "runs" / name / "scores.jsonl", lines=True)
        sc = sc[sc.result.isin(["pass", "fail"])]
        txt = sc[sc.test_type.map(vocab.FAMILIES) == "text"]
        by = txt.groupby(txt.page_id.map(kind)).result.apply(lambda r: 100 * (r == "pass").mean())
        tab = sc[sc.test_type == "table_cell"]
        print(f"{name:28s} {by.get('PDF', np.nan):10.1f} {by.get('image', np.nan):8.1f} "
              f"{100 * (txt.result == 'pass').mean():6.1f} {100 * (tab.result == 'pass').mean():8.1f}")
    fam = s["families"]
    return f"text layer, no OCR: text {100 * fam['text']['score']:.1f}%, tables {100 * fam['tables']['score']:.1f}% on the 50 pages"
 
 
byo_step()

Any parser can be graded without an adapter: we write one predictions file per page and call benchmark.grade, declaring the outputs we cannot produce as unsupported. Our parser reads a PDF’s embedded text layer with pypdfium2 and returns an empty string for images, which have none. On PDF pages it passes exactly as many text tests as Tesseract, 42.3% each, without any OCR, while on images it has nothing and Indra OCR still passes 43.1%. Plain text fails every table test, since a pass needs cell structure, so the mix of PDFs and images matters whenever two parsers are compared.

@section("11. The launch claims, checked against the files")
def claims_step():
    a, t = TABLE.loc["Datalab accurate"], TABLE.loc["Tesseract"]
    g = TABLE.loc["Gemini 3.8 Flash", "headline"]
    c = TABLE.loc["Claude Sonnet 5.5"]
    tags = TESTS.tags
    langs = {x for ts in tags for x in ts if re.fullmatch("[a-z]{3}", x)} - {"und", "zxx"}
    pkg = Path(vocab.__file__).parent       # the scorer and the modules it reads; data.py and the harness only fetch and run
    scoring = sorted(pkg.glob("scorers/**/*.py")) + [pkg / f"{m}.py" for m in ("normalize", "tables", "equations", "views", "vocab", "markdown")]
    clients = [f.name for f in scoring if re.search(r"^\s*(import|from)\s+(httpx|requests|urllib|huggingface_hub|openai|anthropic|google"
                                                    r"|transformers|torch|omni_parse_bench\.harness)\b", f.read_text(), re.M)]
    n_eng, n_table = tags.apply(lambda x: "eng" in x).sum(), tags.apply(lambda x: "table" in x).sum()
    rows = [
        ("16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents", f"{len(TESTS):,} / {TESTS.page_id.nunique():,} / {TESTS.document.nunique():,}",
         (len(TESTS), TESTS.page_id.nunique(), TESTS.document.nunique()) == (16288, 2937, 2343)),
        ("92 languages", f"{len(langs)} codes besides und and zxx", len(langs) == 92),
        ("10,089 English tests, 6,767 table tests", f"{n_eng:,} and {n_table:,}", (n_eng, n_table) == (10089, 6767)),
        ("Datalab accurate scores 92.7", f"{a.headline:.2f} in results.parquet", round(a.headline, 1) == 92.7),
        ("Datalab accurate ranks second, behind Gemini", f"{a.headline:.3f} vs {g:.3f}", a.headline < g),
        ("Claude Sonnet 5.5: text 93.1, tables 95.4, layout 77.5", f"{c.text:.1f} / {c.tables:.1f} / {c.layout:.1f}",
         [round(c[k], 1) for k in ("text", "tables", "layout")] == [93.1, 95.4, 77.5]),
        ("Tesseract: no headline, text 17.6, tables 0.0",
         f"{'none' if pd.isna(t.headline) else round(t.headline, 1)} / {t.text:.1f} / {t.tables:.1f}",
         pd.isna(t.headline) and round(t.text, 1) == 17.6 and round(t.tables, 1) == 0.0),
        ("no model judges the outputs", f"{len(clients)} of {len(scoring)} scorer modules import a model or HTTP client", not clients),
    ]
    print(f"{'claim (launch article and blog)':56s} {'what the files say':38s} verdict")
    for text, found, ok in rows:
        print(f"{text:56s} {found:38s} {'holds' if ok else 'does not hold'}")
        claim(text, ok)
    print("\nnot checkable from these files: latency, price per 1,000 pages, the other benchmarks' test counts")
    return f"{sum(bool(ok) for *_, ok in rows)} of {len(rows)} launch claims hold against the files"
 
 
claims_step()

Instead of repeating the launch claims, we check each one against the files. The counts hold exactly, from tests and pages to languages and subsets, and the Claude and Tesseract rows match. Datalab‘s own row does not: the launch article and blog give Datalab an accurate 92.7 and place it second behind Gemini, while the released verdicts give 92.92 against 92.89, a tie that rounds to the same figure. The no-judge claim holds for the scorer itself, whose modules import no model or HTTP client; KaTeX runs in an embedded JavaScript engine to compare equations. Latency and price cannot be checked from these files.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
banner("SUMMARY")
for name, res in RESULTS.items():
    print(f"  {name:<100s}  {res}")
print("\nchecks decided in this run:")
for step, text, held in CLAIMS:
    print(f"   [{'held' if held else 'did not hold'}] step {step}: {text}")
failed = [k for k, v in RESULTS.items() if str(v).startswith("SKIPPED")]
print(f"\n{sum(h for *_, h in CLAIMS)} of {len(CLAIMS)} checks held; steps failed or skipped: {failed or 'none'}")
print(f"omni-parse-bench {md.version('omni-parse-bench')}, dataset @ {REV[:7]}, Python {platform.python_version()}, {SYSTEM}")
print("not run here: the hosted parsers (paid API keys), the GPU models, latency and cost, all 2,937 pages")

The summary prints each step’s one-line result and every check the run decided, marking which held and which did not: 13 of 17 held, and the four that did not are findings rather than failures, namely the placebo gap, Indra’s reproduction and Datalab’s two launch figures. It also lists what we did not run here: the hosted parsers that need paid keys, the GPU models, latency and cost, and the full set of 2,937 pages.

In conclusion, OmniParseBench is a benchmark we can audit end to end: the scorer is open code that calls no model, the verdicts are released, and every entry on the card can be rebuilt from them. The top two parsers are statistically tied, pooling tests instead of families changes the order, and a different parser comes first on handwriting, rotated pages, tables and several scripts. The two models named on the card fall less far than the others on tests a model corrected, which we report as a flag rather than proof. Tesseract’s published verdicts reproduced exactly on our sample, while Indra OCR’s agreed on 92% of tests. The practical lesson is to slice the benchmark to our own documents, report intervals, and pin every version.

items.title: OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.summary: OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). In addition to Open Responses, OpenSandbox , Anthropic’s Agent Skills , and HuggingFace’s OpenEv framework for agent environments are also joining the AAIF. The join other AAIF projects like the MCP and A2A protocols, AGENTS.md (also from OpenAI), the open source AI agent goose, agentgateway, and Agent Router. The foundation, which is part of the Linux Foundation, launched in December 2025, with MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md as its first projects. As for Open Responses, the core idea here is to provide developers with a set of core API calls that should work across LLM providers. When OpenAI first announced the specification in January, the team behind the project noted that virtually all LLM providers now offer the same building blocks (messages, tool calls, function calling, etc.), but that they also all represent them differently in their APIs. Agentic AI Foundation projects. Credit: The New Stack. Open Responses aims to create a spec that standardizes these primitives so that developers don’t have to translate between each vendor’s idiosyncratic API when they switch between models. “When we co-founded AAIF, we contributed AGENTS.md, a way to give coding agents project-specific instructions,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The New Stack. “Open Responses addresses another part of building agents by giving developers a shared format for working with models across endpoints that support it, so they have fewer provider-specific integrations to maintain. Vercel AI Gateway and Databricks Model Serving already implement it, and AAIF will provide a neutral home for developers and providers to continue developing the specification together.” Why a neutral home matters It’s this neutral home that is generally the reason why companies donate projects to a foundation. The AAIF is part of the Linux Foundation, which has become somewhat of the de facto standard for providing vendor-neutral homes for popular open source projects, with a technical steering committee , which will initially be made up of project maintainers, handling the technical discussions. Who already supports it — and who doesn’t There is already wide support for the spec, with the likes of AWS (in Bedrock), Databricks, LM Studio, Ollama, Hugging Face, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Red Hat, Vercel, and open source projects like vLLM and OGC (previously Llama Stack) supporting it. Among the names that are missing from this list is OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which defines its own Messages API for giving developers access to its models. Anthropic is a member of the AAIF, so maybe we’ll see the company adopt this spec at some point in the future. With the Interactions API, Google, too, has its default for letting developers work with its models. Open Responses doesn’t hide its lineage. The project’s own contributor guide notes that its core schema files are copied from OpenAI’s API. And while OpenAI’s earlier Chat Completions API became an early standard that others used to model their offerings after, Anthropic’s Messages API has now also left a clear mark (in large part thanks to the success of Claude Code), with the likes of DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, and others exposing Anthropic-compatible endpoints, too. That split is exactly the kind of fragmentation a vendor-neutral spec like this is meant to fix, of course.

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. items.summary_html:
At a glance
  • Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.
  • Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.
  • Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.
  • Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another.

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations.: We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: 

  • (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select?
  • (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data?

Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face:

  • High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time.
  • Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them.

These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions.

Flint-interactive

Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications.

Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use

1. Use Flint in your chat

Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation.

Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns.

2. Build an interactive app with Flint

Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas.

Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa.

3. Create bespoke interactions

To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks.

Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works
