  • Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. 
Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable cand cost effective.

This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards.

items.title: OpenAI’s COBOL migration score has made a striking leap
items.summary: This week, OpenAI put COBOL in the spotlight. It announced benchmark results suggesting its latest models are getting much better at migrating COBOL programs and building software in languages with less code and documentation for models to learn from. On OpenAI’s own COBOL migration test, GPT-6.1 Sol reached 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, up from GPT-5.6 Sol’s 5.4%, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, the newer model reached 97.9%. But the evidence behind the two evaluations is uneven. OpenAI has not published the details of its evaluation of COBOL (“Common Business-Oriented Language”; the programming language that AI coding tools may help maintain or migrate). It has released the MultiLangBench setup and test suite on GitHub . That benchmark tests whether models can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 programming languages. OpenAI’s announcement calls the results “substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.” Those results could matter to teams maintaining and modernizing legacy software. But without public COBOL test cases, developers cannot independently inspect that evaluation. Is there finally some hope for modernizing COBOL? Per OpenAI, its new COBOL migration evaluation “tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior.” Specifically, it’s testing migrations from COBOL to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust. To succeed, each migration must pass a series of hidden tests that require “byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs.” And with markedly greater accuracy than its predecessor, GPT-6.1 Sol is, indeed, showing substantial progress. Source: OpenAI The measured gains are striking, though OpenAI is not the first company to bring AI to COBOL modernization. Even though COBOL underpins much of the world’s financial transactions and business records — IBM reports COBOL underpins over 40% of all online banking systems, supports 80% of in-person credit card transactions, and handles 95% of all ATM transactions — it remains a difficult target for AI coding tools. Compared with Python and JavaScript, models have less COBOL code and documentation to learn from. Experienced COBOL developers can also be hard to find, and documentation often lags behind the systems they maintain. AI coding gains across 20 languages Alongside its COBOL migration tests, OpenAI developed a second evaluation to measure models’ ability to build software from scratch, MultiLangBench. This benchmark “tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 different programming languages.” First, the program gets a database and SQL query. Then, it produces a modified database. The reference SQLite implementation serves as the ground truth to check if the resulting database contains the expected data. Source: OpenAI On average, GPT-6 Astra — OpenAI’s flagship model — achieved an 87.4% test pass rate across 20 programming languages, a hefty jump from GPT-5.6 Sol’s modest 26.8%. It scored above 83% on 19 out of 20 languages and made improvements on all of them. GPT-6 Luna , predictably, didn’t do as well as Astra, with the lower-cost option only achieving an average pass rate of 40.3%. That said, it did manage to outperform GPT-5.6 Sol on every language tested, with an approximate 78% lower estimated API cost. All right, then. Keep your secrets. OpenAI reports promising results from its COBOL migration evaluation and MultiLangBench, but benchmarks don’t tell the whole story. As of Thursday, Real-SWE 1.1 , which uses private codebases, lists Claude Opus 5.5 in first place at 56.8% resolution. An earlier Real-SWE run covered by The New Stack had a different leader and lower scores. Plus, developers still can’t inspect OpenAI’s COBOL migration benchmark. The announcement credits feedback from developers and enterprise customers for guiding the work, but without the underlying tests and dataset, outsiders can’t independently check the results. OpenAI acknowledges a key limitation, noting that “applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.” OpenAI is entering a field others have been working on for some time. Anthropic outlined how Claude Code could assist COBOL modernization on February 23 . As The New Stack reported, AWS introduced AI agents for mainframe migrations in 2024.

items.title: This Woman's Living a CashApp Scam Nightmare
items.summary: GM! We have a few bangers for you today. First: Can you imagine sitting in jail for days without knowing why, and then finding out that it's because someone hacked CashApp to impersonate you? I would be kind of mad! And elsewhere on 404 this morning, we have some prescient thoughts from an autonomous weapons expert on the state of AI in war, what's going on with cybersecurity experts in the wake of the PHPocalypse, and more insights into how cops view anti-Flock activists. Let's get into it. IMAGE: SPUMONI COOPERATIVE FOR 404 MEDIA Someone Opened a CashApp In Her Name. She Faces Years in Prison Amanda Smith answered the door one afternoon in April and came face to face with the local Sheriff’s department in upstate Pennsylvania. The officers said they had a warrant for her arrest for a crime she had allegedly committed more than a thousand miles away in Arkansas. “I was completely confused,” Smith recalled. For one, she had never been to Arkansas. Second, the warrant was for computer fraud. By her own admission, Smith was not a very tech savvy person. She had a feeling she was being set up. After discussing with the officers the practicalities of what was about to happen — she was allowed to get her contact lenses — they took her away in handcuffs to the local jail where she spent three nights. The reason for Smith’s arrest, she learned later, was that a scammer had tricked someone on Facebook Marketplace into sending $1,000 to a CashApp account in her name that the scammer controlled. The scammer created the account using her Social Security number and date of birth. Smith said she has never used CashApp. What developed over the next few days, and has now stretched across six months, is a Kafkaesque situation in which Smith, in her telling, is being asked to prove her innocence in an ongoing criminal case, while CashApp refuses to provide her any information about the account because she couldn’t prove that she was the owner. Read the rest of this story here. MORE FROM 404 MEDIA “Suspicious behavior:” A federal intelligence center warned police that city council meetings about Flock “may be viewed by extremists as a desirable target,” and told them to be on the lookout for “emotional confrontations” between people who oppose surveillance and government officials, according to a copy of the warning obtained by 404 Media. “Black October?” For much of the last month, many cybersecurity experts have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, saying they’re alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents to find and exploit previously unknown bugs. So, what’s really going on? The UN met this week to discuss autonomous weapons. “The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning,” Laurent Gisel, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) legal warfare team, told 404 Media. Gisel was in NYC this week to address the UN about all the things that are driving conflict across the planet. His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and, of course, AI. FROM AROUND THE WEB That’s a W for the Rebel Alliance. In San Diego, where Darth Vader famously spoke in favor of Flock cameras and mass surveillance, the city council just voted to end its contract with Flock. The decision still has to be confirmed, NBC 7 reports , but this is huge news for a city where council members have voted multiple times to keep Flock watching its citizens.

His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and, of course, AI.

FROM AROUND THE WEB 

That’s a W for the Rebel Alliance. In San Diego, where Darth Vader famously spoke in favor of Flock cameras and mass surveillance, the city council just voted to end its contract with Flock. The decision still has to be confirmed, NBC 7 reports, but this is huge news for a city where council members have voted multiple times to keep Flock watching its citizens.

items.summary: Looped transformers, targeted data, continued pretraining: each under 1 point. Swapping in a bigger encoder: +5.3. Lessons from Yama. Disclosure: this article was drafted with help from an AI assistant, and the charts were made with AI-assisted code from my own results. The model, experiments, results and decisions are my own. Every number was checked against the model card or my training logs. Yama returns a calibrated probability for every label you define. Image by the author. That model is Yama. It succeeds my earlier model, laya-indic, which is still available. XLM-RoBERTa-large [6] has about 300M in its transformer layers, roughly three times as much network. Corpus size isn’t the explanation: mmBERT was actually pretrained on more text. So I trained XLM-R-large on the same data. mmBERT-base and XLM-RoBERTa-large on the same training data, both after three epochs. The subtitle shows where v3’s six points came from. These are internal ablation runs; only v2 and v3 are on the model card. Chart by the author. The settings weren’t perfectly matched: the XLM-R run needed bf16 and a lower learning rate (more on that below). One difference favours mmBERT: its encoder had extra Indian-language pretraining, and XLM-R’s did not. IndicCOPA went from 0.531, barely above the 0.5 coin-flip line, to 0.624. Three lessons 1. Check the encoder before you invent architecture. Everything clever I tried was worth less than a point. The swap was worth more than five. I’d now run the bigger-encoder baseline first. 2. Big encoders can fail silently. My first XLM-R run collapsed. Around step 28,000 the running loss roughly doubled, from about 0.65 to 1.35, and never recovered. Large encoders often overflow in fp16, the 16-bit format I was using; bf16 has a wider range. Switching to bf16 and halving the learning rate fixed it. I also added a guard that rolls back and lowers the learning rate on a loss spike. It never had to fire, but I’d keep it. 3. Continued pretraining helped the small encoder, not the large one. Extra masked-language-model training on Indian-language text [7] gave mmBERT about +0.7 points in a pilot. On XLM-R, it cut that pretraining loss by 6–14% in every language, but the downstream result was a tie (0.861 against 0.862). My guess is that XLM-R had already seen plenty of Indian-language text. How it compares I scored Yama and four popular open zero-shot classifiers with the same harness on the same test samples. The headline set contains only datasets Yama never saw any data from. That is 33 pick-one-label tasks: SIB-200 topic classification in 19 languages [8] IndicSentiment, and IndicCOPA, where you pick the more plausible cause or effect [9] AG News [10] and Emotion [11] Zero-shot accuracy on 33 tasks from datasets Yama never trained on (it did train on similar task types). On the 22 Indian-language tasks alone: Yama 0.813, bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0 0.753. Chart by the author. The closest competitor, bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0, is the same size class (568M). Yama beats it on 29 of the 33 tasks, loses on 3 (AG News, Emotion and Marathi IndicCOPA) and ties on 1. For a rough sense of scale I also asked an LLM the same questions zero-shot: Gemma 4, a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters [12]. On a slightly different 64-task set, with 200-sample subsets, it scored 0.850 against Yama’s 0.855. Treat that as “roughly level”, not a ranking. Benchmark tables are easy to tilt, so here is what to keep in mind: An unseen dataset is not an unseen task type. Yama trained on topic questions about Indian-language text, on cause/effect questions in the COPA format, and on synthetic sentiment and emotion questions. None of it came from the test sets, but the tasks are similar. Only pick-one-label tasks are compared. NLI models have no native yes/no or rating mode, so they turn each option into the hypothesis “This text is about {option}.” The harness doesn’t handicap the other models. It gives bart-large-mnli 0.785 accuracy on AG News, against 0.703 macro-F1 reported for it on the bge-m3-zeroshot card, and 0.491 against 0.455 on Emotion. bge-m3’s wins on AG News and Emotion are probably not zero-shot. Its model card reports those datasets from a run that trained on them, and its scores here match. They are still in its 0.770 average. Calibration on unseen tasks is a tie. Expected calibration error (lower is better) is 0.092 for both models. The model card lists every per-task number. How it works How Yama scores a question (simplified). Architecture and training method from THX-01 [13]. Diagram by the author. Yama uses the THX-01 decision architecture, its training method and its open-source thx01 library [13]. It does not use THX-01's weights, and I'm not affiliated with its authors. Packing. The question, the options and the text are packed into one sequence, and each option is preceded by its own mask marker. Encoder. XLM-RoBERTa-large, with 560M parameters, reads the sequence. Every token can see the question, all the options and the text at once. Decision head. A question-type embedding is added and two more transformer layers run over the sequence. A small shared scorer then turns the hidden state at each marker into one logit. Probabilities. The logits are divided by a temperature fitted for each question type and softmaxed into probabilities. The labels are part of the input, so a new label set needs no retraining. Yes/no questions get two markers (“false” and “true”), and ratings get one marker per level. Training uses THX-01’s RLCD method [13]: The model samples answers and is rewarded with a strictly proper scoring rule [14]. That is a reward that is maximised only by reporting honest probabilities. This is combined with ordinary cross-entropy on slightly smoothed targets. After training, one temperature per question type is fitted on held-out data [15]. Expected calibration error is 0.070 on the 67-task benchmark and 0.092 on the unseen tasks above. The data All training data is public and permissively licensed: CC0, CC-BY, Apache-2.0 or MIT, with no ShareAlike or NonCommercial sources. As far as I can verify, none of it is output from proprietary models. The one exception I couldn’t fully check is NVIDIA’s Nemotron Safety Guard v3 [16], which doesn’t name the models used to generate it. The training set has four parts: 285k decisions from 17 public datasets. These include MASSIVE intents [17], news categories, emotions, toxicity, safety categories and Hinglish voice-assistant requests. 173k synthetic questions written by open-weights Qwen3 [18]. The pipeline works label-first: decide the answers, write a text that makes them true, have a smaller Qwen3 model answer blind, and keep only the questions where the two agree. 118k questions about real Indian-language web text from AI4Bharat’s Sangraha corpus [19]. Roughly half were written by Qwen3. The newer 54k were written by Gemma 4 and checked by Qwen3.6 [20], a different model family. 15k cause/effect and passage yes/no questions , written the same way. I built in one experiment. Telugu and Gujarati were left out of the cause/effect questions, and Hindi out of the yes/no questions. Any gain in those languages would then be transfer, not format memorisation. The result was mixed: Telugu and Gujarati IndicCOPA improved like the other languages, but only once I switched to the bigger encoder. Hindi BoolQ (yes/no questions about a passage, from the THX-01 benchmark [13]) didn’t move: 0.618 → 0.616. All training text was deduplicated against every test set by normalised exact match. The new data is published as arunp0/yama-indic-gemma . Limitations Reasoning is still weak. IndicCOPA is 0.62. BoolQ-hi is also 0.62, which is about what you’d get by always answering “yes”, so there’s essentially no signal there. On smaller samples, Gemma 4 scores roughly 0.80–0.85 on both, so there is plenty of room left. Inputs are capped at 512 tokens, down from 1,024 in v2. XLM-R’s tokenizer uses 25–40% fewer tokens on Indian scripts, which offsets part of the cut. Each decision costs about twice v2’s compute. About half the labels come from language models, checked by another language model rather than by people. Recalibrate before you set thresholds. Calibration is good on average but poor on the reasoning tasks. Benchmark coverage is uneven. There’s no Odia test set here. The only real-world Hinglish test set, Hinglish-TOP, comes from a dataset whose training split Yama used. It isn’t a tested moderation system, even though it can classify that kind of content. Why “Yama”? In Indian tradition Yama is also Dharmaraja , the judge who weighs what is placed before him and gives a verdict. A model that weighs the options you give it and returns a verdict with a confidence seemed a fair fit. Try it Model (Apache-2.0): huggingface.co/arunp0/yama-indic New training data (CC-BY-4.0): huggingface.co/datasets/arunp0/yama-indic-gemma Everything in one place: the Yama collection This is a personal project. If you try it on your own data, tell me where it breaks. That’s the most useful feedback I can get. items.summary_html:
Looped transformers, targeted data, continued pretraining: each under 1 point. Swapping in a bigger encoder: +5.3. Lessons from Yama.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with help from an AI assistant, and the charts were made with AI-assisted code from my own results. The model, experiments, results and decisions are my own. Every number was checked against the model card or my training logs.

Yama returns a calibrated probability for every label you define. Image by the author.

TL;DR

  • Yama is an open-weights (Apache-2.0), 586M-parameter model. You give it a text in any of 11 Indian languages, Hinglish or English, plus a question and labels you write at inference time.
  • On 33 tasks from datasets it never trained on, it scores 0.814, against 0.770 for the strongest open zero-shot classifier I tested.
  • On my 67-task benchmark, looped transformers, targeted data and continued pretraining each moved the score by less than a point. Swapping in a larger encoder moved it by 5.3 points.
The problem

Here is a typical customer message:

Kal se mera UPI payment fail ho raha hai, paise kat gaye par merchant ko nahi mile

(“My UPI payment has been failing since yesterday; the money was debited but the merchant never got it.”)

The questions you want answered change all the time. Today: is this a failed payment, a refund request or a login problem? Is it urgent? How annoyed is the customer? Tomorrow: the same kind of questions about Tamil product reviews or Bengali headlines, with different labels.

The usual tools all have a catch for Indian languages:

  • A fine-tuned classifier per task works well, but every new label set needs labelled data and a training run.
  • Zero-shot NLI models such as bart-large-mnli [1, 2] learn from English or machine-translated inference data. On the Indian-language tasks in my tests, three of the four I tried scored between 0.35 and 0.59; one of them, bart-large-mnli, is English-only. The best, bge-m3-zeroshot [3, 4], reached 0.75.
  • An LLM call per message works, but it is slow and costly at volume, and you end up parsing free text and fighting prompt drift.

I wanted one small, open model that takes the question and labels at inference time and returns one calibrated probability per label in a single forward pass. “Calibrated” means that when it says 0.8, it is right about 80% of the time. That model is Yama. It succeeds my earlier model, laya-indic, which is still available.

What a call looks like
import thx01   # pip install thx01
agent = thx01.load("arunp0/yama-indic")
text = "Kal se mera UPI payment fail ho raha hai, paise kat gaye par merchant ko nahi mile"
out = agent.system_one(text, {
    "topic":  {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What is the customer writing about?",
               "criteria": {"failed_payment": "payment failed or money debited but not received",
                            "refund": "asking for a refund", "account": "login or account access", "other": None}},
    "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer need help urgently?"},
    "anger":  {"type": "score", "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?",
               "criteria": ["calm", "mildly annoyed", "clearly frustrated", "furious"]},
})
print(out["answers"]["topic"]["probabilities"])
# {'failed_payment': 0.9629, 'refund': 0.0125, 'account': 0.0123, 'other': 0.0124}
# other answers from the same call: urgent P(yes) = 0.74, anger "clearly frustrated" 0.88

That is real output. One call answered three kinds of question:

  • choice picks one of the options you define; descriptions are optional.
  • noul is yes/no and returns the probability of “yes”.
  • score is an ordinal rating over levels you define.

Write the questions in English and leave the text in its own language and script. Yama covers:

  • Hindi (Devanagari or romanised) and Hinglish
  • Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu and Odia
  • English

It is an encoder, not a text generator, so it is fast and deterministic:

  • about 17 ms per decision on an NVIDIA H100, or about 1,400 decisions per second batched
  • about 120 ms on 8 AMD EPYC CPU threads
What didn’t work

The first two versions used mmBERT-base [5] as the encoder, and v2 reached 0.800. Every number in this section is on the same 67-task benchmark the model card uses; the intermediate runs are internal and not on the card. Here is what I tried to push that score higher.

Targeted data. Reasoning was the weakest area. I added 15k cause/effect and passage yes/no questions, written by Gemma 4 from real Indian-language text. Under the same three-epoch schedule, the overall score went from 0.804 without them to 0.809 with them. The two tasks they targeted barely moved.

Looped transformers in the head. I let the decision head take several passes over its own output and let the options attend to each other. The new blocks sat behind gates initialised to zero, so training started exactly at the baseline. The result was 0.806, against 0.809 for the same model trained for the same extra epoch without loops. The gates learned to stay almost closed.

Looped transformers in the encoder. I re-ran the top six encoder layers three times. The result was 0.808 against 0.809. Again, the gates barely opened.

One caveat: I added the loops to an already-trained model at a low learning rate, which favours the existing weights. Trained from scratch, they might behave differently.

A bigger encoder. At this point the pattern suggested that depth and wiring weren’t the bottleneck; capacity was:

  • mmBERT-base has 307M parameters, but only 110M sit outside its large vocabulary embeddings.
  • XLM-RoBERTa-large [6] has about 300M in its transformer layers, roughly three times as much network.
  • Corpus size isn’t the explanation: mmBERT was actually pretrained on more text.

So I trained XLM-R-large on the same data.

mmBERT-base and XLM-RoBERTa-large on the same training data, both after three epochs. The subtitle shows where v3’s six points came from. These are internal ablation runs; only v2 and v3 are on the model card. Chart by the author.

The settings weren’t perfectly matched: the XLM-R run needed bf16 and a lower learning rate (more on that below). One difference favours mmBERT: its encoder had extra Indian-language pretraining, and XLM-R’s did not. IndicCOPA went from 0.531, barely above the 0.5 coin-flip line, to 0.624.

Three lessons

1. Check the encoder before you invent architecture. Everything clever I tried was worth less than a point. The swap was worth more than five. I’d now run the bigger-encoder baseline first.

2. Big encoders can fail silently. My first XLM-R run collapsed. Around step 28,000 the running loss roughly doubled, from about 0.65 to 1.35, and never recovered. Large encoders often overflow in fp16, the 16-bit format I was using; bf16 has a wider range. Switching to bf16 and halving the learning rate fixed it. I also added a guard that rolls back and lowers the learning rate on a loss spike. It never had to fire, but I’d keep it.

3. Continued pretraining helped the small encoder, not the large one. Extra masked-language-model training on Indian-language text [7] gave mmBERT about +0.7 points in a pilot. On XLM-R, it cut that pretraining loss by 6–14% in every language, but the downstream result was a tie (0.861 against 0.862). My guess is that XLM-R had already seen plenty of Indian-language text.

How it compares

I scored Yama and four popular open zero-shot classifiers with the same harness on the same test samples. The headline set contains only datasets Yama never saw any data from. That is 33 pick-one-label tasks:

  • SIB-200 topic classification in 19 languages [8]
  • IndicSentiment, and IndicCOPA, where you pick the more plausible cause or effect [9]
  • AG News [10] and Emotion [11]

Zero-shot accuracy on 33 tasks from datasets Yama never trained on (it did train on similar task types). On the 22 Indian-language tasks alone: Yama 0.813, bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0 0.753. Chart by the author.

The closest competitor, bge-m3-zeroshot-v2.0, is the same size class (568M). Yama beats it on 29 of the 33 tasks, loses on 3 (AG News, Emotion and Marathi IndicCOPA) and ties on 1.

For a rough sense of scale I also asked an LLM the same questions zero-shot: Gemma 4, a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters [12]. On a slightly different 64-task set, with 200-sample subsets, it scored 0.850 against Yama’s 0.855. Treat that as “roughly level”, not a ranking.

Benchmark tables are easy to tilt, so here is what to keep in mind:

  • An unseen dataset is not an unseen task type. Yama trained on topic questions about Indian-language text, on cause/effect questions in the COPA format, and on synthetic sentiment and emotion questions. None of it came from the test sets, but the tasks are similar.
  • Only pick-one-label tasks are compared. NLI models have no native yes/no or rating mode, so they turn each option into the hypothesis “This text is about {option}.”
  • The harness doesn’t handicap the other models. It gives bart-large-mnli 0.785 accuracy on AG News, against 0.703 macro-F1 reported for it on the bge-m3-zeroshot card, and 0.491 against 0.455 on Emotion.
  • bge-m3’s wins on AG News and Emotion are probably not zero-shot. Its model card reports those datasets from a run that trained on them, and its scores here match. They are still in its 0.770 average.
  • Calibration on unseen tasks is a tie. Expected calibration error (lower is better) is 0.092 for both models.

The model card lists every per-task number.

How it works

How Yama scores a question (simplified). Architecture and training method from THX-01 [13]. Diagram by the author.

Yama uses the THX-01 decision architecture, its training method and its open-source thx01 library [13]. It does not use THX-01's weights, and I'm not affiliated with its authors.

  1. Packing. The question, the options and the text are packed into one sequence, and each option is preceded by its own mask marker.
  2. Encoder. XLM-RoBERTa-large, with 560M parameters, reads the sequence. Every token can see the question, all the options and the text at once.
  3. Decision head. A question-type embedding is added and two more transformer layers run over the sequence. A small shared scorer then turns the hidden state at each marker into one logit.
  4. Probabilities. The logits are divided by a temperature fitted for each question type and softmaxed into probabilities.

The labels are part of the input, so a new label set needs no retraining. Yes/no questions get two markers (“false” and “true”), and ratings get one marker per level.

Training uses THX-01’s RLCD method [13]:

  • The model samples answers and is rewarded with a strictly proper scoring rule [14]. That is a reward that is maximised only by reporting honest probabilities.
  • This is combined with ordinary cross-entropy on slightly smoothed targets.
  • After training, one temperature per question type is fitted on held-out data [15].

Expected calibration error is 0.070 on the 67-task benchmark and 0.092 on the unseen tasks above.

The data

All training data is public and permissively licensed: CC0, CC-BY, Apache-2.0 or MIT, with no ShareAlike or NonCommercial sources. As far as I can verify, none of it is output from proprietary models. The one exception I couldn’t fully check is NVIDIA’s Nemotron Safety Guard v3 [16], which doesn’t name the models used to generate it.

The training set has four parts:

  • 285k decisions from 17 public datasets. These include MASSIVE intents [17], news categories, emotions, toxicity, safety categories and Hinglish voice-assistant requests.
  • 173k synthetic questions written by open-weights Qwen3 [18]. The pipeline works label-first: decide the answers, write a text that makes them true, have a smaller Qwen3 model answer blind, and keep only the questions where the two agree.
  • 118k questions about real Indian-language web text from AI4Bharat’s Sangraha corpus [19]. Roughly half were written by Qwen3. The newer 54k were written by Gemma 4 and checked by Qwen3.6 [20], a different model family.
  • 15k cause/effect and passage yes/no questions, written the same way.

I built in one experiment. Telugu and Gujarati were left out of the cause/effect questions, and Hindi out of the yes/no questions. Any gain in those languages would then be transfer, not format memorisation. The result was mixed:

  • Telugu and Gujarati IndicCOPA improved like the other languages, but only once I switched to the bigger encoder.
  • Hindi BoolQ (yes/no questions about a passage, from the THX-01 benchmark [13]) didn’t move: 0.618 → 0.616.

All training text was deduplicated against every test set by normalised exact match. The new data is published as arunp0/yama-indic-gemma.

Limitations
  • Reasoning is still weak. IndicCOPA is 0.62. BoolQ-hi is also 0.62, which is about what you’d get by always answering “yes”, so there’s essentially no signal there. On smaller samples, Gemma 4 scores roughly 0.80–0.85 on both, so there is plenty of room left.
  • Inputs are capped at 512 tokens, down from 1,024 in v2. XLM-R’s tokenizer uses 25–40% fewer tokens on Indian scripts, which offsets part of the cut. Each decision costs about twice v2’s compute.
  • About half the labels come from language models, checked by another language model rather than by people.
  • Recalibrate before you set thresholds. Calibration is good on average but poor on the reasoning tasks.
  • Benchmark coverage is uneven. There’s no Odia test set here. The only real-world Hinglish test set, Hinglish-TOP, comes from a dataset whose training split Yama used.
  • It isn’t a tested moderation system, even though it can classify that kind of content.
Why “Yama”?

In Indian tradition Yama is also Dharmaraja, the judge who weighs what is placed before him and gives a verdict. A model that weighs the options you give it and returns a verdict with a confidence seemed a fair fit.

Try it
  • Model (Apache-2.0): huggingface.co/arunp0/yama-indic
  • New training data (CC-BY-4.0): huggingface.co/datasets/arunp0/yama-indic-gemma
  • Everything in one place: the Yama collection

This is a personal project. If you try it on your own data, tell me where it breaks. That’s the most useful feedback I can get.

Thanks to AI4Bharat for Sangraha, to the THX-01 authors for the architecture, training method and thx01 library, and to the teams behind XLM-RoBERTa, Qwen and Gemma for releasing open weights.

items.title: LAI #148: What Happens Between Prompt and Output?
items.summary: Agent traces, LLM observability, reliable webhooks, safer secrets, source filtering, and dropout explained. Good morning, AI enthusiasts! A lot of the frustrating bugs in AI systems now happen after the model has already done its part. The policy agent gets the right answer, but drops an important condition when it hands the task off. The batch job finishes, but your app never hears about it. Your latency dashboard looks fine, but the user is still waiting too long for the first token. Or the coding agent completes the command and leaves the credential sitting in its transcript. This week’s issue has a lot of useful examples of how to deal with those problems. You’ll learn: Which metrics actually help debug LLM latency and cost How to evaluate what happens between multiple agents How to make batch webhooks survive retries and duplicates How coding agents can use secrets without exposing them in chat Why research agents should filter for novelty, not just relevance How dropout reduces overfitting in neural networks Let’s get into it! What’s AI Weekly https://medium.com/media/a35dcc74c91b16f962be9e21597b0fb4/href This week in What’s AI, I’m sharing the setup I now use to switch between Claude Code and Codex without rebuilding context every time. The main change was moving my notes, skills, scripts, meeting recaps, and recurring instructions into an Obsidian vault that both agents can read. An index tells them what to load for each task, so I can give an agent the context it needs without passing my entire archive into every prompt. I also keep feedback with each skill, so repeated corrections can become part of the default workflow. I still use Codex, but I often let Claude Code plan the work and call Codex through MCP to execute it. I also move non-urgent jobs, such as daily news recaps, into scheduled runs so they do not compete with my daytime usage. The idea is to keep useful context and skills outside any one model or coding tool, so changing agents doesn’t mean starting over. The full article goes through the vault structure, the role of skills and feedback files, how I split planning from execution, and how the setup follows me across devices. Read it here or watch the video on YouTube . AI Tip of the Day When developers first give an agent search access, relevance is often the main filter: find pages related to the query, then let the model read them. That becomes expensive as the system scales. More searches bring in more pages, and relevant pages often overlap. You waste context, add latency, and spend money processing the same information multiple times. We ran into this while scaling Nova, the research agent we built in Agent Engineering . Its searches kept surfacing shady blogs, sales pitches, low-quality pages, and several sources making essentially the same point. So we stopped ranking sources on relevance alone. Nova now checks three things: Trust: is the source reliable enough to use? Relevance: does it answer the research question? Novelty: does it add information the agent does not already have? Sources that pass the first filters stay in the research file as short summaries. Nova then chooses only five to read in full, partly based on whether they add something missing from the material already collected. If your agent already ranks search results by relevance, add novelty before loading the full page. Compare each source with what the agent already has. If it mostly repeats the same information, keep the summary or skip it. — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI Co-founder & Head of Community My AI Engineer talk on why AI writing still reads like slop is now live on YouTube! https://medium.com/media/bfe42abad29717ee8e6d1344158f9538/href I walk through ToneBench, where we tested 78 models across 127 configurations using 6,350 generated scripts and 25,400 judge assessments. I cover how we measure tone, substance, structure, hooks, slop, and consistency, and what the results show about model choice, reasoning effort, and cost. I also get into one of the harder parts of benchmarking writing: the judges themselves have measurable preferences, even when model identities are hidden. Watch the full talk here. Learn AI Together Community Section! Featured Community post from the Discord Panelreader. built a neural network from scratch in Python and NumPy to understand what frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow handle behind the scenes. The project implements a 2 → 3 → 1 XOR network with forward propagation, backpropagation, and gradient descent written manually. After 5,000 training epochs, the network correctly predicted all four XOR cases with a final MSE of 0.004715. The repo also includes mathematical explanations, training visualizations, and 12 editable diagrams that walk through how the network works. Check it out on GitHub and support a fellow community member. If you have feedback on the code or documentation, share it in the thread ! Collaboration Opportunities The Learn AI Together Discord community is flooding with collaboration opportunities. If you are excited to dive into applied AI, want a study partner, or even want to find a partner for your passion project, join the collaboration channel ! Keep an eye on this section, too — we share cool opportunities every week! 1. Hendrickop is looking for an AI/ML learning partner. He is a beginner but wants to learn quickly and work on projects. If you are following the same path, connect with him in the thread ! 2. Martocierny is putting together a team to build a 2D multiplayer sandbox in the browser and is looking for coders, artists, testers, and even complete beginners. This is a hobby project, but if it sounds fun, reach out to him in the thread ! 3. Gian_16992 is moving from backend orientation to AI engineering and is looking for people to discuss ideas, share resources, make projects, etc. If this sounds like a good next step for you, reach out to them in the thread ! Meme of the week! Meme shared by bin4ry_d3struct0r TAI Curated Section Article of the week Dropout Finally Explained: Why Breaking Half Your Neural Networks Makes It Smarter by Simple ML Neural networks can fit their training data closely but still perform much worse on new examples. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing units during training, so the network repeatedly trains different weight-sharing subnetworks instead of allowing the same neurons to depend on one another. This article works through the original dropout paper, explains co-adaptation and the weight-scaling rule, and connects dropout to regularization in linear models. It also reviews results across vision, speech, text, and genetics, along with practical guidance on keep probabilities, network size, max-norm constraints, and the additional training time dropout requires. Our must-read articles 1. LLM Observability in Production: Metrics, Logs, Traces by Ray Hu Traditional API monitoring misses several problems specific to LLM applications. A streaming request can have acceptable total latency while still making the user wait too long for the first token, and token usage adds a cost dimension that normal request metrics don’t track. This article shows how to measure time to first token, time per output token, token usage, and cost with Prometheus, separate high-volume metadata from full prompt logs, and connect requests across OpenTelemetry traces with a shared trace_id. It also covers redaction, sampling, and alerting so teams can trace a slow or expensive request back to the component that caused it. 2. Multi-Agent Trajectory Evaluation, Explained Simply by Satsawat Natakarnkitkul A multi-agent system can return the correct final message even when one agent makes a serious mistake along the way. In the article’s example, a policy tool correctly returned that a damaged item had to be sent back before a refund, but the policy agent omitted that condition when handing the case to the orchestrator, so billing issued the refund immediately. The article shows how to evaluate each agent’s tool use, the information passed between agents, and the final outcome separately. It also runs cases multiple times to detect inconsistent behavior and uses step-level failure attribution to identify where the error entered the trajectory. 3. LLM Batch Webhooks: 5 Mechanisms, Zero Lost Jobs by Ray Hu Polling a batch API creates a failure case when the batch finishes, but the process checking its status stops running. This article replaces polling with a TypeScript webhook flow designed for duplicate deliveries, temporary failures, and unavailable downstream services. It implements signature verification, atomic deduplication, idempotent side effects, exponential backoff, a dead-letter queue for failed events, and a circuit breaker for unhealthy endpoints. It also compares how providers handle batch completion and retries, and shows how to replay failed deliveries without processing the same job twice. 4. The Key Is in the Clipboard by Enzo Lombardi Coding agents often need credentials to run commands, but pasting a password or API key into chat leaves it in the model context and can also store it in local session transcripts. After examining 661 Claude Code transcripts, this article builds lsv, a Rust vault that lets an agent pass a secret into a command without providing a normal command for reading the value back. Secrets enter through the clipboard, appear as redacted references during use, and require Touch ID approval before access. items.summary_html:
Agent traces, LLM observability, reliable webhooks, safer secrets, source filtering, and dropout explained.

Good morning, AI enthusiasts!

A lot of the frustrating bugs in AI systems now happen after the model has already done its part.

The policy agent gets the right answer, but drops an important condition when it hands the task off. The batch job finishes, but your app never hears about it. Your latency dashboard looks fine, but the user is still waiting too long for the first token. Or the coding agent completes the command and leaves the credential sitting in its transcript.

This week’s issue has a lot of useful examples of how to deal with those problems. You’ll learn:

  • Which metrics actually help debug LLM latency and cost
  • How to evaluate what happens between multiple agents
  • How to make batch webhooks survive retries and duplicates
  • How coding agents can use secrets without exposing them in chat
  • Why research agents should filter for novelty, not just relevance
  • How dropout reduces overfitting in neural networks

Let’s get into it!

What’s AI Weeklyhttps://medium.com/media/a35dcc74c91b16f962be9e21597b0fb4/href

This week in What’s AI, I’m sharing the setup I now use to switch between Claude Code and Codex without rebuilding context every time.

The main change was moving my notes, skills, scripts, meeting recaps, and recurring instructions into an Obsidian vault that both agents can read. An index tells them what to load for each task, so I can give an agent the context it needs without passing my entire archive into every prompt. I also keep feedback with each skill, so repeated corrections can become part of the default workflow.

I still use Codex, but I often let Claude Code plan the work and call Codex through MCP to execute it. I also move non-urgent jobs, such as daily news recaps, into scheduled runs so they do not compete with my daytime usage. The idea is to keep useful context and skills outside any one model or coding tool, so changing agents doesn’t mean starting over.

The full article goes through the vault structure, the role of skills and feedback files, how I split planning from execution, and how the setup follows me across devices. Read it here or watch the video on YouTube.

AI Tip of the Day

When developers first give an agent search access, relevance is often the main filter: find pages related to the query, then let the model read them.

That becomes expensive as the system scales. More searches bring in more pages, and relevant pages often overlap. You waste context, add latency, and spend money processing the same information multiple times.

We ran into this while scaling Nova, the research agent we built in Agent Engineering. Its searches kept surfacing shady blogs, sales pitches, low-quality pages, and several sources making essentially the same point.

So we stopped ranking sources on relevance alone. Nova now checks three things:

  • Trust: is the source reliable enough to use?
  • Relevance: does it answer the research question?
  • Novelty: does it add information the agent does not already have?

Sources that pass the first filters stay in the research file as short summaries. Nova then chooses only five to read in full, partly based on whether they add something missing from the material already collected.

If your agent already ranks search results by relevance, add novelty before loading the full page. Compare each source with what the agent already has. If it mostly repeats the same information, keep the summary or skip it.

— Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI Co-founder & Head of Community

My AI Engineer talk on why AI writing still reads like slop is now live on YouTube!

https://medium.com/media/bfe42abad29717ee8e6d1344158f9538/href

I walk through ToneBench, where we tested 78 models across 127 configurations using 6,350 generated scripts and 25,400 judge assessments. I cover how we measure tone, substance, structure, hooks, slop, and consistency, and what the results show about model choice, reasoning effort, and cost.

I also get into one of the harder parts of benchmarking writing: the judges themselves have measurable preferences, even when model identities are hidden.

Watch the full talk here.

Learn AI Together Community Section!Featured Community post from the Discord

Panelreader. built a neural network from scratch in Python and NumPy to understand what frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow handle behind the scenes. The project implements a 2 → 3 → 1 XOR network with forward propagation, backpropagation, and gradient descent written manually. After 5,000 training epochs, the network correctly predicted all four XOR cases with a final MSE of 0.004715. The repo also includes mathematical explanations, training visualizations, and 12 editable diagrams that walk through how the network works. Check it out on GitHub and support a fellow community member. If you have feedback on the code or documentation, share it in the thread!

Collaboration Opportunities

The Learn AI Together Discord community is flooding with collaboration opportunities. If you are excited to dive into applied AI, want a study partner, or even want to find a partner for your passion project, join the collaboration channel! Keep an eye on this section, too — we share cool opportunities every week!

1. Hendrickop is looking for an AI/ML learning partner. He is a beginner but wants to learn quickly and work on projects. If you are following the same path, connect with him in the thread!

2. Martocierny is putting together a team to build a 2D multiplayer sandbox in the browser and is looking for coders, artists, testers, and even complete beginners. This is a hobby project, but if it sounds fun, reach out to him in the thread!

3. Gian_16992 is moving from backend orientation to AI engineering and is looking for people to discuss ideas, share resources, make projects, etc. If this sounds like a good next step for you, reach out to them in the thread!

Meme of the week!

Meme shared by bin4ry_d3struct0r

TAI Curated SectionArticle of the week

Dropout Finally Explained: Why Breaking Half Your Neural Networks Makes It Smarter by Simple ML

Neural networks can fit their training data closely but still perform much worse on new examples. Dropout addresses this by randomly removing units during training, so the network repeatedly trains different weight-sharing subnetworks instead of allowing the same neurons to depend on one another. This article works through the original dropout paper, explains co-adaptation and the weight-scaling rule, and connects dropout to regularization in linear models. It also reviews results across vision, speech, text, and genetics, along with practical guidance on keep probabilities, network size, max-norm constraints, and the additional training time dropout requires.

Our must-read articles

1. LLM Observability in Production: Metrics, Logs, Traces by Ray Hu

Traditional API monitoring misses several problems specific to LLM applications. A streaming request can have acceptable total latency while still making the user wait too long for the first token, and token usage adds a cost dimension that normal request metrics don’t track. This article shows how to measure time to first token, time per output token, token usage, and cost with Prometheus, separate high-volume metadata from full prompt logs, and connect requests across OpenTelemetry traces with a shared trace_id. It also covers redaction, sampling, and alerting so teams can trace a slow or expensive request back to the component that caused it.

2. Multi-Agent Trajectory Evaluation, Explained Simply by Satsawat Natakarnkitkul

A multi-agent system can return the correct final message even when one agent makes a serious mistake along the way. In the article’s example, a policy tool correctly returned that a damaged item had to be sent back before a refund, but the policy agent omitted that condition when handing the case to the orchestrator, so billing issued the refund immediately. The article shows how to evaluate each agent’s tool use, the information passed between agents, and the final outcome separately. It also runs cases multiple times to detect inconsistent behavior and uses step-level failure attribution to identify where the error entered the trajectory.

3. LLM Batch Webhooks: 5 Mechanisms, Zero Lost Jobs by Ray Hu

Polling a batch API creates a failure case when the batch finishes, but the process checking its status stops running. This article replaces polling with a TypeScript webhook flow designed for duplicate deliveries, temporary failures, and unavailable downstream services. It implements signature verification, atomic deduplication, idempotent side effects, exponential backoff, a dead-letter queue for failed events, and a circuit breaker for unhealthy endpoints. It also compares how providers handle batch completion and retries, and shows how to replay failed deliveries without processing the same job twice.

4. The Key Is in the Clipboard by Enzo Lombardi

Coding agents often need credentials to run commands, but pasting a password or API key into chat leaves it in the model context and can also store it in local session transcripts. After examining 661 Claude Code transcripts, this article builds lsv, a Rust vault that lets an agent pass a secret into a command without providing a normal command for reading the value back. Secrets enter through the clipboard, appear as redacted references during use, and require Touch ID approval before access.

items.title: Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
items.summary: At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU , a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available on GitHub . AWS also launched TorchNeuron in public beta, its open-source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, also available on GitHub . Both releases seem aimed at making it easier for developers to move beyond Nvidia GPUs, whose CUDA software ecosystem has long dominated AI development. But while Google and AWS’s new offerings do ease some of the challenges of switching hardware, getting top-tier performance still isn’t straightforward. For developers eager for more computing options, it’s promising but somewhat disappointing. Google wants to make TPUs more PyTorch-friendly Google put TorchTPU in preview with select customers in April (PyTorch says Google’s been working on the project since mid-2025), teasing a simpler way to run PyTorch workloads on Google’s AI chips. PyTorch support has long been an awkward dance, so the new backend could make it easier to run existing models on TPUs. Google says it wants to make its TPU software ecosystem more open and developer-friendly for the PyTorch community, as it works to make the chips a more practical option for developers already using PyTorch. Developed in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU allows developers to run existing PyTorch workloads without JAX dependencies in the runtime. This way, rather than requiring extensive code changes, developers can migrate existing workloads with only “trivial code changes,” according to PyTorch. Specifically, developers can use eager execution to debug models and torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. The new PyTorch stack from Google and Meta comes alongside a slew of other products and integrations announced at the conference, which Google says are “designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure.” Google also announced integrations involving Hugging Face, vLLM , SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray and TorchRec, while contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch ecosystem. AWS wants in, too AWS’s release extends the same PyTorch-native approach to its own AI chips. Like TorchTPU, TorchNeuron gives developers a way to natively experiment and build models with PyTorch — this time for Trainium , AWS’s portfolio of AI chips designed for deep learning training and inference workloads. The public beta supports Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. AWS says moving a model to Trainium can be as simple as switching to .to(‘neuron’) for eager execution. Compiled models also need the Neuron backend selected, either as the default or in a torch.compile call. TorchNeuron also integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface ( NKI ) — a bare-metal language and compiler for programming AWS Trainium and Inferentia NeuronDevices — so developers can create custom operators and optimize performance on Trainium. AWS and PyTorch have published more detailed guidance on the backend’s execution modes and performance tradeoffs. Both are getting closer, but not there yet While TorchTPU and TorchNeuron are notable steps forward in opening up more hardware choices for PyTorch developers, neither is a silver bullet. PyTorch says a simple code change can get models running on TPUs, but peak performance can require TPU-specific optimization. For distributed workloads, PyTorch says TorchTPU’s default Skinny Collectives approach can incur an end-to-end performance penalty of roughly 30–40% compared with an optimized approach because it prevents the XLA compiler from overlapping computation and communication. For workloads seeking peak performance, PyTorch recommends additional tuning and production-grade stacks: “Of course, for production workloads seeking peak performance we would absolutely recommend pursuing an optimal approach based on Pallas kernels and production-grade stacks such as vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, or TorchTitan-TorchTPU, as examples.” TorchNeuron is in public beta. In a separate blog post , AWS says teams can try Trainium with a configuration change instead of a code or model rewrite “in most cases,” leaving open which workloads need more changes. In a case study , AWS describes how its Generative AI Innovation Center worked with AI research and technology company i14 to adapt its Laplace 3B model for Trainium2. The implementation required three changes: 1) using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel; 2) redesigning how Muon communicates; 3) compiling the sequential backward pass. The releases give PyTorch developers more options beyond Nvidia GPUs. For now, moving existing code is easier than getting peak performance on unfamiliar chips.
items.summary_html:
At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available on GitHub. AWS also launched TorchNeuron in public beta, its open-source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, also available on GitHub.

Both releases seem aimed at making it easier for developers to move beyond Nvidia GPUs, whose CUDA software ecosystem has long dominated AI development. But while Google and AWS’s new offerings do ease some of the challenges of switching hardware, getting top-tier performance still isn’t straightforward. 

For developers eager for more computing options, it’s promising but somewhat disappointing.

Google wants to make TPUs more PyTorch-friendly

Google put TorchTPU in preview with select customers in April (PyTorch says Google’s been working on the project since mid-2025), teasing a simpler way to run PyTorch workloads on Google’s AI chips. PyTorch support has long been an awkward dance, so the new backend could make it easier to run existing models on TPUs.

Google says it wants to make its TPU software ecosystem more open and developer-friendly for the PyTorch community, as it works to make the chips a more practical option for developers already using PyTorch. 

Developed in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU allows developers to run existing PyTorch workloads without JAX dependencies in the runtime. This way, rather than requiring extensive code changes, developers can migrate existing workloads with only “trivial code changes,” according to PyTorch. 

Specifically, developers can use eager execution to debug models and torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. 

The new PyTorch stack from Google and Meta comes alongside a slew of other products and integrations announced at the conference, which Google says are “designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure.” Google also announced integrations involving Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray and TorchRec, while contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch ecosystem. 

AWS wants in, too

AWS’s release extends the same PyTorch-native approach to its own AI chips.

Like TorchTPU, TorchNeuron gives developers a way to natively experiment and build models with PyTorch — this time for Trainium, AWS’s portfolio of AI chips designed for deep learning training and inference workloads. The public beta supports Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. 

AWS says moving a model to Trainium can be as simple as switching to .to(‘neuron’) for eager execution. Compiled models also need the Neuron backend selected, either as the default or in a torch.compile call.

TorchNeuron also integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) — a bare-metal language and compiler for programming AWS Trainium and Inferentia NeuronDevices — so developers can create custom operators and optimize performance on Trainium. AWS and PyTorch have published more detailed guidance on the backend’s execution modes and performance tradeoffs.

Both are getting closer, but not there yet

While TorchTPU and TorchNeuron are notable steps forward in opening up more hardware choices for PyTorch developers, neither is a silver bullet.

PyTorch says a simple code change can get models running on TPUs, but peak performance can require TPU-specific optimization.

For distributed workloads, PyTorch says TorchTPU’s default Skinny Collectives approach can incur an end-to-end performance penalty of roughly 30–40% compared with an optimized approach because it prevents the XLA compiler from overlapping computation and communication.

For workloads seeking peak performance, PyTorch recommends additional tuning and production-grade stacks: 

“Of course, for production workloads seeking peak performance we would absolutely recommend pursuing an optimal approach based on Pallas kernels and production-grade stacks such as vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, or TorchTitan-TorchTPU, as examples.”

TorchNeuron is in public beta. In a separate blog post, AWS says teams can try Trainium with a configuration change instead of a code or model rewrite “in most cases,” leaving open which workloads need more changes.

In a case study, AWS describes how its Generative AI Innovation Center worked with AI research and technology company i14 to adapt its Laplace 3B model for Trainium2. The implementation required three changes: 1) using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel; 2) redesigning how Muon communicates; 3) compiling the sequential backward pass.

The releases give PyTorch developers more options beyond Nvidia GPUs. For now, moving existing code is easier than getting peak performance on unfamiliar chips.

items.title: Head of Instagram Says He Has No Idea How to Deal With Wave of Horrible AI Slop
items.summary: AI slop purveyors are stealing comedians’ jokes to create viral Instagram videos of fake comics. And Adam Mosseri, the longtime head of Instagram, says he doesn’t know what to do about it. As Wired reported last week , a recent trend among AI sloppers is to steal the work of real comedians and repackage it in AI-manipulated clips in which the human performers are replaced by fake AI ones. The AI performers in the videos are often depicted as voluptuous young women and direct viewers to OnlyFans pages, where they’re encouraged to pay for more content. George Brett Olson, a comedian whose work was ripped off by a thieving AI account with more than 300,000 followers, published a video earlier this month detailing how his work — and even his outfit — were stolen by the AI fake. This prompted a response from Mosseri, who commented that he doesn’t “think it’s practical for us to try and ban Al content from the platform. It’s gonna be harder and harder to identify, and it’s not all bad content (though yes, there is plenty of slop).” “But we are very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an Al creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that,” Mosseri continued. “I’m not sure what it would be, but I’ll make sure to talk to the team and look into it.” View this post on Instagram This past weekend, in response to a completely different type of content that was ripped off from a creator and rehashed as AI slop — in this case, a video of a visual artist’s work — Mosseri waded into the AI ripoff trend once again, writing that it’s a “tricky problem” and Instagram is still trying to figure out what to do. “To be clear, I am very worried about this trend. We are actively working out what to do; it’s just a tricky problem,” Mosseri wrote in a comment on Threads , again in response to Olson. “We already let people make copyright claims against content and take stolen copyrighted material.” “That’s not enough, though, as I assume many comedians and dancers haven’t gone through the trouble to copyright their material,” he added. “We need a way to help those creatives without letting bad actors make more fake claims (happens all the time unfortunately).” Given Meta’s stake in the AI race, it’s unlikely that the tech giant will move to rid any of its social media platforms of AI content. And to Mosseri’s point, theft and copyright infringement isn’t exactly a new problem. But while stealing someone else’s work and passing it off as your own is an old problem, AI makes it easer than ever to rip people off with basically zero effort. You no longer have to get on stage and perform a standup set to pilfer from a fellow comic, let alone record it and then post it online; to filch someone’s artwork, you don’t have to actually draw or paint. In other words, the barrier of entry is now amazingly low: all you have to do is set up an AI workflow and hit generate, and you have endless low-effort slop to pump out to the masses. (And if you’re able to convince people that you’re not a thieving sloperator and are instead a hot human woman, you might just rake in some extra cash via OnlyFans in the process.) It’ll be interesting to see how Meta moves to combat this kind of abuse across its social media platforms, Instagram included — or if it’ll continue to be up to creators to find and report individual instances of abuse piecemeal, and at the mercy of the platform’s tepid moderation efforts. More on AI ripoffs: Recipe Scammers Are Using an AI-Generated Emily Blunt as a Slop Puppet to Promote Their Garbage
