items.title: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
items.summary: At 2:07 a.m., an AI agent starts failing. The application is still running, but requests are timing out because a downstream API is returning errors. The agent has already retried twice, using more tokens than usual, and its response time has roughly doubled. The first question should not be: “Which model should we use?” It should be: “Who owns this system right now?” That question is easy to overlook when building AI agents . Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk. “Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.” A production agent needs an owner, boundaries, telemetry, failure policies, escalation paths, and a clear distinction between what the system may automate and what requires human intervention. A production agent should not have a direct path from reasoning to action. Each tool invocation should pass through explicit controls, remain observable, and have a defined path to human intervention . Here’s a practical way to build those controls. Step 1: Treat the agent as a production service An agent should have the same operational identity as any other production service. Start by defining its ownership metadata. Python from pydantic import BaseModel class AgentService(BaseModel): name: str owner_team: str service_tier: str escalation_channel: str agent_service = AgentService( name="incident-command-agent", owner_team="platform-engineering", service_tier="critical", escalation_channel="#platform-oncall", ) This may look simple, but it changes the conversation. The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path. “The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.” You can later attach the same metadata to logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and deployment records. Step 2: Define what the agent is allowed to do Ownership also means being clear about what an agent is allowed to do. An agent that can only read telemetry carries far less risk than one that can restart production services, change infrastructure, or deploy code. That’s why I prefer an explicit tool allowlist, which limits the agent to the actions you’ve deliberately granted it. Python ALLOWED_TOOLS = { "get_service_health", "get_recent_deployments", "search_runbooks", "summarize_incident", } class ToolAuthorizationError(Exception): """Raised when an agent attempts to use an unapproved tool.""" def authorize_tool(tool_name: str) -> None: if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS: raise ToolAuthorizationError( f"Tool '{tool_name}' is not authorized." ) The guiding principle is deny by default . Adding a new capability should be an intentional engineering decision, not something that happens because a tool became available to the agent. For destructive operations, authorisation should be even stricter. A production restart or deployment should require authenticated human approval, not the agent’s own judgment. Step 3: Put budgets around agent execution An agent that can reason indefinitely is difficult to operate. Every production workflow should have limits around execution time, model calls, tool calls, and ideally token consumption. Python import os class ExecutionBudget: def __init__( self, max_steps: int | None = None, max_tools: int | None = None, ): self.steps = 0 self.tool_calls = 0 self.max_steps = ( max_steps if max_steps is not None else int(os.getenv("MAX_AGENT_STEPS", "5")) ) self.max_tools = ( max_tools if max_tools is not None else int(os.getenv("MAX_TOOL_CALLS", "8")) ) if self.max_steps <= 0 or self.max_tools <= 0: raise ValueError( "Execution budget limits must be positive." ) def check_step(self) -> None: if self.steps >= self.max_steps: raise RuntimeError( "Agent step budget exceeded." ) self.steps += 1 def check_tool_call(self) -> None: if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tools: raise RuntimeError( "Agent tool-call budget exceeded." ) self.tool_calls += 1 Execution limits should be configurable rather than buried in application code. By passing these limits through the constructor, engineers can assign different budgets to different agents without changing global settings. A diagnostic agent might need only three steps, while a more complex research workflow may require considerably more. When no limits are supplied, the class falls back to environment variables. What matters is that every workflow has a defined ceiling, and that the same budget is enforced throughout its execution. Step 4: Make model calls observable An owner cannot operate what they cannot see. At minimum, record: request latency; model used; success/failure; tool calls; token usage where available; correlation or request ID; escalation events. A simple wrapper provides a useful boundary. Python import logging import time import uuid logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) def invoke_model(model, messages): request_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) started = time.perf_counter() # Extract the model name across different provider libraries. model_name = ( getattr(model, "model_name", None) or getattr(model, "model", None) or "unknown_model" ) try: response = model.invoke(messages) elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started logger.info( "agent_model_call_success", extra={ "request_id": request_id, "model": model_name, "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3), }, ) return response except Exception: elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started logger.exception( "agent_model_call_failed", extra={ "request_id": request_id, "model": model_name, "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3), }, ) raise The request ID becomes especially valuable when an incident involves several services. An engineer should be able to move from an alert to the agent request and then to the underlying model and tool calls. In production, supplement this logging layer with distributed tracing and metrics for a more complete view of system behaviour and performance. Step 5: Separate failure from escalation A failed model call does not necessarily mean the entire service should fail. Likewise, a successful model call does not mean the agent’s recommendation should execute automatically. These are different decisions. Python def handle_agent_failure(error: Exception) -> dict: logger.error( "Agent execution failed; escalating to human.", exc_info=( type(error), error, error.__traceback__, ), ) return { "status": "escalated", "message": ( "The AI agent could not complete the operation. " "Human intervention is required." ), "error_type": type(error).__name__, } This distinction matters during a real incident. The agent might go down, but the engineering team should still be able to respond using the underlying workflows and runbooks. That is what graceful degradation looks like in practice. Step 6: Make high-risk actions human-gated One of the most useful patterns for enterprise agents is separating recommendation from execution . For example: Telemetry ↓ AI Agent ↓ Diagnosis ↓ Recommended Action ↓ Risk Check ↓ Human Approval ↓ Production Change The agent might recommend: “Increase the database connection pool.” But it shouldn’t push that change to production just because the model generated the recommendation. Here’s what a simple approval boundary looks like: Python def execute_action( action: str, approved_by: str | None, ) -> dict: if not approved_by: return { "status": "awaiting_approval", "action": action, } return { "status": "approved", "action": action, "approved_by": approved_by, } A real system needs a more sophisticated implementation, but the architectural boundary is what matters. “The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.” The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation. Step 7: Give the agent a health check A production agent needs a health endpoint just like any other service. With FastAPI: `Python import os import httpx from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, status app = FastAPI() SERVICE_NAME = "incident-command-agent" @app.get("/health/live") async def liveness(): """Check whether the application process is responsive.""" return { "status": "alive", "service": SERVICE_NAME, } async def check_provider() -> bool: """Check a configured provider health endpoint.""" health_url = os.getenv("MODEL_PROVIDER_HEALTH_URL") if not health_url: return False try: async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client: result = await client.get(health_url) return result.status_code == 200 except httpx.RequestError: return False @app.get("/health/ready") async def readiness(response: Response): """Check whether required dependencies are available.""" if not await check_provider(): response.status_code = ( status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE ) return { "status": "unhealthy", "reason": "Model provider unavailable", } return { "status": "ready", "service": SERVICE_NAME, } Liveness and readiness serve different purposes. The liveness endpoint confirms that the application process is responsive, while readiness checks whether the service can handle requests based on the availability of its required dependencies. In this example, the readiness endpoint checks a configured model-provider health URL and returns HTTP 503 when the check fails. The check is deliberately lightweight and time-limited to avoid introducing unnecessary delays or costs. In production, teams should adapt it to their provider’s supported health-check mechanism and other critical dependencies, such as a vector database or configuration service. Keeping these checks separate lets orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes distinguish between an application that needs restarting and one that can’t serve traffic temporarily. Step 8: Fail closed when safety controls break One of the worst failure modes is letting an agent keep running after its safety mechanisms go down. For example: Python def run_controlled_agent( tool_name: str, model, messages, budget: ExecutionBudget, ): try: authorize_tool(tool_name) # Reuse the budget across agent steps and tool calls. budget.check_step() budget.check_tool_call() return invoke_model( model, messages, ) except ToolAuthorizationError: logger.exception( "Agent authorisation check failed." ) return { "status": "blocked", "message": ( "The requested operation is not authorised." ), } except RuntimeError: logger.exception( "Agent execution budget exceeded." ) return { "status": "escalated", "message": ( "The agent exceeded its execution budget. " "Human investigation is required." ), } except Exception as exc: return handle_agent_failure(exc) Notice that different failures produce different outcomes. An authorisation failure should block the requested operation, while an exhausted execution budget should trigger escalation rather than another retry. A temporary model failure, meanwhile, should follow the system’s defined failure-handling policy. Another important detail: the execution budget must persist throughout the agent’s workflow. Creating a new budget for every invocation would reset its counters, allowing repeated calls to bypass the intended limits. Instead, create the budget once and pass it into each successive invocation, as shown below. Python # Create one budget for the entire agent workflow. budget = ExecutionBudget( max_steps=5, max_tools=8, ) # Reuse the same budget across successive invocations. for tool_name in planned_tools: result = run_controlled_agent( tool_name=tool_name, model=model, messages=messages, budget=budget, ) if isinstance(result, dict) and result.get( "status" ) in {"blocked", "escalated"}: break With the same budget shared across invocations, each counted step and tool call contributes to the workflow’s overall limit. Once that limit is reached, the agent stops rather than continuing with a fresh budget. These controls only work if they remain effective throughout execution, especially when an agent encounters repeated failures. Step 9: Define the 2 a.m. runbook This is where operational ownership becomes real. Suppose the agent starts failing at 2 a.m. The on-call engineer should be able to answer five questions quickly: Is the agent itself healthy? Is the model provider healthy? Are retrieval or tool dependencies failing? Has the agent exceeded its normal cost or latency envelope? What happens if we disable it? The last question matters most. Every production AI system should have a clear degradation path. For an incident-response agent, that might mean: AI Agent unavailable ↓ Incident still created ↓ Telemetry remains available ↓ Standard runbook activated ↓ Human engineer continues investigation The AI system should speed up operations, not become something the organisation can’t operate without. So, who owns the agent? The answer should never simply be: “The AI Team.” Production ownership needs to be explicit. Someone owns: deployment; infrastructure; model configuration; tool permissions; monitoring; incident response; cost; security; rollback; the decision to disable the agent. That doesn’t mean one person has to handle everything. It means everyone knows their role well enough that, when an incident hits, the team isn’t wasting time figuring out who should take charge. The real test of an AI agent The easiest time to operate an AI agent is during business hours when everything is working. The real test comes at 2 a.m. A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget that prevents runaway behaviour, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries that constrain what it can do, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it. The goal isn’t to take humans out of the loop. “A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.” It’s to make it clear where the agent’s responsibility ends and where a human needs to step in. Because when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., the question isn’t whether the model was smart enough. It’s whether the system was designed well enough that the person on call knows what happened, what the agent did, and what to do next.

A production agent needs an owner, boundaries, telemetry, failure policies, escalation paths, and a clear distinction between what the system may automate and what requires human intervention.

A production agent should not have a direct path from reasoning to action. Each tool invocation should pass through explicit controls, remain observable, and have a defined path to human intervention.

Here’s a practical way to build those controls.

Step 1: Treat the agent as a production service

An agent should have the same operational identity as any other production service.

Start by defining its ownership metadata.

Python
from pydantic import BaseModel


class AgentService(BaseModel):
    name: str
    owner_team: str
    service_tier: str
    escalation_channel: str


agent_service = AgentService(
    name="incident-command-agent",
    owner_team="platform-engineering",
    service_tier="critical",
    escalation_channel="#platform-oncall",
)

This may look simple, but it changes the conversation.

The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.

“The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.”

You can later attach the same metadata to logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and deployment records.

Step 2: Define what the agent is allowed to do

Ownership also means being clear about what an agent is allowed to do.

An agent that can only read telemetry carries far less risk than one that can restart production services, change infrastructure, or deploy code.

That’s why I prefer an explicit tool allowlist, which limits the agent to the actions you’ve deliberately granted it.

Python
ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "get_service_health",
    "get_recent_deployments",
    "search_runbooks",
    "summarize_incident",
}


class ToolAuthorizationError(Exception):
    """Raised when an agent attempts to use an unapproved tool."""


def authorize_tool(tool_name: str) -> None:
    if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:
        raise ToolAuthorizationError(
            f"Tool '{tool_name}' is not authorized."
        )

The guiding principle is deny by default.

Adding a new capability should be an intentional engineering decision, not something that happens because a tool became available to the agent.

For destructive operations, authorisation should be even stricter. A production restart or deployment should require authenticated human approval, not the agent’s own judgment.

Step 3: Put budgets around agent execution

An agent that can reason indefinitely is difficult to operate.

Every production workflow should have limits around execution time, model calls, tool calls, and ideally token consumption.

Python
import os


class ExecutionBudget:
    def __init__(
        self,
        max_steps: int | None = None,
        max_tools: int | None = None,
    ):
        self.steps = 0
        self.tool_calls = 0

        self.max_steps = (
            max_steps
            if max_steps is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_AGENT_STEPS", "5"))
        )

        self.max_tools = (
            max_tools
            if max_tools is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_TOOL_CALLS", "8"))
        )

        if self.max_steps <= 0 or self.max_tools <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Execution budget limits must be positive."
            )

    def check_step(self) -> None:
        if self.steps >= self.max_steps:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent step budget exceeded."
            )

        self.steps += 1

    def check_tool_call(self) -> None:
        if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tools:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent tool-call budget exceeded."
            )

        self.tool_calls += 1

Execution limits should be configurable rather than buried in application code. By passing these limits through the constructor, engineers can assign different budgets to different agents without changing global settings. A diagnostic agent might need only three steps, while a more complex research workflow may require considerably more. When no limits are supplied, the class falls back to environment variables. What matters is that every workflow has a defined ceiling, and that the same budget is enforced throughout its execution.

Step 4: Make model calls observable

An owner cannot operate what they cannot see.

At minimum, record:

  • request latency;
  • model used;
  • success/failure;
  • tool calls;
  • token usage where available;
  • correlation or request ID;
  • escalation events.

A simple wrapper provides a useful boundary.

Python
import logging
import time
import uuid

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def invoke_model(model, messages):
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    started = time.perf_counter()

    # Extract the model name across different provider libraries.
    model_name = (
        getattr(model, "model_name", None)
        or getattr(model, "model", None)
        or "unknown_model"
    )

    try:
        response = model.invoke(messages)

        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started

        logger.info(
            "agent_model_call_success",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )

        return response

    except Exception:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started

        logger.exception(
            "agent_model_call_failed",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )

        raise

The request ID becomes especially valuable when an incident involves several services.

An engineer should be able to move from an alert to the agent request and then to the underlying model and tool calls.

In production, supplement this logging layer with distributed tracing and metrics for a more complete view of system behaviour and performance.

Step 5: Separate failure from escalation

A failed model call does not necessarily mean the entire service should fail.

Likewise, a successful model call does not mean the agent’s recommendation should execute automatically.

These are different decisions.

Python
def handle_agent_failure(error: Exception) -> dict:
    logger.error(
        "Agent execution failed; escalating to human.",
        exc_info=(
            type(error),
            error,
            error.__traceback__,
        ),
    )

    return {
        "status": "escalated",
        "message": (
            "The AI agent could not complete the operation. "
            "Human intervention is required."
        ),
        "error_type": type(error).__name__,
    }

This distinction matters during a real incident.

The agent might go down, but the engineering team should still be able to respond using the underlying workflows and runbooks. That is what graceful degradation looks like in practice.

Step 6: Make high-risk actions human-gated

One of the most useful patterns for enterprise agents is separating recommendation from execution.

For example:

Telemetry
    ↓
AI Agent
    ↓
Diagnosis
    ↓
Recommended Action
    ↓
Risk Check
    ↓
Human Approval
    ↓
Production Change

The agent might recommend:

	“Increase the database connection pool.”

But it shouldn’t push that change to production just because the model generated the recommendation.

Here’s what a simple approval boundary looks like:

Python
def execute_action(
    action: str,
    approved_by: str | None,
) -> dict:
    if not approved_by:
        return {
            "status": "awaiting_approval",
            "action": action,
        }

    return {
        "status": "approved",
        "action": action,
        "approved_by": approved_by,
    }

A real system needs a more sophisticated implementation, but the architectural boundary is what matters.

“The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.”

The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.

Step 7: Give the agent a health check

A production agent needs a health endpoint just like any other service.

With FastAPI:

`Python
import os

import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, status

app = FastAPI()

SERVICE_NAME = "incident-command-agent"


@app.get("/health/live")
async def liveness():
    """Check whether the application process is responsive."""
    return {
        "status": "alive",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }


async def check_provider() -> bool:
    """Check a configured provider health endpoint."""
    health_url = os.getenv("MODEL_PROVIDER_HEALTH_URL")

    if not health_url:
        return False

    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
            result = await client.get(health_url)
            return result.status_code == 200
    except httpx.RequestError:
        return False


@app.get("/health/ready")
async def readiness(response: Response):
    """Check whether required dependencies are available."""
    if not await check_provider():
        response.status_code = (
            status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
        )
        return {
            "status": "unhealthy",
            "reason": "Model provider unavailable",
        }

    return {
        "status": "ready",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }

Liveness and readiness serve different purposes. The liveness endpoint confirms that the application process is responsive, while readiness checks whether the service can handle requests based on the availability of its required dependencies.

In this example, the readiness endpoint checks a configured model-provider health URL and returns HTTP 503 when the check fails. The check is deliberately lightweight and time-limited to avoid introducing unnecessary delays or costs. In production, teams should adapt it to their provider’s supported health-check mechanism and other critical dependencies, such as a vector database or configuration service.

Keeping these checks separate lets orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes distinguish between an application that needs restarting and one that can’t serve traffic temporarily.

Step 8: Fail closed when safety controls break

One of the worst failure modes is letting an agent keep running after its safety mechanisms go down.

For example:

Python
def run_controlled_agent(
    tool_name: str,
    model,
    messages,
    budget: ExecutionBudget,
):
    try:
        authorize_tool(tool_name)

        # Reuse the budget across agent steps and tool calls.
        budget.check_step()
        budget.check_tool_call()

        return invoke_model(
            model,
            messages,
        )

    except ToolAuthorizationError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent authorisation check failed."
        )

        return {
            "status": "blocked",
            "message": (
                "The requested operation is not authorised."
            ),
        }

    except RuntimeError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent execution budget exceeded."
        )

        return {
            "status": "escalated",
            "message": (
                "The agent exceeded its execution budget. "
                "Human investigation is required."
            ),
        }

    except Exception as exc:
        return handle_agent_failure(exc)

Notice that different failures produce different outcomes. An authorisation failure should block the requested operation, while an exhausted execution budget should trigger escalation rather than another retry. A temporary model failure, meanwhile, should follow the system’s defined failure-handling policy.

Another important detail: the execution budget must persist throughout the agent’s workflow. Creating a new budget for every invocation would reset its counters, allowing repeated calls to bypass the intended limits. Instead, create the budget once and pass it into each successive invocation, as shown below.

Python
# Create one budget for the entire agent workflow.
budget = ExecutionBudget(
    max_steps=5,
    max_tools=8,
)

# Reuse the same budget across successive invocations.
for tool_name in planned_tools:
    result = run_controlled_agent(
        tool_name=tool_name,
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        budget=budget,
    )

    if isinstance(result, dict) and result.get(
        "status"
    ) in {"blocked", "escalated"}:
        break

With the same budget shared across invocations, each counted step and tool call contributes to the workflow’s overall limit. Once that limit is reached, the agent stops rather than continuing with a fresh budget. These controls only work if they remain effective throughout execution, especially when an agent encounters repeated failures.

Step 9: Define the 2 a.m. runbook

This is where operational ownership becomes real.

Suppose the agent starts failing at 2 a.m.

The on-call engineer should be able to answer five questions quickly:

  1. Is the agent itself healthy?
  2. Is the model provider healthy?
  3. Are retrieval or tool dependencies failing?
  4. Has the agent exceeded its normal cost or latency envelope?
  5. What happens if we disable it?

The last question matters most.

Every production AI system should have a clear degradation path.

For an incident-response agent, that might mean:

AI Agent unavailable
        ↓
Incident still created
        ↓
Telemetry remains available
        ↓
Standard runbook activated
        ↓
Human engineer continues investigation

The AI system should speed up operations, not become something the organisation can’t operate without.

So, who owns the agent?

The answer should never simply be:

	“The AI Team.”

Production ownership needs to be explicit.

Someone owns:

  • deployment;
  • infrastructure;
  • model configuration;
  • tool permissions;
  • monitoring;
  • incident response;
  • cost;
  • security;
  • rollback;
  • the decision to disable the agent.

That doesn’t mean one person has to handle everything. It means everyone knows their role well enough that, when an incident hits, the team isn’t wasting time figuring out who should take charge.

The real test of an AI agent

The easiest time to operate an AI agent is during business hours when everything is working. 

The real test comes at 2 a.m. 

A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget that prevents runaway behaviour, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries that constrain what it can do, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.

The goal isn’t to take humans out of the loop.

“A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.”

It’s to make it clear where the agent’s responsibility ends and where a human needs to step in.

Because when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., the question isn’t whether the model was smart enough.

It’s whether the system was designed well enough that the person on call knows what happened, what the agent did, and what to do next.

items.title: Space Force scrambles as Elon Musk's SpaceX retires its major rocket
items.summary: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket returns at Cape Canaveral, Florida, after launching a Crew Dragon capsule into orbit on October 1, 2026. Marco Bello / AFP via Getty Images SpaceX is phasing out its popular Falcon 9 rocket in favor of its much larger Starship rocket. That presents a headache for the US Space Force, POLITICO reports . The Space Force has said it's open to eventually using SpaceX's Starship. But there are engineering challenges to overcome. SpaceX's plans to retire its most popular rocket could jeopardize the United States' ability to launch military satellites — a plight compounded by the Pentagon's dependence on Elon Musk's company. SpaceX is by far the dominant player in the rocket business and indispensable to the military, dwarfing competitors and accounting for 85% of US launches in 2025. The company is phasing out its Falcon 9 rocket to make way for Starship, a massive new vehicle that SpaceX says will be more efficient and profitable, but which many military satellites aren't designed to fit. The situation leaves the Space Force in a launch crunch that could affect the military's ability to put its advanced satellites in orbit — and on time. The Pentagon has few alternatives to ferry its equipment, and SpaceX's competitors are likely years away from being able to offer comparable services, reports POLITICO, which — like Business Insider — is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. "Everybody's having problems, so the Space Force is freaking out a little bit about launch," one former Space Force official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive issue. It also highlights the scale of Musk's company's footprint and the way its business decisions can affect the security of countries including the United States. From the battlefield in Ukraine, where Kyiv is dependent on his Starlink satellite internet service, to cutting-edge artificial intelligence and SpaceX's stranglehold over the pathways to orbit, the world's first trillionaire has a direct hand in the technology that will shape the future. The Space Force recently tried to book rides for three future satellite missions, but SpaceX declined to offer its services, according to two people familiar with the missions. No other rocket companies offered to take them either, the people said. A top official at the Space Force downplayed the problem about finding rockets to launch military satellites. "I wouldn't say there [are] missions I'm worried about being able to fly; I would say we're working through the right way to support those customers," said Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the Space Force's acting portfolio acquisition executive for space access. But Zarybnisky acknowledged growing pains for the government and space industry as demand for rockets increases. "Temporarily, there are some things we'll need to work through, again, as we get new providers flying," he said. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The three Space Force missions that didn't find a ride were listed through the National Security Space Launch initiative, or NSSL — the program the service uses to buy rocket launches for its satellites. Two of the missions were for the Space Development Agency, according to the people. The agency is a branch of the Space Force that's building a network of hundreds of military satellites in low-Earth orbit to provide expanded data services, and missile warning and tracking capabilities. Details about the third Space Force mission or the precise date for when the Space Force hoped to launch the missions are unclear. The Space Force has set up a two-lane system for buying its launches, one for less demanding efforts and another for more challenging missions. The hope was that new competitors, such as Rocket Lab, Stoke Space and Relativity, would have an easier time winning contracts for the lower-risk missions. But SpaceX has dominated both lanes with its Falcon rocket, and other providers have been slow to scale up. The Space Force hopes to use two large rockets from SpaceX competitors to ferry key military satellites into orbit: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan and Blue Origin's New Glenn. But the Vulcan rocket has struggled to launch consistently and was grounded earlier this year after problems with its solid rocket boosters. Space Force officials have been frustrated by ULA's delays and have moved missions slated for a Vulcan to a SpaceX Falcon. Meanwhile, Blue Origin's New Glenn program had a devastating setback in May when a rocket exploded on the company's only launchpad in Florida — putting the rocket out of commission likely until next year. The Space Force has said it's open to eventually using SpaceX's Starship. But there are engineering challenges to overcome because Starship is designed for "flat stack" satellites such as Starlink, while most military satellites are designed for a larger cargo bay. And it's unclear when SpaceX will have the capacity to meet the Pentagon's needs, given its plans to use Starship to build out orbital data-centers and other company priorities. Other newer companies may have some solutions. Stoke Space, Relativity and Rocket Lab are all working on medium-lift rockets that could help meet the military's needs. But none of those companies has flown successful test flights of their new vehicles, meaning it could take years for them to start launching reliably and frequently. Zarybnisky remained optimistic that Blue Origin and ULA will work through their technical problems and that new competitors will get up and running in time. "We're excited to see where those new providers come on board and are able to support the national security base launches that we need," he said. It's not just the Pentagon feeling the pinch. The move to decommission the Falcon 9 rocket and focus on Starship has sent the entire space industry into panic — especially commercial satellite builders. Some of those firms have been unable to secure Falcon 9 flights after 2028 . The Space Force didn't disclose a set date for when it will fly its last Falcon mission, but Zarybnisky said the service is "actively talking to SpaceX and understanding where the spacecraft programs are, where they are in their build and test cycle. The end date will really be driven by the spacecraft customers that we have launch service contracts for already." It's unclear what happens after the Space Force runs through that batch of missions. An industry representative warned that the service is unprepared to deal with the crisis coming its way as demand for rockets increases across the space industry. New rocket companies can't bid on a Space Force launch until they've demonstrated the ability to successfully fly, part of an effort to keep vaporware companies from winning government business. But commercial satellite companies are not restricted in the same way and have been buying up early launches on rockets that haven't even flown yet. This puts more pressure on the Space Force to find future launches. The launch crunch "probably requires the Space Force to get creative and figure out a way to start buying capacity now before it's too late," the representative said. Another person familiar with the issue said that Space Force officials need to work with Congress to "fundamentally rethink" how the military acquires launch. "The Space Force needs to be allowed to reserve multiple launches at a time, much further out into the 2030s, for vehicles that have yet to fly," the person said. "Yes, it's taking on more risk … [but] if it waits for new rockets to prove themselves, it may find they're already sold out." This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms. items.title: Recursive shows first result of its AI-driven research process with Flint
items.summary: The AI startup Recursive is unveiling Flint, its first language model, a 40-billion-parameter MoE for local coding developed by former DeepMind researchers. It was created in four months using the company's in-house AI system, "Eureka Machine," which independently tests and optimizes architectures. Recursive has yet to prove whether this approach will actually lead to self-improving AI. The article Recursive shows first result of its AI-driven research process with Flint appeared first on The Decoder .

items.title: Billionaires fleeing California's wealth tax could cost the state more than the levy makes, Stanford economists say
items.summary: A Stanford paper warns that California could lose more in future income taxes than it would raise from a one-time billionaire tax. Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images Several billionaires have left or plan to leave California over its proposed wealth tax. The departures could mean that the state loses more in the long term than the one-time tax brings in. That's according to a working paper shared by a pair of Stanford economists. Supporters of California’s proposed billionaire tax say it could raise about $100 billion. But a new paper puts the takings closer to $30 billion and warns that the state could ultimately lose money if its richest residents flee. Proposition 40, which goes before voters on November 3, would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, with their wealth valued at the end of the year. Most of the tax proceeds would go toward healthcare. In a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper released this week, Stanford economists Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh estimate the tax would collect between $28 billion and $36 billion — far short of supporters' $100 billion projection. They point to billionaires moving away before the residency cutoff. Their estimate also assumes legal challenges could prevent California from collecting some of the remaining tax. The authors identified seven billionaires reported to have left the state before the cutoff: Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, investor Peter Thiel, director Steven Spielberg, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, investor David Sacks, and car loan tycoon Don Hankey. Together, they accounted for nearly 30% of the wealth the researchers considered potentially taxable. The researchers noted that moving out of the state does not, by itself, settle someone's tax residency. The authors' bigger concern is what happens afterward. California would collect the wealth tax only once, but billionaires who leave could stop paying state income taxes year after year. If those departures and lost payments last, their model projects an average net loss of $38.9 billion. The researchers said they ran 100,000 simulations, and that in 85% of scenarios, losses outweighed revenues from the tax. The forecast depends on who actually left and whether they stay away. California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office offers a less stark view. It expects tens of billions in tax revenue and a possible ongoing drop of less than $1 billion a year in billionaire income-tax payments. Brin is fighting the proposal on another front, too. He has given at least $102 million to Building a Better California, a group backing efforts to defeat or block Proposition 40. Two competing measures on the same ballot could keep Proposition 40 from taking effect, even if voters approve it. While some billionaires have been vocal in their opposition to the tax, some have welcomed it. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CBS News last month that being able to pay an estimated $8 billion over five years would be a "privilege." In filings released this week, it was revealed that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had considered moving out of California due to the tax, but ultimately decided to stay. To ensure that Zuckerberg has sufficient liquidity to pay without diluting his control of the company, Meta created a new class of shares. Many economists back the plans. Six Nobel Prize winners — Daron Acemoglu, Abhijit Banerjee, Peter Diamond, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman, and Joseph Stiglitz — signed a letter in September calling the proposal the "first opportunity for the people to start reining in the power of billionaires." At the time, Acemoglu said it could counter years of tax avoidance by the very wealthy and curb their political influence. He said that while the proposal isn’t perfect, it "deserves support." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them
items.summary: One of the biggest security scares to hit the web is causing widespread disruption, prompting businesses, hospitals, schools, and government agencies to temporarily shut down websites and online services as they scramble to protect themselves against two critical vulnerabilities in PHP , the programming language underpinning much of the internet. The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell , could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers. Major technology companies have been racing to protect users, with Cloudflare deploying firewall protections and Automattic confirming that websites hosted across its platforms, including WordPress.com, WordPress VIP and Tumblr, have been secured. The Wikimedia Foundation, meanwhile, took several supporting services offline until they can be patched. The PHP project released emergency fixes on Wednesday for versions 8.2 through 8.5. Older versions are no longer officially supported, although some distributions and vendors provide legacy fixes, and PHP has published limited patches for versions 7.4 through 8.1. But while the PHP vulnerabilities are a major deal in their own right, the circumstances surrounding their discovery, remediation, and disclosure offer a revealing glimpse into the growing pressures facing the open-source community, as AI makes it easier to uncover serious security flaws. “Find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”: Prompt discovery News of the impending patches emerged on Tuesday , after details leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The following day, OpenAI revealed that security firm Calif had discovered one of the flaws using its GPT-5.6 Sol model , while Google-owned Wiz had independently identified both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said it spent two months coordinating a response involving PHP maintainers, the security researchers, Cloudflare, and government cybersecurity agencies, as part of its Patch the Planet initiative . The effort was disrupted when software supply-chain security company Chainguard released patched PHP container images more than six hours before the agreed time. CEO Dan Lorenc acknowledged on LinkedIn that he made the call, noting that Chainguard had independently rediscovered the flaw using a frontier AI model and the simple prompt “ find bad vulnerabilities in PHP “. Lorenc defended the decision by pointing to reports of attacks and the ease of reproducing the vulnerability. The PHP Foundation, for its part, argued that the early release could help attackers while other vendors were still preparing their patches. “This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the Foundation notes . Nils Adermann , a PHP Foundation board member and creator and co-maintainer of Composer , says that “there were no confirmed exploits,” adding that any identified activity was merely people attempting exploits. “The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional.” “There was a clear embargo until the time of disclosure and public release, that was discussed and evaluated repeatedly as information arrived, weighing the risk of exploitation vs protection from publishing patches without complete updates,” Adermann writes in response to Lorenc’s post. “The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional. The proper thing to do here is apologize, not to justify your clear misbehavior.” The new normal The PHP pandemonium highlights a larger concern, however: AI is making it easier to find security flaws, faster than the people responsible for fixing them can respond. And as Lorenc himself put it: “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry.” Just a day before OpenAI’s disclosure, Anthropic published research showing that Claude had identified 493 security issues across 25 open-source projects encompassing more than five million lines of code. One configuration flaw had gone unnoticed for 21 years, and had the potential to disable an authentication requirement, allowing unauthorised clients to reach a supposedly restricted server. While not all of Anthropic’s findings were exploitable vulnerabilities, they underline a growing problem: AI can uncover security weaknesses at scale, but assessing them and developing reliable fixes still takes time and expertise. Christopher Robinson , CTO of Akrites and CTO / chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation ( OpenSSF ), says the PHP emergency is also a reminder of the importance of being ready to respond when serious vulnerabilities do emerge. “The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen.” “The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen,” Robinson tells The New Stack . “Having a vulnerability management process and understanding who can assist when issues become too complex are the best things that both open source projects and commercial entities can do.” When finding bugs becomes easier than fixing them For Michelle Tilley , software engineer and CTO of Atuin , an open-source developer tool with more than 32,000 GitHub stars , the kind of emergency response mounted for PHP would be difficult to replicate for smaller open-source projects. “The response here looked like a vendor emergency, with a coalition, government agencies, and WAF (web application firewall) rules,” Tilley tells The New Stack . “This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.” “This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.” Atuin itself is already receiving more AI-generated bug reports and pull requests, Tilley says. While her company has enough engineering resources to handle them, many smaller projects depend on unpaid maintainers working in their spare time, who can become overwhelmed and walk away. “These developers can, and do, burn out,” Tilley continues. “Sometimes they arrange for someone else to take over the project; often, they simply stop working on it, and downstream consumers never know. That’s how projects end up with vulnerabilities that will never be patched.” Ultimately, she wants more responsibility to fall on researchers and businesses that rely on the code. “There’s no single fix, but the direction is clear,” Tilley says. “The cost of remediation has to move toward the people finding the bugs and the companies depending on the code.” That pressure extends to larger projects, too. Madelyn Olson , an AWS principal engineer and maintainer of the Valkey database, says that it too is finding and fixing far more security bugs this year than before. “The hardest part has shifted from finding bugs to fixing them,” Olson tells The New Stack . “PHP is a good example.” A PHP developer first identified the underlying problem behind one of this week’s vulnerabilities while fixing an issue uncovered during a 2024 security audit , which was organised by the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund ( OSTIF ). However, attempts to resolve it stalled because proposed fixes risked breaking compatibility, affecting performance or disrupting third-party extensions. Few engineers had the expertise to resolve those trade-offs, according to the PHP Foundation. “AI is getting very good at finding bugs,” Olson says. “Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.” “AI is getting very good at finding bugs. Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.” To manage the influx, Valkey is narrowing its definition of a security vulnerability, using AI to inspect its own code, and making backports and releases easier to produce. The Chainguard brouhaha also raises the question of whether disclosure timelines need to change. Olson recalls three researchers independently reporting the same Valkey bug in one week, each using LLMs. Valkey is now working toward shorter embargoes — although that is a different matter from breaking an agreed release date. “If you found a bug with an LLM, it’s safe to say someone else can find it too,” Olson says. “That argues for shorter embargoes and faster releases, and Valkey is working toward shorter embargoes now, which is a trend we’re seeing across most large projects.” A growing security backlog Derek Zimmer , executive director of OSTIF, said the volume of both legitimate discoveries and poor-quality reports is creating backlogs, with maintainers spending scarce engineering time just establishing which issues are real. “Maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage.” “The reality in 2026 is that finding serious bugs is easier than ever, and maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage,” Zimmer tells The New Stack . To help, OSTIF is trialling initiatives such as Project V-LAT , which embeds engineers in projects to review findings and develop fixes, while helping maintainers improve how reports are processed. Robinson also emphasises the need for shared security expertise and dedicated engineers who can support upstream projects. He rejects the suggestion that exposing more flaws necessarily makes open source less secure, pointing to the opportunity for companies that depend on the code to contribute fixes. Yet, many projects have neither the money nor the expertise to respond independently. “Most upstream maintainers are also acting as volunteers within the projects, with little to no budget, infrastructure, or supporting tools,” Robinson says. “There will be no ‘one size fits all’ approach here, we’ll need to approach this situation using multiple, parallel approaches to get the broadest chance for successful outcomes.”

A PHP developer first identified the underlying problem behind one of this week’s vulnerabilities while fixing an issue uncovered during a 2024 security audit, which was organised by the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF). However, attempts to resolve it stalled because proposed fixes risked breaking compatibility, affecting performance or disrupting third-party extensions. Few engineers had the expertise to resolve those trade-offs, according to the PHP Foundation.

“AI is getting very good at finding bugs,” Olson says. “Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”

“AI is getting very good at finding bugs. Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”

To manage the influx, Valkey is narrowing its definition of a security vulnerability, using AI to inspect its own code, and making backports and releases easier to produce.

The Chainguard brouhaha also raises the question of whether disclosure timelines need to change. Olson recalls three researchers independently reporting the same Valkey bug in one week, each using LLMs. Valkey is now working toward shorter embargoes — although that is a different matter from breaking an agreed release date.

“If you found a bug with an LLM, it’s safe to say someone else can find it too,” Olson says. “That argues for shorter embargoes and faster releases, and Valkey is working toward shorter embargoes now, which is a trend we’re seeing across most large projects.”

A growing security backlog

Derek Zimmer, executive director of OSTIF, said the volume of both legitimate discoveries and poor-quality reports is creating backlogs, with maintainers spending scarce engineering time just establishing which issues are real.

“Maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage.”

“The reality in 2026 is that finding serious bugs is easier than ever, and maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage,” Zimmer tells The New Stack.

To help, OSTIF is trialling initiatives such as Project V-LAT, which embeds engineers in projects to review findings and develop fixes, while helping maintainers improve how reports are processed.

Robinson also emphasises the need for shared security expertise and dedicated engineers who can support upstream projects. He rejects the suggestion that exposing more flaws necessarily makes open source less secure, pointing to the opportunity for companies that depend on the code to contribute fixes. Yet, many projects have neither the money nor the expertise to respond independently.

“Most upstream maintainers are also acting as volunteers within the projects, with little to no budget, infrastructure, or supporting tools,” Robinson says. “There will be no ‘one size fits all’ approach here, we’ll need to approach this situation using multiple, parallel approaches to get the broadest chance for successful outcomes.”
