items.title: Migrating from Databricks to Fabric: When to Move and When Not To
items.summary: Databricks to Fabric migration makes sense when Microsoft Fabric better fits your analytics operating model, Microsoft ecosystem, and reporting needs. However, Databricks remains suitable for advanced data engineering, machine learning, and specialized workloads. The right choice in the Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks comparison depends on technical requirements, costs, and business goals. Organizations can also adopt a hybrid approach. Organizations with established Databricks workloads must evaluate whether Microsoft Fabric better supports their evolving analytics needs. Platform consolidation, Power BI integration, operating complexity, and workload requirements influence this decision. This guide examines Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks to help organizations choose migration, coexistence, or continued investment in Databricks. Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: What Actually Changes? Platform architecture and operating model Microsoft Fabric is a SaaS analytics platform that combines data integration, engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, and Power BI. Its services share a common environment, reducing the need to manage separate analytics tools. Microsoft Fabric OneLake provides a unified logical data lake for storing and accessing organizational data. Databricks is a data and AI platform built on lakehouse architecture. It supports Spark-based processing, SQL analytics, data engineering, and machine learning. Its capabilities suit organizations building customized data pipelines and advanced AI workloads. The key difference in Databricks vs Microsoft Fabric architecture is the operating model. Fabric emphasizes integrated analytics within Microsoft’s cloud ecosystem. Databricks offers broader architectural flexibility across supported cloud providers. Storage, processing, and governance OneLake and Delta Lake serve different purposes. OneLake is Fabric’s logical data lake, while Delta Lake is a storage layer and table format supporting reliable data operations. Both platforms support Delta Lake, but feature compatibility does not guarantee identical APIs, optimizations, or behavior. Fabric integrates governance capabilities across its environment. Databricks uses Unity Catalog for centralized governance of data and AI assets. Both support access controls and data management, but their configurations and integrations differ. Migration therefore involves more than transferring data. Teams must assess compute behavior, permissions, governance policies, and workload dependencies. Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: Key Differences Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks The practical choice depends on existing investments, workload requirements, and team expertise. Fabric can simplify analytics integration for Microsoft-oriented organizations. When Does Migrating from Databricks to Fabric Make Sense? Your organization depends heavily on Power BI Microsoft Fabric and Power BI integration can simplify the path from data preparation to business reporting. Teams can build pipelines, prepare data, and develop semantic models within one environment. Direct Lake can enable Power BI to access supported OneLake data without traditional import duplication, depending on configuration and architecture. You want fewer separate analytics services Microsoft Fabric migration may reduce integration overhead when ingestion, transformation, warehousing, and reporting currently span multiple services. However, the benefits depend on your existing architecture and which services Fabric can replace. Your team prefers an integrated SaaS operating model Fabric offers standardized administration, shared data access, and integrated analytics capabilities. This approach may suit teams seeking fewer independently managed platform components and simpler operational workflows. Your cost analysis supports the move Evaluate Microsoft Fabric cost using actual workload performance, licensing, capacity utilization, engineering effort, and ongoing operations. Pricing alone cannot establish savings. Benchmark representative workloads before committing. Reader takeaway: Migration deserves serious evaluation when Fabric solves a specific operational problem, improves reporting workflows, or reduces measurable complexity. Microsoft Fabric benefits matter most when they align with business priorities and technical requirements. Databricks can remain valuable when teams need specialized processing, machine learning workflows, or multi-cloud flexibility. Neither platform removes the need to evaluate governance, performance, and compatibility before migration. When Should You NOT Migrate from Databricks to Fabric? Your workloads rely on advanced Spark engineering Databricks may remain the better fit for complex Spark pipelines, specialized runtime configurations, custom libraries, and workload-specific optimizations. Moving these workloads may require code changes, compatibility testing, or architectural redesign. Assess whether Fabric can meet existing performance and processing requirements before migrating. Machine learning is central to your platform Established model-training pipelines, feature engineering, experiment tracking, model lifecycle management, and deployment dependencies deserve careful evaluation. Compare each requirement against current Fabric capabilities. Avoid migration if critical workflows cannot transfer without unacceptable compromises. You need cloud flexibility Organizations operating across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud may value Databricks’ multicloud deployment options. Cloud strategy, data residency requirements, and existing infrastructure investments can make migration less attractive. Migration risk exceeds the expected benefit Regulated workloads, critical production dependencies, complex orchestration, strict service-level objectives, and limited engineering capacity can increase migration risks. Rebuilding pipelines or changing governance controls may introduce operational disruption. The Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks decision should reflect measurable business needs, not platform availability alone. Teams should estimate migration effort, validate compatibility, and test representative workloads before committing. Decision rule: If Databricks already meets your performance, governance, and cost requirements, do not migrate simply because Fabric is available. Retaining a proven platform can be more practical than introducing unnecessary change. Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: Cost, Performance, and Architecture Compare total cost of ownership The Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks cost comparison should consider total cost of ownership (TCO), not headline pricing alone. Fabric: Assess capacity pricing, licensing requirements, utilization, and existing Power BI entitlements. Databricks: Include compute, cloud storage, networking, and associated infrastructure costs. Migration: Account for engineering, testing, staff training, and parallel-running expenses. Operations: Evaluate idle capacity, workload concurrency, and unpredictable processing demand. Existing investments can significantly influence the financial outcome. Model both platforms using equivalent workloads and measured consumption before estimating potential savings. Benchmark performance before deciding Microsoft Fabric performance and Databricks performance depend on workload characteristics, configuration, and resource allocation. Compare representative SQL queries, Spark jobs, data refreshes, concurrency, and latency requirements. Include routine operations and peak workloads. Measure execution times, resource consumption, reliability, and scaling behavior under realistic conditions. Test data volumes and query patterns that reflect production requirements. Architecture also affects results. Fabric’s integrated environment may simplify data access and reporting workflows. Databricks may better suit workloads requiring specialized Spark configurations or advanced engineering controls. Decision rule: Choose the platform that meets performance and reliability requirements at an acceptable total operating cost. Validate the results through controlled benchmarks rather than pricing assumptions or isolated performance tests. How to Migrate from Databricks to Microsoft Fabric? A successful Databricks to Fabric migration requires workload assessment, compatibility checks, data planning, and controlled deployment. Moving Delta tables or importing notebooks alone will not reproduce an existing production environment. Follow a phased approach to manage dependencies, validate results, and reduce operational risk. Step 1: Inventory existing Databricks workloads Document notebooks, jobs, Delta tables, streaming pipelines, external dependencies, Unity Catalog permissions, custom libraries, and downstream consumers. Record business criticality, data volumes, refresh schedules, recovery requirements, and service-level objectives. This inventory establishes migration scope and identifies workloads requiring additional testing. Step 2: Assess compatibility and choose a migration pattern Classify workloads into four groups: Limited changes: Workloads compatible with Fabric after basic configuration. Refactoring required: Workloads needing code changes or architectural redesign. Retain on Databricks: Workloads dependent on specialized capabilities. Hybrid deployment: Workloads benefiting from both platforms. Check Databricks-specific utilities, APIs, runtime settings, custom libraries, and governance policies before selecting a migration path. Step 3: Plan data access and movement Choose the appropriate data strategy for each workload. OneLake shortcuts: Reference supported external data without copying underlying files. Unity Catalog integration: Evaluate metadata mirroring and shortcut-based access for supported configurations. Data movement: Use ingestion pipelines or other supported methods when replication, transformation, or destination requirements demand it. These options have limitations. Not every Unity Catalog object, security policy, or table format transfers seamlessly. Verify supported configurations, permissions, and access requirements before implementation. Step 4: Rebuild and validate workloads Port compatible notebooks and orchestration into the selected Fabric services. Replace unsupported dependencies and configure libraries, secrets, identities, and permissions. Validate output accuracy, performance, failure recovery, and costs against the existing Databricks environment. Test representative workloads before production deployment. Step 5: Run a controlled cutover Run both platforms in parallel where appropriate, comparing results and operational behavior. Define rollback criteria, communicate downtime requirements, and prepare production consumers for the transition. Switch workloads only after validation and stakeholder approval. Implementation consideration: Microsoft Fabric implementation services can help assess dependencies, plan migration patterns, and validate workloads. However, teams should retain clear ownership of architecture decisions, acceptance criteria, and production readiness. Should You Migrate, Stay, or Use Both? The right choice in the Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks decision depends on workload requirements, existing investments, and measurable business benefits. Databricks and Fabric integration can support coexistence when teams need specialized engineering alongside integrated reporting. However, a hybrid model introduces additional governance, monitoring, and operational considerations. These recommendations are starting points, not universal rules. Before committing, validate workload compatibility, security, governance, performance, total costs, and team readiness. Choose the approach that solves actual business problems without introducing unnecessary complexity. Conclusion: Make the Decision Based on Workloads A successful Databricks to Fabric migration starts with measurable business value, not platform popularity. Assess existing workloads and run a representative pilot before committing. Migrate only workloads that meet compatibility, governance, and performance requirements. For organizations evaluating their options, Microsoft Fabric implementation services can help assess architecture, plan migration, and validate outcomes, supporting informed decisions without unnecessary disruption or unsupported performance expectations. Frequently asked questions Is Microsoft Fabric better than Databricks? Neither platform is universally better. Fabric integrates data engineering, warehousing, analytics, and Power BI. Databricks can suit organizations with demanding Spark engineering, data science, and machine learning requirements. The right choice depends on workloads. Can you migrate Databricks notebooks to Microsoft Fabric? Some notebook code can be reused, but compatibility is not guaranteed. Databricks-specific utilities, libraries, configurations, and APIs may require changes. Test migrated notebooks and their dependencies before production deployment. Does Microsoft Fabric support Delta Lake? Yes. Fabric uses Delta Lake as its standard analytics table format. However, supported features and behavior can differ across engines. Validate advanced Delta Lake features before migrating dependent workloads. Can Microsoft Fabric access Databricks data without copying it? Yes, supported Unity Catalog data can be accessed through metadata mirroring and OneLake shortcuts. However, supported table formats, security behavior, and other limitations must be checked before implementation. Should an organization run Databricks and Fabric together? Yes, where each platform serves a distinct purpose. For example, Databricks may handle specialized engineering while Fabric supports reporting. Evaluate governance, access controls, operating costs, and duplicated processing before adopting both. Migrating from Databricks to Fabric: When to Move and When Not To was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Databricks to Fabric migration makes sense when Microsoft Fabric better fits your analytics operating model, Microsoft ecosystem, and reporting needs. However, Databricks remains suitable for advanced data engineering, machine learning, and specialized workloads. The right choice in the Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks comparison depends on technical requirements, costs, and business goals. Organizations can also adopt a hybrid approach.

Organizations with established Databricks workloads must evaluate whether Microsoft Fabric better supports their evolving analytics needs. Platform consolidation, Power BI integration, operating complexity, and workload requirements influence this decision. This guide examines Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks to help organizations choose migration, coexistence, or continued investment in Databricks.

Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: What Actually Changes?Platform architecture and operating model

Microsoft Fabric is a SaaS analytics platform that combines data integration, engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, and Power BI. Its services share a common environment, reducing the need to manage separate analytics tools. Microsoft Fabric OneLake provides a unified logical data lake for storing and accessing organizational data.

Databricks is a data and AI platform built on lakehouse architecture. It supports Spark-based processing, SQL analytics, data engineering, and machine learning. Its capabilities suit organizations building customized data pipelines and advanced AI workloads.

The key difference in Databricks vs Microsoft Fabric architecture is the operating model. Fabric emphasizes integrated analytics within Microsoft’s cloud ecosystem. Databricks offers broader architectural flexibility across supported cloud providers.

Storage, processing, and governance

OneLake and Delta Lake serve different purposes. OneLake is Fabric’s logical data lake, while Delta Lake is a storage layer and table format supporting reliable data operations. Both platforms support Delta Lake, but feature compatibility does not guarantee identical APIs, optimizations, or behavior.

Fabric integrates governance capabilities across its environment. Databricks uses Unity Catalog for centralized governance of data and AI assets. Both support access controls and data management, but their configurations and integrations differ.

Migration therefore involves more than transferring data. Teams must assess compute behavior, permissions, governance policies, and workload dependencies.

Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: Key DifferencesMicrosoft Fabric vs Databricks
The practical choice depends on existing investments, workload requirements, and team expertise. Fabric can simplify analytics integration for Microsoft-oriented organizations.
When Does Migrating from Databricks to Fabric Make Sense?Your organization depends heavily on Power BI

Microsoft Fabric and Power BI integration can simplify the path from data preparation to business reporting. Teams can build pipelines, prepare data, and develop semantic models within one environment. Direct Lake can enable Power BI to access supported OneLake data without traditional import duplication, depending on configuration and architecture.

You want fewer separate analytics services

Microsoft Fabric migration may reduce integration overhead when ingestion, transformation, warehousing, and reporting currently span multiple services. However, the benefits depend on your existing architecture and which services Fabric can replace.

Your team prefers an integrated SaaS operating model

Fabric offers standardized administration, shared data access, and integrated analytics capabilities. This approach may suit teams seeking fewer independently managed platform components and simpler operational workflows.

Your cost analysis supports the move

Evaluate Microsoft Fabric cost using actual workload performance, licensing, capacity utilization, engineering effort, and ongoing operations. Pricing alone cannot establish savings. Benchmark representative workloads before committing.

Reader takeaway: Migration deserves serious evaluation when Fabric solves a specific operational problem, improves reporting workflows, or reduces measurable complexity. Microsoft Fabric benefits matter most when they align with business priorities and technical requirements.
Databricks can remain valuable when teams need specialized processing, machine learning workflows, or multi-cloud flexibility. Neither platform removes the need to evaluate governance, performance, and compatibility before migration.
When Should You NOT Migrate from Databricks to Fabric?Your workloads rely on advanced Spark engineering

Databricks may remain the better fit for complex Spark pipelines, specialized runtime configurations, custom libraries, and workload-specific optimizations. Moving these workloads may require code changes, compatibility testing, or architectural redesign. Assess whether Fabric can meet existing performance and processing requirements before migrating.

Machine learning is central to your platform

Established model-training pipelines, feature engineering, experiment tracking, model lifecycle management, and deployment dependencies deserve careful evaluation. Compare each requirement against current Fabric capabilities. Avoid migration if critical workflows cannot transfer without unacceptable compromises.

You need cloud flexibility

Organizations operating across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud may value Databricks’ multicloud deployment options. Cloud strategy, data residency requirements, and existing infrastructure investments can make migration less attractive.

Migration risk exceeds the expected benefit

Regulated workloads, critical production dependencies, complex orchestration, strict service-level objectives, and limited engineering capacity can increase migration risks. Rebuilding pipelines or changing governance controls may introduce operational disruption.

The Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks decision should reflect measurable business needs, not platform availability alone. Teams should estimate migration effort, validate compatibility, and test representative workloads before committing.

Decision rule: If Databricks already meets your performance, governance, and cost requirements, do not migrate simply because Fabric is available. Retaining a proven platform can be more practical than introducing unnecessary change.
Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks: Cost, Performance, and ArchitectureCompare total cost of ownership

The Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks cost comparison should consider total cost of ownership (TCO), not headline pricing alone.

  • Fabric: Assess capacity pricing, licensing requirements, utilization, and existing Power BI entitlements.
  • Databricks: Include compute, cloud storage, networking, and associated infrastructure costs.
  • Migration: Account for engineering, testing, staff training, and parallel-running expenses.
  • Operations: Evaluate idle capacity, workload concurrency, and unpredictable processing demand.

Existing investments can significantly influence the financial outcome. Model both platforms using equivalent workloads and measured consumption before estimating potential savings.

Benchmark performance before deciding

Microsoft Fabric performance and Databricks performance depend on workload characteristics, configuration, and resource allocation. Compare representative SQL queries, Spark jobs, data refreshes, concurrency, and latency requirements.

Include routine operations and peak workloads. Measure execution times, resource consumption, reliability, and scaling behavior under realistic conditions. Test data volumes and query patterns that reflect production requirements.

Architecture also affects results. Fabric’s integrated environment may simplify data access and reporting workflows. Databricks may better suit workloads requiring specialized Spark configurations or advanced engineering controls.

Decision rule: Choose the platform that meets performance and reliability requirements at an acceptable total operating cost. Validate the results through controlled benchmarks rather than pricing assumptions or isolated performance tests.
How to Migrate from Databricks to Microsoft Fabric?

A successful Databricks to Fabric migration requires workload assessment, compatibility checks, data planning, and controlled deployment. Moving Delta tables or importing notebooks alone will not reproduce an existing production environment. Follow a phased approach to manage dependencies, validate results, and reduce operational risk.

Step 1: Inventory existing Databricks workloads

Document notebooks, jobs, Delta tables, streaming pipelines, external dependencies, Unity Catalog permissions, custom libraries, and downstream consumers. Record business criticality, data volumes, refresh schedules, recovery requirements, and service-level objectives. This inventory establishes migration scope and identifies workloads requiring additional testing.

Step 2: Assess compatibility and choose a migration pattern

Classify workloads into four groups:

  • Limited changes: Workloads compatible with Fabric after basic configuration.
  • Refactoring required: Workloads needing code changes or architectural redesign.
  • Retain on Databricks: Workloads dependent on specialized capabilities.
  • Hybrid deployment: Workloads benefiting from both platforms.

Check Databricks-specific utilities, APIs, runtime settings, custom libraries, and governance policies before selecting a migration path.

Step 3: Plan data access and movement

Choose the appropriate data strategy for each workload.

  • OneLake shortcuts: Reference supported external data without copying underlying files.
  • Unity Catalog integration: Evaluate metadata mirroring and shortcut-based access for supported configurations.
  • Data movement: Use ingestion pipelines or other supported methods when replication, transformation, or destination requirements demand it.

These options have limitations. Not every Unity Catalog object, security policy, or table format transfers seamlessly. Verify supported configurations, permissions, and access requirements before implementation.

Step 4: Rebuild and validate workloads

Port compatible notebooks and orchestration into the selected Fabric services. Replace unsupported dependencies and configure libraries, secrets, identities, and permissions. Validate output accuracy, performance, failure recovery, and costs against the existing Databricks environment. Test representative workloads before production deployment.

Step 5: Run a controlled cutover

Run both platforms in parallel where appropriate, comparing results and operational behavior. Define rollback criteria, communicate downtime requirements, and prepare production consumers for the transition. Switch workloads only after validation and stakeholder approval.

Implementation consideration: Microsoft Fabric implementation services can help assess dependencies, plan migration patterns, and validate workloads. However, teams should retain clear ownership of architecture decisions, acceptance criteria, and production readiness.
Should You Migrate, Stay, or Use Both?

The right choice in the Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks decision depends on workload requirements, existing investments, and measurable business benefits.

Databricks and Fabric integration can support coexistence when teams need specialized engineering alongside integrated reporting. However, a hybrid model introduces additional governance, monitoring, and operational considerations.

These recommendations are starting points, not universal rules. Before committing, validate workload compatibility, security, governance, performance, total costs, and team readiness. Choose the approach that solves actual business problems without introducing unnecessary complexity.

Conclusion: Make the Decision Based on Workloads

A successful Databricks to Fabric migration starts with measurable business value, not platform popularity. Assess existing workloads and run a representative pilot before committing. Migrate only workloads that meet compatibility, governance, and performance requirements. For organizations evaluating their options, Microsoft Fabric implementation services can help assess architecture, plan migration, and validate outcomes, supporting informed decisions without unnecessary disruption or unsupported performance expectations.

Frequently asked questionsIs Microsoft Fabric better than Databricks?

Neither platform is universally better. Fabric integrates data engineering, warehousing, analytics, and Power BI. Databricks can suit organizations with demanding Spark engineering, data science, and machine learning requirements. The right choice depends on workloads.

Can you migrate Databricks notebooks to Microsoft Fabric?

Some notebook code can be reused, but compatibility is not guaranteed. Databricks-specific utilities, libraries, configurations, and APIs may require changes. Test migrated notebooks and their dependencies before production deployment.

Does Microsoft Fabric support Delta Lake?

Yes. Fabric uses Delta Lake as its standard analytics table format. However, supported features and behavior can differ across engines. Validate advanced Delta Lake features before migrating dependent workloads.

Can Microsoft Fabric access Databricks data without copying it?

Yes, supported Unity Catalog data can be accessed through metadata mirroring and OneLake shortcuts. However, supported table formats, security behavior, and other limitations must be checked before implementation.

Should an organization run Databricks and Fabric together?

Yes, where each platform serves a distinct purpose. For example, Databricks may handle specialized engineering while Fabric supports reporting. Evaluate governance, access controls, operating costs, and duplicated processing before adopting both.

Migrating from Databricks to Fabric: When to Move and When Not To was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: AI Is Changing Everything About Hacking. No One Knows What Happens Next
items.summary: For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs. The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to vagueposting about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the internet was nice while it lasted,’ to outright prepper-level terror . To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, posted “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper , suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios. And all those posts came before people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in eMudhra (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), Node.js (an alternative to PHP), Gitlab (a software development platform), Plex (media server software), Railway (a cloud provider), OpenCode (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers from Wiz , Calif , and OpenAI discovered using AI. Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet , posted , “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this. But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something. Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models. In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no. AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation , said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. In a LinkedIn post, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc said that his company independently found the same bugs by typing “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP” into a frontier AI model. Amazon, meanwhile, said that it saw exploit attempts before the official disclosure. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning. After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the National Security Agency , the Prime Minister of Japan , and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. 4chan , several Wikimedia services , and Archive.org were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated. As The Atlantic has already suggested , one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost. For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Various low-effort, LLM-developed exploits have been dropped online; many of them will not work. A blog post called “There isn’t an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability,” written by Elias Taylor, quickly went viral and was dissected on Hacker News , especially by people pointing out that the website eliastaylor.com had been recently registered and that it wasn’t clear who Elias Taylor was. 404 Media reached Taylor by Signal; he said “I am real and on a delayed train.” “Lots of people are being tricked by AI into thinking they have an exploit when they don't, because they can't read or understand what the LLM gave them,” Taylor told 404 Media. “It doesn't appear to be anywhere near as exploitable as the other ‘stop the world’ vulnerabilities i.e log4j, heartbleed. But patch your servers, it’s still a vulnerability. Please do not paraphrase me as saying ‘there is no vulnerability’ for any reason. There is, and people should patch.” Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI on the Patch the Planet initiative, posted that his company had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.” It should also be noted that Taylor’s other blog post is called “Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces,” which includes the lines “software engineers have spent the past 40 years writing vulnerable, dogshit software. LLMs are easily above the bar needed to break into said software.” It remains unclear, at the moment, what the ultimate impact of all of this is going to be, or where we’ll be in one hour, one week, one year, or 10 years. But AI is changing how cybersecurity and hacking works. It is making finding and exploiting bugs faster and easier. We’re about to find out how insecure the internet really is.

For much of the last month, many of the cybersecurity experts I talk to and follow have been posting like they are very scared. Many have been warning of an AI-powered “Black Swan” event, have been alarmed by the number of vulnerabilities suddenly discovered, and of the apparent power of AI agents and large language models more broadly to find and exploit previously unknown bugs. 

The rhetoric has ranged from worried-but-measured (things are about to get weird), to run-of-the-mill advice like update your software and make sure you have two-factor authentication on, to vagueposting about AI-powered attacks, to things like ‘the internet was nice while it lasted,’ to outright prepper-level terror. 

To give you a sense of what I’m seeing, Matthew Green, a Johns Hopkins professor and one of the most respected cryptographers in the world, posted  “we’re in the part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the zombies and hope it slows them down,” and “so many people discovering that the whole Internet is dry tinder and the only thing keeping it from burning is the fact that teenagers haven’t found the matches yet,” Green is alluding to the fact that hackers and researchers driving AI tools and agents are getting better at finding and exploiting all sorts of bugs in important systems. I’ve also seen numerous AI employees, as mentioned, go full prepper, suggesting people pull money out of their bank accounts, disconnect from the internet, purchase shelf-stable food, hoard water, put money in gold and cash, and purchase hand-crank emergency radios.

And all those posts came before people using AI-powered tools found vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers much of the internet. In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in eMudhra (an Indian entity that provides website security certificates), Node.js (an alternative to PHP), Gitlab (a software development platform), Plex (media server software), Railway (a cloud provider), OpenCode (a coding agent platform), and several other companies and services, though, rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers from Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI discovered using AI. 

Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a service that has wide insight into the general health of the internet, posted, “In the 10 hours before [PHP2Shell] was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.” 

So much is happening, and so quickly, that it has been difficult for me — someone who has been reporting and editing stories on security and hacking for a decade — to fully understand what’s going on, to have a sense of what could happen next, or predict where this is going. And I think that that is largely where we are at the moment, as I am writing this. 

But it has become clear that AI, broadly defined, has fundamentally changed both offensive hacking and defensive cybersecurity. This is not because AI has become sentient or because human beings have lost control of it or because of “swarms” of “rogue agents,” but because AI is proving something that we have always known: much of the software that runs the internet, our devices, our accounts, and our lives is vulnerable, or out of date, or has security flaws that human beings never noticed, or was installed by someone at a company who left the company six years ago and has been replaced four times and no one knows how to find them now or how to update it. This doesn’t mean that all of the vulnerabilities that have been found with the help of AI have been obvious or trivial; skilled hackers and researchers, driving AI tools, seem to be better than humans alone at finding vulnerabilities. But, critically, AI and large language models have made it extremely easy to essentially brute force the internet; if every piece of software is a door, AI makes it exceptionally easy to turn turn the knobs of every door to see if it’s unlocked, even on buildings that human beings had never really bothered to try to open. What we are learning at an alarmingly fast pace is that not only are some of the locks easy to pick, in some cases the door is wide open or there’s a giant hole in the wall. The recent spate of people using AI to hack their internet of things devices to run new software shows that, in some cases, it takes essentially no expertise to actually use AI to hack something.

Meanwhile, we've seen the rise of "abliterated" AI models that are designed to not say no and open weights models that can be used for pentesting and potentially offensive hacks without the guardrails that exist in many off-the-shelf commercial models.

In a blog post explaining the PHP vulnerability discovery, OpenAI said the findings highlight “how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” OpenAI basically argues that it did all of this research ethically, and that its discovery opened a “Defender’s Window” that allowed governments and critical infrastructure to prepare for the disclosure of the bug. ‘Researcher finds bug, ethically discloses it to company, company fixes it’ is the preferred course of action in cybersecurity, but AI is shortening the window for all of this, is leading more people to do more research more easily, and is making both bug finding and bug fixing much faster. Whether those fixes are actually deployed by individual companies any faster is another, much more complicated question. The answer in many cases is, probably, no. 

AI is also making all of this much more unpredictable. The security company Chainguard was criticized for breaking the embargo on the PHP vulnerability disclosure because it posted fixes for the vulnerabilities several hours before it was officially disclosed. Critics, including the PHP Foundation, said this could have let attackers figure out how to exploit the issues before website owners had a chance to protect their systems. These facts raise questions about whether the bug was exceptionally easy to find, whether the AI models that originally found the vulnerabilities incorporated that information into the model somehow therefore making it easier for someone else to find, or whether there was a leak along the way from someone connected to the disclosure process. Any option is concerning.

After the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were discovered, some infosec experts started calling this “Black October,” and highlighted the fact that the National Security Agency, the Prime Minister of Japan, and various governments around the world told people to patch their websites and services immediately, and to take down services that couldn’t be patched. 4chan, several Wikimedia services, and Archive.org were all temporarily taken offline so that they could be updated. 

As The Atlantic has already suggested, one of the biggest impacts of PHP2Shell could be the fact that many historic websites can’t or won’t be updated, may be proactively pulled offline, might eventually be hacked, and might never come back. The link rot could be horrendous, and a lot of history could be lost. 

For such a high-profile incident, most of the actual impacts thus far have been related to the proactive patching or removal of potentially insecure websites, and we have not seen immediate, widespread exploitation of the bug. Dan Guido, the CEO of Trail of Bits, a well-respected cybersecurity company that partners with OpenAI on the Patch the Planet initiative, posted that his company had created “a working exploit,” and that “Will Tan built it in 1 day with Codex, drawing on ~10 years of system security and vulnerability research. AI accelerates exploit development. Knowing how to turn a bug into a shell still takes expertise. AI makes that expertise more productive.” 

It should also be noted that Taylor’s other blog post is called “Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces,” which includes the lines “software engineers have spent the past 40 years writing vulnerable, dogshit software. LLMs are easily above the bar needed to break into said software.”

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
items.summary: DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to i ts Flash model . Its change log says the update cuts task runtime and output length. It lists 11 benchmark scores, including 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Developers can use it through DeepSeek’s API or a service like OpenRouter. Because it’s an open-weight model , they can also download it from Hugging Face and run it on their own servers. I tested it through OpenRouter on DeepSeek’s own servers, at DeepSeek’s prices. DeepSeek’s model card compares the update with several rivals, but not Haiku 5.5, so I picked it for this hands-on comparison. Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest model at standard speed, aimed at high-volume tasks such as classification, summarization, and database queries. Anthropic notes that its Opus models run faster in Fast Mode. Anthropic reports 39.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 3.1 percentage points below DeepSeek’s reported score. These are vendor-reported results, rather than a controlled head-to-head test. Haiku costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, then $0.50 and $2.50 above that. DeepSeek’s off-peak rates are $0.15 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens, and $0.60 per million output tokens; peak rates are twice those amounts. Comparing uncached input and output rates, Haiku is cheaper on short prompts, and DeepSeek is cheaper on long ones. Actual charges also depend on tokenization, caching, and the provider route. I built three tests around what each company says its model does well to see which one performs better in practice. The tests I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to DeepSeek’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default settings. I pinned DeepSeek to model ID 1017 and ran everything off-peak. A script graded every answer against keys I built and checked with a second method before either model saw them. Agentic bug fix : A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap. Database queries : A fake CI platform database with 20 questions, answered by writing SQL. Traps include soft deletes, mixed casing, retried builds, time zones, and currency conversion. Two questions can’t be answered from the data. Triage : 400 developer error reports, each needing a category, a severity, a service, and a team. That’s 1,600 scored fields. The prompt counted as 153,082 input tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku, past Haiku’s 100,000-token price threshold. Agentic bug fix DeepSeek started strong, beating Haiku’s accuracy on the first test. DeepSeek scored 6 of 6. Haiku scored 5 of 6. Both found the first bug even though the error pointed at the wrong file, fixed the third, broke no regression tests, and flagged the wrong test without touching it. Haiku missed one of six hidden tests on the second bug, and DeepSeek didn’t. Haiku finished in eight turns and 21.6 seconds. DeepSeek took 12 turns and 49.6 seconds but still cost less because it automatically cached most of the repeated input. I didn’t turn on Anthropic’s prompt caching , which requires an opt-in. This compares the caching settings used in these runs; enabling Haiku’s caching could change the cost comparison. The numbers: DeepSeek: 12 calls, 190,139 in, 7,877 out, $0.009, 49.6 s. Haiku: 8 calls, 100,461 in, 3,255 out, $0.012, 21.6 s. Database queries This is the only test where both models tied for accuracy, both scoring 20 out of 20. Both caught every trap and answered “unknown” to both questions the data couldn’t answer rather than hallucinating. Haiku got the answers in fewer calls and less time. DeepSeek cost about half as much. The numbers: DeepSeek: 12 calls, 75,151 in, 4,608 out, $0.004, 34.9 s. Haiku 7 calls, 55,304 in, 5,917 out, $0.009, 28.4 s. Triage Here’s where the accuracy differences are clearest. DeepSeek got all 1,600 fields right. Haiku got 1,596. Two of its misses were severity ratings. The routing guide rates a report sev4 if it affects fewer than 50 users or has an error rate under 1%. Haiku rated a report with 49 affected customers as sev3, and another with a 0.8% error rate as sev3. Both should have been sev4. Haiku’s other two misses were routing mistakes. The guide says one service moved to a new team on August 1 and that reports should be routed by the date in their header. Haiku sent two reports filed after August 1 to the old team. Each mentioned an earlier July date in its body, but the outputs alone don’t explain why Haiku chose the old team. The same prompt was counted as 153,082 tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku. Because the models use different tokenizers, identical text can produce different token counts. That puts Haiku at a higher long-prompt rate. It costs $0.28, compared with DeepSeek’s $0.06. The numbers: DeepSeek: 153,082 in, 58,923 out, $0.058, 188.3 s. Haiku 216,811 in, 69,354 out, $0.282, 228.9 s. Results Test DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 Claude Haiku 5.5 Agentic bug fix 6 of 6 5 of 6 Database queries 20 of 20 20 of 20 Triage fields 1,600 of 1,600 1,596 of 1,600 Total tokens in / out 418,372 / 71,408 372,576 / 78,526 Total cost $0.07 $0.30 Total model time 272.8 s 278.9 s DeepSeek and Haiku came out close on accuracy. DeepSeek edged ahead on the bug fix and the triage job, and they tied on the database queries. Speed was close too: Haiku was faster on the tool-based tests, and DeepSeek was faster on the big triage prompt. Cost was the real difference. DeepSeek came in at $0.07 to Haiku’s $0.30, and most of that gap came from the one long prompt that pushed Haiku onto its higher rate. What do I think? For these three runs, I’d pick DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017: it earned full marks on my scoring keys and cost less with the settings I used. Haiku was faster on both tool-based tests, while DeepSeek was faster on triage and slightly faster across the three runs combined. I ran each model only once per test, so these results don’t establish a general accuracy or speed advantage, or show how either model performs at scale. I’d test both on my own workload before making a production choice.

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to its Flash model. Its change log says the update cuts task runtime and output length. It lists 11 benchmark scores, including 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0.

Developers can use it through DeepSeek’s API or a service like OpenRouter. Because it’s an open-weight model, they can also download it from Hugging Face and run it on their own servers. I tested it through OpenRouter on DeepSeek’s own servers, at DeepSeek’s prices.

DeepSeek’s model card compares the update with several rivals, but not Haiku 5.5, so I picked it for this hands-on comparison. Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest model at standard speed, aimed at high-volume tasks such as classification, summarization, and database queries.

Anthropic notes that its Opus models run faster in Fast Mode. Anthropic reports 39.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 3.1 percentage points below DeepSeek’s reported score. These are vendor-reported results, rather than a controlled head-to-head test.

Haiku costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, then $0.50 and $2.50 above that. DeepSeek’s off-peak rates are $0.15 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens, and $0.60 per million output tokens; peak rates are twice those amounts.

Comparing uncached input and output rates, Haiku is cheaper on short prompts, and DeepSeek is cheaper on long ones. Actual charges also depend on tokenization, caching, and the provider route.

I built three tests around what each company says its model does well to see which one performs better in practice.

The tests

I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to DeepSeek’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default settings. I pinned DeepSeek to model ID 1017 and ran everything off-peak. A script graded every answer against keys I built and checked with a second method before either model saw them.

  • Agentic bug fix: A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
  • Database queries: A fake CI platform database with 20 questions, answered by writing SQL. Traps include soft deletes, mixed casing, retried builds, time zones, and currency conversion. Two questions can’t be answered from the data.
  • Triage: 400 developer error reports, each needing a category, a severity, a service, and a team. That’s 1,600 scored fields. The prompt counted as 153,082 input tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku, past Haiku’s 100,000-token price threshold.
Agentic bug fix

DeepSeek started strong, beating Haiku’s accuracy on the first test. DeepSeek scored 6 of 6. Haiku scored 5 of 6. Both found the first bug even though the error pointed at the wrong file, fixed the third, broke no regression tests, and flagged the wrong test without touching it. Haiku missed one of six hidden tests on the second bug, and DeepSeek didn’t.

Haiku finished in eight turns and 21.6 seconds. DeepSeek took 12 turns and 49.6 seconds but still cost less because it automatically cached most of the repeated input. I didn’t turn on Anthropic’s prompt caching, which requires an opt-in. This compares the caching settings used in these runs; enabling Haiku’s caching could change the cost comparison.

The numbers:

  • DeepSeek: 12 calls, 190,139 in, 7,877 out, $0.009, 49.6 s.
  • Haiku: 8 calls, 100,461 in, 3,255 out, $0.012, 21.6 s.
Database queries

This is the only test where both models tied for accuracy, both scoring 20 out of 20. Both caught every trap and answered “unknown” to both questions the data couldn’t answer rather than hallucinating. Haiku got the answers in fewer calls and less time. DeepSeek cost about half as much.

The numbers:

  • DeepSeek: 12 calls, 75,151 in, 4,608 out, $0.004, 34.9 s.
  • Haiku 7 calls, 55,304 in, 5,917 out, $0.009, 28.4 s.
Triage

Here’s where the accuracy differences are clearest. DeepSeek got all 1,600 fields right. Haiku got 1,596. Two of its misses were severity ratings. The routing guide rates a report sev4 if it affects fewer than 50 users or has an error rate under 1%. Haiku rated a report with 49 affected customers as sev3, and another with a 0.8% error rate as sev3. Both should have been sev4. 

Haiku’s other two misses were routing mistakes. The guide says one service moved to a new team on August 1 and that reports should be routed by the date in their header. Haiku sent two reports filed after August 1 to the old team. Each mentioned an earlier July date in its body, but the outputs alone don’t explain why Haiku chose the old team.

The same prompt was counted as 153,082 tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku. Because the models use different tokenizers, identical text can produce different token counts. That puts Haiku at a higher long-prompt rate. It costs $0.28, compared with DeepSeek’s $0.06.

The numbers:

  • DeepSeek: 153,082 in, 58,923 out, $0.058, 188.3 s.
  • Haiku 216,811 in, 69,354 out, $0.282, 228.9 s.
Results
TestDeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017Claude Haiku 5.5Agentic bug fix6 of 65 of 6Database queries20 of 2020 of 20Triage fields1,600 of 1,6001,596 of 1,600Total tokens in / out418,372 / 71,408372,576 / 78,526Total cost$0.07$0.30Total model time272.8 s278.9 s

DeepSeek and Haiku came out close on accuracy. DeepSeek edged ahead on the bug fix and the triage job, and they tied on the database queries. Speed was close too: Haiku was faster on the tool-based tests, and DeepSeek was faster on the big triage prompt. Cost was the real difference. DeepSeek came in at $0.07 to Haiku’s $0.30, and most of that gap came from the one long prompt that pushed Haiku onto its higher rate.

What do I think?

For these three runs, I’d pick DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017: it earned full marks on my scoring keys and cost less with the settings I used. Haiku was faster on both tool-based tests, while DeepSeek was faster on triage and slightly faster across the three runs combined. I ran each model only once per test, so these results don’t establish a general accuracy or speed advantage, or show how either model performs at scale. I’d test both on my own workload before making a production choice.

items.title: AI Is Already 'Amplifying the Destruction' of War
items.summary: The UN met this week to discuss, among other things, the threat of autonomous weapons. “The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning,” Laurent Gisel, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) legal warfare team, told 404 Media. Gisel was in NYC this week to address the UN about all the things that are driving conflict across the planet. His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and – of course – AI. Autonomous weapons have been a hot topic at the UN this year . In September, the UN attempted to pass a treaty that would govern the use of killer AI weapons. Diplomats from Russia and the US stripped it of its power . But the UN has pressed forward. On Tuesday, the international governing body announced a new initiative that would grapple with the issue. But, as Gisel said: “multilateral processes take quite some time” and “we already see the effects on the battlefield.” AI is already picking targets and killing people. Gisel said the technology is “amplifying the destruction, amplifying the violation of the law, amplifying the humanitarian harm caused by conflicts.” Israel used an AI powered by Microsoft to pick targets in Gaza . In Ukraine, AI-powered Russian drones are deciding which humans to kill . The United States military is pitching itself as an “AI-first” fighting force . Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth recently announced Project Meridian, an initiative to guide the AI-powered autonomous weapons of the future. Three of Meridian's leads are Elon Musk, defense contractor Palmer Luckey, and Newt Gingrich. For Gisel, one of the biggest dangers of AI is how fast it is. A core selling point for the tech is that it can help commanders make decisions faster. But that also accelerates the pace of mistakes. “Targets are created at higher speed and higher frequency, and are actually then prosecuted quicker, and with that give us great concerns in terms of the level of human control that is retained,” he said. “The human is supposed to remain in the loop.” The human does not always remain in the loop. The Israel Defense Forces told journalists it did not thoroughly vet the kill lists generated by Lavender, the AI system it used to pick targets in Gaza. “It's known in the [civilian world] [...] that humans tend to trust the systems,” Gisel said. “That it's more the case when the humans are tired, when the humans are under stress, when the humans have to deliver quickly, and that's of course exactly the situation in which soldiers are in. So all of that gives us a lot of concerns in terms of retaining control on the use of force in armed conflict.” AI boosters often pitch AI as an “easy button,” a way for people to brute force a complicated task and get it over with. But the consequences are much different when someone in Silicon Valley is parsing spreadsheets or reverse engineering code than when they’re prosecuting a war in the Middle East. “That's something that the developers of those systems don't necessarily realize either, because some of those systems are developed by technological companies very far away from the battlefield, and they are not naturally all developed for battlefield use,” Gisel said. International humanitarian law is an ever-evolving legal negotiation between world powers meant to limit the devastating effects of war. It’s imperfect and countries with vast armies like the US and Russia often do not abide by it. The ICRC, which Gisel represents, exists explicitly to shape these rules and laws. Some of the laws are old, far older than AI, but according to Gisel humanitarian law applies to “all weapons, means, and methods of warfare. Those of yesterday, those of today, and those of tomorrow.” Beyond the opportunity to code humanitarian law into AI, Gisel said there should be new rules and regulations for the new technology. “Not to prohibit them all, but to prohibit specific categories of autonomous weapon systems and put specific restrictions on others,” he said. "...Once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle" But he does have redlines. The first is any AI support system that removes a human being from the kill chain. “That requires specific limits and guardrails and restrictions from our perspective,” he said. “The other type of autonomous weapon system that we recommend prohibiting is those that would target human beings directly, where the target profile is the human being, as opposed to a tank, weapon systems, or another typical military objective, and the reason why is based on ethical concerns, humanitarian concerns, and a moral line,” he added. Autonomous weapons have existed for a long time. Some US warships have gatling guns that track and destroy incoming targets automatically. The difference is that those weapons track ships and missiles, not human beings. According to Gisel, one problem with autonomous weapons that target humans or AI support systems that pick targets is that they’re unpredictable. He said banning unpredictable weapons should be a non-brainer. “Military discipline is about your forces [...] delivering the commander's intent,” he said. “If you have a weapon that is unpredictable in its effect, how can you deliver the commander's intent?” Data Centers Are War Targets Now "Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes?" But it’s been a sticking point in negotiations. “We would have thought, military considerations, would align. But actually, that has also faced quite some pushback. Strangely enough,” he said. He spoke about the negotiations in August and September from earlier in the year . “There were references in the last proposal by the chair of the group on precisely all those questions: that the autonomous weapon systems need to be reliable, explainable, understandable, and predictable. And all of that was taken out by some states.” Gisel also opposes AI in nuclear command and control. In 1983, the Soviet Union’s early warning systems reported that the US had launched a nuclear weapon at the country. Soviet lieutenant colonel Stanislav Petrov decided the computer had made a mistake and decided not to report the attacks up the chain. He was right. “States will continue to use satellite systems and therefore algorithms that go with those satellites,” he said. “But it's so important to ensure that it remains entirely under human control and a really meaningful human control.” While the UN deliberates and the ICRC wrangles with how to regulate all this, the wars continue and military forces continue to embrace AI. “That's why it's urgent to have decisions being made by the international community on what to prohibit and what to restrict [...] once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle,” he said. Gisel said the world needs to act now. “Otherwise, it's the technology that will decide what is acceptable, and that's not the world we want to live in, right?”
items.summary_html:
The UN met this week to discuss, among other things, the threat of autonomous weapons.

“The technology is developing at a pace that is very concerning,” Laurent Gisel, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s (ICRC) legal warfare team, told 404 Media. Gisel was in NYC this week to address the UN about all the things that are driving conflict across the planet. His prepared remarks include a statement on the illegal arms trade, nuclear weapons, mines, and – of course – AI.

Autonomous weapons have been a hot topic at the UN this year. In September, the UN attempted to pass a treaty that would govern the use of killer AI weapons. Diplomats from Russia and the US stripped it of its power. 

But the UN has pressed forward. On Tuesday, the international governing body announced a new initiative that would grapple with the issue. But, as Gisel said: “multilateral processes take quite some time” and  “we already see the effects on the battlefield.” 

AI is already picking targets and killing people. Gisel said the technology is “amplifying the destruction, amplifying the violation of the law, amplifying the humanitarian harm caused by conflicts.”

Israel used an AI powered by Microsoft to pick targets in Gaza. In Ukraine, AI-powered Russian drones are deciding which humans to kill. The United States military is pitching itself as an “AI-first” fighting force. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth recently announced Project Meridian, an initiative to guide the AI-powered autonomous weapons of the future. Three of Meridian's leads are Elon Musk, defense contractor Palmer Luckey, and Newt Gingrich.

For Gisel, one of the biggest dangers of AI is how fast it is. A core selling point for the tech is that it can help commanders make decisions faster. But that also accelerates the pace of mistakes. “Targets are created at higher speed and higher frequency, and are actually then prosecuted quicker, and with that give us great concerns in terms of the level of human control that is retained,” he said. “The human is supposed to remain in the loop.”

The human does not always remain in the loop. The Israel Defense Forces told journalists it did not thoroughly vet the kill lists generated by Lavender, the AI system it used to pick targets in Gaza. “It's known in the [civilian world] [...] that humans tend to trust the systems,” Gisel said. “That it's more the case when the humans are tired, when the humans are under stress, when the humans have to deliver quickly, and that's of course exactly the situation in which soldiers are in. So all of that gives us a lot of concerns in terms of retaining control on the use of force in armed conflict.”

AI boosters often pitch AI as an “easy button,” a way for people to brute force a complicated task and get it over with. But the consequences are much different when someone in Silicon  Valley is parsing spreadsheets or reverse engineering code  than when they’re prosecuting a war in the Middle East.

“That's something that the developers of those systems don't necessarily realize either, because some of those systems are developed by technological companies very far away from the battlefield, and they are not naturally all developed for battlefield use,” Gisel said.

International humanitarian law is an ever-evolving legal negotiation between world powers meant to limit the devastating effects of war. It’s imperfect and countries with vast armies like the US and Russia often do not abide by it. The ICRC, which Gisel represents, exists explicitly to shape these rules and laws. Some of the laws are old, far older than AI, but according to Gisel humanitarian law applies to “all weapons, means, and methods of warfare. Those of yesterday, those of today, and those of tomorrow.”

Beyond the opportunity to code humanitarian law into AI, Gisel said there should be new rules and regulations for the new technology. “Not to prohibit them all, but to prohibit specific categories of autonomous weapon systems and put specific restrictions on others,” he said.

"...Once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle"

But he does have redlines. The first is any AI support system that removes a human being from the kill chain. “That requires specific limits and guardrails and restrictions from our perspective,” he said.

“The other type of autonomous weapon system that we recommend prohibiting is those that would target human beings directly, where the target profile is the human being, as opposed to a tank, weapon systems, or another typical military objective, and the reason why is based on ethical concerns, humanitarian concerns, and a moral line,” he added.

Autonomous weapons have existed for a long time. Some US warships have gatling guns that track and destroy incoming targets automatically. The difference is that those weapons track ships and missiles, not human beings.

According to Gisel, one problem with autonomous weapons that target humans or AI support systems that pick targets is that they’re unpredictable. He said banning unpredictable weapons should be a non-brainer. “Military discipline is about your forces [...] delivering the commander's intent,” he said. “If you have a weapon that is unpredictable in its effect, how can you deliver the commander's intent?”

Data Centers Are War Targets Now
"Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes?"

But it’s been a sticking point in negotiations. “We would have thought, military considerations, would align. But actually, that has also faced quite some pushback. Strangely enough,” he said. He spoke about the negotiations in August and September from earlier in the year. “There were references in the last proposal by the chair of the group on precisely all those questions: that the autonomous weapon systems need to be reliable, explainable, understandable, and predictable. And all of that was taken out by some states.”

Gisel also opposes AI in nuclear command and control. In 1983, the Soviet Union’s early warning systems reported that the US had launched a nuclear weapon at the country. Soviet lieutenant colonel Stanislav Petrov decided the computer had made a mistake and decided not to report the attacks up the chain. He was right.

“States will continue to use satellite systems and therefore algorithms that go with those satellites,” he said. “But it's so important to ensure that it remains entirely under human control and a really meaningful human control.”

While the UN deliberates and the ICRC wrangles with how to regulate all this, the wars continue and military forces continue to embrace AI. “That's why it's urgent to have decisions being made by the international community on what to prohibit and what to restrict [...] once the genie is out of the bottle, it's very, very much difficult to put it back in the bottle,” he said.

Gisel said the world needs to act now. “Otherwise, it's the technology that will decide what is acceptable, and that's not the world we want to live in, right?”
