items.title: You are the Team  — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
items.summary: Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year. When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book. At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader. They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring. Watch the episode Watch Anekha Sokhal on YouTube Show notes Moshi — Anekha’s company Anekha Sokhal — background and work GIQ research paper — research discussed in the interview Reducto — document extraction AI Engineer New York Timestamps 0:00 — AI Engineer New York and “you are the team” 0:54 — Meet Anekha Sokhal 2:09 — From mathematics to energy derivatives 3:46 — The Fulbright and becoming a founder 5:45 — What Moshi does for traders 6:10 — Processing a flood of market data 9:03 — Bloomberg and market workflows 10:03 — Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix 12:03 — From dashboards to workflows 15:03 — Trusted sources and signal 17:13 — Build or buy models and document extraction 18:20 — AI Engineer New York 20:32 — Customer meetings and community 23:54 — Hiring and talking to customers 25:55 — swyx’s path into AI Transcript Automated transcript; wording may contain errors. Speaker labels are omitted. 0:00 So I’ve actually extended my stay in New York, because we’ve like now, I was meant to leave today. We’ve now got meetings on Thursday, extended it another day, Friday, extended it another day, Monday. And then I’ve got now meetings where people are like, hey, we’re in energy. Let’s talk in Houston. So we’ve like filled up a week after the conference of meetings. AI engineers was an interesting one, because a lot of them are feeling like overwhelmed with the pressure from management. To do what? Because people now say, we don’t need a team, you are the team. And so it’s like, hey, I need to now build this whole system myself. But that system would be typically done by 10 people. Okay, we are in the studio. Last podcast of AIE for me with Anekha from Moshi. Welcome. Thank you so much. 1:01 Did I get it right, Anekha? Yes, you did. So your background caught my interest because I was a former trader and you’re now a founder. Yes. And you also were telling me just about your experience. I kind of want to hear about it from you. As far as I know, this is your first AIE. How did you hear about us? What was the experience like giving your talk and what happened after? Yeah, well, first of all, thank you to everyone at AIE because it’s been such a fantastic experience. And thank you for inviting me on the podcast as well. I’m so excited to just share my experience. And also, I think we’re living in such a fast moving time and everyone I speak to is like very overwhelmed. So it’s really helpful to be able to kind of share everything that I’ve had in my experience because I did my undergrad in statistics and math, which is now what everyone calls AI. And so it’s really interesting to speak about that and the evolution of that and also to always speak to a former trader as well. 2:02 And just to share like war scars on that. Did you do financial calculus, like stochastic calculus? Yeah, I did that. And I so my undergraduate degree was mathematics, operational research, statistics and economics, Morse at Warwick. And it was what everyone was just like, oh, my God, so nerdy. And I hated telling people. And now it’s like, wow. Yeah, everyone’s like, oh, my God, machine learning, AI. Yeah. Yeah. And then derivatives. So I did that. So my background was started in that at Warwick in England and then knew I wanted to work in trading. I don’t know what what your story to go into trading was, but I wanted something which was fast paced and to do with data, like absolutely love data. And it was when I read about what trading was. I could not imagine myself being in any other career. So I was just set on doing that. So I got my first internship in investment banking and trading and then got an internship at JP Morgan where I started. 3:04 And I started on the emerging markets desk and then moved to commodities and did derivative trading there. So most of my career has been in energy derivatives. And because I have that data background, I always looked at the market from I wanted to break it down into all the different parts. So, for example, in commodities, a lot is about the fundamentals and about the different news and the different the physical happening. And so I was always fascinated by like building out from zero. And so when I was trade trade trading, I saw this shift where it’s like a data and then something was going to happen. And that’s when I left JP Morgan to to actually I wanted to be an entrepreneur and and a founder. But I wanted to have a data company. So I got the Fulbright scholarship to come to the US because you guys have such an incredible venture. Just casually got a Fulbright. 4:06 Yeah, I guess the way I say a funny story, I was doing a yoga class in London. I was like, so my parents have a jewelry business. I side hustled a computer vision startup before my startup at university. And so I was like, oh, what are the problems in the jewelry space? Oh, like virtual try on. So that led to me wanting to be a founder. And I thought, how could I be a founder in the best country to be a founder in? And I thought, what I want to be a founder who can talk about the technology. So this was back in like 2020, 2021. And I found Fulbright had a data scholarship and they gave one in the whole of the UK. So I was like, my way to get here is a Fulbright scholarship and they only give one. And this is really funny because I don’t know if you remember 2020 when it was COVID and gas markets were going crazy. So there was there was like gas markets had insane 5:06 volatility. And so when I did my Fulbright interview, they asked me, how do you like, how do you see the future? And I talked about the like global issue of everyone is having the energy market crisis and how data relates to that. And everyone could relate to what I was talking to because like gas prices were crazy. Their electricity bills were going crazy. And so that led me to the US, came here, was deep in machine learning research, published at ICLR with Stability AI, worked in collaboration with NASA, did a lot of a lot of super interesting work, which then led me to Moshi. And what is Moshi? So Moshi, we are building the program that I wish I had when I was trading. So what we do is we provide real time insights for financial traders, starting with commodity and energy markets and macro markets. So what we do is we process more data than is humanly possible to tell you everything that matters to your portfolio right 6:09 now. What kind of data would you be processing that give us an idea of maybe types and an order of magnitude? Types and order of magnitude. So let me start with order of magnitude. So a fun way I explain it to people is it takes me four seconds to say the sentence to you. And in the same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things. So that’s the type of volume of data that we process. In terms of the types of data, this very much comes to me like geeking out about how I would trade. I would break the market up into all the different types of data, which a trader looks at to decide what trade to put on and how to manage the risk. So what I do is I take the market and I say, well, there’s structured data and unstructured data. There’s the time series of the futures market and there’s all of the technical analysis around it. So we’re looking at all of this like statistical indicated, all of the different technical indicators, all of the moving averages. 7:11 That’s one data set. And obviously that is updating constantly. The next data set we look at is the time series for fundamentals markets. So especially in some commodity markets, there’s a lot of demand and supply. And then we look at the unstructured data. So the news is the obvious one. But then there’s also all this alternative data that exists. For example, there’s X data. There’s audio data on podcasts. X Twitter. X Twitter, yes. You read Twitter. OK. So understanding all of these different types of data. And that I would say is the like public availability of data. And there’s this whole other type of data, which is the user’s private data. So I’m sure you had that when you were trading, which is you have the analysts you care about. I can’t come and tell you, hey, you should, you know, read this person because you have who you need. And then you’re going to have your subscriptions that you care about. You’ll have your internal data, right? 8:11 Like some of the companies we speak to, if they are trading markets, trading energy markets, they will have their person for the amount of LNG ships going through the Strait of Hormuz. And so there’s all this data which is personal to the user. So we take those two data points together, do all of the data cleaning, data transformation. We then look at the statistics and machine learning, tag it, kind of create our whole ontology on top of it. And then we put it into the Moshi, like n-dimensional graph. And then we produce the output, which is a piece of software which pushes data to you. So every time you open Moshi, you see something new related to your portfolio. And you can pull data. So LLM, I’m going to give you answers in 30 seconds, which would take you typically days. So do people often say new Bloomberg or is that something that you disagree? You don’t like being characterized as new Bloomberg? Yeah, that’s an interesting question. 9:13 Because obviously that’s the 800 pound gorilla or whatever the British version of saying 800 pound gorilla is. Yeah, you know, I think Bloomberg has certain features, which the Bloomberg chat, it’s a fantastic aspect of the platform. Yeah, for those who don’t know, like traders would transact billions of dollars in chat. And there’s a standardized formula. When my entry into NLP was actually parsing Bloomberg chat into a structured pricing sheet for my logs. And that’s how we did option pricing. Yeah, there’s the Bloomberg chat, which is one thing. I wouldn’t say we’re a new Bloomberg. I’d say we’re a different type of software, which is not. I think this is the easiest way to say it. And I don’t know how controversial this is. But if Bloomberg and Claude and Netflix had a baby. Netflix. It would be Moshi. You have videos? Netflix. 10:14 We actually have a recommendation system, which we’ve internally built, which is if you’re a trader and you’re looking at one thing, you actually care about the second and third order derivatives right now, which you wouldn’t immediately know. I see. And so we’ve built a whole recommendation system where a simple thing, if you’re, let’s bring it back to like an oil trader, and there’s an energy equities company that’s doing something which would indirectly impact oil, you need to know that right now. You’re not going to get that from like a news stream. You will get that from a connected graph, which is showing that to you. Because if those two information points are coming out right now, the only way you can do it is either a human, which is being able to like connect those, or by a mimicking human, sort of like a recommendation system, which can do that. But that’s what we try and do, because I like wish I had that when I was trading. Yeah. Well, you know, there’s a whole addictiveness element of Netflix, which is bad. 11:15 There is. But yeah, it’s very interesting. I think like RecSys is one of the most important parts of AI. And as a curator of AIEs, I actually have every year an LLM RecSys track. And engineers often don’t appreciate how important it is. Like it’s not very well attended, even though some of the people powering these things, I mean, they run RecSys for YouTube, they run Netflix for Netflix, for Instagram and TikTok. And then like nobody shows up. And I’m like, what do you mean? Like you’re not interested in RecSys? You know, I find it really interesting. I think part of it is they make it seem so easy. And it’s like, oh, this is so like... This is the most important system in the entire, you know, company. Exactly. And I’d say there’s arguably something linked to it, which I think some companies do really well, like Spotify, Instagram, which is one thing that people have come out with AI 12:15 is everyone now can build their own Claude dashboards, right? It’s like, hey, I built this myself. Great. Great. If you want to get someone else to use it, that’s your brain in a dashboard or your brain in something. Try and get someone new to incorporate that into their workflow. You’re then no longer dealing with a problem. You’re dealing with a UI problem, which is how did they interact with it? Because sometimes users don’t always use that. One thing that these platforms do really well is they push data to you, which like hooks you. So you naturally don’t even realize you’re on the platform and you’re like, oh, I want that. No, no, I actually want that. And so we’ve been trying to internally as a company understand how does UI relate to a recommendation system? Because our thesis is if you solve for one, you’re naturally also solving for the other. And I think that’s a big thing right now, which is if everyone’s building software, how do you get it to actually be software that people will use? It’s a bit of an interesting take. 13:19 Yeah, a bit of chicken and egg. Well, anyway, I forgot to mention also my background to this. I used to trade currency options in London, actually. And then I spent some time in rates. And it had a very similar career path where you start with EMEA and then you go into maybe G10. Yeah. At least that’s what we call it for currencies. And you ingest a lot of information and really probably LLMs can process it better. So we didn’t have the tooling back when I did this 10 years ago. But now I see that. And then I moved to the buy side where you start paying for alternative data exactly like you did. We were actually one of the very first few at Balyasny to do the X fire hose or Twitter fire hose. Yeah. That’s something like a stupidly expensive, like $300,000 a month data thing that you have to pay for to get all tweets. It used to be free. And you sort of parse them. 14:19 I don’t think I don’t know if it was ever free. It was free for researchers. Okay. But then if you’re like a hedge fund, like you have to buy that. And it’s very noisy. And so my eyes go up because I don’t know if I would trade on those things because sometimes people do just talk random crap. And sometimes people try to manipulate markets by saying stuff. And it just doesn’t matter that much. But we would also have alternative data like satellite information or credit card information or whatever. And so on the buy side, my number one question is, are you looking at my data? Which is probably not. But how do you assure people? How do you integrate with systems that you don’t necessarily even see? Yeah. And I think there’s two questions in there, which is the first one is, if there’s so much data available, how do you know what’s important? So when we’re looking at X data, it’s a natural conversation when we speak to people or let’s even expand it out to any types of data. 15:20 One thing we found with people is they really will have their trusted people who they’ll follow of these voices in industry, especially in commodities. There’ll be the suppliers of commodities. There’ll be the LNG, all of these facilities who will be active on there because it’s the quickest way for them to also give a status update. Wow. So it’s interesting because we found that a lot of our users will tell us about this. So it’s like, oh, OK, so you find it as a trusted source because you believe this certain individual. Sketchy. Right. And so it’s one of those things where we have found a way to try and filter out as much as possible. But when we are showing it to someone, we give a confidence score of, OK, someone is saying this one thing, but this is everything else happening around the conversation. Because what’s interesting to people is if there are divergent sources, like an example would be how many 16:21 ships are going, how many planes are going above us right now. If Reuters is saying something or Bloomberg is saying something, a Wall Street Journal is saying something, they may not all agree. But the fact that they don’t agree is a point of data because is there an opportunity there? Because no one knows. So that’s how we try and give people information. And then the second question is, you know, people’s data sits everywhere. And I think there’s different types of integration. The first one is what about like their messy PDF data? That data is what we’ve built is like a vision language model to understand it. So we’ll take the data that they can upload to their cloud version of Moshi. And then we actually go and we break it down and then build it up in our database. And there are certain types of data where you just have to connect to their systems. And then that’s like more of a conversation. Is it important to, I assume you’re running this vision language model yourself, is it important to own that? Or would you want to lay out, I mean, there’s any number of vendors, Reducto 17:24 is like a non-documenting processing one. How important is it to have your own models versus just use whatever’s off the shelf? I think that’s a question that a lot of companies are battling with right now. The first question for us is we, if someone’s giving us their data, we don’t want to be sending it to a third party. Because there are systems out there which can do these things for you. But you want to make sure that you’ve got that agreement on how are they processing that data? What are they doing with it? That’s the first question. The second one is, if you don’t have a team of engineers, then that is a great solution. But if you do have a team of engineers like us, a fun fact is most of the team has in some capacity worked with NASA, then they want to build the models. But not everyone has that. And so, you know, I think it really depends like where you are as a team. Yeah, got it. Okay, and then coming into your talk, you apparently had a lot of inbound from it. 18:28 This is our first finance focused one. So I was genuinely unsure who we could get in the door. Obviously, we like pitch it and market it very heavily for this crew. What kind of people did you end up talking to? Yeah, we, it was a like fantastic opportunity because we have been like back to back speaking to people. And what we initially thought would be the interest, we’ve had people like, in the past hour messaging me on LinkedIn saying, hey, I saw your court talk. Are you’re in Houston? Can we get a meeting? Or hey, are you in New York? Can we get a meeting? The types of people we’ve had a lot of traders, either at funds, consulting, and then AI engineers was an interesting one, because a lot of them are feeling like overwhelmed with the pressure from management. To do what? Because people now say, we don’t need a team, you are the team. And so it’s like, hey, I need to now build this whole system 19:31 myself. But that system would be typically done by 10 people. So a lot of people have talked to us and they’re like, hey, I need to build a system. But like, you know, do I need to have a swarm of agents? But then like, what if something breaks? Something interesting is, hey, I built the system. People told me they needed it. It’s in their email. No one’s, no one’s clicking it. But they complain that they have this problem. Like, what do I do? So that was one area. And then partnerships. You know, we’ve been meeting people and people like, hey, you’re doing this. That’s interesting, because we’re doing this. Let’s have a conversation after. So I’ve actually extended my stay in New York, because we’ve like now, I was meant to leave today. We’ve now got meetings on Thursday, extended it another day, Friday, extended it another day, Monday. And then I’ve got now meetings where people are like, hey, we’re in energy. Let’s talk in Houston. So we’ve like filled up a week after the conference of meetings. Oh my god. Yeah. And my team was like, hey, Anekha, another person signed up. Another person signed up. So it’s super cool. 20:32 Is it interesting to do these one to one? I guess because they need to ask you things in private. It just seems very inefficient to set up so many meetings when you could be doing building a business or building the product. Yeah. We try and be as helpful to people where we will have an initial meeting, but then really we want to be able to understand what the problem is that you’re solving for and then have a plan after that. So we have got things that we’re doing now to stream that because like we’re hosting our first webinar because of the amount of inbound that we have. We just can’t always do these one to ones. And so more generally, when I was in the buy side, the banks would actually set up these meetings for us. Yeah. And they’d come to little rooms like this. There’d be sort of a round table. I would meet five at once. So like I’d say I’m a CFO of a company and I need to do investor relations. 21:33 I’m meeting five funds at once and I would be one of the five funds. And I imagine what we could do for you in future, which I haven’t, I have not got this off the ground yet, but we should do the meetings on site. Like you’ve, that makes sense. People like saw your talk. They want to speak more with you. They should be able to sign up and you can do five on one. And probably all these questions are the exact same. And like, that would be a great idea actually, because another, because we used to do this in finance, like that, that is such a good idea. Cause we had one where, um, sometimes you like don’t know what the person you’re meeting looks like as well. Okay. So you’re trying to like take pictures of where you are. Really? It’s like, Hey, meet me here, meet me here and like call them. So an idea like that would be great. So just like an assigned meeting room. Yeah. It’s like, Hey, like. I mean, this whole floor is that, but we had to pre-assign it to other speakers, but, um, we, we wanted to do some dynamic allocation. I just don’t know how to, you know, get that going. I’m trying to fill it out with you. So like, you’re not having to like fly to Houston or even like, even if they’re in New York, you don’t even have to go to their office. 22:34 Everyone just gets in here, gets their meetings done. You’re out. I actually think that would be a great idea. Like have a 30 minute slot for this person and then like sign up. Just like whatever you want. Yeah. Like smaller one, one. That is a great idea. Yeah. Yeah. Uh, I mean anything else that like we, I guess we could do better or like other experiences from the conference that you’re, I think this has been the best organized conference I’ve been to like, no, no, seriously. Like the amount of good quality guidelines I’ve had, and it was super clear, like the speaker team, the breakout rooms, um, the speaker lounge having, I feel like the lounge was never this good. Uh, yeah. So haircut. I know. I didn’t do a facial. I did a facial and a massage. Yeah. I know you got your haircut. I did get my haircut. Yeah. Um, I, I, I mean, we do want to swallow speakers. Uh, this was definitely, uh, over and above and that’s thanks to the cognition for doing that. But, uh, yeah, I mean, uh, organizing is one thing. 23:38 I do think like in terms of business value and efficiency, I think that’s an important, uh, element. Um, because I think what we have with hiring is we get continuous inbound from LinkedIn. Really? Yeah. I had, we had one job up. We had to close it. It was open for four days. We had 2,500 applicants. Okay. Um, and so it’s like, that’s tough to deal with in itself, but meeting people who like want to buy and people who, because I think there’s people who have the problem, but they don’t want to buy. And there’s people who have the problem and want to buy. And then you who are trying to find that match that is, 24:39 I haven’t found any person who’s done that. Um, well, but so I really like your one-on-one idea. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, so basically I’m, I’m transferring over what I used to have as a hedge fund person to this market, which is AI and finance. Yeah. Um, well, we’ll try to do that next year. We’ll try to be the definitive thing. Um, and I think on hiring side, so that that’s buying and then that’s clear. I think, I think I can definitely help you better there. Uh, on the hiring side, I also want to help you. Right. Okay. Like 2,500 is too much and most of it’s noise. And so you need a better filter. Um, I’m just appreciative that you’re spending some time with us and congrats on your success. Thank you so much. I’d love, I have one question, which is how you went, you moved into AI. items.summary_html:
Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year.

When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book.

At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader.

They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring.

0:00 So I’ve actually extended my stay in New York, because we’ve like now, I was meant to leave today. We’ve now got meetings on Thursday, extended it another day, Friday, extended it another day, Monday. And then I’ve got now meetings where people are like, hey, we’re in energy. Let’s talk in Houston. So we’ve like filled up a week after the conference of meetings. AI engineers was an interesting one, because a lot of them are feeling like overwhelmed with the pressure from management. To do what? Because people now say, we don’t need a team, you are the team. And so it’s like, hey, I need to now build this whole system myself. But that system would be typically done by 10 people. Okay, we are in the studio. Last podcast of AIE for me with Anekha from Moshi. Welcome. Thank you so much.

1:01 Did I get it right, Anekha? Yes, you did. So your background caught my interest because I was a former trader and you’re now a founder. Yes. And you also were telling me just about your experience. I kind of want to hear about it from you. As far as I know, this is your first AIE. How did you hear about us? What was the experience like giving your talk and what happened after? Yeah, well, first of all, thank you to everyone at AIE because it’s been such a fantastic experience. And thank you for inviting me on the podcast as well. I’m so excited to just share my experience. And also, I think we’re living in such a fast moving time and everyone I speak to is like very overwhelmed. So it’s really helpful to be able to kind of share everything that I’ve had in my experience because I did my undergrad in statistics and math, which is now what everyone calls AI. And so it’s really interesting to speak about that and the evolution of that and also to always speak to a former trader as well.

2:02 And just to share like war scars on that. Did you do financial calculus, like stochastic calculus? Yeah, I did that. And I so my undergraduate degree was mathematics, operational research, statistics and economics, Morse at Warwick. And it was what everyone was just like, oh, my God, so nerdy. And I hated telling people. And now it’s like, wow. Yeah, everyone’s like, oh, my God, machine learning, AI. Yeah. Yeah. And then derivatives. So I did that. So my background was started in that at Warwick in England and then knew I wanted to work in trading. I don’t know what what your story to go into trading was, but I wanted something which was fast paced and to do with data, like absolutely love data. And it was when I read about what trading was. I could not imagine myself being in any other career. So I was just set on doing that. So I got my first internship in investment banking and trading and then got an internship at JP Morgan where I started.

3:04 And I started on the emerging markets desk and then moved to commodities and did derivative trading there. So most of my career has been in energy derivatives. And because I have that data background, I always looked at the market from I wanted to break it down into all the different parts. So, for example, in commodities, a lot is about the fundamentals and about the different news and the different the physical happening. And so I was always fascinated by like building out from zero. And so when I was trade trade trading, I saw this shift where it’s like a data and then something was going to happen. And that’s when I left JP Morgan to to actually I wanted to be an entrepreneur and and a founder. But I wanted to have a data company. So I got the Fulbright scholarship to come to the US because you guys have such an incredible venture. Just casually got a Fulbright.

4:06 Yeah, I guess the way I say a funny story, I was doing a yoga class in London. I was like, so my parents have a jewelry business. I side hustled a computer vision startup before my startup at university. And so I was like, oh, what are the problems in the jewelry space? Oh, like virtual try on. So that led to me wanting to be a founder. And I thought, how could I be a founder in the best country to be a founder in? And I thought, what I want to be a founder who can talk about the technology. So this was back in like 2020, 2021. And I found Fulbright had a data scholarship and they gave one in the whole of the UK. So I was like, my way to get here is a Fulbright scholarship and they only give one. And this is really funny because I don’t know if you remember 2020 when it was COVID and gas markets were going crazy. So there was there was like gas markets had insane

5:06 volatility. And so when I did my Fulbright interview, they asked me, how do you like, how do you see the future? And I talked about the like global issue of everyone is having the energy market crisis and how data relates to that. And everyone could relate to what I was talking to because like gas prices were crazy. Their electricity bills were going crazy. And so that led me to the US, came here, was deep in machine learning research, published at ICLR with Stability AI, worked in collaboration with NASA, did a lot of a lot of super interesting work, which then led me to Moshi. And what is Moshi? So Moshi, we are building the program that I wish I had when I was trading. So what we do is we provide real time insights for financial traders, starting with commodity and energy markets and macro markets. So what we do is we process more data than is humanly possible to tell you everything that matters to your portfolio right

6:09 now. What kind of data would you be processing that give us an idea of maybe types and an order of magnitude? Types and order of magnitude. So let me start with order of magnitude. So a fun way I explain it to people is it takes me four seconds to say the sentence to you. And in the same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things. So that’s the type of volume of data that we process. In terms of the types of data, this very much comes to me like geeking out about how I would trade. I would break the market up into all the different types of data, which a trader looks at to decide what trade to put on and how to manage the risk. So what I do is I take the market and I say, well, there’s structured data and unstructured data. There’s the time series of the futures market and there’s all of the technical analysis around it. So we’re looking at all of this like statistical indicated, all of the different technical indicators, all of the moving averages.

7:11 That’s one data set. And obviously that is updating constantly. The next data set we look at is the time series for fundamentals markets. So especially in some commodity markets, there’s a lot of demand and supply. And then we look at the unstructured data. So the news is the obvious one. But then there’s also all this alternative data that exists. For example, there’s X data. There’s audio data on podcasts. X Twitter. X Twitter, yes. You read Twitter. OK. So understanding all of these different types of data. And that I would say is the like public availability of data. And there’s this whole other type of data, which is the user’s private data. So I’m sure you had that when you were trading, which is you have the analysts you care about. I can’t come and tell you, hey, you should, you know, read this person because you have who you need. And then you’re going to have your subscriptions that you care about. You’ll have your internal data, right?

8:11 Like some of the companies we speak to, if they are trading markets, trading energy markets, they will have their person for the amount of LNG ships going through the Strait of Hormuz. And so there’s all this data which is personal to the user. So we take those two data points together, do all of the data cleaning, data transformation. We then look at the statistics and machine learning, tag it, kind of create our whole ontology on top of it. And then we put it into the Moshi, like n-dimensional graph. And then we produce the output, which is a piece of software which pushes data to you. So every time you open Moshi, you see something new related to your portfolio. And you can pull data. So LLM, I’m going to give you answers in 30 seconds, which would take you typically days. So do people often say new Bloomberg or is that something that you disagree? You don’t like being characterized as new Bloomberg? Yeah, that’s an interesting question.

9:13 Because obviously that’s the 800 pound gorilla or whatever the British version of saying 800 pound gorilla is. Yeah, you know, I think Bloomberg has certain features, which the Bloomberg chat, it’s a fantastic aspect of the platform. Yeah, for those who don’t know, like traders would transact billions of dollars in chat. And there’s a standardized formula. When my entry into NLP was actually parsing Bloomberg chat into a structured pricing sheet for my logs. And that’s how we did option pricing. Yeah, there’s the Bloomberg chat, which is one thing. I wouldn’t say we’re a new Bloomberg. I’d say we’re a different type of software, which is not. I think this is the easiest way to say it. And I don’t know how controversial this is. But if Bloomberg and Claude and Netflix had a baby. Netflix. It would be Moshi. You have videos? Netflix.

10:14 We actually have a recommendation system, which we’ve internally built, which is if you’re a trader and you’re looking at one thing, you actually care about the second and third order derivatives right now, which you wouldn’t immediately know. I see. And so we’ve built a whole recommendation system where a simple thing, if you’re, let’s bring it back to like an oil trader, and there’s an energy equities company that’s doing something which would indirectly impact oil, you need to know that right now. You’re not going to get that from like a news stream. You will get that from a connected graph, which is showing that to you. Because if those two information points are coming out right now, the only way you can do it is either a human, which is being able to like connect those, or by a mimicking human, sort of like a recommendation system, which can do that. But that’s what we try and do, because I like wish I had that when I was trading. Yeah. Well, you know, there’s a whole addictiveness element of Netflix, which is bad.

11:15 There is. But yeah, it’s very interesting. I think like RecSys is one of the most important parts of AI. And as a curator of AIEs, I actually have every year an LLM RecSys track. And engineers often don’t appreciate how important it is. Like it’s not very well attended, even though some of the people powering these things, I mean, they run RecSys for YouTube, they run Netflix for Netflix, for Instagram and TikTok. And then like nobody shows up. And I’m like, what do you mean? Like you’re not interested in RecSys? You know, I find it really interesting. I think part of it is they make it seem so easy. And it’s like, oh, this is so like... This is the most important system in the entire, you know, company. Exactly. And I’d say there’s arguably something linked to it, which I think some companies do really well, like Spotify, Instagram, which is one thing that people have come out with AI

12:15 is everyone now can build their own Claude dashboards, right? It’s like, hey, I built this myself. Great. Great. If you want to get someone else to use it, that’s your brain in a dashboard or your brain in something. Try and get someone new to incorporate that into their workflow. You’re then no longer dealing with a problem. You’re dealing with a UI problem, which is how did they interact with it? Because sometimes users don’t always use that. One thing that these platforms do really well is they push data to you, which like hooks you. So you naturally don’t even realize you’re on the platform and you’re like, oh, I want that. No, no, I actually want that. And so we’ve been trying to internally as a company understand how does UI relate to a recommendation system? Because our thesis is if you solve for one, you’re naturally also solving for the other. And I think that’s a big thing right now, which is if everyone’s building software, how do you get it to actually be software that people will use? It’s a bit of an interesting take.

13:19 Yeah, a bit of chicken and egg. Well, anyway, I forgot to mention also my background to this. I used to trade currency options in London, actually. And then I spent some time in rates. And it had a very similar career path where you start with EMEA and then you go into maybe G10. Yeah. At least that’s what we call it for currencies. And you ingest a lot of information and really probably LLMs can process it better. So we didn’t have the tooling back when I did this 10 years ago. But now I see that. And then I moved to the buy side where you start paying for alternative data exactly like you did. We were actually one of the very first few at Balyasny to do the X fire hose or Twitter fire hose. Yeah. That’s something like a stupidly expensive, like $300,000 a month data thing that you have to pay for to get all tweets. It used to be free. And you sort of parse them.

14:19 I don’t think I don’t know if it was ever free. It was free for researchers. Okay. But then if you’re like a hedge fund, like you have to buy that. And it’s very noisy. And so my eyes go up because I don’t know if I would trade on those things because sometimes people do just talk random crap. And sometimes people try to manipulate markets by saying stuff. And it just doesn’t matter that much. But we would also have alternative data like satellite information or credit card information or whatever. And so on the buy side, my number one question is, are you looking at my data? Which is probably not. But how do you assure people? How do you integrate with systems that you don’t necessarily even see? Yeah. And I think there’s two questions in there, which is the first one is, if there’s so much data available, how do you know what’s important? So when we’re looking at X data, it’s a natural conversation when we speak to people or let’s even expand it out to any types of data.

15:20 One thing we found with people is they really will have their trusted people who they’ll follow of these voices in industry, especially in commodities. There’ll be the suppliers of commodities. There’ll be the LNG, all of these facilities who will be active on there because it’s the quickest way for them to also give a status update. Wow. So it’s interesting because we found that a lot of our users will tell us about this. So it’s like, oh, OK, so you find it as a trusted source because you believe this certain individual. Sketchy. Right. And so it’s one of those things where we have found a way to try and filter out as much as possible. But when we are showing it to someone, we give a confidence score of, OK, someone is saying this one thing, but this is everything else happening around the conversation. Because what’s interesting to people is if there are divergent sources, like an example would be how many

16:21 ships are going, how many planes are going above us right now. If Reuters is saying something or Bloomberg is saying something, a Wall Street Journal is saying something, they may not all agree. But the fact that they don’t agree is a point of data because is there an opportunity there? Because no one knows. So that’s how we try and give people information. And then the second question is, you know, people’s data sits everywhere. And I think there’s different types of integration. The first one is what about like their messy PDF data? That data is what we’ve built is like a vision language model to understand it. So we’ll take the data that they can upload to their cloud version of Moshi. And then we actually go and we break it down and then build it up in our database. And there are certain types of data where you just have to connect to their systems. And then that’s like more of a conversation. Is it important to, I assume you’re running this vision language model yourself, is it important to own that? Or would you want to lay out, I mean, there’s any number of vendors, Reducto

17:24 is like a non-documenting processing one. How important is it to have your own models versus just use whatever’s off the shelf? I think that’s a question that a lot of companies are battling with right now. The first question for us is we, if someone’s giving us their data, we don’t want to be sending it to a third party. Because there are systems out there which can do these things for you. But you want to make sure that you’ve got that agreement on how are they processing that data? What are they doing with it? That’s the first question. The second one is, if you don’t have a team of engineers, then that is a great solution. But if you do have a team of engineers like us, a fun fact is most of the team has in some capacity worked with NASA, then they want to build the models. But not everyone has that. And so, you know, I think it really depends like where you are as a team. Yeah, got it. Okay, and then coming into your talk, you apparently had a lot of inbound from it.

18:28 This is our first finance focused one. So I was genuinely unsure who we could get in the door. Obviously, we like pitch it and market it very heavily for this crew. What kind of people did you end up talking to? Yeah, we, it was a like fantastic opportunity because we have been like back to back speaking to people. And what we initially thought would be the interest, we’ve had people like, in the past hour messaging me on LinkedIn saying, hey, I saw your court talk. Are you’re in Houston? Can we get a meeting? Or hey, are you in New York? Can we get a meeting? The types of people we’ve had a lot of traders, either at funds, consulting, and then AI engineers was an interesting one, because a lot of them are feeling like overwhelmed with the pressure from management. To do what? Because people now say, we don’t need a team, you are the team. And so it’s like, hey, I need to now build this whole system

19:31 myself. But that system would be typically done by 10 people. So a lot of people have talked to us and they’re like, hey, I need to build a system. But like, you know, do I need to have a swarm of agents? But then like, what if something breaks? Something interesting is, hey, I built the system. People told me they needed it. It’s in their email. No one’s, no one’s clicking it. But they complain that they have this problem. Like, what do I do? So that was one area. And then partnerships. You know, we’ve been meeting people and people like, hey, you’re doing this. That’s interesting, because we’re doing this. Let’s have a conversation after. So I’ve actually extended my stay in New York, because we’ve like now, I was meant to leave today. We’ve now got meetings on Thursday, extended it another day, Friday, extended it another day, Monday. And then I’ve got now meetings where people are like, hey, we’re in energy. Let’s talk in Houston. So we’ve like filled up a week after the conference of meetings. Oh my god. Yeah. And my team was like, hey, Anekha, another person signed up. Another person signed up. So it’s super cool.

20:32 Is it interesting to do these one to one? I guess because they need to ask you things in private. It just seems very inefficient to set up so many meetings when you could be doing building a business or building the product. Yeah. We try and be as helpful to people where we will have an initial meeting, but then really we want to be able to understand what the problem is that you’re solving for and then have a plan after that. So we have got things that we’re doing now to stream that because like we’re hosting our first webinar because of the amount of inbound that we have. We just can’t always do these one to ones. And so more generally, when I was in the buy side, the banks would actually set up these meetings for us. Yeah. And they’d come to little rooms like this. There’d be sort of a round table. I would meet five at once. So like I’d say I’m a CFO of a company and I need to do investor relations.

21:33 I’m meeting five funds at once and I would be one of the five funds. And I imagine what we could do for you in future, which I haven’t, I have not got this off the ground yet, but we should do the meetings on site. Like you’ve, that makes sense. People like saw your talk. They want to speak more with you. They should be able to sign up and you can do five on one. And probably all these questions are the exact same. And like, that would be a great idea actually, because another, because we used to do this in finance, like that, that is such a good idea. Cause we had one where, um, sometimes you like don’t know what the person you’re meeting looks like as well. Okay. So you’re trying to like take pictures of where you are. Really? It’s like, Hey, meet me here, meet me here and like call them. So an idea like that would be great. So just like an assigned meeting room. Yeah. It’s like, Hey, like. I mean, this whole floor is that, but we had to pre-assign it to other speakers, but, um, we, we wanted to do some dynamic allocation. I just don’t know how to, you know, get that going. I’m trying to fill it out with you. So like, you’re not having to like fly to Houston or even like, even if they’re in New York, you don’t even have to go to their office.

22:34 Everyone just gets in here, gets their meetings done. You’re out. I actually think that would be a great idea. Like have a 30 minute slot for this person and then like sign up. Just like whatever you want. Yeah. Like smaller one, one. That is a great idea. Yeah. Yeah. Uh, I mean anything else that like we, I guess we could do better or like other experiences from the conference that you’re, I think this has been the best organized conference I’ve been to like, no, no, seriously. Like the amount of good quality guidelines I’ve had, and it was super clear, like the speaker team, the breakout rooms, um, the speaker lounge having, I feel like the lounge was never this good. Uh, yeah. So haircut. I know. I didn’t do a facial. I did a facial and a massage. Yeah. I know you got your haircut. I did get my haircut. Yeah. Um, I, I, I mean, we do want to swallow speakers. Uh, this was definitely, uh, over and above and that’s thanks to the cognition for doing that. But, uh, yeah, I mean, uh, organizing is one thing.

23:38 I do think like in terms of business value and efficiency, I think that’s an important, uh, element. Like we want to make this, uh, and you know, something that’s useful for you for both hiring and selling, you know, and I don’t know how to balance that because yeah, are you even, what’s, what’s more important to you hiring or selling? So in terms of we’ve just hired and we plan to hire, um, we’re always meeting people, but the priority right now is to meet clients and that’s a priority, not necessarily hiring. Um, because I think what we have with hiring is we get continuous inbound from LinkedIn. Really? Yeah. I had, we had one job up. We had to close it. It was open for four days. We had 2,500 applicants. Okay. Um, and so it’s like, that’s tough to deal with in itself, but meeting people who like want to buy and people who, because I think there’s people who have the problem, but they don’t want to buy. And there’s people who have the problem and want to buy. And then you who are trying to find that match that is,

24:39 I haven’t found any person who’s done that. Um, well, but so I really like your one-on-one idea. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, so basically I’m, I’m transferring over what I used to have as a hedge fund person to this market, which is AI and finance. Yeah. Um, well, we’ll try to do that next year. We’ll try to be the definitive thing. Um, and I think on hiring side, so that that’s buying and then that’s clear. I think, I think I can definitely help you better there. Uh, on the hiring side, I also want to help you. Right. Okay. Like 2,500 is too much and most of it’s noise. And so you need a better filter. I have a strong opinion. Okay. Go ahead. The amount of people who are also doing it in a way where it’s like undercover, not it’s they’re shopping, they’re spying. You have that, but you also have, it’s that like legally not allowed to work. So there’s so much noise in that. It’s like visas and there’s so much noise around that as well. And so when I was a first time, like I am a first time founder, when I first

25:41 started, you don’t know those things. You don’t know the like market. Right. And there’s a lot of noise related to that. Yeah. Okay. Well, we’ll, we’ll try to get that higher signal for you. We want to be a high signal conference. Um, I’m just appreciative that you’re spending some time with us and congrats on your success. Thank you so much. I’d love, I have one question, which is how you went, you moved into AI. Uh, just, just decided to start. Uh, well, I, I left, uh, the hedge fund worlds. I moved into tech and then when the AI wave happens, I realized that I better move very, very quickly to, uh, establish this field. And, um, so I did the AI engineering post and, uh, started this, this conference and the media stuff because I’m, I’m very much of a media person. Yeah. Uh, at my heart. Um, I do miss trading a little bit, but this is very fulfilling because I get to meet real people instead of stare at a screen all day. Uh, yeah, I feel the same. Well, thank you. I think we have to go. Thank you so much. Thanks. Thanks.

When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book.

4:06 Yeah, I guess the way I say a funny story, I was doing a yoga class in London. I was like, so my parents have a jewelry business. 5:06 volatility. And so when I did my Fulbright interview, they asked me, how do you like, how do you see the future? 6:09 now. What kind of data would you be processing that give us an idea of maybe types and an order of magnitude? Types and order of magnitude. So let me start with order of magnitude. items.title: Utopai Becomes a Unicorn as Video AI Takes Off
items.summary: While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI , video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI’s Sora app to launch a new AI film company . Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI , the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology , raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer. The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios , a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential.

items.title: Designing Tools Well
items.summary: This is Chapter 4 of MCP in Practice , a book for software engineers building production-ready MCP tools. Previously: Chapter 1 — The Integration Problem, Chapter 2 — MCP Core Concepts, and Chapter 3 — Your First MCP Server. Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author. Designing Tools Well The tool definition is the user interface the model actually reads What you will understand Why the tool description is the model’s user interface, and the five elements it must carry How to name tools so the model picks the right one without reading your code How to design input schemas the model can fill correctly on the first try When to split one tool into two, and when to merge two into one How to write errors, annotations, and versions that survive contact with real agents The description is the model’s user interface Your server’s code never reaches the model. What reaches it is the tools/list response: a name, a description, an input schema, and a few annotations. That is the entire user interface. Chapter 2 gave you a five-element checklist for judging descriptions — data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, side effects. This chapter puts that checklist to work, because each element answers a question the model or the host is actively asking at the moment of the call. Watch what happens with a weak description. Suppose the http-status server from Chapter 3 had shipped this instead of the description it actually carries: { "name": "lookup_http_status", "description": "Looks up HTTP status codes." } The model learns nothing it needs: which codes are covered, what comes back, whether the call is safe to make without asking the user. A host deciding whether to auto-approve the call is equally blind — “looks up” could mean reading a built-in table or scraping a website. Now the revision the server actually ships: “description”: “Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code. Searches a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes; it makes no network calls. Returns the code’s category, standard phrase, and a one-line usage note. Read-only: it never modifies anything. Accepts integer codes from 100 to 599 and raises an error for anything outside that range.” Read it against the checklist, and notice what each element buys: Data source: “a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes.” The model will not assume it can verify against the live web, and it will not ask the user which table you meant. Scope: “integer codes from 100 to 599.” The model knows what to pass and — just as important — what will be rejected, so it can validate its own arguments before calling. Time behavior: a fixed reference table. The answer is deterministic and does not go stale, which tells the model there is no reason to call twice “just to check.” Result limits: “the code’s category, standard phrase, and a one-line usage note.” One record per call, in a known shape — the model can plan what to do with the result before it arrives. Side effects: “Read-only: it never modifies anything.” This sentence is not for the model at all. It is for the host, which uses it — along with the annotations below — to decide whether the call needs the user’s confirmation. Figure 4.1 What the model and host read in tools/list Notice what the description does not do: it does not teach the model HTTP. The model already knows, roughly, what a 404 is. The description teaches the model about your tool — its boundaries, its cost, its shape. Write for the tool, not the domain. A description that explains the subject matter is documentation for a human; a description that explains the contract is an interface for the model. Name tools like the model is reading a menu When a host shows the model twenty tools from six servers, the model scans names first. Names are compared side by side, sometimes truncated in a user interface, and matched against the user’s words. A good name does half the description’s job before the description is even read. Lead with a specific verb. lookup_http_status beats get_data; search_production_traces beats query. “Get,” “run,” “process,” and “handle” describe nothing — they are the verbs you reach for when you have not decided what the tool does. Name the domain, not the implementation. lookup_http_status, not query_reference_table. The model thinks in tasks, not in your storage layout, and the name should meet it where it thinks. Keep names comparable across a server. If one tool is list_invoices, its sibling is get_invoice, not fetchBill. Every inconsistency forces the model to memorize your thesaurus instead of your tools. Respect the spec’s naming guidance: names should stay within 1 to 128 characters, are case-sensitive, and should stick to letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, and dot — no spaces. Uniqueness within a server is not a nicety; it is how a tool gets addressed at all. Compare two catalogs for the same server: get_data, fetch_info, run_query lookup_http_status, lookup_status_by_category The first catalog forces the model to read every description just to tell the tools apart — and descriptions are longer than names, which means more tokens spent before the first decision is even made. The second catalog decides at the name. That is not a cosmetic difference; it is fewer chances to choose wrong, on every single call, for the life of the server. A useful test: cover the descriptions and read only the names. Can you still tell which tool does what — and, harder, which two are dangerously similar? If lookup_http_status and lookup_http_category blur together at a glance, the names are not doing their job. That blur is also a design signal, and the next section gives it a structural answer. Design the input schema as a contract The input schema is where the model’s creativity meets your server’s discipline. The model is a fluent writer of JSON and an unreliable follower of implications. Every constraint you leave unstated becomes a guess, and every guess becomes a failed call the model must recover from. The schema is the one place where you can remove guessing entirely — treat it as a contract, not a suggestion. Make required truly required and optional truly optional. FastMCP derives this from your function signature: parameters with defaults become optional. If the tool cannot do its job without an argument, give it no default and say so. Prefer enums over free text wherever the valid set is closed. A category parameter typed as a bare string invites “client-errors,” “4xx,” and “client error” — three spellings of one idea. An enum of five fixed values removes the negotiation before it starts: "category": { "type": "string", "enum": ["informational", "success", "redirection", "client_error", "server_error"], "description": "Which 1xx–5xx class to list. Use the singular lowercase value exactly." } Describe every parameter. The per-parameter description is the model’s inline help at the exact moment it fills the argument: the units, the format, and one example. A parameter without a description is a question you declined to answer. Never build a mega-parameter: one query: str that accepts “anything the user might mean.” If the tool needs a service, a time window, and a filter, those are three parameters with three types — not one string your server parses with hope. Bound what the domain bounds. maxLength on free text, minimum and maximum on numbers. The schema rejects cheaply what your code would otherwise reject expensively, and the rejection happens before your function ever runs. Test the schema the way the model will use it: hand the tools/list output to someone who has never seen your server and ask them to write three calls — one normal, one edge case, one deliberately wrong. Every hesitation is a description you still owe, and every wrong guess is a parameter that needs a tighter type. One job per tool: when to split and when to merge Chapter 3’s first mistake was the everything server. The subtler version is the everything tool: one tool that grows a second job because “it’s related.” Related is not the test. The test is whether the two jobs share the same contract with the caller — the same side effects, the same trust, the same approval story. When they don’t, one tool is really two tools wearing a trench coat. Split when any of these differ: Side effects. A tool that reads and a tool that writes must never be one tool with a mode flag. The host approves tools, not modes — it cannot auto-approve half a tool, and the model cannot tell which half it just invoked. Data source or authority. lookup_http_status reads a built-in table. A tool that fetched live definitions from the web would carry different freshness, latency, and trust. Different descriptions, different tools. Approval needs. If one job needs the user to confirm and the other does not, they are two tools. Approval attaches to the tool, never to a parameter value. Failure modes. If half the calls fail for reasons the other half never encounters, the error story has already split — the tool should follow. Merge when the job is genuinely one job and only the parameters vary: an optional verbose flag beats a second tool when the data source, side effects, and result shape are identical and only the detail level changes. The flowchart below is the whole decision: Figure 4.2 Split or merge: one flowchart for the decision When in doubt, split. Two narrow tools with clear names are easier for the model to choose between than one broad tool whose description is full of “or.” Merging is cheap later; untangling a tool that callers already depend on is not — which is a versioning problem, and we will get there. Write errors the model can recover from Chapter 3 drew the line: invalid input raises and becomes an error result; a valid query with a negative answer returns a normal result. That line is the foundation. This section is the architecture built on it — because errors are the model’s only debugging channel, and a tool whose errors don’t teach is a tool the model will misuse twice. The spec gives tools two error channels, and the distinction matters for design. Protocol errors report problems with the request itself — an unknown tool, a malformed envelope — things the model is unlikely to fix. Tool execution errors report problems with the operation: a validation failure, a downstream outage, a business rule. Clients are expected to hand execution errors to the model so it can self-correct, which makes the error message the most leveraged text you will write after the description. A recoverable error has four parts: Name what was wrong, with the value. “code must be between 100 and 599, got 99” lets the model see its mistake and the fix in one line. “Invalid input” names nothing and fixes nothing. Say what to do next. Append the remedy to the message: “Pass an integer from 100 to 599.” An error without a next step is a dead end the model must reason its way around, usually by guessing again. Keep the shape machine-readable. A stable code the caller can switch on, plus the human message — correlated to the request by id, exactly as Chapter 3 showed. Humans read the message; programs read the code; both need to be there. Say whether retrying helps. A validation error is retryable with different arguments; an expired handle means create a new one first (Chapter 2’s stateful-tools pattern); a downstream outage means wait or tell the user. Name the category, or the model will retry the unretryable and abandon the fixable. The difference in practice: Bad: “Invalid input.” Good: “code must be between 100 and 599, got 99. Pass an integer from 100 to 599.” The first message ends the conversation — there is nothing in it to act on, so the model either retries the identical call or abandons the task. The second contains the value, the rule, and the remedy in one line. Write every error as if the reader is a capable colleague who simply cannot see your code, because that is exactly who it is. And one prohibition: never leak internals. No stack traces, no file paths, no SQL, no secret-adjacent detail. The model does not need your traceback to fix its arguments, and the user should never see it. Log the internals to stderr for yourself; send the caller only what the caller can act on. Annotate behavior honestly Descriptions tell the model what a tool does. Annotations tell the host what kind of thing it is. The spec defines an optional annotations object carrying four behavior hints — readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint — plus a human-readable title. They are hints: advisory metadata a client may use for confirmation dialogs and display. They are not enforcement. Your server enforces its own safety; annotations merely advertise it, and the host decides what to believe. readOnlyHint: true means the tool modifies nothing. Set it on lookup_http_status — it is the difference between the host auto-approving the call and interrupting the user to ask. A read-only tool without the hint gets treated with suspicion it has not earned. destructiveHint: true marks irreversible change. Note the spec’s defaults are deliberately conservative: an unannotated tool is treated as potentially destructive, non-idempotent, and externally reaching. Silence is not neutral — it is the strictest possible reading of your tool. idempotentHint: true promises that repeating the call with the same arguments has no additional effect. Claim it only when it is true; hosts and models lean on it when deciding whether a retry is safe. openWorldHint: true means the tool reaches outside the server — network calls, external APIs. Our http-status tool reads a built-in table, so its honest value is false. The day the table becomes a live fetch, the annotation must change with the code. title gives humans a display name — “Look up HTTP status code” — so name can stay a programmatic identifier. Names are for addressing; titles are for reading. As it appears in tools/list, the whole declaration is small and worth getting exactly right: "annotations": { "title": "Look up HTTP status code", "readOnlyHint": true, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true, "openWorldHint": false } The honesty rule is absolute: annotate what the tool does, not what you wish it did. A read-only tool that secretly writes is not a documentation bug — it is a trust violation the host cannot detect, because the host’s approval policy reads your annotations, not your intentions. Review annotations with the same seriousness as the description, and re-review them every time the tool’s behavior changes. Design for retries: idempotency and side effects Networks fail, hosts time out, and models retry. Any tool with a side effect will eventually be called twice for one intention — once by the user, once by the retry. The second call is not a bug in the caller; it is a fact about distributed systems. Design for it before it happens, because retrofitting safety onto a tool that already mutates is where outages are born. Make side-effecting tools idempotent where the domain allows. Accept a client-supplied idempotency key and key the operation on it, or define the operation so repetition converges: setting a value, not incrementing one; ensuring a state, not appending to it. Read before you write. A tool that checks current state before changing it turns “create” into “ensure,” and “ensure” survives retries that would duplicate a blind “create.” Offer a dry run where the stakes are high. A preview parameter that returns what would happen without doing it gives the model a safe way to confirm its plan — and gives the user something concrete to approve. Keep approval in the host. Chapter 2 placed policy there for a reason: the server validates inputs and enforces its own authorization, and the host decides whether the user must confirm. Do not invent a private confirmation dance inside the tool — the host cannot see it, audit it, or apply policy to it, which makes it theater, not safety. Tools are a public API with an unusual property — one of the clients is a language model whose knowledge of your names came from context it may never see again. Version accordingly. Add; don’t change. New optional parameters, new tools, new enum values. Never rename a tool, remove a parameter, or narrow an accepted type. Additive changes are invisible to existing callers; anything else is a migration you are imposing on strangers. A new required parameter is a breaking change, full stop. If the job genuinely needs new input, ship a new tool and deprecate the old one in its description: “Prefer lookup_http_status_v2; this tool remains for compatibility.” Two tools with an honest pointer beat one tool with a surprise. Deprecation lives in the description, because that is where the model actually reads. Say what replaces the tool and, if you know it, when the old one stops working. A deprecated tool that still works is a courtesy; a removed tool is an outage wearing a version number. A deprecation done well reads like this, in the old tool’s description: “Deprecated: use lookup_http_status_v2, which adds an optional detail parameter. This tool remains available and unchanged.” The model sees the pointer at decision time and simply never chooses the old tool again. No migration guide, no breakage — the catalog heals itself one call at a time. Treat tools/list as the live contract. If your catalog changes, the listChanged capability and subscription notifications exist so hosts can refresh — Chapter 2’s advice to design for catalogs that change applies to your own server first. Seven tool-design traps These are not hypothetical. They are the failures that show up in real tool catalogs, including the author’s, usually discovered by watching a model misuse a tool that tested perfectly by hand. The helpful description. “Searches things and returns stuff.” Vague descriptions don’t fail loudly — they fail as wrong tool choices you will never see, because the model quietly picks the wrong tool and moves on. The host approves tools, not modes, so half your tool inherits the other’s trust level. The fix is a split, however inelegant two tools feel. The mind-reading schema. query: str, options: dict — parameters the model must guess at. Every guess is a failed call followed by a recovery, and recoveries cost the user’s patience before they cost tokens. The fix is narrow types, enums, and a description on every parameter. The fix is honesty in both places: the description names everything the tool does, and the annotations match. The dead-end error. “Invalid input.” No value, no rule, no next step. The clever rename. lookup_http_status becomes getHttpStatus for “consistency,” and every saved workflow, prompt, and host config breaks at once. The fix is additive change only, with deprecation declared in the description where the model will actually read it. The untested choice. You tested the tool; you never tested whether the model picks it. Descriptions are UI, and UI gets usability-tested. The fix is adversarial selection testing in the Inspector: give the model a task and two similar tools, and watch which one it reaches for before you ship the catalog. Chapter checkpoint The tools/list response — name, description, input schema, annotations — is the entire user interface the model sees. Design it like one. A strong description carries five elements: data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, and side effects. Each answers a question the model or host is asking right now. Names are scanned side by side: lead with a specific verb, name the domain, keep siblings consistent, and follow the spec’s naming guidance. Input schemas are contracts. Required means required, enums beat free text, every parameter gets a description, and mega-parameters are a design smell. Errors are the model’s debugging channel: name the value, the rule, and the remedy; keep the shape machine-readable and correlated by id; never leak internals. Annotations are honest, advisory metadata — readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint, plus title. Defaults are conservative; silence reads as dangerous. Version additively: new optional parameters and new tools, never renames or removals. Deprecation belongs in the description. The seven traps: the helpful description, the mode flag, the mind-reading schema, the silent side effect, the dead-end error, the clever rename, the untested choice. The model fills arguments from it, and the server validates against it before the tool runs. Output schema: An optional JSON Schema describing the structure of a tool’s result, letting clients validate responses and models parse them reliably. Side effects determine approval needs and must be declared, never silent. Tool names should follow the spec’s naming guidance (1–128 characters, case-sensitive, limited character set). Annotations are advisory hints for hosts — enforce safety in your server code, not in metadata. Check the current specification before treating any detail as settled. Next: Chapter 5 — Resources and Prompts: when the model should read instead of act. Follow to get it when it drops.
