This is Chapter 4 of MCP in Practice, a book for software engineers building production-ready MCP tools.Previously: Chapter 1 — The Integration Problem, Chapter 2 — MCP Core Concepts, and Chapter 3 — Your First MCP Server.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

Designing Tools WellThe tool definition is the user interface the model actually readsWhat you will understand
  • Why the tool description is the model’s user interface, and the five elements it must carry
  • How to name tools so the model picks the right one without reading your code
  • How to design input schemas the model can fill correctly on the first try
  • When to split one tool into two, and when to merge two into one
  • How to write errors, annotations, and versions that survive contact with real agents
The description is the model’s user interface

Your server’s code never reaches the model. What reaches it is the tools/list response: a name, a description, an input schema, and a few annotations. That is the entire user interface. Chapter 2 gave you a five-element checklist for judging descriptions — data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, side effects. This chapter puts that checklist to work, because each element answers a question the model or the host is actively asking at the moment of the call.

Watch what happens with a weak description. Suppose the http-status server from Chapter 3 had shipped this instead of the description it actually carries:

{
"name": "lookup_http_status",
"description": "Looks up HTTP status codes."
}

The model learns nothing it needs: which codes are covered, what comes back, whether the call is safe to make without asking the user. A host deciding whether to auto-approve the call is equally blind — “looks up” could mean reading a built-in table or scraping a website. Now the revision the server actually ships:

“description”: “Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code. Searches a built-in table of standard

HTTP status codes; it makes no network calls. Returns the code’s category, standard phrase, and a

one-line usage note. Read-only: it never modifies anything. Accepts integer codes from 100 to 599

and raises an error for anything outside that range.”

Read it against the checklist, and notice what each element buys:

  • Data source: “a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes.” The model will not assume it can verify against the live web, and it will not ask the user which table you meant.
  • Scope: “integer codes from 100 to 599.” The model knows what to pass and — just as important — what will be rejected, so it can validate its own arguments before calling.
  • Time behavior: a fixed reference table. The answer is deterministic and does not go stale, which tells the model there is no reason to call twice “just to check.”
  • Result limits: “the code’s category, standard phrase, and a one-line usage note.” One record per call, in a known shape — the model can plan what to do with the result before it arrives.
  • Side effects: “Read-only: it never modifies anything.” This sentence is not for the model at all. It is for the host, which uses it — along with the annotations below — to decide whether the call needs the user’s confirmation.
Figure 4.1 What the model and host read in tools/list

Notice what the description does not do: it does not teach the model HTTP. The model already knows, roughly, what a 404 is. The description teaches the model about your tool — its boundaries, its cost, its shape. Write for the tool, not the domain. A description that explains the subject matter is documentation for a human; a description that explains the contract is an interface for the model.

Name tools like the model is reading a menu

When a host shows the model twenty tools from six servers, the model scans names first. Names are compared side by side, sometimes truncated in a user interface, and matched against the user’s words. A good name does half the description’s job before the description is even read.

  • Lead with a specific verb. lookup_http_status beats get_data; search_production_traces beats query. “Get,” “run,” “process,” and “handle” describe nothing — they are the verbs you reach for when you have not decided what the tool does.
  • Name the domain, not the implementation. lookup_http_status, not query_reference_table. The model thinks in tasks, not in your storage layout, and the name should meet it where it thinks.
  • Keep names comparable across a server. If one tool is list_invoices, its sibling is get_invoice, not fetchBill. Every inconsistency forces the model to memorize your thesaurus instead of your tools.
  • Respect the spec’s naming guidance: names should stay within 1 to 128 characters, are case-sensitive, and should stick to letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, and dot — no spaces. Uniqueness within a server is not a nicety; it is how a tool gets addressed at all.

Compare two catalogs for the same server:

get_data, fetch_info, run_query

lookup_http_status, lookup_status_by_category

The first catalog forces the model to read every description just to tell the tools apart — and descriptions are longer than names, which means more tokens spent before the first decision is even made. The second catalog decides at the name. That is not a cosmetic difference; it is fewer chances to choose wrong, on every single call, for the life of the server.

A useful test: cover the descriptions and read only the names. Can you still tell which tool does what — and, harder, which two are dangerously similar? If lookup_http_status and lookup_http_category blur together at a glance, the names are not doing their job. That blur is also a design signal, and the next section gives it a structural answer.

Design the input schema as a contract

The input schema is where the model’s creativity meets your server’s discipline. The model is a fluent writer of JSON and an unreliable follower of implications. "category": {
  "type": "string",
  "enum": ["informational", "success", "redirection", "client_error", "server_error"],
  "description": "Which 1xx–5xx class to list. Use the singular lowercase value exactly."
}

  • Bound what the domain bounds. maxLength on free text, minimum and maximum on numbers. The schema rejects cheaply what your code would otherwise reject expensively, and the rejection happens before your function ever runs.

Figure 4.2 Split or merge: one flowchart for the decision

Bad: “Invalid input.”

Good: “code must be between 100 and 599, got 99. Pass an integer from 100 to 599.”

  • Keep approval in the host. Chapter 2 placed policy there for a reason: the server validates inputs and enforces its own authorization, and the host decides whether the user must confirm. Do not invent a private confirmation dance inside the tool — the host cannot see it, audit it, or apply policy to it, which makes it theater, not safety.
Version tools without breaking callers

The first time you rename a tool, you learn who your callers are: every host configuration, every saved prompt, every agent workflow that named the old string breaks at once. Tools are a public API with an unusual property — one of the clients is a language model whose knowledge of your names came from context it may never see again. Version accordingly.

  • Add; don’t change. New optional parameters, new tools, new enum values. Never rename a tool, remove a parameter, or narrow an accepted type. Additive changes are invisible to existing callers; anything else is a migration you are imposing on strangers.
  • A new required parameter is a breaking change, full stop. If the job genuinely needs new input, ship a new tool and deprecate the old one in its description: “Prefer lookup_http_status_v2; this tool remains for compatibility.” Two tools with an honest pointer beat one tool with a surprise.
  • Deprecation lives in the description, because that is where the model actually reads. Say what replaces the tool and, if you know it, when the old one stops working. A deprecated tool that still works is a courtesy; a removed tool is an outage wearing a version number.

A deprecation done well reads like this, in the old tool’s description: “Deprecated: use lookup_http_status_v2, which adds an optional detail parameter. This tool remains available and unchanged.” The model sees the pointer at decision time and simply never chooses the old tool again. No migration guide, no breakage — the catalog heals itself one call at a time.

  • Treat tools/list as the live contract. If your catalog changes, the listChanged capability and subscription notifications exist so hosts can refresh — Chapter 2’s advice to design for catalogs that change applies to your own server first.
Seven tool-design traps

These are not hypothetical. They are the failures that show up in real tool catalogs, including the author’s, usually discovered by watching a model misuse a tool that tested perfectly by hand.

  1. The helpful description. “Searches things and returns stuff.” Vague descriptions don’t fail loudly — they fail as wrong tool choices you will never see, because the model quietly picks the wrong tool and moves on. The fix is the five-element checklist, applied to every tool, not just the important ones.
  2. The mode flag. One tool, one boolean, two jobs: read versus write, preview versus execute. The host approves tools, not modes, so half your tool inherits the other’s trust level. The fix is a split, however inelegant two tools feel.
  3. The mind-reading schema. query: str, options: dict — parameters the model must guess at. Every guess is a failed call followed by a recovery, and recoveries cost the user’s patience before they cost tokens. The fix is narrow types, enums, and a description on every parameter.
  4. The silent side effect. A “lookup” tool that also logs, caches, or notifies — undeclared, unannotated. The host auto-approved a read and got a write. The fix is honesty in both places: the description names everything the tool does, and the annotations match.
  5. The dead-end error. “Invalid input.” No value, no rule, no next step. The model retries the identical call or abandons the task. The fix names the value, the rule, and the remedy — and says whether retrying helps.
  6. The clever rename. lookup_http_status becomes getHttpStatus for “consistency,” and every saved workflow, prompt, and host config breaks at once. The fix is additive change only, with deprecation declared in the description where the model will actually read it.
  7. The untested choice. You tested the tool; you never tested whether the model picks it. Descriptions are UI, and UI gets usability-tested. The fix is adversarial selection testing in the Inspector: give the model a task and two similar tools, and watch which one it reaches for before you ship the catalog.
Chapter checkpoint
  • The tools/list response — name, description, input schema, annotations — is the entire user interface the model sees. Design it like one.
  • A strong description carries five elements: data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, and side effects. Each answers a question the model or host is asking right now.
  • Names are scanned side by side: lead with a specific verb, name the domain, keep siblings consistent, and follow the spec’s naming guidance.
  • Input schemas are contracts. Required means required, enums beat free text, every parameter gets a description, and mega-parameters are a design smell.
  • Split tools when side effects, data sources, approval needs, or failure modes differ; merge when only parameters vary. When in doubt, split.
  • Errors are the model’s debugging channel: name the value, the rule, and the remedy; keep the shape machine-readable and correlated by id; never leak internals.
  • Annotations are honest, advisory metadata — readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint, plus title. Defaults are conservative; silence reads as dangerous.
  • Design side-effecting tools for the inevitable retry: idempotency keys, read-before-write, dry runs — with approval living in the host, not the tool.
  • Version additively: new optional parameters and new tools, never renames or removals. Deprecation belongs in the description.
  • The seven traps: the helpful description, the mode flag, the mind-reading schema, the silent side effect, the dead-end error, the clever rename, the untested choice.
Design exercise

Take the http-status server from Chapter 3 and put its tool through the full design checklist:

  1. Rewrite the tool description from memory against the five-element checklist. Compare it with the chapter’s version — which element did you drop first?
  2. Invent a second tool for the server, e.g. listing codes by category. Argue split versus merge in two sentences, using the flowchart.
  3. Write the error message for a category outside the enum. Does it name the value, the rule, and the remedy — and does it say whether retrying helps?
  4. Set all four annotations and the title. Then change one fact — the table becomes a live fetch — and list everything that must change with it.
  5. Rename lookup_http_status in your head. List everything that breaks. Now write the deprecation description instead, and notice how much cheaper honesty is than migration.

Keep the answers. The chapters ahead put this tool into production settings, where every design choice made here gets tested under real load.

Key terms

Tool annotation: Optional metadata on a tool definition — readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint, and title — advising the host about the tool’s behavior. Hints inform confirmation and display; they do not enforce safety.

Idempotent tool: A tool for which repeating the call with the same arguments produces no additional effect. Idempotency makes retries safe and should be claimed in annotations only when it is genuinely true.

Input schema: The JSON Schema describing a tool’s accepted parameters. The model fills arguments from it, and the server validates against it before the tool runs.

Output schema: An optional JSON Schema describing the structure of a tool’s result, letting clients validate responses and models parse them reliably.

Side effect: Any change a tool makes beyond returning a value — writing data, calling external systems, sending notifications. Side effects determine approval needs and must be declared, never silent.

References and further reading
  1. Model Context Protocol, “Tools” (Specification, 2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools
  2. Model Context Protocol, “Tool annotations” (blog, 2026–03–16). https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/
  3. Model Context Protocol, Python SDK. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk
  4. Model Context Protocol, “Architecture overview” (2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture

Version note: This chapter targets MCP specification revision 2026–07–28. Tool names should follow the spec’s naming guidance (1–128 characters, case-sensitive, limited character set). Annotations are advisory hints for hosts — enforce safety in your server code, not in metadata. Check the current specification before treating any detail as settled.

Next: Chapter 5 — Resources and Prompts: when the model should read instead of act. Follow to get it when it drops.

items.title: AI agent security is a lifecycle — not a gatekeeper
items.summary: Enterprise security has traditionally operated on a relatively straightforward premise: establish identity, authenticate the requester, determine what that identity can access, and enforce those permissions. AI agents introduce a fundamental complication. They don’t simply access systems. They interpret objectives, select tools, create sub-agents, make decisions, and execute actions, often using credentials and permissions inherited from humans. The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform. And unlike conventional software, agents can change their execution paths dynamically in pursuit of an objective. “The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform.” This creates a new operational requirement: security must evaluate not only who or what is acting, but what an agent is attempting to do, on whose authority, and under which policy. Meeting that requirement takes more than a security checkpoint. It requires a continuous agent security lifecycle. Defense-in-depth needs action-level authorization Every passing day further shows that agent security is a defense-in-depth problem. Network security controls how agents communicate. Endpoint and runtime protections constrain where and how code executes. Infrastructure and silicon-based protections establish a foundation for trusted execution. Model guardrails help shape behavior. These layers complement each other, and enterprises need them to work together. But consider an agent that attempts to delete a production database using a developer’s legitimate credentials. Network controls may see authorized traffic. The runtime may see an approved process. An identity provider may confirm that the credentials are valid. All three could be working as designed. The missing question is whether this particular agent should be allowed to perform this particular action, even if the human whose credentials it inherited could legitimately do so. That requires identity context and authorization at the point of action . In practical terms, an authorization decision should consider the agent’s identity, the human or service that delegated its authority, the requested operation, the target resource, and applicable policy. Enforce that decision before the operation executes. The agent harness (the execution layer that connects an AI model to tools, application programming interfaces (APIs), files, and external systems) is an important place to apply that control. Other trusted enforcement points, including tool services and resource APIs, provide additional protection. The goal isn’t to replace existing defenses. It’s to make authorization integral to agent execution. But even that is only a partial answer because what is needed is a new framework — an agent security lifecycle. Four disciplines, one continuous security lifecycle A practical agent security architecture needs four interconnected disciplines: Observe. Enforce. Build. Deploy. These aren’t sequential gates every organization must pass through. They form a continuous lifecycle, and organizations can enter at whichever point reflects their existing infrastructure and maturity. A company with agents already running in production may begin by observing their behavior. A development team creating a new agent may start by building authorization directly into its architecture. An enterprise expanding an existing deployment may discover new activity that requires revisiting its policies. Each stage informs the others. The cycle never really ends. Observe: Understand what agents actually do Most enterprises have some form of application inventory. Increasingly, they’re extending that inventory to AI agents. That’s a useful starting point, but knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does. Security teams need visibility into the actions agents actually attempt: Which tools and APIs are being invoked? What commands are being executed? Which systems and sensitive resources are being accessed? What credentials and delegated permissions are being used? What sub-agents are being created, and what authority do they inherit? Which actions would violate a proposed security policy? Architectural diagrams or agent configuration files alone can’t reliably answer these questions. The important evidence exists in execution, which is why agent observability must extend beyond conventional logs and application monitoring. Security teams need to connect observed actions with identity, delegation, and authorization context. “Knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does. You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed.” Equally important, observation should support evaluating potential policies without immediately disrupting production activity. There are useful precedents here. When intrusion prevention systems and web application firewalls became widely adopted, organizations learned that immediately enabling aggressive blocking rules could interrupt legitimate applications. Monitoring first, establishing behavioral baselines, and progressively enforcing policies proved more practical. AI agents require similar discipline, although their behavior can be substantially more dynamic. For organizations already deploying agents, the priority may not be to block more activity. It may be to understand what activity is actually occurring. You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed. Enforce: Put deterministic boundaries around probabilistic behavior Once organizations understand how agents behave, they can begin defining and enforcing boundaries. The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. An agent might interpret instructions differently across executions. It may choose different tools, sequence operations differently, or discover alternative ways to accomplish an objective. A security policy cannot depend on the model consistently choosing the safest option. Consider a coding agent with permission to work in a source repository. Reading a file might be permitted. Modifying a protected branch might require human approval. Deleting the repository might be prohibited. All three actions could originate from the same authenticated agent operating in the same environment. But they require different authorization decisions. “The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting. It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent.” Effective enforcement means evaluating the attempted action against policy before execution. A simplified authorization request might contain: Actor: Coding agent 42 Delegated authority: Developer account 17 Requested action: Delete repository Target: Production source repository Policy decision: Deny The important architectural distinction is that the permission check occurs at a trusted enforcement point, not merely within a prompt instructing the model to behave. For high-risk operations, the system may deny execution or require explicit human approval. Lower-risk operations may proceed automatically. Enforcement also needs to account for agents attempting alternative execution paths. A harness-level check only protects actions routed through that harness. Robust designs therefore combine action-level authorization with independently enforced permissions at APIs, tool servers, and underlying resources. The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting. It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent. Build: Make identity and authorization part of the agent architecture Observation and enforcement help organizations secure existing agents. But the greatest long-term benefit comes when those lessons influence how agents are built. Today, developers may implement AI agents using different models, frameworks, tool protocols, and execution environments. If every team must independently design identity propagation, delegated permissions, authorization policies, and audit logging, security becomes inconsistent and difficult to maintain. Instead, these capabilities should be available as reusable infrastructure. Software development kits (SDKs), APIs, and shared authorization services can make it easier to incorporate controls directly into agent applications. That means establishing several architectural expectations from the beginning. An agent should have an identifiable execution context. Its authority should be explicitly delegated and constrained. Sensitive tool invocations should require authorization. Security decisions and consequential actions should be auditable. Importantly, an agent shouldn’t automatically inherit every permission available to the human initiating it. Consider an employee using an AI assistant to reconcile invoices. The employee may have permission to review invoices, approve payments, and update vendor records. The agent’s assigned task requires only invoice retrieval and reconciliation. The correct architecture delegates the permissions required for that task, not the employee’s entire authority. That distinction matters even more when an agent creates sub-agents or invokes tools under different service identities. Developers need mechanisms to preserve and constrain delegated authority throughout those interactions. Security should also be portable across implementations. Organizations shouldn’t have to reconstruct their authorization architecture every time a development team adopts a new framework or model. This is why identity and authorization should be infrastructure, not application-specific features. Done correctly, security becomes something developers build with, rather than something security teams attempt to bolt on after an application is complete. Deploy: Make consistent security possible at machine scale Building a secure agent is one challenge. Operating thousands of agents across applications, departments, cloud environments, and business processes is another. At that scale, manually reviewing permissions or trusting individual development teams to implement controls consistently becomes unsustainable. Agents may invoke new tools, coordinate with other agents, and participate in workflows that span multiple authorization domains. Security controls need to follow them. That requires a deployment architecture that consistently applies identity context, delegated authority, authorization policy, and audit requirements across supported environments. The underlying model or framework shouldn’t determine whether security controls exist. Nor should adopting a new tool require rebuilding the entire security architecture. This is where framework-independent interfaces and centrally managed policy become especially valuable. Organizations can maintain consistent security expectations while allowing development teams to use the technologies best suited to their applications. Deployment also changes the meaning of scale. With traditional applications, scale generally means handling more users, transactions, or workloads. With agents, scale can also mean more independent actors making more decisions, invoking more tools, and creating additional agents. The number of consequential actions can increase much faster than the number of deployed applications. Security architectures must therefore operate automatically and consistently at the pace of machine-generated activity. Deployment creates something else: new evidence. Production activity reveals unexpected workflows, new dependencies, authorization gaps, and opportunities to refine policy. That information feeds directly back into observation and enforcement and informs how the next generation of agents is built. The lifecycle continues. The shift from security as a checkpoint to security as infrastructure The underlying security principles aren’t new. Least privilege, zero trust, separation of duties, identity federation, and defense in depth remain foundational. What’s changing is how consistently those principles must be applied throughout an agent’s lifecycle, and how close enforcement must be to the actions agents take. Traditional security architectures often assume that controlling system access is enough to govern what happens afterward. AI agents challenge that assumption because they can make consequential decisions independently within the access they’ve already been granted. As a result, the security model needs to evolve in three important ways. First, visibility must be based on actual agent behavior rather than configuration alone. Second, authorization must evaluate individual actions in the context of identity, delegation, and policy. Third, these capabilities must become reusable infrastructure that accompanies agents from development through production and back into continuous improvement. This is why treating agent security as a lifecycle, rather than a collection of isolated controls, matters. Observation supplies evidence. Enforcement establishes boundaries. Development incorporates those boundaries into applications. Deployment extends them consistently across environments and feeds new evidence into the cycle. Each stage makes the others more effective. Securing the agentic era without slowing it down Organizations face two tempting extremes. One is to trust agents too broadly, assuming that legitimate credentials and well-written instructions provide sufficient protection. The other is to constrain agents so aggressively that the productivity gains motivating their adoption disappear. Neither is a sustainable long-term strategy. “Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable.” A better approach is to establish the visibility, accountability, and controls that make greater autonomy possible. That means knowing what agents actually do, enforcing what they’re permitted to do, building those controls into the development process, and deploying them consistently at scale. It also means recognizing that the work is never finished. New models, frameworks, tools, and workflows will continuously introduce new behaviors and risks. Agent security cannot be a one-time approval at the beginning of a deployment. It must be a continuous discipline that evolves with the agents themselves. Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable. It takes a continuous lifecycle, not a gatekeeper.
items.summary_html:
Enterprise security has traditionally operated on a relatively straightforward premise: establish identity, authenticate the requester, determine what that identity can access, and enforce those permissions.

AI agents introduce a fundamental complication. They don’t simply access systems. They interpret objectives, select tools, create sub-agents, make decisions, and execute actions, often using credentials and permissions inherited from humans.

The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform. And unlike conventional software, agents can change their execution paths dynamically in pursuit of an objective.

“The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform.”

This creates a new operational requirement: security must evaluate not only who or what is acting, but what an agent is attempting to do, on whose authority, and under which policy. Meeting that requirement takes more than a security checkpoint. It requires a continuous agent security lifecycle.

Defense-in-depth needs action-level authorization

Every passing day further shows that agent security is a defense-in-depth problem. Network security controls how agents communicate. Endpoint and runtime protections constrain where and how code executes. Infrastructure and silicon-based protections establish a foundation for trusted execution. Model guardrails help shape behavior. These layers complement each other, and enterprises need them to work together.

But consider an agent that attempts to delete a production database using a developer’s legitimate credentials. Network controls may see authorized traffic. The runtime may see an approved process. An identity provider may confirm that the credentials are valid. All three could be working as designed.

The missing question is whether this particular agent should be allowed to perform this particular action, even if the human whose credentials it inherited could legitimately do so.

That requires identity context and authorization at the point of action.

In practical terms, an authorization decision should consider the agent’s identity, the human or service that delegated its authority, the requested operation, the target resource, and applicable policy. Enforce that decision before the operation executes.

The agent harness (the execution layer that connects an AI model to tools, application programming interfaces (APIs), files, and external systems) is an important place to apply that control. Other trusted enforcement points, including tool services and resource APIs, provide additional protection.

The goal isn’t to replace existing defenses. It’s to make authorization integral to agent execution. But even that is only a partial answer because what is needed is a new framework — an agent security lifecycle.

Four disciplines, one continuous security lifecycle

A practical agent security architecture needs four interconnected disciplines:

Observe. Enforce. Build. Deploy.

These aren’t sequential gates every organization must pass through. They form a continuous lifecycle, and organizations can enter at whichever point reflects their existing infrastructure and maturity.

A company with agents already running in production may begin by observing their behavior. A development team creating a new agent may start by building authorization directly into its architecture. An enterprise expanding an existing deployment may discover new activity that requires revisiting its policies.

Each stage informs the others. The cycle never really ends.

Observe: Understand what agents actually do

Most enterprises have some form of application inventory. Increasingly, they’re extending that inventory to AI agents.

That’s a useful starting point, but knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does.

Security teams need visibility into the actions agents actually attempt:

  • Which tools and APIs are being invoked?
  • What commands are being executed?
  • Which systems and sensitive resources are being accessed?
  • What credentials and delegated permissions are being used?
  • What sub-agents are being created, and what authority do they inherit?
  • Which actions would violate a proposed security policy?

Architectural diagrams or agent configuration files alone can’t reliably answer these questions. The important evidence exists in execution, which is why agent observability must extend beyond conventional logs and application monitoring. Security teams need to connect observed actions with identity, delegation, and authorization context.

“Knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does. You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed.”

Equally important, observation should support evaluating potential policies without immediately disrupting production activity. There are useful precedents here. When intrusion prevention systems and web application firewalls became widely adopted, organizations learned that immediately enabling aggressive blocking rules could interrupt legitimate applications. Monitoring first, establishing behavioral baselines, and progressively enforcing policies proved more practical.

AI agents require similar discipline, although their behavior can be substantially more dynamic.

For organizations already deploying agents, the priority may not be to block more activity. It may be to understand what activity is actually occurring.

You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed.

Enforce: Put deterministic boundaries around probabilistic behavior

Once organizations understand how agents behave, they can begin defining and enforcing boundaries.

The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. An agent might interpret instructions differently across executions. It may choose different tools, sequence operations differently, or discover alternative ways to accomplish an objective.

A security policy cannot depend on the model consistently choosing the safest option. Consider a coding agent with permission to work in a source repository. Reading a file might be permitted. Modifying a protected branch might require human approval. Deleting the repository might be prohibited.  All three actions could originate from the same authenticated agent operating in the same environment. But they require different authorization decisions.

“The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting. It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent.”

Effective enforcement means evaluating the attempted action against policy before execution. A simplified authorization request might contain:

  • Actor: Coding agent 42
  • Delegated authority: Developer account 17
  • Requested action: Delete repository
  • Target: Production source repository
  • Policy decision: Deny

The important architectural distinction is that the permission check occurs at a trusted enforcement point, not merely within a prompt instructing the model to behave. For high-risk operations, the system may deny execution or require explicit human approval. Lower-risk operations may proceed automatically.

Enforcement also needs to account for agents attempting alternative execution paths. A harness-level check only protects actions routed through that harness. Robust designs therefore combine action-level authorization with independently enforced permissions at APIs, tool servers, and underlying resources.

The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting.

It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent.

Build: Make identity and authorization part of the agent architecture

Observation and enforcement help organizations secure existing agents. But the greatest long-term benefit comes when those lessons influence how agents are built.

Today, developers may implement AI agents using different models, frameworks, tool protocols, and execution environments. If every team must independently design identity propagation, delegated permissions, authorization policies, and audit logging, security becomes inconsistent and difficult to maintain.

Instead, these capabilities should be available as reusable infrastructure. Software development kits (SDKs), APIs, and shared authorization services can make it easier to incorporate controls directly into agent applications. That means establishing several architectural expectations from the beginning.

An agent should have an identifiable execution context. Its authority should be explicitly delegated and constrained. Sensitive tool invocations should require authorization. Security decisions and consequential actions should be auditable.

Importantly, an agent shouldn’t automatically inherit every permission available to the human initiating it. Consider an employee using an AI assistant to reconcile invoices. The employee may have permission to review invoices, approve payments, and update vendor records. The agent’s assigned task requires only invoice retrieval and reconciliation. The correct architecture delegates the permissions required for that task, not the employee’s entire authority.

That distinction matters even more when an agent creates sub-agents or invokes tools under different service identities. Developers need mechanisms to preserve and constrain delegated authority throughout those interactions.

Security should also be portable across implementations. Organizations shouldn’t have to reconstruct their authorization architecture every time a development team adopts a new framework or model. This is why identity and authorization should be infrastructure, not application-specific features.

Done correctly, security becomes something developers build with, rather than something security teams attempt to bolt on after an application is complete.

Deploy: Make consistent security possible at machine scale

Building a secure agent is one challenge. Operating thousands of agents across applications, departments, cloud environments, and business processes is another. At that scale, manually reviewing permissions or trusting individual development teams to implement controls consistently becomes unsustainable. 

Agents may invoke new tools, coordinate with other agents, and participate in workflows that span multiple authorization domains. Security controls need to follow them. That requires a deployment architecture that consistently applies identity context, delegated authority, authorization policy, and audit requirements across supported environments.

The underlying model or framework shouldn’t determine whether security controls exist. Nor should adopting a new tool require rebuilding the entire security architecture. This is where framework-independent interfaces and centrally managed policy become especially valuable. Organizations can maintain consistent security expectations while allowing development teams to use the technologies best suited to their applications.

Deployment also changes the meaning of scale. With traditional applications, scale generally means handling more users, transactions, or workloads. With agents, scale can also mean more independent actors making more decisions, invoking more tools, and creating additional agents. The number of consequential actions can increase much faster than the number of deployed applications. Security architectures must therefore operate automatically and consistently at the pace of machine-generated activity.

Deployment creates something else: new evidence. Production activity reveals unexpected workflows, new dependencies, authorization gaps, and opportunities to refine policy. That information feeds directly back into observation and enforcement and informs how the next generation of agents is built.

The lifecycle continues.

The shift from security as a checkpoint to security as infrastructure

The underlying security principles aren’t new. Least privilege, zero trust, separation of duties, identity federation, and defense in depth remain foundational.

What’s changing is how consistently those principles must be applied throughout an agent’s lifecycle, and how close enforcement must be to the actions agents take. Traditional security architectures often assume that controlling system access is enough to govern what happens afterward. 

AI agents challenge that assumption because they can make consequential decisions independently within the access they’ve already been granted. As a result, the security model needs to evolve in three important ways.

First, visibility must be based on actual agent behavior rather than configuration alone.

Second, authorization must evaluate individual actions in the context of identity, delegation, and policy.

Third, these capabilities must become reusable infrastructure that accompanies agents from development through production and back into continuous improvement.

This is why treating agent security as a lifecycle, rather than a collection of isolated controls, matters. Observation supplies evidence. Enforcement establishes boundaries. Development incorporates those boundaries into applications. Deployment extends them consistently across environments and feeds new evidence into the cycle.

Each stage makes the others more effective.

Securing the agentic era without slowing it down

Organizations face two tempting extremes. One is to trust agents too broadly, assuming that legitimate credentials and well-written instructions provide sufficient protection. The other is to constrain agents so aggressively that the productivity gains motivating their adoption disappear. Neither is a sustainable long-term strategy.

“Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable.”

A better approach is to establish the visibility, accountability, and controls that make greater autonomy possible. That means knowing what agents actually do, enforcing what they’re permitted to do, building those controls into the development process, and deploying them consistently at scale. It also means recognizing that the work is never finished. New models, frameworks, tools, and workflows will continuously introduce new behaviors and risks.

Agent security cannot be a one-time approval at the beginning of a deployment. It must be a continuous discipline that evolves with the agents themselves. Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable.

It takes a continuous lifecycle, not a gatekeeper.
