Sure.

We built price signals to deal with scarcity, to say, “Let’s encourage people to be brain surgeons because we have a shortage of brain surgeons,” and that’s very hard to do. As you move into abundance, you don’t need those price signals.

But again, my issue, my prescriptions thinking, is about how we get through this 20-year period. The questions that are deeply religious, philosophical, social behavior-related — do humans feel a strong sense of purpose and get along in that period of abundance? — that’s not the thing I’m going to solve.

You’re worried about the disruption now.

The Gates Foundation lives in a world where when we started, we had 10 million children dying every year. Now we have five million. That’s a good thing.

All of my resources will be spent over the next 19 years to eradicate a number of diseases and cut those deaths in half again, from five million a year down below two and a half million per year. That’s all about shortages — “Okay, we need to invent a vaccine, we need to make drugs less expensive, we need to get great medical advice to pregnant women.”

The industry has largely stopped talking about how it’s going to kill everyone and take the jobs away. They’ve pivoted to “AI will cure all diseases.” I hear this from various AI CEOs all the time.

I actually asked Mustafa about that change in tone over the conversations we have had over the past year or so. The idea that there are huge positive benefits from AI at scale seems to have come back to the forefront, rather than some of the doomer impulses that maybe a year or two ago were there.

It strikes me that AI curing all diseases is right in your strike zone. It’s something the Gates Foundation has been working on in global health for years and years. It doesn’t seem as easy as just telling the model to cure cancer. You have to do trials, you have to manufacture the drugs, you have to distribute the drugs, you have to make sure they work.

How do you think that’s going to go? Is that in the same 20-year time period as the robots building our houses? Is it faster, or is it slower?

This is my full-time job as chairman of the Gates Foundation. In fact, this month we do two weeks of strategy reviews to decide how we’ll spend our money next year on tuberculosis, HIV, and malaria. It’s fantastic how we’re using AI, not only on the drug discovery side, but also as we get the African languages to be properly understood by these models, which is an initiative we announced with 60 partners last month.

Healthcare discovery and delivery will be incredibly accelerated by AI, and that’s very exciting — better seeds, better livestock genetics, weather forecast for farmers in Africa, who never had any of those things. So yes, that’s good stuff that AI enables during the remaining 19 years of the Gates Foundation.

The good stuff does take time. Some of the things, like cyberattacks and the job market thing, even in the next two to three years, you’ll see significant negative effects in those two areas

Do you think that that is enough to overcome people’s skepticism or fear of the AI models they encounter today? Because that is very much how the companies think about it.

No, come on. I think it’s unfair to say they were totally on a doomer message and now they’ve switched to some other message. These two things are deeply entangled.

AI will eventually be able to model human biology in such a way that you’ll understand the side effects of a drug without having to do human trials. We’re not there, but in the next five to 10 years, there’s a very good chance these in silico models will give us that capability. Biology is very complex, AI is extremely good given enough data, and there are new tools to gather and feed it more data. It’s very, very good at dealing with complex systems, so it’s almost perfect for biology.

But no, that doesn’t mean that people will feel good about the downsides. How quickly do the good things arrive? How quickly do you look at your medical bill and go, “Wow, that’s really low”? Or you say, “I want to buy a new house, wow, these houses are sure cheap”? The good stuff does take time. Some of the things, like cyberattacks and the job market thing, even in the next two to three years, you’ll see significant negative effects in those two areas.

You have a number of ideas for how you would stop those negative effects, or prevent or at least mitigate them, in your letter.

Moderate them, yes.

Ameliorate might be the right word.

Yes, exactly.

And they’re not small. You have a quote here that says, “We need a response far greater than the United States national security response in the wake of 9/11.” You want to set up an international body that somehow makes everyone do the right thing. These are challenging ideas.

Absolutely. When we blew off nuclear bombs in World War II, did we expect that we’d go 80 more years without that happening? I’d give us a good grade on that. Things like caring for poor countries and helping them out — although right now we’re not prioritizing that as much as I think we should or we did in the past, we’ve done a very good job on that. This will be a greater challenge than anything humanity’s ever achieved.

One of the things that strikes me about the comparison to nuclear, which has come up quite a bit on Decoder recently, is the government built the nuclear weapons. Sure, they had some contractors, but these were government projects and eventually the technology was in control of the government, and we never let regular people have it.

Think about Muse in the context of nuclear weapons. Do you think it’s a mistake to have consumer agentic AI products like Muse and Dots that might not have the controls?

Muse happens to be powered by Meta’s model, which is still a closed-source model. I do think allowing people through open weights to remove all safeguards is irresponsible in terms of the cyber and bio risk that comes from that.

For these agents, there’ll be some early problems in terms of how they’re set up, but I fundamentally think people will have personal agents. Muse is a very nice step forward. I talked to Alexandr Wang about it, congratulated him, and even though it’ll have challenges, personal agents will help people get things done.

Muse is the first truly great consumer AI product. One of the reasons people don’t like AI a lot in a diffuse way is they experience cheap free models and AI overviews or they use the free ChatGPT and it hallucinates and it lies to them, but Muse actually does things and it’s a good consumer product.

But I wonder — in the nuclear age, we were not saying, “Everyone is going to have a nuclear reactor at home that we haven’t built the safety guards for.” There’s something here.

The notion of letting everybody make smallpox at home or make nuclear weapons at home, of course, and you can parody some of these people saying, “Don’t worry about safeguards.” It’s taking that position. “We are not serious about the safety things.”

But the personal agent thing is an expected development. AIs are really cool just as I intellectually explore things, even the work of the Gates Foundation. I’m far more empowered. But I agree with you, it’ll get out to more people in this personal agent form.

The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd

All the models we’ve been talking about right now effectively run on data centers owned by big companies. One of the arguments here is, “If they do something really wrong, you can just sue them and that will provide a deterrent or at least an incentive to create safety systems.”

I’m not sure product liability is the way to go, but it has come up a lot that product liability itself will keep the industry in line. Then there’s the flip side, which is that you can just go buy a Mac Studio and run an open source and open weight model on it and it can do whatever you want.

I’m not sure where any of that liability would lie or what would control or align the behaviors of those open source models. Do you think that that is an ever-growing risk? Do you think that that can be controlled?

The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd. When bad people do bioattacks, you don’t go to the court and say, “Oh, okay.” Even for finding who is doing these attacks, the liability model fails in every respect because it’s not the AI companies themselves. It’s the people who take particularly the models without safeguards and do these things.

We will take AI safety more seriously than we take airline safety, drug safety, and car safety. That is guaranteed. Whether it’s going to be enough… This is harder, harder than nuclear weapons, harder than any of those other domains.

But what are you going to do about an open source model running on a PC that somebody built with just a random Nvidia graphics card in it?

I would hope that with models above a certain capability, we find a way to require the safeguards and monitoring to be maintained in those models. I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see.

But where do you impose the limit?

A sovereign country says that models that are capable of sophisticated cyberattacks have to have safeguards kept in them.

Sure.

You can be open in the sense that you’re free, you can be open in the sense that you’re totally customizable, but you have to stay on platforms where, as you customize it, it’s checking to see if you’re customizing out the safeguards and monitoring and refusing to let you do that. So it means sovereigns go and say, “Are these trusted platforms able to perform this function or not?”

I’m asking very nuts and bolts. Where would you technically implement that regulation?

Through the laws of the United States.

Sure, but you have to put them somewhere. Is it at the Hugging Face, which distributes some of these models? Is it at the chip level?

No, it’s exactly what I said: Models above a certain capacity can only be run on platforms that certify that, as they’re customized, it’s not taking out the safeguards.

I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see

Just to pull this apart, maybe I’m not quite getting it — is the Mac Studio a platform in that case that would have to pay attention to what code it’s running?

You would not let a model past a certain capability be copied down to a client machine unless you’d somehow figured out how to monitor down to that client machine, which is very doable.

But in the near term, most of these really frontier models are going to run more on Hugging Face or you could have them on GitHub. You can have all sorts of people be in the business of providing the platforms that maintain safeguards.

Just to get this right, it seems like you would enforce the regulation at the platform and distribution level and not so much at the chip level.

Not at the chip level, no.

Because it feels to me at some point even the cheap, free, open source models will be capable enough as the models we have today.

That’s right.

And then you will have a big problem.

If those are open weights in such a way that all safeguards can be removed, then you’re going to have a very high level of cyberattacks and bioattacks. You can then say, “Okay, let’s rewrite all the code that we have today to be less subject to attack or let’s do biosurveillance in a very deep way,” which are things I believe we need to do in addition to these other restrictions.

We’re proposing again a lot of new capabilities, right?

Yeah.

We’re going to impose some restrictions on GitHub. GitHub does not have a lot of restrictions on what code it can distribute today. It has some, but it doesn’t have this kind of set of restrictions.

When you put a state-of-the-art model that’s capable of profound cyberattacks or bioattacks on GitHub, it would say, “I’ve gone to the U.S. government and certified that I don’t let people customize out the safeguards.”

I do not think that we currently live in a time of high trust in institutions. It just doesn’t feel that way to me. In fact, mostly we’ve torn them down. Elon Musk showed up and he tore down USAID. I know you have strong feelings about that.

That was a mistake.

We have mostly torn down our institutions, for good and bad.

No, that’s a little too strong. Our institutions-

They’re weakened.

They’re somewhat weakened, yeah.

Somewhat weakened. It’s a very nice way of putting it. Trust in them is very low. We could probably do another full hour on AI drug discovery and whether a significant part of the population will trust the products of that work because they don’t trust pharma companies today.

They don’t have to trust pharma companies today. They have to trust the FDA review process.

I’m not sure they trust that either. Across the board, trust is low.

Then they can walk away from taking them. When they get cancer, they can say, “No, I don’t want to take that cancer drug.” As far as I know, people do take drugs. It’s a thriving business and people take them because they have proven benefits.

All I’m saying is, right now it feels like trust in institutions, particularly in America but around the world, is in decline. You are proposing a new class of institutions, potentially a new class of global institutions that might impose restrictions that are novel.

At some point we need to say open source models, open weight models cannot do things and the government is going to reach into them and say whether or not they can do the things.

No, they’ll make sure that the platforms don’t allow the safeguards to be taken away.

How do you regain the institutional trust to impose these controls?

Let’s say we don’t do this and we let models go off and do cyberattacks and bioattacks. Do you think that’s going to increase trust or human wellbeing? That’s the alternative.

This is why I’m asking about it. This is why I asked about my kids and nihilism. I truly wonder about this.

I’m not sure we’ll succeed at this, but I guarantee you this is doable. The FDA is very complex. The airline safety regulations are very complex. Now with AI, you can do an even better job with the same number of people in those organizations.

It’s this weirdly recursive thing where AI will be involved in AI safety and auditing and a variety of things like that. Yes, this requires taking action, and I’m suggesting it’s only a matter of how bad the incidents are before we take action.

People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices

I can sense your urgency about the harms. I can also sense your enthusiasm about the benefits over the long term, but we’re sitting here talking about trust. We’re going to put this on YouTube. I know you know what some of the YouTube commenters are going to say.

They’re going to say, “Why should we trust Bill Gates? He had a relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.” How do you respond to that? Is it that the urgency is over that, or do you have a more specific response?

People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices.

I’ve been in the technology industry thinking about AI my whole life, writing software, thinking about the power of software. I admit I was very fascinated as AI started to finally make progress. It was actually pretty slow until recently.

I’m amazed and it’s actually helping me do my job in some incredible ways. But yes, I’m just one voice, an imperfect voice. I doubt you’ll find a perfect voice, but people can judge it however they like.

I would say voices people trust are in short supply.

I agree with that.

When you go and talk to the people in this industry, it’s a bunch of young CEOs building huge companies. That is something you have some experience with. Do you think they’re going about this the right way? Do you think that they have the right intentions?

Our problem today is not in the industry. Our problem is not that Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella, or Sundar Pichai don’t understand that there are some grave challenges here. I talk less to Elon than other people, but even his public statements about summoning the demon are exactly what we’re discussing here.

Why is there not the political energy to do the things you’re suggesting?

As you said, the government didn’t fund this work. This is private sector company work. The government is not the key customer for this work, not like rockets and weapons and things like that. When somebody comes along and says all other previous technology advances are trivial compared to this one, people should have a high degree of skepticism about that.

Is life really going to be significantly different 10 years from now because of AI? People should say, “Those guys just got overexcited about this one thing.” But I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this. I’m suggesting some precautions and safeguards are absolutely needed.

What do you make of the difference in the tenor of conversation in the United States versus in China, where it’s often reported that optimism around AI is much higher? Why do you think there’s a difference there?

Most of those people don’t spend that much time in China. The concern about job markets in China is very, very high and you can’t characterize China as one monolith. There are the private companies doing the AI work like we have in the United States and then there’s the Chinese government.

For example, when it came to whether crypto should be allowed, they said no. Should young people be gambling all the time? They said no. When it came to whether kids should have relationships with AIs, they said no. On a lot of these things, including usage of AI, they’re showing a willingness to do things on behalf of society.

I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this

The fervor is a tiny bit less there, because their economy isn’t as AI-centric as ours is right at the moment. In the end, [when it comes to] the human value of not wanting cyberattacks or bioterrorism or trying to figure out what do we do when jobs go away, I don’t think there’s some difference between Chinese people and Americans and all the rest of the humans in terms of how they’re going to view this.

Do you think it’s going to take something actually bad happening to get the political capital of the United States to make these changes?

Probably yes. We get ready for earthquakes because there are small earthquakes. I thought after we had the COVID pandemic, that would cause us to be more ready for future pandemics. That one didn’t work the way I expected.

But usually that galvanizes our attention. Over the next several years, certainly in the cyber domain, because there’s a business model there, you will see a lot of attacks different in terms of scale than anything we’ve seen in the past.

There is one thing that, again, I’ll come back to and I just want to end here. I am worried about young people and nihilism. I sense it in our audience all the time. We have a young audience.

There are some things about AI that are just legitimately the coolest things I’ve ever seen a computer do. There’s something there that can be fun and interesting and fascinating and change your entire relationship with the very notion of living in a digital world.

Then there are obviously horrible things. What I see more often than not is a sense of distrust, not just in institutions, but also in the companies, in capitalism itself, in the notion that we should change how we tax labor and capital, which I know is another one of your ideas. The idea that, I don’t know, we should even have more kids. It’s all done. They’re going to kill us all and we should just take a beat.

There is a lot of nihilism out there. I feel it very keenly. If you were a young person today and you were listening to Bill Gates say it’s about 20 years of disruption and at the end of it, robots might be building houses, what would you hold onto as a source of hope?

Throughout human history, we’ve been dealing with the shortage of food and disease and war. [Historian] Yuval Noah Harari writes eloquently about the past. And it is ironic that now that we have this sort of Pandora’s box that will take food shortage — which is still a real thing, not in the U.S., but in Africa — will take diseases, where human suffering is unbelievable, and solve all these things, it comes with it such an effect on jobs and our sense of unique contribution.

I think, “The way I orchestrate resources to eradicate malaria, I’m pretty unique in my life experience that lets me do that.” But when the AI says to me, “No, I’m better than you. You go play pickleball and I’ll get back to you. I’m going to take care of this,” it’s humorous, but it’s not humorous. For somebody who is young today and wants to make a unique contribution, it is very intimidating that the AI is so powerful.

That’s why the crisis in the math community is going to be mirrored everywhere. If you’re in your twenties today, during this 20-year period, you can take the things AI still can’t do, and you can use AI and you can have a lot of good impact, and you can suggest policies. We may need to develop the taste to actually not use technology to its maximum.

Even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history

When I was talking with Claude about human-reserved job categories and trying to get that up to, say, 40 percent of the labor market — so you could use early retirement, restricted work weeks, and things like that to still get something like we have today — its response was always, “You’re artificially restricting the AI from doing these things.” I couldn’t get to a very high percentage without doing that.

We’re going to have real choices. We have had groups — not large groups, but like the Amish — who don’t live at the technology frontier. A lot of humanity may choose not to live at the technological frontier because of things we get from helping each other or coming up with unique ideas.

On the idea that young people are concerned because of the disruption that’s coming — that even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history — I hate being the bearer of concerning news on this, but it’s even worse not to tell people that this is coming. We have choices as humans to make about how we shape it.

Bill, I appreciate you sounding the alarm and I appreciate you being on Decoder. Thank you so much.

Thank you.

items.title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
items.summary: A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review. By Sergio De Simone

items.title: The Lazy Python Tutor: I built a tutor for people who don't want a tutorial
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest 2026 DEV Challenge — Week 3: Slow and Steady. What I built The Lazy Python Tutor — ask any Python question, get a plain-English explanation first, then a short runnable example, then one tiny optional practice prompt. That's it. No 40-minute video. No 12 documentation tabs. No homework list. Live app: https://lazy-py-tpvbo7rexyrv4af4lv64qb.streamlit.app/ Repo: https://github.com/ashleygirl3723/lazy-python-tutor Try asking: What is a variable? How do loops work? Why does my code say IndentationError? — paste your broken code and it names the most likely problem, shows the fixed version, and says what changed in one sentence. It remembers the conversation, so follow-ups build on what you already asked. Why I built this — honestly I'm learning Python myself, in a 30-day self-paced course, mostly on my laptop between caregiving shifts. I know exactly where beginners quit: not because Python is hard, but because every small question turns into a huge tutorial. "What does elif mean?" should not require watching half a course. I kept wishing I could just ask — in plain words, get a plain answer, see one tiny example, and move on with my day. So for "Slow and Steady" — build something with open-weight AI that rewards laziness — I built the tutor I wanted. Laziness here isn't cutting corners. It's respecting your time and energy. Slow and steady is literally how I'm learning: one small question at a time. The design enforces that in the system prompt, which is the whole brain of the app: Plain English first — no jargon without immediately explaining it Then a short example — usually under 10 lines, nothing extra Then one tiny practice prompt — labeled "Feeling ambitious? Try this:" — genuinely tiny, always optional Hard rules in that prompt: keep it under ~200 words plus code, never dump code without explaining it first, and if code is broken, name the one most likely problem — not a lecture. That last part matters to me personally. My most common mistakes are picky syntax things — capitalized If/Print (phone autocorrect loves that one), missing colons, missing indents, dropping the variable after elif. A good lazy tutor spots the one thing, fixes it kindly, and doesn't make you feel dumb for it. How it's built Streamlit chat interface, Python, deployed free on Streamlit Cloud — runs in any browser, phone included Open-weight models via OpenRouter's free tier — openrouter/free auto-router picks a working free open-weight model per call. No credit card, no paid API. One system prompt does the teaching — the tutor's personality, answer shape, and honesty rules all live in one readable block at the top of app.py. Anyone who forks this can retune the tutor by editing plain English, not code logic. Conversation memory via Streamlit session state — follow-ups keep context. Total running cost: $0. Why open innovation matters for this build I'm a caregiver learning to code on the side. I don't have a budget for AI APIs, and a learning tool that charges per question would teach me to stop asking questions — the exact opposite of learning. Open weights fix that: Asking is free. Every "wait, why?" costs nothing. A beginner can ask the dumb question, the follow-up, and the follow-up to the follow-up without a meter running. That's how slow-and-steady learning actually works. No one can pull the plug. If a closed provider raises prices, retires a model, or changes terms, a closed-API tutor dies on their schedule. With open weights + an open router, when one free model is busy, the request goes to another — the app keeps working. The tutor is forkable, not rented. The whole thing is one app.py and a prompt written in plain English. Another beginner can clone it, make it stricter, make it funnier, make it teach JavaScript instead — without asking anyone's permission. That's open innovation at the smallest, most personal scale: one learner's tool becomes the next learner's starting point. This is my Week 1 and Week 2 lesson too, now for the third time: the auto-router is what makes free actually reliable. Openness isn't one model — it's having many, so no single point of failure can take your tool away. What I'd do next A "explain my error" paste box with even simpler language for total first-week beginners Voice input — asking out loud is even lazier than typing, and helps on a phone A "review what I learned" button that turns your chat history into 5 tiny recap cards But the core promise is done: one question, one plain answer, one tiny example — back to your day. Slow and steady wins.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest 2026 DEV Challenge — Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I built
The Lazy Python Tutor — ask any Python question, get a plain-English explanation first, then a short runnable example, then one tiny optional practice prompt. That's it. No 40-minute video. No 12 documentation tabs. No homework list.

Live app: https://lazy-py-tpvbo7rexyrv4af4lv64qb.streamlit.app/
Repo: https://github.com/ashleygirl3723/lazy-python-tutor

Try asking:
What is a variable?
How do loops work?
Why does my code say IndentationError? — paste your broken code and it names the most likely problem, shows the fixed version, and says what changed in one sentence.
It remembers the conversation, so follow-ups build on what you already asked.

Why I built this — honestly
I'm learning Python myself, in a 30-day self-paced course, mostly on my laptop between caregiving shifts. I know exactly where beginners quit: not because Python is hard, but because every small question turns into a huge tutorial.
"What does elif mean?" should not require watching half a course. I kept wishing I could just ask — in plain words, get a plain answer, see one tiny example, and move on with my day.
So for "Slow and Steady" — build something with open-weight AI that rewards laziness — I built the tutor I wanted. Laziness here isn't cutting corners. It's respecting your time and energy. Slow and steady is literally how I'm learning: one small question at a time.
The design enforces that in the system prompt, which is the whole brain of the app:
Plain English first — no jargon without immediately explaining it
Then a short example — usually under 10 lines, nothing extra
Then one tiny practice prompt — labeled "Feeling ambitious? Try this:" — genuinely tiny, always optional
Hard rules in that prompt: keep it under ~200 words plus code, never dump code without explaining it first, and if code is broken, name the one most likely problem — not a lecture.
That last part matters to me personally. My most common mistakes are picky syntax things — capitalized If/Print (phone autocorrect loves that one), missing colons, missing indents, dropping the variable after elif. A good lazy tutor spots the one thing, fixes it kindly, and doesn't make you feel dumb for it.

How it's built
Streamlit chat interface, Python, deployed free on Streamlit Cloud — runs in any browser, phone included
Open-weight models via OpenRouter's free tier — openrouter/free auto-router picks a working free open-weight model per call. No credit card, no paid API.

Why open innovation matters for this build
I'm a caregiver learning to code on the side. I don't have a budget for AI APIs, and a learning tool that charges per question would teach me to stop asking questions — the exact opposite of learning.
Open weights fix that:
Asking is free. Every "wait, why?" costs nothing. A beginner can ask the dumb question, the follow-up, and the follow-up to the follow-up without a meter running. That's how slow-and-steady learning actually works.
No one can pull the plug. If a closed provider raises prices, retires a model, or changes terms, a closed-API tutor dies on their schedule. With open weights + an open router, when one free model is busy, the request goes to another — the app keeps working.
The tutor is forkable, not rented. The whole thing is one app.py and a prompt written in plain English. Another beginner can clone it, make it stricter, make it funnier, make it teach JavaScript instead — without asking anyone's permission. That's open innovation at the smallest, most personal scale: one learner's tool becomes the next learner's starting point.
This is my Week 1 and Week 2 lesson too, now for the third time: the auto-router is what makes free actually reliable. Openness isn't one model — it's having many, so no single point of failure can take your tool away.

A "explain my error" paste box with even simpler language for total first-week beginners
Voice input — asking out loud is even lazier than typing, and helps on a phone
A "review what I learned" button that turns your chat history into 5 tiny recap cards
But the core promise is done: one question, one plain answer, one tiny example — back to your day. Slow and steady wins.

items.title: Your AI Eraser Redraws the Whole Photo: Inside a Label-Then-Edit Object Remover
items.summary: This week two of our own help pages contradicted each other. MagicRemover's passersby page promised that only the area you brush changes; the people page said the whole image may shift slightly. Only one could be true, so I read our pipeline end to end instead of trusting either page. The people page was right. An instruction-based eraser doesn't fill a hole: it re-renders the entire photo from a text instruction, and your brush stroke only decides what that instruction says. This post walks through how that pipeline works in production, why it was worth switching to, and what it costs the pixels you never touched. Disclosure: I build MagicRemover, the browser-based AI eraser this post is about. The draft was written with AI assistance and every code excerpt and number was checked against the repository and production logs. Two ways to build an eraser There are two broad designs, and they fail in opposite ways. Mask inpainting takes the image plus a binary mask. The model generates pixels only inside the mask, and the pipeline copies everything outside it straight from the original. Outside the brush, the result is pixel-identical to your upload. The weakness is context: if you brush a person but not their shadow, the shadow stays, because the model was only allowed to touch the mask. Instruction editing takes the image plus a sentence such as "remove the man in the blue shirt". The model returns a complete new image. Because it understands the scene, it can remove the shadow and the reflection you didn't brush. The cost is that every pixel in the output was generated, including the ones you wanted left alone. MagicRemover's photo tools ran on mask inpainting until May 2026. In early May we added a labelling step; in June we replaced the backend with an instruction-following image editor that takes only an image and a prompt. Fills got noticeably more coherent, especially around shadows. What we didn't do was update every sentence on the site that still described the old behaviour. How a brush stroke becomes a sentence Here is the path a removal takes today. 1. The browser shrinks the photo to about 1 megapixel Every upload goes through one helper before anything leaves the browser: /** Cap uploads at ~1 megapixel (matches the model's ~1MP working resolution). */ export const MAX_PIXELS = 1 _000_000 ; /** Secondary edge cap for very wide panoramas. */ export const MAX_EDGE = 2048 ; export function fitTarget ( w : number , h : number ) { let scale = 1 ; const pixels = w * h ; if ( pixels > MAX_PIXELS ) scale = Math . sqrt ( MAX_PIXELS / pixels ); const longest = Math . max ( w , h ) * scale ; if ( longest > MAX_EDGE ) scale *= MAX_EDGE / longest ; return { width : Math . max ( 1 , Math . round ( w * scale )), height : Math . max ( 1 , Math . round ( h * scale )), }; } A 4000×3000 phone photo becomes 1155×866. There is no point sending more: the editing model works at roughly one megapixel and returns an image at that size, so extra pixels would only make the request slower and bigger. 2. The browser sends two copies The editor posts the clean, downscaled original and a second copy with the user's brush strokes filled solid red. The red copy is never edited; it exists so the next step can see what was marked. 3. A vision model names what is under the red A vision-language model receives both images and a tool-specific instruction. The people tool's instruction starts like this: Identify the person or people inside the red-marked region of image 2. Your reply MUST uniquely identify ONLY the red-marked subjects so they can be deleted without affecting any similar-looking person ... It answers with a short label, along the lines of "the man in the blue shirt on the left". In the nine removals logged since our latest deploy, all nine got a label, and the labelling step took about 2.5 seconds on average. That's a small sample, but it matches what we see day to day. 4. The editor gets the clean photo and a sentence The label is dropped into a per-tool template. The people tool uses: Completely remove {label} from the photo, leaving no trace, shadow, or outline, and realistically reconstruct the background and scene behind them. Keep everyone and everything else exactly unchanged. The editor receives the clean original, never the red copy, so there's no risk of red pixels leaking into the result. 5. If labelling fails, fall back to the red copy When the vision model can't produce a label, the editor gets the red-marked copy and a generic instruction instead: Completely remove whatever the red area covers, then remove the red marking itself and fill the space with background that naturally matches the surroundings. Leave no trace, shadow, or outline. Keep everything outside the red area exactly unchanged. That keeps the tool working when the labeller is down, at the cost of slightly worse results, because "the red area" is a vaguer target than "the man in the blue shirt". Why the whole photo changes Notice the last sentence of both prompts: "Keep everything else exactly unchanged." It's a request, not a guarantee. The model regenerates the full frame, and nothing in the pipeline copies the original pixels back. In practice the untouched parts of the photo look the same, but they aren't bit-identical. The things most likely to drift are fine repeating textures (fabric, foliage, gravel), small text away from the brushed area, and faces in the background. Colour can shift slightly across the whole image too. That's acceptable for the use most people have: a holiday photo going to Instagram or a chat. It's not acceptable for an e-commerce product shot that has to match its colour profile, or a scanned document where every other character must survive untouched. So the pages now say it plainly: changes concentrate in the brushed area, the rest looks the same but isn't pixel-identical. Why we don't paste the original back (yet) The obvious fix is to composite: keep the edited pixels inside the brushed area, take the original's pixels everywhere else. It's about twenty lines with sharp. This is an example, not production code; it's tested with sharp 0.34.5 on Node 24: import sharp from " sharp " ; const { width , height } = await sharp ( " original.png " ). metadata (); // 1. Grow the brushed area so the seam lands outside the object's edge: // blur the mask, then turn every non-black pixel white. const blurred = await sharp ( " mask.png " ). resize ( width , height ). blur ( 8 ). toBuffer (); const grown = await sharp ( blurred ). threshold ( 1 ). toBuffer (); // 2. Feather the grown edge and keep a single raw channel to use as alpha. const alpha = await sharp ( grown ). blur ( 6 ). extractChannel ( 0 ). raw (). toBuffer (); // 3. The edited image at the original's size, with that alpha channel. const rgb = await sharp ( " edited.png " ). resize ( width , height ). removeAlpha (). toBuffer (); const patch = await sharp ( rgb ) . joinChannel ( alpha , { raw : { width , height , channels : 1 } }) . png () . toBuffer (); // 4. Lay the patch over the untouched original. await sharp ( " original.png " ). composite ([{ input : patch }]). toFile ( " result.png " ); Two gotchas cost me time while testing it. sharp applies operations in a fixed internal order, not in the order you chain them, so blur, threshold and blur again only behave as written when each runs in its own pipeline. And removeAlpha() chained after joinChannel() quietly strips the channel you just joined, which is why step 3 builds the RGB buffer first. So why isn't this in production? Because it gives back what instruction editing bought us. Shadows come back. The editor removes a person's shadow even if the user brushed only the person. Composite outside the mask and the shadow is pasted right back from the original. Growing the mask helps a little; it can't know where a long evening shadow ends. Seams appear. The editor relights the area it rebuilt. Where its version meets the original, a feathered edge turns a sharp seam into a soft halo, but on a flat sky or a white wall you can still see the step in brightness. Resolution stays the same. Compositing keeps the original pixels outside the mask, but if you composite onto the downscaled original, the output is still about one megapixel. To get full resolution back you'd upscale the patch onto the full-size upload, and a 1 MP patch dropped into a 12 MP photo looks soft next to its neighbours. A hybrid is on our list: composite only when the brushed area is small and far from strong shadows, and leave the full regeneration otherwise. Until then, the honest move was to change the copy rather than the pipeline. When an instruction editor is the wrong tool You need everything outside the mask to stay bit-identical: product photos with strict colour, documents, anything used as a record. Use mask inpainting with compositing, or Photoshop's Remove Tool on the full-resolution file. You need print resolution. Any eraser that works at about one megapixel, MagicRemover included, will hand you back a smaller image. The image is dense with text you want to keep. Regenerating the frame can subtly alter characters far from the brush. Where MagicRemover fits MagicRemover is a browser-based AI eraser: you upload a photo, brush over a person, object, text, sticker or watermark, and it returns the photo with that thing removed, usually in well under a minute. It's built for photos headed to the web and social media, with 2 free removals a day without an account and 2 more after Google sign-in. Don't use it when you need full resolution or pixel-exact output outside the brushed area; for those jobs a desktop editor on the original file is the right call. The tool walkthroughs, including the people remover discussed above, are at magicremover.org . If you've shipped an eraser yourself: do you composite the original back, and how do you deal with shadows that fall outside the user's mask?
items.summary_html:
This week two of our own help pages contradicted each other. MagicRemover's passersby page promised that only the area you brush changes; the people page said the whole image may shift slightly. Only one could be true, so I read our pipeline end to end instead of trusting either page.

The people page was right. An instruction-based eraser doesn't fill a hole: it re-renders the entire photo from a text instruction, and your brush stroke only decides what that instruction says. This post walks through how that pipeline works in production, why it was worth switching to, and what it costs the pixels you never touched.

Disclosure: I build MagicRemover, the browser-based AI eraser this post is about. The draft was written with AI assistance and every code excerpt and number was checked against the repository and production logs.

Two ways to build an eraser

There are two broad designs, and they fail in opposite ways.

Mask inpainting takes the image plus a binary mask. The model generates pixels only inside the mask, and the pipeline copies everything outside it straight from the original. Outside the brush, the result is pixel-identical to your upload. The weakness is context: if you brush a person but not their shadow, the shadow stays, because the model was only allowed to touch the mask.

Instruction editing takes the image plus a sentence such as "remove the man in the blue shirt". The model returns a complete new image. Because it understands the scene, it can remove the shadow and the reflection you didn't brush. The cost is that every pixel in the output was generated, including the ones you wanted left alone.

MagicRemover's photo tools ran on mask inpainting until May 2026. In early May we added a labelling step; in June we replaced the backend with an instruction-following image editor that takes only an image and a prompt. Fills got noticeably more coherent, especially around shadows. What we didn't do was update every sentence on the site that still described the old behaviour.

How a brush stroke becomes a sentence

Here is the path a removal takes today.

1. The browser shrinks the photo to about 1 megapixel

Every upload goes through one helper before anything leaves the browser:

/** Cap uploads at ~1 megapixel (matches the model's ~1MP working resolution). */
export const MAX_PIXELS = 1_000_000;
/** Secondary edge cap for very wide panoramas. */
export const MAX_EDGE = 2048;

export function fitTarget(w: number, h: number) {
  let scale = 1;
  const pixels = w * h;
  if (pixels > MAX_PIXELS) scale = Math.sqrt(MAX_PIXELS / pixels);
  const longest = Math.max(w, h) * scale;
  if (longest > MAX_EDGE) scale *= MAX_EDGE / longest;
  return {
    width: Math.max(1, Math.round(w * scale)),
    height: Math.max(1, Math.round(h * scale)),
  };
}

A 4000×3000 phone photo becomes 1155×866. There is no point sending more: the editing model works at roughly one megapixel and returns an image at that size, so extra pixels would only make the request slower and bigger.

2. The browser sends two copies

The editor posts the clean, downscaled original and a second copy with the user's brush strokes filled solid red. The red copy is never edited; it exists so the next step can see what was marked.

3. A vision model names what is under the red

A vision-language model receives both images and a tool-specific instruction. The people tool's instruction starts like this:

Identify the person or people inside the red-marked region of image 2.
Your reply MUST uniquely identify ONLY the red-marked subjects so they can
be deleted without affecting any similar-looking person ...

It answers with a short label, along the lines of "the man in the blue shirt on the left". In the nine removals logged since our latest deploy, all nine got a label, and the labelling step took about 2.5 seconds on average. That's a small sample, but it matches what we see day to day.

4. The editor gets the clean photo and a sentence

The label is dropped into a per-tool template. The people tool uses:

Completely remove {label} from the photo, leaving no trace, shadow, or
outline, and realistically reconstruct the background and scene behind
them. Keep everyone and everything else exactly unchanged.

The editor receives the clean original, never the red copy, so there's no risk of red pixels leaking into the result.

5. If labelling fails, fall back to the red copy

When the vision model can't produce a label, the editor gets the red-marked copy and a generic instruction instead:

Completely remove whatever the red area covers, then remove the red marking
itself and fill the space with background that naturally matches the
surroundings. Leave no trace, shadow, or outline. Keep everything outside
the red area exactly unchanged.

That keeps the tool working when the labeller is down, at the cost of slightly worse results, because "the red area" is a vaguer target than "the man in the blue shirt".

Why the whole photo changes

Notice the last sentence of both prompts: "Keep everything else exactly unchanged." It's a request, not a guarantee. The model regenerates the full frame, and nothing in the pipeline copies the original pixels back.

In practice the untouched parts of the photo look the same, but they aren't bit-identical. The things most likely to drift are fine repeating textures (fabric, foliage, gravel), small text away from the brushed area, and faces in the background. Colour can shift slightly across the whole image too.

That's acceptable for the use most people have: a holiday photo going to Instagram or a chat. It's not acceptable for an e-commerce product shot that has to match its colour profile, or a scanned document where every other character must survive untouched. So the pages now say it plainly: changes concentrate in the brushed area, the rest looks the same but isn't pixel-identical.

Why we don't paste the original back (yet)

The obvious fix is to composite: keep the edited pixels inside the brushed area, take the original's pixels everywhere else. It's about twenty lines with sharp. This is an example, not production code; it's tested with sharp 0.34.5 on Node 24:

import sharp from "sharp";

const { width, height } = await sharp("original.png").metadata();

// 1. Grow the brushed area so the seam lands outside the object's edge:
//    blur the mask, then turn every non-black pixel white.
const blurred = await sharp("mask.png").resize(width, height).blur(8).toBuffer();
const grown = await sharp(blurred).threshold(1).toBuffer();

// 2. Feather the grown edge and keep a single raw channel to use as alpha.
const alpha = await sharp(grown).blur(6).extractChannel(0).raw().toBuffer();

// 3. The edited image at the original's size, with that alpha channel.
const rgb = await sharp("edited.png").resize(width, height).removeAlpha().toBuffer();
const patch = await sharp(rgb)
  .joinChannel(alpha, { raw: { width, height, channels: 1 } })
  .png()
  .toBuffer();

// 4. Lay the patch over the untouched original.
await sharp("original.png").composite([{ input: patch }]).toFile("result.png");

Two gotchas cost me time while testing it. sharp applies operations in a fixed internal order, not in the order you chain them, so blur, threshold and blur again only behave as written when each runs in its own pipeline. And removeAlpha() chained after joinChannel() quietly strips the channel you just joined, which is why step 3 builds the RGB buffer first.

So why isn't this in production? Because it gives back what instruction editing bought us.

  • Shadows come back. The editor removes a person's shadow even if the user brushed only the person. Composite outside the mask and the shadow is pasted right back from the original. Growing the mask helps a little; it can't know where a long evening shadow ends.
  • Seams appear. The editor relights the area it rebuilt. Where its version meets the original, a feathered edge turns a sharp seam into a soft halo, but on a flat sky or a white wall you can still see the step in brightness.
  • Resolution stays the same. Compositing keeps the original pixels outside the mask, but if you composite onto the downscaled original, the output is still about one megapixel. To get full resolution back you'd upscale the patch onto the full-size upload, and a 1 MP patch dropped into a 12 MP photo looks soft next to its neighbours.

A hybrid is on our list: composite only when the brushed area is small and far from strong shadows, and leave the full regeneration otherwise. Until then, the honest move was to change the copy rather than the pipeline.

When an instruction editor is the wrong tool
  • You need everything outside the mask to stay bit-identical: product photos with strict colour, documents, anything used as a record. Use mask inpainting with compositing, or Photoshop's Remove Tool on the full-resolution file.
  • You need print resolution. Any eraser that works at about one megapixel, MagicRemover included, will hand you back a smaller image.
  • The image is dense with text you want to keep. Regenerating the frame can subtly alter characters far from the brush.
Where MagicRemover fits

MagicRemover is a browser-based AI eraser: you upload a photo, brush over a person, object, text, sticker or watermark, and it returns the photo with that thing removed, usually in well under a minute. It's built for photos headed to the web and social media, with 2 free removals a day without an account and 2 more after Google sign-in. Don't use it when you need full resolution or pixel-exact output outside the brushed area; for those jobs a desktop editor on the original file is the right call.

The tool walkthroughs, including the people remover discussed above, are at magicremover.org.

If you've shipped an eraser yourself: do you composite the original back, and how do you deal with shadows that fall outside the user's mask?

items.title: I cut my AI agent's reading by 78%. It lost 2 answers to a missing folder name.
items.summary: TL;DR A context-shrinking MCP tool cut what my agent sent to the model by a median 78%, on every question. It answered 7 of 10 correctly, against 9 of 10 with full files. Every miss traced back to one small detail: a file shown without its folder. Along the way, I found a bug the founder fixed within two days, and a flaw in my own test. Coding agents read a lot of code. Every file you paste into the prompt costs tokens, time and money, so a new kind of tool has appeared: send it your files, and it hands the model a trimmed view instead. Showing that the token count goes down is easy. The harder question is the one that matters: Does the agent still get the right answer? I picked one of these tools, Hexum, a hosted MCP server, and set up a fair fight to find out. The fight I wrote 10 questions about real open-source Python and TypeScript libraries: things like "which function calls this helper?" and "what does this function return for an empty input?" Then I asked Gemini each question three ways: Full files. Everything goes into the prompt. Hexum. The model gets Hexum's trimmed view, plus a tool to expand any function it wants to read in full. No files at all. Just the question, to see how much the model already knows from memory. To keep myself honest, I froze the grading rule, the prompts and all 10 questions in a git tag before the first real call , and checked every answer key against the source code by hand. That way, I couldn't move the goalposts after seeing results. The rule was simple: Hexum counts as "not worse" if it gets at most one question fewer right than the full files. The results Correct Tokens sent to the model Full files 9 of 10 511,004 Hexum 7 of 10 108,653 No files 3 of 10 3,348 On tokens, it's a clear win. Hexum sent less to the model on every single question , with a median cut of 77.7%, and up to 97% on some. On correctness, it lost two answers. Under my own frozen rule, "not worse" does not hold. So the interesting part isn't the score. It's why it lost. The misses had one thing in common I went through every failed answer, step by step. All three Hexum misses looked the same. Hexum's view shows each file with its path. Except, in every miss, the file holding the answer was shown by its bare name : The answer lived in source/utils/body.ts . The view just said body.ts . So the agent guessed. It looked for the function in source/core/Ky.ts , got back NOT_FOUND with no hint, tried again, and ran out of steps. The same thing happened with recipes.py and core.py in the other two misses. One missing folder name, and the agent was lost. A full path in the label, or a hint in the error message, would likely have fixed at least some of these. Twist 1: the tool forgot my code Before any of this, my first pilot run showed something stranger. When I asked Hexum to shrink the same files a second time, even in a brand new session, it returned an empty view . It remembered what it had already sent and skipped it, so the agent saw no code at all. I wrote up an exact reproduction (the arguments, the verbatim responses, the timestamps) and sent it to the founder, Vijay Harre. He shipped a fix within two days. I confirmed it with a probe, restarted the whole run on the fixed server, and kept the earlier run in the repo, labelled "before the fix". Twist 2: my own test was part of the problem It would be easy to stop here and blame the tool. But my harness had flaws too: The agent never saw the file list. In the Hexum arm, it only saw the view. An agent working inside a real editor would know every path in the project. My harness blocked one of Hexum's chances. In one miss, the agent tried to expand recipes.py , the exact name Hexum had shown it. My harness only accepted full paths, so it refused the call before it ever reached Hexum. Whether Hexum would have found the file, I don't know. I also caught a bug in how my harness handled Hexum's NOT_FOUND errors partway through the run. It was fixed before the affected question was rerun, and it's documented in the repo. 5 things I'd check before trusting any context-shrinking tool Measure correctness next to tokens, on the same questions. A token chart alone tells you nothing about whether the answers survived. Run a no-files baseline. The model got 3 of 10 right with no code at all. On famous libraries, part of any "success" may just be memory. Look at what the agent can navigate. Here, one missing folder name decided the outcome. Check paths, labels and error messages. Count tokens on both sides. Hexum itself received the full files on every call. Fewer tokens to the model is not automatically a lower bill, and I didn't measure cost. Freeze your rules before you look. Otherwise it's too easy to "fix" the test until it says what you hoped. What this doesn't show It's 10 questions, one model and one run: a signal, not a verdict. I didn't test edits, Hexum's other tools, or an agent that greps and reads a few files instead. Everything is public The harness, the frozen rules, every raw run record and the full results are on GitHub: https://github.com/sravya520/hexum-eval If you've measured accuracy with a context tool yourself, I'd like to hear what you saw. Did your agent lose answers too?
items.summary_html:
TL;DR

  • A context-shrinking MCP tool cut what my agent sent to the model by a median 78%, on every question.
  • It answered 7 of 10 correctly, against 9 of 10 with full files.
  • Every miss traced back to one small detail: a file shown without its folder.
  • Along the way, I found a bug the founder fixed within two days, and a flaw in my own test.

Coding agents read a lot of code. Every file you paste into the prompt costs tokens, time and money, so a new kind of tool has appeared: send it your files, and it hands the model a trimmed view instead.

Showing that the token count goes down is easy. The harder question is the one that matters:

Does the agent still get the right answer?

I picked one of these tools, Hexum, a hosted MCP server, and set up a fair fight to find out.

The fight

I wrote 10 questions about real open-source Python and TypeScript libraries: things like "which function calls this helper?" and "what does this function return for an empty input?"

Then I asked Gemini each question three ways:

  1. Full files. Everything goes into the prompt.
  2. Hexum. The model gets Hexum's trimmed view, plus a tool to expand any function it wants to read in full.
  3. No files at all. Just the question, to see how much the model already knows from memory.

To keep myself honest, I froze the grading rule, the prompts and all 10 questions in a git tag before the first real call, and checked every answer key against the source code by hand. That way, I couldn't move the goalposts after seeing results.

The rule was simple: Hexum counts as "not worse" if it gets at most one question fewer right than the full files.

The results
Correct Tokens sent to the model Full files 9 of 10 511,004 Hexum 7 of 10 108,653 No files 3 of 10 3,348

On tokens, it's a clear win. Hexum sent less to the model on every single question, with a median cut of 77.7%, and up to 97% on some.

On correctness, it lost two answers. Under my own frozen rule, "not worse" does not hold.

So the interesting part isn't the score. It's why it lost.

The misses had one thing in common

I went through every failed answer, step by step. All three Hexum misses looked the same.

Hexum's view shows each file with its path. Except, in every miss, the file holding the answer was shown by its bare name:

The answer lived in source/utils/body.ts. The view just said body.ts.

So the agent guessed. It looked for the function in source/core/Ky.ts, got back NOT_FOUND with no hint, tried again, and ran out of steps. The same thing happened with recipes.py and core.py in the other two misses.

One missing folder name, and the agent was lost. A full path in the label, or a hint in the error message, would likely have fixed at least some of these.

Twist 1: the tool forgot my code

Before any of this, my first pilot run showed something stranger.

When I asked Hexum to shrink the same files a second time, even in a brand new session, it returned an empty view. It remembered what it had already sent and skipped it, so the agent saw no code at all.

I wrote up an exact reproduction (the arguments, the verbatim responses, the timestamps) and sent it to the founder, Vijay Harre. He shipped a fix within two days. I confirmed it with a probe, restarted the whole run on the fixed server, and kept the earlier run in the repo, labelled "before the fix".

Twist 2: my own test was part of the problem

It would be easy to stop here and blame the tool. But my harness had flaws too:

  • The agent never saw the file list. In the Hexum arm, it only saw the view. An agent working inside a real editor would know every path in the project.
  • My harness blocked one of Hexum's chances. In one miss, the agent tried to expand recipes.py, the exact name Hexum had shown it. My harness only accepted full paths, so it refused the call before it ever reached Hexum. Whether Hexum would have found the file, I don't know.

I also caught a bug in how my harness handled Hexum's NOT_FOUND errors partway through the run. It was fixed before the affected question was rerun, and it's documented in the repo.

5 things I'd check before trusting any context-shrinking tool
  1. Measure correctness next to tokens, on the same questions. A token chart alone tells you nothing about whether the answers survived.
  2. Run a no-files baseline. The model got 3 of 10 right with no code at all. On famous libraries, part of any "success" may just be memory.
  3. Look at what the agent can navigate. Here, one missing folder name decided the outcome. Check paths, labels and error messages.
  4. Count tokens on both sides. Hexum itself received the full files on every call. Fewer tokens to the model is not automatically a lower bill, and I didn't measure cost.
  5. Freeze your rules before you look. Otherwise it's too easy to "fix" the test until it says what you hoped.
What this doesn't show

It's 10 questions, one model and one run: a signal, not a verdict. I didn't test edits, Hexum's other tools, or an agent that greps and reads a few files instead.

Everything is public

The harness, the frozen rules, every raw run record and the full results are on GitHub: https://github.com/sravya520/hexum-eval

If you've measured accuracy with a context tool yourself, I'd like to hear what you saw. Did your agent lose answers too?

items.title: I replaced 4 discontinued Flutter packages. Here's what I learned.
items.summary: When the Flutter team announced they were discontinuing six first-party packages (flutter_markdown, palette_generator, flutter_adaptive_scaffold, flutter_image, ios_platform_images, css_colors), they left the community a single sentence: "we encourage members of the community to coordinate on establishing forks." Six packages. Millions of combined downloads. And no plan. What I did about it I didn't set out to maintain replacements. I set out to fix my own problem — I needed markdown rendering after flutter_markdown died. But once I shipped one replacement and watched the issue threads fill up with "so what do we use now?", the pattern became obvious: every discontinued package leaves behind a large, orphaned user base with nowhere to go. So I built the Prism family — 15 pure-Flutter packages, no platform channels, all six platforms. Four of them replace discontinued packages directly: Discontinued My replacement Orphaned likes flutter_markdown prism_markdown ~330+ palette_generator prism_palette 678 flutter_adaptive_scaffold prism_adaptive_scaffold — flutter_image prism_image 102 What I learned 1. The issue threads are a product roadmap. When flutter_markdown was discontinued, the old backlog was full of years-old feature requests with hundreds of reactions. The top one — maxLines/overflow truncation — had 59 upvotes and was never implemented. I shipped it in my first replacement release. That's not feature planning, that's just listening. 2. Maintainability beats features. When palette_generator died, Flutter's own team pointed people at material_color_utilities — the pro-grade color science library bundled with Flutter. Instead of copying the old code, I built my replacement on that foundation. The existing community forks copied first; the ones built on better foundations are the ones that keep working. 3. Testing discontinued-package replacements is hard — but not optional. The old packages were battle-tested by years of production use. My replacements start from zero. For prism_image, that meant spinning up a real local HTTP server in the test suite and verifying retry behavior against actual failures — not mocked promises. Two tests are still skipped pending on-device verification, and I say so publicly rather than pretend the coverage is complete. 4. Open source feedback loops are fast — when you're responsive. A maintainer on one of my other PRs suggested a better approach I hadn't considered (parsing data from a URL instead of hardcoding it). Implementing his suggestion within a day turned a "requested changes" review into approval-ready. Responsiveness is the cheapest credibility there is. items.summary_html:
When the Flutter team announced they were discontinuing six first-party
packages (flutter_markdown, palette_generator, flutter_adaptive_scaffold,
flutter_image, ios_platform_images, css_colors), they left the community a
single sentence: "we encourage members of the community to coordinate on
establishing forks."

Six packages. Millions of combined downloads. And no plan.

What I did about it

I didn't set out to maintain replacements. I set out to fix my own problem —
I needed markdown rendering after flutter_markdown died. But once I shipped
one replacement and watched the issue threads fill up with "so what do we use
now?", the pattern became obvious: every discontinued package leaves behind
a large, orphaned user base with nowhere to go.

So I built the Prism family — 15 pure-Flutter packages, no platform channels,
all six platforms. Four of them replace discontinued packages directly:

Discontinued My replacement Orphaned likes flutter_markdown prism_markdown ~330+ palette_generator prism_palette 678 flutter_adaptive_scaffold prism_adaptive_scaffold — flutter_image prism_image 102
What I learned

1. The issue threads are a product roadmap.
When flutter_markdown was discontinued, the old backlog was full of
years-old feature requests with hundreds of reactions. The top one —
maxLines/overflow truncation — had 59 upvotes and was never implemented.
I shipped it in my first replacement release. That's not feature planning,
that's just listening.

2. Maintainability beats features.
When palette_generator died, Flutter's own team pointed people at
material_color_utilities — the pro-grade color science library bundled
with Flutter. Instead of copying the old code, I built my replacement on
that foundation. The existing community forks copied first; the ones
built on better foundations are the ones that keep working.

3. Testing discontinued-package replacements is hard — but not optional.
The old packages were battle-tested by years of production use. My
replacements start from zero. For prism_image, that meant spinning up a
real local HTTP server in the test suite and verifying retry behavior
against actual failures — not mocked promises. Two tests are still skipped
pending on-device verification, and I say so publicly rather than pretend
the coverage is complete.

4. Open source feedback loops are fast — when you're responsive.
A maintainer on one of my other PRs suggested a better approach I hadn't
considered (parsing data from a URL instead of hardcoding it). Implementing
his suggestion within a day turned a "requested changes" review into
approval-ready. Responsiveness is the cheapest credibility there is.

chat completions that works with OpenAI, Ollama, Groq, DeepSeek and any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with typed events instead of heavyweight
frameworks. It pairs with prism_markdown for live-rendering AI responses.

items.title: Hundreds of Protestors Descend on Meta Corporate Office Depicting Zuck as the Devil
items.summary: Meta’s corporate offices in São Paulo are the site of ongoing protests against election interference in the crucial national run-off elections in Brazil. Hundreds of protestors rallied at the company’s offices on Tuesday, carrying effigies mocking Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg as the devil incarnate, Venezuelan publication TeleSur reported . The demonstration coincided with an order by Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court demanding that Meta release proof it was providing equitable treatment to both of Brazil’s presidential candidates. Meta’s moderation methods came under international scrutiny earlier this month, after the company restricted over 1,000 social media accounts belonging to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who’s viewed as something like the Bernie Sanders of the Brazilian political scene. At the same time, Lula’s allies have accused Meta of artificially boosting content from the far-right contender for the office, Flávio Bolsonaro. Outraged at the perceived election meddling, protestors descended on Meta’s offices with Zuckerberg masks, signs, and massive paper heads. One protest sign showed a scowling Zuckerberg with dollar signs over his eyes and “bilionario safado” scrawled in blood-red paint, translating roughly to “billionaire scoundrel.” Others carried signs demanding “não se Meta,” or “Meta stay out,” putting extra public pressure behind the judicial demand. For its part, Meta has publicly denied any wrongdoing with its handling of the Brazilian election materials, insisting that any perceived imbalance was caused by two global service outages, per the Associated Press . Whether intentional or not, Brazil isn’t the only country whose political direction is quietly being dictated by the whims of a trillion-dollar tech corporation. Over the weekend, the Guardian reported that Meta had temporarily suspended Instagram accounts belonging to the No Kings coalition, a broad-tent liberal grouping which has been mobilizing protests and voter-registration drives across the US. It all comes as higher-ups at Instagram admit they have no clue how to stem the tide of AI content flooding onto the app. Until Meta submits its explanation to the Superior Electoral Court, it remains to be seen how the extremely powerful media platform can simultaneously censor thousands of political accounts during a pivotal election cycle, while being powerless to stop the deluge of harmful AI slop suffocating its users. More on protests: 78-Year-Old Woman Hauled Off In Handcuffs After Blocking Delivery Robot

items.title: I Built AgentSpend: A Rust CLI That Automatically Tracks AI Agent Usage and Finds Wasted Tokens
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built AgentSpend is a local-first Rust CLI that scans local Codex session files for token usage and saves deduplicated totals to a local SQLite database. Digging through agent log files to figure out your usage is annoying and tedious. I built this to make collecting that data automatic and private—everything stays on your machine. Note: This is an early MVP. Cost calculations, waste detection and AI recommendations aren't built yet. Demo If you have Codex session records on your machine, you can run: agentspend doctor agentspend scan agentspend status (I haven't attached a video or terminal recording yet since I still need to verify the build and run live CLI tests.) Code Repository: https://github.com/aunjum/AgentSpend Installation: Run cargo install --path . in the root directory. How I Built It Rust & Clap: For building a fast, lightweight native CLI. Serde: To parse event metadata from session logs. SQLite: To store usage totals locally without duplicates. The log connector uses turn-level counters so it doesn't double-count cumulative thread totals. To keep things secure, prompt and response text are ignored entirely and local API credentials are never touched. Note on Gemma: I plan to integrate Gemma down the road, but since it’s not working yet I'm not submitting this for the Gemma prize category. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Local, open-source dev tools give you complete control over your data. You can inspect exactly how log collection works, adapt connectors to your own workflow and ensure your usage data never leaves your hardware. My Agent Session Omitted—I haven't collected structured metrics on the agent session used to build this yet. The Lazy Payoff No more grepping through log folders or manually tallying up session files. The scanner runs in seconds and handles the tracking for you. Prize Categories Primary: Overall Hacktoberfest Challenge Gemma Category: Skipped for now (waiting until integration is functional). Limitations and testing Imports: Claude and Gemini log parsing aren't implemented yet. Features: Cost tracking, real-time TUI and Ollama/Gemma log analysis are still on the roadmap. Testing: Needs broader testing across different real-world session setups.
items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

AgentSpend is a local-first Rust CLI that scans local Codex session files for token usage and saves deduplicated totals to a local SQLite database.

Digging through agent log files to figure out your usage is annoying and tedious. I built this to make collecting that data automatic and private—everything stays on your machine.

Note: This is an early MVP. Cost calculations, waste detection and AI recommendations aren't built yet.

Demo

If you have Codex session records on your machine, you can run:

agentspend doctor
agentspend scan
agentspend status

(I haven't attached a video or terminal recording yet since I still need to verify the build and run live CLI tests.)

Code
  • Repository: https://github.com/aunjum/AgentSpend
  • Installation: Run cargo install --path . in the root directory.
How I Built It
  • Rust & Clap: For building a fast, lightweight native CLI.
  • Serde: To parse event metadata from session logs.
  • SQLite: To store usage totals locally without duplicates.

The log connector uses turn-level counters so it doesn't double-count cumulative thread totals. To keep things secure, prompt and response text are ignored entirely and local API credentials are never touched.

Note on Gemma: I plan to integrate Gemma down the road, but since it’s not working yet I'm not submitting this for the Gemma prize category.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Local, open-source dev tools give you complete control over your data. You can inspect exactly how log collection works, adapt connectors to your own workflow and ensure your usage data never leaves your hardware.

My Agent Session

Omitted—I haven't collected structured metrics on the agent session used to build this yet.

The Lazy Payoff

No more grepping through log folders or manually tallying up session files. The scanner runs in seconds and handles the tracking for you.

Prize Categories
  • Primary: Overall Hacktoberfest Challenge
  • Gemma Category: Skipped for now (waiting until integration is functional).
Limitations and testing
  • Imports: Claude and Gemini log parsing aren't implemented yet.
  • Features: Cost tracking, real-time TUI and Ollama/Gemma log analysis are still on the roadmap.
  • Testing: Needs broader testing across different real-world session setups.
