items.summary_html:
Spark’s lineage is the most elegant recovery mechanism in distributed computing — until your iterative job’s DAG grows so long that remembering how the data was built costs more than the data itself. Checkpointing cuts the chain. The question is what you pay for the scissors, and most teams get the answer wrong in both directions.

Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII

The Job That Got Slower Every Single Iteration

The entity-resolution job ran 120 iterations. Iteration 1 took 42 seconds. Iteration 30 took 6 minutes. By iteration 90, each pass was taking 14 minutes, and the whole thing was on track to blow past its 12-hour SLA window before iteration 110. Nobody had changed the code in weeks. The data volume was flat. The cluster was healthy. The job was simply, deterministically, getting slower every single time it looped — like a runner accumulating weights.

Then came the real incident. At 4:12 AM, on iteration 118 of 120, a spot instance was reclaimed and took two executors with it. Spark did exactly what it was designed to do: it recomputed the lost partitions from lineage. The problem was the lineage. To rebuild those partitions, it had to replay 117 iterations of joins and aggregations — every shuffle, every stage, all the way back to the raw input. Recovery took 6 hours and 40 minutes. The two lost executors cost us nearly seven hours of cluster time and a missed downstream SLA that paged three teams.

The post-mortem was one line long: we had 118 iterations of lineage and zero checkpoints. The DAG the driver was carrying had grown to tens of thousands of nodes. DAGScheduler was spending longer planning each iteration than the executors spent running it — planning cost grows with DAG depth, and we had built the deepest DAG in the company’s history one innocent loop at a time. The driver was also spending 40% of its time in garbage collection just holding the lineage graph (Part V’s memory lesson, applied to the driver instead of the heap).

So: when does remembering how your data was built become more expensive than the data itself — and what does it actually cost to forget on purpose?

The Mechanic Underneath: Lineage Is a Promise, and Promises Compound

Spark’s core fault-tolerance idea is disarmingly simple: instead of replicating data, remember how it was built. Every RDD and DataFrame carries its lineage — the graph of transformations from the source. Lose a partition, and Spark replays the lineage to rebuild exactly that partition. No replication overhead, no write-ahead cost during the happy path. For a ten-stage ETL, this is nearly free and brilliantly robust.

But lineage is a promise that compounds. In an iterative algorithm — PageRank, ALS, K-means, our entity-resolution loop — each iteration appends to the DAG. After n iterations, the lineage graph has depth n, and three costs grow with it. First, recovery cost: rebuilding a lost partition means replaying every stage back to the last materialization point, so recovery time is roughly lineage depth × per-stage cost. Our 6h40m recovery was not bad luck; it was arithmetic. Second, scheduling cost: the DAGScheduler traverses the DAG to plan each job, and planning time grows with graph size — at iteration 90, planning alone took minutes. Third, driver memory: the entire lineage graph lives on the driver, and tens of thousands of nodes with their metadata will eventually push the driver into GC hell. Lineage is free until the day it is the most expensive thing in your architecture.

Checkpointing is the deliberate decision to stop paying the compounding cost: materialize the data to stable storage (or executor memory), and cut the lineage at that point. Everything before the checkpoint is forgotten; recovery replays only from the checkpoint forward. You trade write cost now for bounded recovery cost later. The entire art of this topic is choosing where to cut, how often, and which kind of scissors to use — because each choice has a failure mode that teams discover at 4 AM.

Reliable Checkpointing Cuts the Chain — For a Price

RDD.checkpoint() (and Dataset.checkpoint()) writes the data to the checkpoint directory — HDFS, S3, any reliable filesystem you configure via sparkContext.setCheckpointDir() — and then truncates the lineage, pointing the RDD's parent at the checkpointed files instead of the full history. Recovery from a checkpoint replays at most the stages since the last cut. In our job, checkpointing every 10 iterations would have bounded recovery to 10 stages instead of 118 — turning 6h40m into roughly 25 minutes.

The price is write amplification. A reliable checkpoint is a full materialization: every byte of the checkpointed dataset gets written to durable storage, with all the serialization and I/O cost that implies. Checkpoint a 2TB iterative state every 10 iterations over 120 iterations and you have written 24TB to S3 that your lineage would never have written. On S3 specifically, the cost is worse than it looks — no atomic renames, high per-request latency — and checkpoint writes go through the same object-store path as everything else. Teams that checkpoint every iteration “to be safe” often discover their fault-tolerance mechanism is the slowest stage in the job. The checkpoint directory also needs lifecycle management: Spark does not clean up old checkpoints for RDDs automatically, and an unmonitored checkpoint dir is a slow-growing storage bill with your name on it.

Local Checkpointing Is Faster and Lies About Durability

localCheckpoint() — RDD.localCheckpoint() and Dataset.localCheckpoint() — cuts the lineage too, but materializes the data on the executors' local disks (or in memory, depending on storage level) instead of reliable storage. It is dramatically faster than a reliable checkpoint: no HDFS/S3 round trip, just a local write. For iterative ML loops where the dominant cost is DAG growth rather than executor loss, this is often the right tool.

But read the contract carefully: local checkpoint data dies with the executor. If the executor holding your locally-checkpointed partition is lost, Spark falls back to recomputing from the truncated lineage — which still exists underneath, because local checkpointing does not delete the original lineage, it just stops extending it. In practice this means local checkpointing bounds scheduling cost and driver memory (the DAG stops growing) but only partially bounds recovery cost (the underlying lineage is still replayable, just not re-traversed for planning). It is a scheduler optimization wearing a fault-tolerance costume. Our 4 AM executor loss would still have hurt with local checkpoints — less, but not the 25-minute story. Know which guarantee you are actually buying.

RDD Checkpointing Is Lazy; DataFrame Checkpointing Is Not

A gotcha that has bitten every team exactly once: RDD.checkpoint() is lazy — it marks the RDD for checkpointing, but nothing is written until the next action triggers computation. Dataset.checkpoint() (the DataFrame API), by contrast, is eager — it triggers a job immediately and blocks until the checkpoint is materialized. Mix them in the same codebase without knowing this and you get either checkpoints that never materialize (RDD marked but no action follows before the driver moves on) or mysterious blocking jobs in the middle of your pipeline (DataFrame checkpoint firing eagerly inside a loop). The eager DataFrame behavior is usually what you want in an iterative loop — you want the cut to happen now, deterministically, every k iterations — but you must budget for it: each eager checkpoint inside the loop is a full extra job with its own stages. Count it in your iteration-time math or your "optimization" will look like a regression in the UI.

Streaming Checkpoints Are a Different Animal

Structured Streaming’s checkpointing (Part VIII’s territory) shares the name but not the mechanics. The checkpoint location (checkpointLocation option, or spark.sql.streaming.checkpointLocation) stores three things: source offsets, the write-ahead log of processed batches, and the serialized state store for stateful operations. Recovery replays from the last committed offset — exactly-once semantics depend on the sink supporting idempotent writes, which is why the docs pair checkpointing with foreachBatch idempotency patterns. Two sharp edges: checkpoint state is tied to your query's code — change the projection, the schema, or the stateful logic incompatibly and the old checkpoint becomes unloadable, forcing you to start from a fresh location (or face cryptic deserialization errors); and the default spark.sql.streaming.minBatchesToRetain (100) bounds how much history the checkpoint keeps, which interacts with late-data handling. Streaming checkpointing is not optional — without a checkpoint location, a streaming query cannot recover at all — but it is also not free: state serialization for large keyed state is a real, ongoing write cost on every trigger.

The Fix, and What It Cost

The naive version was our original loop — 120 iterations, pure lineage, no cuts:

# Naive: 120 iterations of pure lineage. DAG depth grows to 120, driver holds
# the entire graph, and ONE executor loss replays ALL 118 prior iterations.
# result = result.join(updates, "id").groupBy("id").agg(...)  # in a loop, no checkpoint
# Optimized: cut the lineage every 10 iterations with a RELIABLE checkpoint.
# Recovery is now bounded to <= 10 stages; driver DAG stays shallow.
sc.setCheckpointDir("s3://our-bucket/checkpoints/entity-resolve")  # reliable store
result = base_df
for i in range(120):
    result = result.join(updates, "id").groupBy("id").agg(...)  # the iterative step
    if i % 10 == 0 and i > 0:
        result = result.checkpoint()  # eager: materializes NOW, truncates lineage
        # checkpoint dir lifecycle: old cuts cleaned by retention job, not Spark

For the tight inner loop of the ML variant we used localCheckpoint() instead — the DAG-growth problem dominated and executor loss was rare on our on-demand pool — reserving reliable checkpoints for every 30th iteration as the durability backstop. Two scissors, each used where its guarantee matches the risk.

The measured result on the next full run: per-iteration time stabilized at 55–70 seconds across all 120 iterations (vs. degrading from 42s to 14min), total runtime 11h20m → 2h35m, and a chaos test — killing two executors at iteration 100 — recovered in 22 minutes instead of 6h40m. The checkpoint writes added ~9 minutes of I/O across the whole run. Nine minutes of writes bought back nine hours of compounding lineage cost. That is the entire trade, expressed as a number.

The Catch: Checkpointing Can Quietly Make Everything Worse

Four ways the cure becomes the disease. First, checkpointing too often: every reliable checkpoint is a full write of the dataset. Checkpoint every iteration of a 2TB state and you have built a write-amplification machine that dwarfs the lineage cost you were avoiding — profile the write cost per checkpoint before choosing the interval. Second, checkpointing on slow storage: S3 checkpoint writes without S3A tuning (or worse, without fs.s3a committer settings) serialize your "fast" iterative loop behind object-store latency; the checkpoint dir belongs on fast storage or a tuned path. Third, localCheckpoint's false confidence: it does not bound recovery the way teams assume — the underlying lineage survives, and executor loss still replays it. If your post-mortem says "but we had checkpoints," check which kind. Fourth, streaming checkpoint incompatibility: evolving a stateful streaming query's logic without migrating the checkpoint location produces failures that look like data corruption but are really version skew — treat checkpoint locations as versioned artifacts, not scratch space. Checkpointing is a sharp tool. Grip it by the handle.

Takeaways
  • Lineage cost compounds with DAG depth: recovery time ≈ depth × stage cost, scheduling time grows with graph size, and the driver holds all of it. Iterative jobs must cut the chain.
  • Reliable checkpointing bounds recovery for a write price: every cut is a full materialization. Size the interval from measured write cost, not from superstition.
  • Local checkpointing is a scheduler optimization, not durability: it stops DAG growth but the underlying lineage survives executor loss. Buy it for planning cost, not for recovery.
  • RDD checkpointing is lazy, DataFrame checkpointing is eager: a marked-but-never-materialized RDD checkpoint protects nothing; an eager DataFrame checkpoint inside a loop is a full extra job per cut.
  • Streaming checkpoints are versioned state: offsets, WAL, and serialized state stores. Change query logic incompatibly and the old checkpoint is unloadable — treat locations as versioned.
  • Clean up after yourself: Spark does not retire old RDD checkpoints. An unmonitored checkpoint directory is a storage bill growing in the dark.

Lineage remembers everything for free, until the remembering costs more than the data. Checkpointing is how you choose what to forget — deliberately, measurably, and before 4 AM chooses for you.

items.title: OpenAI Expands ChatGPT Ads to 26 More Countries, Bringing Availability to 89 Markets
items.summary: OpenAI is expanding advertising in ChatGPT to 26 additional countries, bringing ads to 89 countries worldwide, the company announced on October 21. Ads appear only on the Free and Go plans, while Plus, Pro and Enterprise subscriptions remain ad-free. OpenAI says more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns in ChatGPT since ads launched just over eight months ago. Where ChatGPT Ads Are Launching The expansion follows earlier launches in Mexico and Brazil and recent rollouts across Europe, Southeast Asia and Taiwan. Latin America accounts for the largest share of the new markets, with 14 more countries in the region, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Peru. The remaining launches cover Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia. Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Pakistan are named in the announcement. OpenAI positions the launch as an opening for local businesses and regional brands as well as international companies. L'Oréal is quoted in the announcement as an early tester, describing ChatGPT as a place where consumers now discover and explore beauty products. Businesses in those countries can buy ChatGPT ads through technology partners or through self-service access in OpenAI's Ads Manager. OpenAI puts ChatGPT's audience at more than 1.2 billion people each week and presents advertising as a way to fund free and low-cost access to the chatbot. What Changes for Free and Go Users For users in the new markets, ads can now appear next to conversations on the two cheapest tiers. OpenAI's own example is someone planning meals for race week before a first marathon, who could see an ad for a grocery delivery service related to that conversation. The company lists the rules it says ChatGPT ads follow under its ads principles: conversations are kept private from advertisers OpenAI does not sell customer data ads are clearly labeled and kept separate from ChatGPT's answers advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides Only one way to avoid ads follows from the announcement: a paid Plus, Pro or Enterprise subscription, which OpenAI says will stay ad-free. Free and Go users in the newly added countries should expect ads mainly during shopping, comparison and planning conversations, the moments OpenAI describes as people still evaluating their options before deciding what to buy. The rollout also widens OpenAI's ad business beyond the markets where it first tested the format. According to the company, the next phase of growth will add more ad formats, objectives, buying options and measurement capabilities, and OpenAI is exploring ways for businesses to interact with consumers more natively inside ChatGPT. OpenAI has not published a timeline for those new formats, and the announcement names only some of the 26 new countries rather than the full list. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Microsoft Releases PowerToys 0.102 With Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide Utilities
items.summary: Microsoft has released PowerToys 0.102, a new version of its open-source utility suite for Windows that adds two mouse tools called Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide, according to the release announcement on the company's Windows Command Line blog. The update also brings a quick-access shelf to Command Palette, snip dictation in ZoomIt, and command-line tools for automating PowerToys. Version 0.102 is available now through the built-in updater and the PowerToys release page on GitHub. Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide in PowerToys 0.102 Mouse Button Lock targets long drag and selection operations. Users press and hold a mouse button for a moment and then let go, and Windows keeps treating the button as held until any button is clicked again. Microsoft names gaming, professional applications with heavy dragging and selection work, and accessibility for users who find it hard to hold a button down for extended periods as the main use cases. CursorHide hides the mouse pointer while the user types, after a period of inactivity, or both. The pointer returns as soon as the mouse moves. Both tools build on earlier mouse additions to the suite. PowerToys 0.97 added CursorWrap in January for multi-monitor setups, and Window Hopper arrived in August for switching between an app's windows. Command Palette Shelf, ZoomIt Dictation and Command-Line Tools Command Palette, the PowerToys quick launcher, gets an optional quick-access shelf that shows up to nine pinned commands below the search box while the palette is collapsed. Setting it up takes three steps: Open Command Palette settings and go to Settings > Appearance > Compact mode. Turn on the quick-access shelf and pin frequently used commands, apps, or settings. Press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to run a pinned command, or Alt+Shift plus the number to select it without running it. Other Command Palette changes include fuzzy search in settings, keyboard focus for the dock with Win+Alt+J, support for the Copilot key, and multiple dock clocks with separate time zones. ZoomIt adds Snip with dictation. With the option enabled, pressing Space while dragging out a snip records a spoken description, which ZoomIt transcribes on the device. A single paste then delivers both the screenshot and the text. The new command-line tools cover Advanced Paste, Light Switch, Settings, Peek and PowerDisplay. Settings can enable or disable utilities even while PowerToys is not running, and FancyZones, Image Resizer, File Locksmith and PowerDisplay commands now work from any terminal folder. Keyboard Manager picks up tap-alone remaps, where tapping a key on its own triggers a different action while the key keeps its normal behavior in shortcuts. Large remap lists get search, filters and bulk deletion. Color Picker and Text Extractor move to WinUI 3, and Microsoft says existing shortcuts and settings carry over. The release notes also list fixes for a File Explorer memory leak in New+ and a memory leak in Settings when switching pages, along with a confirmation prompt in Workspaces before launching an unverified app configured to run as administrator. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader.

items.title: Your First MCP Server
items.summary:
This is Chapter 3 of MCP in Practice , a Book for Software Engineers Building Production-ready MCP tools. Previously: Chapter 1 — The Integration Problem and Chapter 2 — MCP Core Concepts. Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author. Your First MCP Server From an empty project to a running server you can inspect and call What you will understand How to lay out a minimal MCP server project with the Python SDK How to define one narrow tool with a precise name, description, and input schema How to add a single resource that contrasts with the tool’s intent How to run the server over stdio and connect the MCP Inspector and an AI host How to walk the full exchange end to end: server/discover → tools/list → tools/call Why logs go to stderr, and the five mistakes that trap every first server Start with one narrow job Chapter 2 ended with an exercise: turn one of your server boundaries into a real server. This chapter does that — but not the server you eventually want. The first server has a different job: to make every concept from Chapter 2 concrete while the moving parts are still few enough to hold in your head. So we will build the smallest useful server we can: it answers one question, “what does this HTTP status code mean?” It exposes exactly one tool, lookup_http_status, and one resource, a short reference of the five status-code categories. It is read-only, self-contained, and deterministic. It makes no network calls, needs no credentials, and holds no secrets — which means there is nothing sensitive to leak while you learn. This choice is deliberate, and it previews a habit worth keeping. A server should do one job that you can state in one sentence. “Look up HTTP status codes” qualifies. “Look up HTTP status codes, and also check the weather, and also read local files” does not — that is three servers wearing one name, and Chapter 2 already showed why that boundary matters. If you cannot describe the server’s job in one sentence, split it. What we are deliberately leaving out is as important as what we include. No authentication: the data is public reference material. No Streamable HTTP: stdio keeps the deployment to a single local process. No prompts, no elicitation, no subscriptions, no tasks. Each of those earns its place in a later chapter, once the basic exchange is second nature. Figure 3.1 One server, one job: a single tool and a single resource Set up the project You need Python 3.10 or newer and a terminal. The official Python SDK is the mcp package; we will use its high-level interface, FastMCP, which handles the JSON-RPC framing, the server/discover response, and the dispatch of list and call operations. That leaves you free to concentrate on the capability surface, which is the part you own. Create a project directory with a single file: http-status-server/ server.py Then make a virtual environment and install the SDK: python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install "mcp[cli]" The [cli] extra adds the command-line helpers used later in this chapter. One caution before you go further: SDKs for a young protocol move quickly. These examples follow the 1.x line of the mcp package. If an import path in your installed version differs from what you see here, check the SDK documentation for your version rather than guessing — the concepts are stable even when the spelling shifts. Verify the install before you write any server code: run python -c “import mcp; print(mcp. version )” inside the virtual environment and confirm it prints a version. If it fails, the usual cause is installing into a different Python than the one you run — which python and which pip should point at the same .venv. Sorting this out now saves a confusing “module not found” later, when the error will surface inside a host process you cannot see into. Define the server before the plumbing Open server.py. The first decisions are the server’s name and its instructions — the two things a host learns about you before anything else. import logging import sys from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.INFO) logger = logging.getLogger("http-status") mcp = FastMCP( name="http-status", instructions="Look up the meaning of HTTP status codes from a built-in reference table.", ) A few things to notice. The name is lowercase, hyphenated, and free of spaces: hosts display it, and a clean name survives being shown in a tool picker. The instructions are one factual sentence. They are not a system prompt and not a place for persuasion; some hosts show them to the model, so state what the server does and nothing more. Treat the instructions as documentation with an audience of two: the person reading the Inspector, and the model deciding whether your tool fits the user’s request. Both read it cold, with no other context about your intentions. That is why “Look up the meaning of HTTP status codes from a built-in reference table” works and “Helps with HTTP stuff” does not — the first lets a stranger predict what the server will and will not do. Like the tool descriptions coming later, review instructions as an interface change whenever you edit them. The logging line deserves attention now because it prevents a failure you will otherwise meet later: it sends logs to standard error. Standard output belongs to the protocol, and we will return to that rule shortly. When a client calls server/discover against this server, the SDK answers with the server’s identity — the name http-status, the instructions, the supported protocol versions — and its capabilities. Because we are about to register a tool and a resource, the capabilities will advertise exactly those two primitives and nothing else. Discovery is honest by construction: it describes what the server actually exposes. Write one tool, and describe it like a public API A tool in FastMCP is a Python function with a decorator. The function name becomes the tool name, the docstring becomes the tool description, and the type annotations become the input schema: STATUS_CODES = { 200: {"phrase": "OK", "category": "Success", "note": "The request succeeded."}, 301: {"phrase": "Moved Permanently", "category": "Redirection", "note": "The resource has a new permanent URL."}, 404: {"phrase": "Not Found", "category": "Client error", "note": "The server has no representation for the target."}, 500: {"phrase": "Internal Server Error", "category": "Server error", "note": "The server failed while processing the request."}, # ... one entry per standard code } @mcp.tool() def lookup_http_status(code: int) -> str: """Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code. Searches a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes; it makes no network calls. Returns the code’s category, standard phrase, and a one-line usage note. Read-only: it never modifies anything. Accepts integer codes from 100 to 599 and raises an error for anything outside that range. """ if not 100 <= code <= 599: raise ValueError(f"code must be between 100 and 599, got {code}") entry = STATUS_CODES.get(code) if entry is None: return f"{code} is not a standard HTTP status code." return f"{code} {entry['phrase']} ({entry['category']}): {entry['note']}" A note on parameters you do not have yet: if a future version of this tool took an optional argument — say, verbose: bool = False — the default would make it optional in the input schema, while the required list would still contain only code. Defaults are a clean way to extend a tool without breaking existing callers, but each new parameter is a new promise in your public interface. For this first server, one required parameter is the whole contract, and that is a feature. Chapter 2 said a tool description should name the data source, the required scope, the time behavior, the result limits, and whether the operation has side effects. Here is that checklist made concrete: Data source: a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes. The description says where the answer comes from, so nobody assumes it queries a live service. Scope: integer codes from 100 to 599. Anything outside that range is rejected, and the description says so up front. Time behavior: the table is fixed reference data. Results are deterministic and do not go stale — which is the honest way to say “no time behavior applies.” Result limits: one record per call. The caller knows exactly what shape to expect. Side effects: none. The word “read-only” appears in the description itself, because a host deciding whether the model may call this without asking should not have to infer it. The input schema comes from the annotation code: int. Before your function ever runs, the SDK validates the incoming arguments against that schema: a missing code, or a value that is not an integer, is rejected at the boundary with an error result. Your own check then handles the domain rule the schema cannot express — that 99 and 600 are integers but not status codes — and raises ValueError with a message that names the bad value. The SDK turns that exception into a JSON-RPC error result, so the host learns the call failed and why. Notice the two different treatments of failure. A code outside 100–599 is invalid input, so it raises. A code inside the range but absent from the table — say, 210 — is a valid query with a negative answer, so it returns a normal result saying so. The distinction matters: an error result means “the call did not do what you asked,” while a result that says “not a standard code” means “the call worked and the answer is no.” Hosts and models treat those differently, so do not blur them. Add one resource for contrast The tool takes an argument and computes an answer. The status-code categories need neither: they are a fixed reference with a stable identity. That makes them a resource, not a second tool. @mcp.resource("http-status://categories") def status_categories() -> str: """The five HTTP status-code categories and the ranges they cover.""" return ( "1xx Informational (100-199): the request was received.
" "2xx Success (200-299): the request was received and accepted.
" "3xx Redirection (300-399): further action is needed.
" "4xx Client error (400-499): the request was invalid.
" "5xx Server error (500-599): the server failed to fulfill a valid request.
" ) A client lists it with resources/list and reads it with resources/read, addressing it by its URI. Compare the two primitives side by side and the intent distinction from Chapter 2 becomes tangible: the resource is retrieved, the tool is performed. A useful test of the boundary: if the categories ever needed an argument — say, a language for the descriptions — the resource would stop being honest, and you would remodel it as a tool. Run it over stdio A stdio server is a program that speaks JSON-RPC on its standard input and output. Add the entry point at the bottom of server.py: if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run() # stdio transport by default Run it: python server.py Nothing visible happens. That is correct: the process is waiting on stdin for a JSON-RPC request, and there is no one to talk to yet. Type a line and press enter and you will get a protocol error back — which, oddly, is a good sign. It means the server is listening. This is also the moment to understand what an AI host does with your file. When the host starts, it spawns python server.py as a child process, connects pipes to its stdin and stdout, and speaks JSON-RPC through those pipes for as long as the host runs. There is no port, no URL, no daemon to manage. The server’s lifetime is the host’s decision: it starts the process when it needs the capability and kills it when it is done. That simplicity is why stdio is the right first transport — deployment is a file path, and the failure modes are process failure modes you already know. Connect the Inspector, then an AI host Talking to the server by hand-typing JSON-RPC gets old after one request. The MCP Inspector gives you a user interface over the same exchange: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py Open the address it prints. The Inspector connects over stdio, calls server/discover, and shows you the server’s identity and capabilities. From there you can list tools, inspect the input schema your annotations produced, and call lookup_http_status with different arguments while watching the raw requests and responses. Every later section of this chapter is easier if you keep the Inspector open beside your editor. In the Inspector, work through three views in order. First, the server view: confirm the name reads http-status and the capabilities list tools and resources. If the name is wrong here, it is wrong everywhere downstream. Second, the tools view: read your own description and input schema as a stranger would, and fix anything that assumes knowledge the reader does not have. Third, the call view: run lookup_http_status with 200, then with 99, then with the argument missing entirely, and watch the three different outcomes — a result, an error result from your range check, and an error result from schema validation. Those three shapes are the whole vocabulary of tool invocation. If the Inspector cannot start your server at all, the cause is almost always the launch command, not your code: the wrong Python, a relative path resolved from the wrong directory, or a virtual environment the Inspector’s shell does not see. Run the exact command yourself in a terminal first. The same advice applies when an AI host reports that the server failed to start — hosts usually surface the child process’s stderr, which is another reason that stream is where your logs belong. To connect an AI host, you tell the host how to launch your server as a child process. The exact configuration shape varies by host; the common form looks like this: { "mcpServers": { "http-status": { "command": "python", "args": ["/path/to/http-status-server/server.py"] } } } Use the full path to your file, and if you installed the SDK in a virtual environment, point command at that environment’s Python. Restart the host, and the tool appears in its catalog. Ask the host “what does a 503 mean?” and watch what happens: the model selects lookup_http_status, the host validates the arguments and sends tools/call, and the answer comes back through the same path you just exercised by hand. Exercise the full flow: discover, list, call Whether the client is the Inspector or an AI host, the exchange follows the same shape. Walk through it once deliberately; this is the protocol from Chapter 2 with the abstractions removed. Step 1: discover The client calls server/discover and the server describes itself: the name http-status, the supported protocol versions, and the capabilities — tools and resources. The client uses the versions to select one both sides support, and every later request carries that version in its _meta field. The server answers from the request alone; it remembers nothing between calls. Step 2: list The client calls tools/list and receives the tool definition exactly as the host and model will see it: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "result": { "tools": [ { "name": "lookup_http_status", "description": "Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code. ...", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "code": { "type": "integer", "title": "Code" } }, "required": ["code"] } } ] } } Read this response as a reviewer, not as the author. The description and the schema are your public interface — the only things a stranger’s host knows about your tool. If the description is vague here, it is vague everywhere. Step 3: call The client sends tools/call with the tool name and arguments: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "lookup_http_status", "arguments": { "code": 404 } }, "_meta": { "protocolVersion": "2026-07-28" } } The server validates the arguments, runs the function, and returns the result: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "result": { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "404 Not Found (Client error): the server has no representation for the target." } ] } } Step 4: fail well Call it with { "code": 99 }. The schema accepts the integer, your range check rejects it, and the client receives an error result naming the invalid input instead of a result pretending everything worked: { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "error": { "code": -32602, "message": "code must be between 100 and 599, got 99" } } (The exact numeric error code is the SDK’s choice; what matters is the shape — an error result, correlated by id, with a message a human can act on.) Figure 3.2 Discover, list, call, and a clean failure When it breaks, check in this order Sooner or later — probably today — something in this setup will not work. Diagnose in this order, because each layer is cheaper to check than the next: Can the process start? Run python server.py by hand. Import errors and syntax errors show up here, with tracebacks you can read. Can it speak the protocol? Connect the Inspector. If it connects, stdio framing is fine and the problem is in your tool logic. If it cannot connect, suspect the launch command or stray output on stdout. Is the surface what you intended? Read the tools/list response in the Inspector. Most “wrong tool behavior” reports are actually wrong descriptions or schemas, discovered here in seconds. Is the call well-formed? Compare your tools/call arguments against the input schema, key by key. The model is a creative writer of JSON; the schema is the editor. What does the server say? Read stderr. If there is nothing there, that is itself a finding — add logging at the boundary where the request enters your code. This order mirrors the debugging lens from Chapter 2: transport, envelope, protocol match, domain operation. The habit of checking layers from the outside in will still be paying off when your servers have authentication, retries, and production traffic. Log to stderr, never stdout Return to the logging line from the start of the chapter, because it is the easiest rule in this book to violate by accident. Over stdio, every byte your process writes to standard output is parsed as protocol. A single print() left over from debugging — a “got here!” or a dumped dictionary — corrupts message framing, and the failure surfaces far from its cause as a cryptic JSON parse error in the host. You will blame the SDK, the host, and the protocol before you find the print statement. Everyone does this once. The fix is a habit, not a trick: configure logging to standard error once at startup, and never write to standard output yourself. Log what helps you diagnose the server — the tool name, the argument keys, timing, the outcome — and leave the values out when they could carry anything sensitive. Even in this toy server, “log shapes, not values” is worth practicing, because the habit transfers to servers that handle credentials. Note what we are not using: the MCP protocol logging primitive. It is deprecated as of the 2026–07–28 revision. For a local stdio server, stderr is the right channel; in production, structured telemetry belongs in OpenTelemetry, as Chapter 2 described. Five mistakes every first server makes These are not hypothetical. They are the failures that appear in every beginner’s server, including the author’s, roughly in this order. 1.The everything server. The lookup tool works, so you add a weather tool “while you’re at it,” then a file reader, then a shell wrapper. Each addition feels small; together they recreate the unscoped capability surface Chapter 2 warned about, and now one process holds every permission the host granted. The fix is the narrow rule from the start of this chapter: one server, one job. When a second job appears, start a second server. 2.Debugging with print(). Covered above, but it belongs on the list because it is the most common way a working server breaks. The fix: logging to stderr from the first line of the project, and a personal ban on print() in server code. 3.Logging secrets. A server that handles API keys or tokens will, sooner or later, log its full arguments to debug a failure — and the secret lands in a log file, a terminal scrollback, or a pasted bug report. The fix: log argument names and shapes, never values, and treat any log line as potentially public. 4.Swallowing errors. The broad except Exception that returns “something went wrong” feels safe; it is the opposite. The host cannot distinguish a transient failure from a bug, the model cannot recover, and you cannot diagnose. The fix: raise specific errors with messages that name the bad input and the rule it broke, and let the SDK turn them into error results. 5.Never testing the real input schema. You tested with {"code": 404} and it worked. The model will send {"code": "404"}, or {"code": 404, "verbose": true}, or omit the argument entirely. The fix: open the Inspector and call your tool the way a stranger would — wrong types, extra fields, missing fields — and decide your coercion and rejection policy deliberately instead of discovering it in production. One more, for readers following older tutorials: if a guide tells you to use sampling — server-initiated model completions — the guide predates the 2026–07–28 revision. Sampling is deprecated. A server that needs model inference integrates directly with a language-model provider under its own controls. Chapter checkpoint You should now be able to build and run a small MCP server without treating the SDK as magic: A first server should do one job statable in one sentence; ours looks up HTTP status codes. FastMCP turns a decorated Python function into a tool: the name, docstring, and annotations become the tool definition. A good tool description names the data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, and side effects. The SDK validates arguments against the input schema before your function runs; your code enforces the domain rules the schema cannot express. Invalid input raises and becomes an error result; a valid query with a negative answer returns a normal result. A resource fits data with a stable identity and no arguments; a tool fits an operation computed from supplied inputs. Over stdio, the server speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout; logs and prints go to stderr. The end-to-end flow is server/discover → tools/list → tools/call, each request self-contained with its version in _meta. The Inspector lets you exercise that flow by hand; an AI host launches the server as a child process from its configuration. The protocol logging primitive and sampling are deprecated in the 2026–07–28 revision; use stderr and provider APIs instead. The five classic mistakes: the everything server, print() on stdout, secrets in logs, swallowed errors, and untested input schemas. Design exercise Pick the server you sketched in Chapter 2’s exercise and shrink it to a first version with one tool and at most one resource. Then answer: State the server’s job in one sentence. If you need “and,” split it. Name the tool. Does the name say what it does without the description? Draft the description against the five-element checklist: data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, side effects. List every invalid input you can think of. Which does the schema reject, and which must your code reject? For each capability, argue tool versus resource in one sentence. How will you test it in the Inspector — including the adversarial inputs? What will you log, and where could a secret plausibly appear in those logs? Keep the answers. In Chapter 4, you will put this server’s tool through the full design checklist — naming, descriptions, schemas, and side-effect discipline. Key terms Error result: A JSON-RPC response carrying an error instead of a result, correlated to its request by id; how a server reports a failed call. FastMCP: The high-level Python interface in the official MCP SDK that maps decorated functions to tools and resources. Input schema: The JSON Schema describing a tool’s accepted arguments, derived here from Python type annotations and enforced by the SDK before the tool function runs. MCP Inspector: A developer tool that connects to an MCP server and lets you exercise discovery, listing, and calls by hand. Read-only tool: A tool that retrieves or computes information without modifying anything; declaring this in the description helps hosts decide when approval is unnecessary. References and further reading Model Context Protocol, “Specification” (2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/index Model Context Protocol, Python SDK. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk Model Context Protocol, “Architecture overview” (2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture Model Context Protocol, “SEP-2575: Make MCP Stateless.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/seps/2575-stateless-mcp Version note: This chapter targets MCP specification revision 2026–07–28. That revision is stateless by default, uses server/discover for server version and capability discovery, and deprecates sampling and the protocol logging primitive. Check the current specification and your SDK’s documentation before implementing version-sensitive behavior. Next: Chapter 4 — Designing Tools Well: names, descriptions, and schemas that models can actually use. Follow to get it when it drops. Your First MCP Server was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

This is Chapter 3 of MCP in Practice, a Book for Software Engineers Building Production-ready MCP tools.Previously: Chapter 1 — The Integration Problem and Chapter 2 — MCP Core Concepts.

Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author.

Your First MCP ServerFrom an empty project to a running server you can inspect and callWhat you will understand
  • How to lay out a minimal MCP server project with the Python SDK
  • How to define one narrow tool with a precise name, description, and input schema
  • How to add a single resource that contrasts with the tool’s intent
  • How to run the server over stdio and connect the MCP Inspector and an AI host
  • How to walk the full exchange end to end: server/discover → tools/list → tools/call
  • Why logs go to stderr, and the five mistakes that trap every first server
Start with one narrow job

Chapter 2 ended with an exercise: turn one of your server boundaries into a real server. This chapter does that — but not the server you eventually want. The first server has a different job: to make every concept from Chapter 2 concrete while the moving parts are still few enough to hold in your head.

So we will build the smallest useful server we can: it answers one question, “what does this HTTP status code mean?” It exposes exactly one tool, lookup_http_status, and one resource, a short reference of the five status-code categories. It is read-only, self-contained, and deterministic. It makes no network calls, needs no credentials, and holds no secrets — which means there is nothing sensitive to leak while you learn.

This choice is deliberate, and it previews a habit worth keeping. A server should do one job that you can state in one sentence. “Look up HTTP status codes” qualifies. “Look up HTTP status codes, and also check the weather, and also read local files” does not — that is three servers wearing one name, and Chapter 2 already showed why that boundary matters. If you cannot describe the server’s job in one sentence, split it.

What we are deliberately leaving out is as important as what we include. No authentication: the data is public reference material. No Streamable HTTP: stdio keeps the deployment to a single local process. No prompts, no elicitation, no subscriptions, no tasks. Each of those earns its place in a later chapter, once the basic exchange is second nature.

Figure 3.1 One server, one job: a single tool and a single resourceSet up the project

You need Python 3.10 or newer and a terminal. The official Python SDK is the mcp package; we will use its high-level interface, FastMCP, which handles the JSON-RPC framing, the server/discover response, and the dispatch of list and call operations. That leaves you free to concentrate on the capability surface, which is the part you own.

Create a project directory with a single file:

http-status-server/
  server.py

Then make a virtual environment and install the SDK:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "mcp[cli]"

The [cli] extra adds the command-line helpers used later in this chapter. One caution before you go further: SDKs for a young protocol move quickly. These examples follow the 1.x line of the mcp package. If an import path in your installed version differs from what you see here, check the SDK documentation for your version rather than guessing — the concepts are stable even when the spelling shifts.

Verify the install before you write any server code: run python -c “import mcp; print(mcp.version)” inside the virtual environment and confirm it prints a version. If it fails, the usual cause is installing into a different Python than the one you run — which python and which pip should point at the same .venv. Sorting this out now saves a confusing “module not found” later, when the error will surface inside a host process you cannot see into.

Define the server before the plumbing

Open server.py. The first decisions are the server’s name and its instructions — the two things a host learns about you before anything else.

import logging
import sys
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger("http-status")
mcp = FastMCP(
    name="http-status",
    instructions="Look up the meaning of HTTP status codes from a built-in reference table.",
)

A few things to notice. The name is lowercase, hyphenated, and free of spaces: hosts display it, and a clean name survives being shown in a tool picker. The instructions are one factual sentence. They are not a system prompt and not a place for persuasion; some hosts show them to the model, so state what the server does and nothing more.

Treat the instructions as documentation with an audience of two: the person reading the Inspector, and the model deciding whether your tool fits the user’s request. Both read it cold, with no other context about your intentions. That is why “Look up the meaning of HTTP status codes from a built-in reference table” works and “Helps with HTTP stuff” does not — the first lets a stranger predict what the server will and will not do. Like the tool descriptions coming later, review instructions as an interface change whenever you edit them.

The logging line deserves attention now because it prevents a failure you will otherwise meet later: it sends logs to standard error. Standard output belongs to the protocol, and we will return to that rule shortly.

When a client calls server/discover against this server, the SDK answers with the server’s identity — the name http-status, the instructions, the supported protocol versions — and its capabilities. Because we are about to register a tool and a resource, the capabilities will advertise exactly those two primitives and nothing else. Discovery is honest by construction: it describes what the server actually exposes.

Write one tool, and describe it like a public API

A tool in FastMCP is a Python function with a decorator. The function name becomes the tool name, the docstring becomes the tool description, and the type annotations become the input schema:

STATUS_CODES = {
    200: {"phrase": "OK", "category": "Success",
          "note": "The request succeeded."},
    301: {"phrase": "Moved Permanently", "category": "Redirection",
          "note": "The resource has a new permanent URL."},
    404: {"phrase": "Not Found", "category": "Client error",
          "note": "The server has no representation for the target."},
    500: {"phrase": "Internal Server Error", "category": "Server error",
          "note": "The server failed while processing the request."},
    # ... one entry per standard code
}
@mcp.tool()
def lookup_http_status(code: int) -> str:
    """Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code.
Searches a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes; it makes no
    network calls. Returns the code’s category, standard phrase, and a
    one-line usage note. Read-only: it never modifies anything. Accepts
    integer codes from 100 to 599 and raises an error for anything
    outside that range.
    """
    if not 100 <= code <= 599:
        raise ValueError(f"code must be between 100 and 599, got {code}")
    entry = STATUS_CODES.get(code)
    if entry is None:
        return f"{code} is not a standard HTTP status code."
    return f"{code} {entry['phrase']} ({entry['category']}): {entry['note']}"

A note on parameters you do not have yet: if a future version of this tool took an optional argument — say, verbose: bool = False — the default would make it optional in the input schema, while the required list would still contain only code. Defaults are a clean way to extend a tool without breaking existing callers, but each new parameter is a new promise in your public interface. For this first server, one required parameter is the whole contract, and that is a feature.

Chapter 2 said a tool description should name the data source, the required scope, the time behavior, the result limits, and whether the operation has side effects. Here is that checklist made concrete:

  • Data source:a built-in table of standard HTTP status codes. The description says where the answer comes from, so nobody assumes it queries a live service.
  • Scope:integer codes from 100 to 599. Anything outside that range is rejected, and the description says so up front.
  • Time behavior:the table is fixed reference data. Results are deterministic and do not go stale — which is the honest way to say “no time behavior applies.”
  • Result limits:one record per call. The caller knows exactly what shape to expect.
  • Side effects:none. The word “read-only” appears in the description itself, because a host deciding whether the model may call this without asking should not have to infer it.

The input schema comes from the annotation code: int. Before your function ever runs, the SDK validates the incoming arguments against that schema: a missing code, or a value that is not an integer, is rejected at the boundary with an error result. Your own check then handles the domain rule the schema cannot express — that 99 and 600 are integers but not status codes — and raises ValueError with a message that names the bad value. The SDK turns that exception into a JSON-RPC error result, so the host learns the call failed and why.

Notice the two different treatments of failure. A code outside 100–599 is invalid input, so it raises. A code inside the range but absent from the table — say, 210 — is a valid query with a negative answer, so it returns a normal result saying so. The distinction matters: an error result means “the call did not do what you asked,” while a result that says “not a standard code” means “the call worked and the answer is no.” Hosts and models treat those differently, so do not blur them.

Add one resource for contrast

The tool takes an argument and computes an answer. The status-code categories need neither: they are a fixed reference with a stable identity. That makes them a resource, not a second tool.

@mcp.resource("http-status://categories")
def status_categories() -> str:
    """The five HTTP status-code categories and the ranges they cover."""
    return (
        "1xx Informational (100-199): the request was received.
"
        "2xx Success (200-299): the request was received and accepted.
"
        "3xx Redirection (300-399): further action is needed.
"
        "4xx Client error (400-499): the request was invalid.
"
        "5xx Server error (500-599): the server failed to fulfill a valid request.
"
    )

A client lists it with resources/list and reads it with resources/read, addressing it by its URI. Compare the two primitives side by side and the intent distinction from Chapter 2 becomes tangible: the resource is retrieved, the tool is performed. A useful test of the boundary: if the categories ever needed an argument — say, a language for the descriptions — the resource would stop being honest, and you would remodel it as a tool.

Run it over stdio

A stdio server is a program that speaks JSON-RPC on its standard input and output. Add the entry point at the bottom of server.py:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()  # stdio transport by default

Run it:

python server.py

Nothing visible happens. That is correct: the process is waiting on stdin for a JSON-RPC request, and there is no one to talk to yet. Type a line and press enter and you will get a protocol error back — which, oddly, is a good sign. It means the server is listening.

This is also the moment to understand what an AI host does with your file. When the host starts, it spawns python server.py as a child process, connects pipes to its stdin and stdout, and speaks JSON-RPC through those pipes for as long as the host runs. There is no port, no URL, no daemon to manage. The server’s lifetime is the host’s decision: it starts the process when it needs the capability and kills it when it is done. That simplicity is why stdio is the right first transport — deployment is a file path, and the failure modes are process failure modes you already know.

Connect the Inspector, then an AI host

Talking to the server by hand-typing JSON-RPC gets old after one request. The MCP Inspector gives you a user interface over the same exchange:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py

Open the address it prints. The Inspector connects over stdio, calls server/discover, and shows you the server’s identity and capabilities. From there you can list tools, inspect the input schema your annotations produced, and call lookup_http_status with different arguments while watching the raw requests and responses. Every later section of this chapter is easier if you keep the Inspector open beside your editor.

In the Inspector, work through three views in order. First, the server view: confirm the name reads http-status and the capabilities list tools and resources. If the name is wrong here, it is wrong everywhere downstream. Second, the tools view: read your own description and input schema as a stranger would, and fix anything that assumes knowledge the reader does not have. Third, the call view: run lookup_http_status with 200, then with 99, then with the argument missing entirely, and watch the three different outcomes — a result, an error result from your range check, and an error result from schema validation. Those three shapes are the whole vocabulary of tool invocation.

If the Inspector cannot start your server at all, the cause is almost always the launch command, not your code: the wrong Python, a relative path resolved from the wrong directory, or a virtual environment the Inspector’s shell does not see. Run the exact command yourself in a terminal first. The same advice applies when an AI host reports that the server failed to start — hosts usually surface the child process’s stderr, which is another reason that stream is where your logs belong.

To connect an AI host, you tell the host how to launch your server as a child process. The exact configuration shape varies by host; the common form looks like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "http-status": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/path/to/http-status-server/server.py"]
    }
  }
}

Use the full path to your file, and if you installed the SDK in a virtual environment, point command at that environment’s Python. Restart the host, and the tool appears in its catalog. Ask the host “what does a 503 mean?” and watch what happens: the model selects lookup_http_status, the host validates the arguments and sends tools/call, and the answer comes back through the same path you just exercised by hand.

Exercise the full flow: discover, list, call

Whether the client is the Inspector or an AI host, the exchange follows the same shape. Walk through it once deliberately; this is the protocol from Chapter 2 with the abstractions removed.

Step 1: discover

The client calls server/discover and the server describes itself: the name http-status, the supported protocol versions, and the capabilities — tools and resources. The client uses the versions to select one both sides support, and every later request carries that version in its _meta field. The server answers from the request alone; it remembers nothing between calls.

Step 2: list

The client calls tools/list and receives the tool definition exactly as the host and model will see it:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "tools": [
      {
        "name": "lookup_http_status",
        "description": "Look up the meaning of an HTTP status code. ...",
        "inputSchema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "code": { "type": "integer", "title": "Code" }
          },
          "required": ["code"]
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

Read this response as a reviewer, not as the author. The description and the schema are your public interface — the only things a stranger’s host knows about your tool. If the description is vague here, it is vague everywhere.

Step 3: call

The client sends tools/call with the tool name and arguments:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "lookup_http_status",
    "arguments": { "code": 404 }
  },
  "_meta": { "protocolVersion": "2026-07-28" }
}

The server validates the arguments, runs the function, and returns the result:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "result": {
    "content": [
      { "type": "text",
        "text": "404 Not Found (Client error): the server has no representation for the target." }
    ]
  }
}
Step 4: fail well

Call it with { "code": 99 }. The schema accepts the integer, your range check rejects it, and the client receives an error result naming the invalid input instead of a result pretending everything worked:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 4,
  "error": { "code": -32602, "message": "code must be between 100 and 599, got 99" }
}

(The exact numeric error code is the SDK’s choice; what matters is the shape — an error result, correlated by id, with a message a human can act on.)

Figure 3.2 Discover, list, call, and a clean failureWhen it breaks, check in this order

Sooner or later — probably today — something in this setup will not work. Diagnose in this order, because each layer is cheaper to check than the next:

  1. Can the process start?Run python server.py by hand. Import errors and syntax errors show up here, with tracebacks you can read.
  2. Can it speak the protocol?Connect the Inspector. If it connects, stdio framing is fine and the problem is in your tool logic. If it cannot connect, suspect the launch command or stray output on stdout.
  3. Is the surface what you intended?Read the tools/list response in the Inspector. Most “wrong tool behavior” reports are actually wrong descriptions or schemas, discovered here in seconds.
  4. Is the call well-formed?Compare your tools/call arguments against the input schema, key by key. The model is a creative writer of JSON; the schema is the editor.
  5. What does the server say?Read stderr. If there is nothing there, that is itself a finding — add logging at the boundary where the request enters your code.

This order mirrors the debugging lens from Chapter 2: transport, envelope, protocol match, domain operation. The habit of checking layers from the outside in will still be paying off when your servers have authentication, retries, and production traffic.

Log to stderr, never stdout

Return to the logging line from the start of the chapter, because it is the easiest rule in this book to violate by accident. Over stdio, every byte your process writes to standard output is parsed as protocol. A single print() left over from debugging — a “got here!” or a dumped dictionary — corrupts message framing, and the failure surfaces far from its cause as a cryptic JSON parse error in the host. You will blame the SDK, the host, and the protocol before you find the print statement. Everyone does this once.

The fix is a habit, not a trick: configure logging to standard error once at startup, and never write to standard output yourself. Log what helps you diagnose the server — the tool name, the argument keys, timing, the outcome — and leave the values out when they could carry anything sensitive. Even in this toy server, “log shapes, not values” is worth practicing, because the habit transfers to servers that handle credentials.

Note what we are not using: the MCP protocol logging primitive. It is deprecated as of the 2026–07–28 revision. For a local stdio server, stderr is the right channel; in production, structured telemetry belongs in OpenTelemetry, as Chapter 2 described.

Five mistakes every first server makes

These are not hypothetical. They are the failures that appear in every beginner’s server, including the author’s, roughly in this order.

1.The everything server.The lookup tool works, so you add a weather tool “while you’re at it,” then a file reader, then a shell wrapper. Each addition feels small; together they recreate the unscoped capability surface Chapter 2 warned about, and now one process holds every permission the host granted. The fix is the narrow rule from the start of this chapter: one server, one job. When a second job appears, start a second server.

2.Debugging with print().Covered above, but it belongs on the list because it is the most common way a working server breaks. The fix: logging to stderr from the first line of the project, and a personal ban on print() in server code.

3.Logging secrets.A server that handles API keys or tokens will, sooner or later, log its full arguments to debug a failure — and the secret lands in a log file, a terminal scrollback, or a pasted bug report. The fix: log argument names and shapes, never values, and treat any log line as potentially public.

4.Swallowing errors.The broad except Exception that returns “something went wrong” feels safe; it is the opposite. The host cannot distinguish a transient failure from a bug, the model cannot recover, and you cannot diagnose. The fix: raise specific errors with messages that name the bad input and the rule it broke, and let the SDK turn them into error results.

5.Never testing the real input schema.You tested with {"code": 404} and it worked. The model will send {"code": "404"}, or {"code": 404, "verbose": true}, or omit the argument entirely. The fix: open the Inspector and call your tool the way a stranger would — wrong types, extra fields, missing fields — and decide your coercion and rejection policy deliberately instead of discovering it in production.

One more, for readers following older tutorials: if a guide tells you to use sampling — server-initiated model completions — the guide predates the 2026–07–28 revision. Sampling is deprecated. A server that needs model inference integrates directly with a language-model provider under its own controls.

Chapter checkpoint

You should now be able to build and run a small MCP server without treating the SDK as magic:

  • A first server should do one job statable in one sentence; ours looks up HTTP status codes.
  • FastMCP turns a decorated Python function into a tool: the name, docstring, and annotations become the tool definition.
  • A good tool description names the data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, and side effects.
  • The SDK validates arguments against the input schema before your function runs; your code enforces the domain rules the schema cannot express.
  • Invalid input raises and becomes an error result; a valid query with a negative answer returns a normal result.
  • A resource fits data with a stable identity and no arguments; a tool fits an operation computed from supplied inputs.
  • Over stdio, the server speaks JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout; logs and prints go to stderr.
  • The end-to-end flow is server/discover → tools/list → tools/call, each request self-contained with its version in _meta.
  • The Inspector lets you exercise that flow by hand; an AI host launches the server as a child process from its configuration.
  • The protocol logging primitive and sampling are deprecated in the 2026–07–28 revision; use stderr and provider APIs instead.
  • The five classic mistakes: the everything server, print() on stdout, secrets in logs, swallowed errors, and untested input schemas.
Design exercise

Pick the server you sketched in Chapter 2’s exercise and shrink it to a first version with one tool and at most one resource. Then answer:

  1. State the server’s job in one sentence. If you need “and,” split it.
  2. Name the tool. Does the name say what it does without the description?
  3. Draft the description against the five-element checklist: data source, scope, time behavior, result limits, side effects.
  4. List every invalid input you can think of. Which does the schema reject, and which must your code reject?
  5. For each capability, argue tool versus resource in one sentence.
  6. How will you test it in the Inspector — including the adversarial inputs?
  7. What will you log, and where could a secret plausibly appear in those logs?

Keep the answers. In Chapter 4, you will put this server’s tool through the full design checklist — naming, descriptions, schemas, and side-effect discipline.

Key terms

Error result: A JSON-RPC response carrying an error instead of a result, correlated to its request by id; how a server reports a failed call.

FastMCP: The high-level Python interface in the official MCP SDK that maps decorated functions to tools and resources.

Input schema: The JSON Schema describing a tool’s accepted arguments, derived here from Python type annotations and enforced by the SDK before the tool function runs.

MCP Inspector: A developer tool that connects to an MCP server and lets you exercise discovery, listing, and calls by hand.

Read-only tool: A tool that retrieves or computes information without modifying anything; declaring this in the description helps hosts decide when approval is unnecessary.

References and further reading
  1. Model Context Protocol, “Specification” (2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/index
  2. Model Context Protocol, Python SDK. https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk
  3. Model Context Protocol, “Architecture overview” (2026–07–28). https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture
  4. Model Context Protocol, “SEP-2575: Make MCP Stateless.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/seps/2575-stateless-mcp

Version note: This chapter targets MCP specification revision 2026–07–28. That revision is stateless by default, uses server/discover for server version and capability discovery, and deprecates sampling and the protocol logging primitive. Check the current specification and your SDK’s documentation before implementing version-sensitive behavior.

Next: Chapter 4 — Designing Tools Well: names, descriptions, and schemas that models can actually use. Follow to get it when it drops.

items.title: Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout
items.summary: Slingshot Insurance, an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth. Ethan Genteman, co-founder and CEO of Slingshot Insurance. (Courtesy photo) Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman, focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it. The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer. Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month. For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself. “We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview. Making the math work on a $25 policy One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season. Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman. He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers. “The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said. Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.” He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin. “That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said. Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check. It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman. A customer helped shape the business The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together. Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up. “We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.” Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said. Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder. The opportunity in vertical SaaS Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry. As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase. A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft. Those are examples of what could be developed, Genteman said. Slingshot aims to help vertical SaaS companies take ideas like those and turn them into insurance they can sell, providing both the software and help navigating the insurance industry and its regulatory requirements. “Insurance becomes another product that can be offered naturally within the existing customer experience,” he said. For Justin Kaufenberg , managing director at Rally Ventures, that opportunity is familiar. Before joining Rally, he ran SportsEngine , where insurance sold through its software became a key revenue source. “That experience gave me firsthand insight into the opportunity for software companies to generate revenue through embedded financial products,” he wrote via email. Kaufenberg sees similar potential across Rally’s portfolio, where most companies combine AI products with financial services. He said founders increasingly want insurance partners that can help them introduce coverage quickly. Rally co-founded Slingshot to bring insurance backing, underwriting, reporting, claims handling and distribution together in one business. “To get the carrier, the reinsurance, the underwriting platform, the data flow engine, the reporting capabilities, the claims handling, the embedded distribution engine, and every other part of the offering from a single vendor is unheard of,” Kaufenberg said. From insurance executive to founder Before starting Slingshot, Genteman was chief actuarial officer at publicly traded Palomar Holdings , where he also led data. He joined in 2019 and helped build its actuarial and data team as the company expanded beyond earthquake insurance into other coverage types. That work led him to explore whether newer technology could reduce the costs of running insurance programs. About a year ago, he began coding and building prototypes in his basement. He started talking with Rally toward the end of 2025 and left Palomar on July 1 to run Slingshot. Related Crunchbase query: Insurtech Startup Funding, 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman
