items.title: This startup raised $34 million to help security teams keep up with AI threats. Read the pitch deck.
items.summary: Guy Eshel and Raziel Oren founded Mave in 2025. Mave Mave has raised $34 million to bring AI agents to companies' security operations. CEO Raziel Oren said old systems can't keep up with how quickly AI is transforming cyberattacks. Business Insider got an exclusive look at the pitch deck Mave used to raise its Series A round. Mave, a cybersecurity startup that uses agents to counter the rise in AI-powered cyberattacks, has raised $34 million in funding. The Israel-based startup says its AI agents pull together information from a company's existing security systems, investigate alerts, filter out false alarms, and take actions approved by human teams. "Security operations is the last gate in any organization," cofounder and CEO Raziel Oren said, comparing it to the physical security guards who monitor a building's live camera footage. "This thing is really broken from the inside. The roots of the solutions there are just not keeping the relevant pace with the emerging threats." AI has transformed cyber threats at a dizzying pace. Attacks can happen much faster and on a much larger scale, and Oren predicted that the increase in agent-powered incidents will be "exponential." Mave says its own agents help human security teams keep up. "You can't hire your way out of this," Oren told Business Insider. "There must be a change in how you do [security operations] in order to protect your organizations." Oren cofounded Mave with Guy Eshel in 2025 after years of friendship. The two met when Oren was Eshel's mentor in unit 8200 of the Israel Defense Forces, which sits under the intelligence corps and gave them firsthand experience with cybersecurity issues. AI agents have come under the spotlight after a string of high-profile security breaches . Corporate leaders have grown increasingly worried about the cybersecurity risks AI poses, and some of Wall Street's executives spent third-quarter earnings calls explaining how they're defending against rogue AI agents. The technology has also been used by researchers to uncover security flaws: this week, OpenAI said one of its AI models had helped identify a vulnerability that puts 70% of the world's websites at risk. Oren said it takes some customers time to become comfortable handing over security operations to agents, but that the product's transparency is key to building trust. Mave says its agents track each step of their thousands of workflows, giving human employees insight into the agents' reasoning and actions. Mave charges its customers a flat rate, depending on the company's size and needs. Other startups have also jumped at the opportunity Mave sees, including agentic cybersecurity companies Dropzone and Prophet Security. Mave's $34 million funding consists of $28 million from a recent Series A round, led by Red Dot Capital Partners and with participation from Lumir Growth Partners, and an earlier $6 million seed round. The startup currently has 30 employees and plans to use some of the fresh capital to continue expanding the team, mainly for go-to-market roles and AI research. Read the pitch deck Mave used to raise its Series A round: The co-founders met in the army. Mave Cyberattacks are happening much faster. Mave Mave consolidates security operations. Mave In one instance, Mave says it stopped ShinyHunters, a cybercriminal group. Mave Customers include Fortune 200 and Fortune 500 companies. Mave Read the original article on Business Insider

  • CEO Raziel Oren said old systems can't keep up with how quickly AI is transforming cyberattacks.
  • Business Insider got an exclusive look at the pitch deck Mave used to raise its Series A round.

Mave, a cybersecurity startup that uses agents to counter the rise in AI-powered cyberattacks, has raised $34 million in funding.

The Israel-based startup says its AI agents pull together information from a company's existing security systems, investigate alerts, filter out false alarms, and take actions approved by human teams.

"Security operations is the last gate in any organization," cofounder and CEO Raziel Oren said, comparing it to the physical security guards who monitor a building's live camera footage. "This thing is really broken from the inside. The roots of the solutions there are just not keeping the relevant pace with the emerging threats."

AI has transformed cyber threats at a dizzying pace. Attacks can happen much faster and on a much larger scale, and Oren predicted that the increase in agent-powered incidents will be "exponential."

Mave says its own agents help human security teams keep up. "You can't hire your way out of this," Oren told Business Insider. "There must be a change in how you do [security operations] in order to protect your organizations."

Oren cofounded Mave with Guy Eshel in 2025 after years of friendship. The two met when Oren was Eshel's mentor in unit 8200 of the Israel Defense Forces, which sits under the intelligence corps and gave them firsthand experience with cybersecurity issues.

AI agents have come under the spotlight after a string of high-profile security breaches. Corporate leaders have grown increasingly worried about the cybersecurity risks AI poses, and some of Wall Street's executives spent third-quarter earnings calls explaining how they're defending against rogue AI agents.

The technology has also been used by researchers to uncover security flaws: this week, OpenAI said one of its AI models had helped identify a vulnerability that puts 70% of the world's websites at risk.

Oren said it takes some customers time to become comfortable handing over security operations to agents, but that the product's transparency is key to building trust. Mave says its agents track each step of their thousands of workflows, giving human employees insight into the agents' reasoning and actions.

Mave charges its customers a flat rate, depending on the company's size and needs. Other startups have also jumped at the opportunity Mave sees, including agentic cybersecurity companies Dropzone and Prophet Security.

Mave's $34 million funding consists of $28 million from a recent Series A round, led by Red Dot Capital Partners and with participation from Lumir Growth Partners, and an earlier $6 million seed round.

The startup currently has 30 employees and plans to use some of the fresh capital to continue expanding the team, mainly for go-to-market roles and AI research.

items.title: Google turns the infrastructure behind Gemini’s agents into a cloud service
items.summary: Google will soon make the infrastructure that powers its Gemini agents available to Google Cloud users in preview. Announced on Thursday at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon+MCPCon in San Jose, Agent Compute Engine will become available in preview to Google Cloud users later this year. It will provide every AI agent with a hardware-isolated microVM that combines the speed of containers with the security of a sandbox. Who else offers agent sandboxes? The idea of agent sandboxes is anything but new, of course. Startups like E2B and Daytona offer them to developers (and support them on any cloud), as does AWS with Bedrock AgentCore . E2B runs each sandbox in a Firecracker microVM, the open source virtualization technology AWS originally built for Lambda. It can pause a sandbox with its memory and filesystem intact and resume it in about a second. Daytona started out with containers but added microVM sandboxes in July. Those can pause a full machine or fork a running one into identical copies. AgentCore also gives every agent session its own microVM . AWS doesn’t charge for CPU while an agent waits on a model or tool call, though memory keeps billing until the runtime reclaims it. Those sessions top out at eight hours. In August, AWS added EC2-based runtime instances that can keep shared sessions alive for up to 14 days. It’s worth noting that Google itself isn’t new to this either. GKE already offers a managed version of Agent Sandbox , the open source Kubernetes project Google launched last November. The company also sells code-execution and computer-use sandboxes through its Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform . Agent Compute Engine, on the other hand, started out as internal infrastructure for Gemini, Antigravity , and Google’s own model training pipelines. Google’s take Few companies — if any — run as many agentic workloads as Google, be that for its own internal use or its customers. According to the company, agentic workloads have quickly become one of the fastest-growing consumers of compute and storage across its fleet. At this scale, the infrastructure services that power all of these autonomous agents don’t just need to be efficient and able to scale, but maybe more than anything, they need to be secure. Google, like some of its competitors, quickly realized that it needed to build a new purpose-built compute service to power all of these agents, similar to how it needed to build Borg , which later inspired Kubernetes, to manage compute in its early data centers. As Rohit Jnagal and Ramanathan Venkatapathy, both distinguished engineers at Google, note in a technical deep dive, traditional VMs provide developers with a lot of control and flexibility, but at the cost of speed when it comes to booting, suspending, and resuming a machine. Given how fast agents start and shut down, that’s not an option. Containers solve some of this, they note, “but there are multiple examples like coding agents and developer assistants that need complete isolation as well as kernel- and root-level control of the agentic environment.” With Agent Compute Engine, Jnagal and Venkatapathy write, the team went back to first principles to build “a unified, agent compute platform for Google” (and now its customers). A persistent computer for every agent At its core, it basically gives every agent a persistent, sandboxed computer to work with. That allows the agents to work with shell scripts, use a headless browser, and write code (with root permissions to that machine) in agent loops that could run for weeks. But the team also built it for large-scale use cases like the eval loops that frontier labs use to test their models, AI benchmarking, and reinforcement learning. In addition, the team also designed Agent Compute Engine to run sandboxed backends for Google’s own services. Jnagal and Venkatapathy also note that agents spend most of their time waiting on the model or the user. So once an agent finishes a tool call, the host checkpoints its microVM, which then uses no active resources until the next call comes in. Nothing to steal inside the sandbox The key feature here, besides speed, is to be able to trust that the agents can’t break out of their sandboxes. We’ve seen what happens when they do, after all. Each agent session runs inside a single-tenant, memory-safe microVM. Those environments hold no secrets in memory or on the disk, and their only identity is a short-lived, session-scoped one delivered through a single per-VM local listener. All traffic is end-to-end encrypted in transit, and snapshots and disks are encrypted at rest. The microVMs don’t get a standard network interface, either. All traffic runs through a proxy outside the sandbox, and when an agent needs to reach a service like Google Drive, Google’s Agent Gateway checks the user’s delegation and the sandbox’s identity before adding the actual credential, outside the sandbox. The underlying host is basically a stateless appliance with a read-only filesystem, with the hardware and firmware cryptographically verified at each boot. All of this is backed by Google’s own Titan and Titanium IPU security platform . The microVMs themselves run on Cloud Hypervisor , an open source virtual machine monitor, and each gets its own guest kernel and root access. Jnagal and Venkatapathy use the example of an enterprise agent that manages a user’s inbox and reads an email with hidden instructions to find any API keys on the machine and send them to an outside address. Most of the time, they note, the model will ignore that, but not always. “We started from one rule: Assume an attacker controls everything inside the sandbox, and make sure they find nothing there to use,” the team writes. Agent Substrate brings the same idea to Kubernetes But not every team will want to have its agents run in a managed Google service. For them, Google also offers Agent Substrate , an open source runtime for the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that it first announced in May. Substrate builds on Agent Sandbox , Google’s Kubernetes project, and adds a lightweight control plane that Google says can handle millions of short-lived tool calls that would swamp Kubernetes. Similar to Agent Compute Engine, Substrate snapshots an idle agent’s memory and returns the machine to the pool until the agent gets more work. Google says that means up to 10 times the density of traditional compute. In a 200,000-agent benchmark, Substrate handled 500 activations per second, with agents suspending and resuming in under half a second, the company says. Teams can isolate each sandbox with a microVM or gVisor , and every agent gets its own cryptographic identity. As with Agent Compute Engine, egress proxies attach credentials outside the sandbox. Substrate runs on any Kubernetes cluster, and Google says it works with any harness, including Claude Code, OpenClaw , and Nous Research’s Hermes . “We built Hermes Enterprise to enable customers to deploy into their existing infrastructure, while handling per-agent isolation and extensible access control,” Hervé Bizira, Nous Research’s chief business officer, notes in the announcement. “Agent Substrate addresses both at the platform layer in a way that also preserves valuable compute resources.”

items.title: Meta investors will get free shares if Mark Zuckerberg hits 'extraordinary' targets
items.summary: Mark Zuckerberg is the founder and CEO of Meta. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta will give its investors free shares if Mark Zuckerberg hits certain "extraordinary" targets. It will pay 1:1 share dividends each time Meta stock doubles and has compounded at over 10% a year. Meta is rolling out Class C shares to address Zuckerberg's tax concerns and keep him in California. Meta stockholders are set to receive free shares if Mark Zuckerberg absolutely crushes it as CEO. The social-media giant revealed in a Wednesday filing that if its upcoming Class C shares double from a baseline price of $580.60 to just over $1,161, and their compound annualized return since September 10 has been at least 10%, shareholders will receive a dividend: a Class C share for every Meta share they own. If Meta stock — specifically its 30-day volume-weighted average price — doubles again to around $2,322, and has risen by at least 10% on average per year, shareholders will receive the same dividend again, and so on. Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and the AI agent Muse , acknowledged how difficult it will be to unlock those dividends, describing the stock price targets as "extraordinary" in its filing. Its stock has already surged more than sevenfold from its November 2022 low, giving Meta a nearly $1.8 trillion market capitalization that ranks it among the 10 most valuable companies in the world. The additional dividends would be paid on top of the initial dividend declared by Meta's board on Wednesday, which will see Class A and Class B shareholders receive Class C shares on a 1:1 basis, likely in late January. Meta is rejigging its share structure in response to Zuckerberg's concerns about California's so-called billionaire tax: a one-off, 5% wealth tax on the roughly 250 billionaires living in the state. Zuckerberg, who ranked fifth on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index with a $247 billion net worth at Wednesday's close, will be able to sell the Class C shares to access the liquidity needed to pay the tax, avoiding a sale of his existing shares that would erode his voting power . Meta's board took action after Zuckerberg said he was considering moving out of California because of the potential tax, and cautioned that the steps involved in relocating, such as listing his home for sale, could spark questions from employees about the company's management, the filing says. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout
items.summary: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program , about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60 per cent report a cut in administrative time. AI scribes are tools that, with the patient’s consent, listen to a clinical visit and automatically draft the physician’s notes. We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). Our observation is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time. But without proper frameworks, it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings. We believe the fix is organizational. Burnout stems from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; not from any single task such as paperwork. One study found electronic health record design and use accounted for just 6.8 per cent of the differences in burnout between clinicians. When work conditions such as a chaotic atmosphere and lack of control over workload were also considered, that number rose to 36.2 per cent. In emergency medicine , physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. No scribe changes that. How AI quietly adds to physicians’ work I think we can all relate to the idea that when you complete one task efficiently and save some time, new demands fill the space, making it seem as though nothing was saved in the first place. But as AI introduces new ways of reducing the time physicians spend on documentation, it comes with novel ways of adding work, too. The time dividend gets spent. Saved time rarely comes back to clinicians. In Canada’s national AI scribe program , half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments. Studies from the United States show the same pattern: AI scribe adopters across five health systems saved 13.4 minutes of daily EHR time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week. Errors do happen and patient safety is at stake. In two simulated tests , Ontario’s auditor general reported that most of the 20 government-approved AI scribes made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province says there are no known reports of patient harm. OntarioMD, a subsidiary of the Ontario Medical Association that helps physicians adopt digital health tools with funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health, responded that physicians “know they must review every clinical note generated by their AI scribe.” That safeguard is essential — and it is also work. Used to be authors and now editors. Automation often leaves humans the hardest job, which is watching for rare but serious errors. When physicians at one U.S. health system got AI-drafted replies to patient messages, replying time did not decline as physicians still have to edit the text to make sure it was accurate. More tools, more switching. In our experience, many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems. As an example, in one of our emergency departments, starting a night shift means logging into the work station, the health record, the dictation system, the imaging viewer, the EKG viewer and, most recently, an AI scribe; six systems before seeing the first patient, and a copy-and-paste at the end of every interaction because the scribe lives outside the chart. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadian physicians named better-connected, interoperable systems as a priority. Always learning because it’s always changing. Keeping up with constant learning is a job demand in its own right and it can wear people down. This is also known as AI fatigue , defined as the overwhelming pressure of keeping up with AI tools for people’s jobs. Change fatigue is a predictable response to how change is managed by the health-care system and health-care leaders and it is not a reflection of someone’s failing to learn or to adapt. A better way We propose a practical framework that can be used by health-care organizations to improve the adoption of AI. This framework, GRACE, was co-developed by one of the authors, Ehsan Etezad, and it sets out five principles for moving toward responsible adoption. GRACE framework for responsible adoption of AI. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY Govern adoption . Include front-line clinicians on AI committees. Give every pilot a stop-rule written in advance. If the pilot doesn’t return measurable time, or audits find errors above an agreed threshold, it ends or is redesigned. Respect autonomy . Keep use voluntary and let clinicians choose among vetted tools. Respecting autonomy is an essential component of responsible AI adoption. Advance access. Build tools into the core clinical record so no one has to copy and paste. Fund access fairly. Cultivate competence. Offer protected, paid learning time and peer “AI champions.” Evaluate effectiveness. Track burnout, after-hours work, note accuracy and whether time actually comes back. Another practical tool, the AI Adoption Matrix, maps organizations on two dimensions. Enablement is how broadly people can access, use and build skills with AI. Governance is how well policies, oversight and accountability work. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant and work toward being “Responsible Pioneers” with GRACE. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY The real test There is increasing pressure to move fast with AI adoption in health-care systems and it will likely continue. We would like to clarify that we’re not arguing against adoption of AI in health care. We actually encourage it and are excited about the future it will bring to all of us. That said, we encourage health-care organizations to adopt AI responsibly because stakes are high in medicine and patient safety could be at risk. We believe success should be measured by how happy a physician can feel at their job and about their job, not just how many patients they can see in one shift. None of us wants our loved ones to be treated by an exhausted and overwhelmed physician, so let’s ask ourselves how can we reimagine a health-care system that won’t burn out our physicians. Ali Abdalvand is the chief medical officer for Elewana Advisory, a consulting firm specialized in health-care digital transformation. He is also a founding director of Western MedTech, a non-for-profit society focused on supporting health-care innovators. Ehsan Etezad provides private consulting at MEUS Science with a focus on Leadership & Culture, Responsible Adoption of AI, and Psychological Health & Safety.
items.summary_html:
AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program, about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60 per cent report a cut in administrative time.

AI scribes are tools that, with the patient’s consent, listen to a clinical visit and automatically draft the physician’s notes.

We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). Our observation is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time. But without proper frameworks, it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings. We believe the fix is organizational.

Burnout stems from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; not from any single task such as paperwork. One study found electronic health record design and use accounted for just 6.8 per cent of the differences in burnout between clinicians. When work conditions such as a chaotic atmosphere and lack of control over workload were also considered, that number rose to 36.2 per cent.

In emergency medicine, physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. No scribe changes that.

How AI quietly adds to physicians’ work

I think we can all relate to the idea that when you complete one task efficiently and save some time, new demands fill the space, making it seem as though nothing was saved in the first place. But as AI introduces new ways of reducing the time physicians spend on documentation, it comes with novel ways of adding work, too.

  1. The time dividend gets spent. Saved time rarely comes back to clinicians. In Canada’s national AI scribe program, half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments. Studies from the United States show the same pattern: AI scribe adopters across five health systems saved 13.4 minutes of daily EHR time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week.

  2. Errors do happen and patient safety is at stake. In two simulated tests, Ontario’s auditor general reported that most of the 20 government-approved AI scribes made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province says there are no known reports of patient harm. OntarioMD, a subsidiary of the Ontario Medical Association that helps physicians adopt digital health tools with funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health, responded that physicians “know they must review every clinical note generated by their AI scribe.” That safeguard is essential — and it is also work.

  3. Used to be authors and now editors. Automation often leaves humans the hardest job, which is watching for rare but serious errors. When physicians at one U.S. health system got AI-drafted replies to patient messages, replying time did not decline as physicians still have to edit the text to make sure it was accurate.

  4. More tools, more switching. In our experience, many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems. As an example, in one of our emergency departments, starting a night shift means logging into the work station, the health record, the dictation system, the imaging viewer, the EKG viewer and, most recently, an AI scribe; six systems before seeing the first patient, and a copy-and-paste at the end of every interaction because the scribe lives outside the chart. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadian physicians named better-connected, interoperable systems as a priority.

  5. Always learning because it’s always changing. Keeping up with constant learning is a job demand in its own right and it can wear people down. This is also known as AI fatigue, defined as the overwhelming pressure of keeping up with AI tools for people’s jobs. Change fatigue is a predictable response to how change is managed by the health-care system and health-care leaders and it is not a reflection of someone’s failing to learn or to adapt.

A better way

We propose a practical framework that can be used by health-care organizations to improve the adoption of AI. This framework, GRACE, was co-developed by one of the authors, Ehsan Etezad, and it sets out five principles for moving toward responsible adoption.

GRACE framework for responsible adoption of AI. (Ehsan Etezad), CC BY

  1. Govern adoption. Include front-line clinicians on AI committees. Give every pilot a stop-rule written in advance. If the pilot doesn’t return measurable time, or audits find errors above an agreed threshold, it ends or is redesigned.

  2. Respect autonomy. Keep use voluntary and let clinicians choose among vetted tools. Respecting autonomy is an essential component of responsible AI adoption.

  3. Advance access. Build tools into the core clinical record so no one has to copy and paste. Fund access fairly.

  4. Cultivate competence. Offer protected, paid learning time and peer “AI champions.”

  5. Evaluate effectiveness. Track burnout, after-hours work, note accuracy and whether time actually comes back.

Another practical tool, the AI Adoption Matrix, maps organizations on two dimensions. Enablement is how broadly people can access, use and build skills with AI. Governance is how well policies, oversight and accountability work. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant and work toward being “Responsible Pioneers” with GRACE.

We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant. (Ehsan Etezad), CC BY The real test

There is increasing pressure to move fast with AI adoption in health-care systems and it will likely continue.

We would like to clarify that we’re not arguing against adoption of AI in health care. We actually encourage it and are excited about the future it will bring to all of us.

That said, we encourage health-care organizations to adopt AI responsibly because stakes are high in medicine and patient safety could be at risk. We believe success should be measured by how happy a physician can feel at their job and about their job, not just how many patients they can see in one shift.

None of us wants our loved ones to be treated by an exhausted and overwhelmed physician, so let’s ask ourselves how can we reimagine a health-care system that won’t burn out our physicians.

Ali Abdalvand is the chief medical officer for Elewana Advisory, a consulting firm specialized in health-care digital transformation. He is also a founding director of Western MedTech, a non-for-profit society focused on supporting health-care innovators.

Ehsan Etezad provides private consulting at MEUS Science with a focus on Leadership & Culture, Responsible Adoption of AI, and Psychological Health & Safety.

items.title: Anthropic’s Financial Situation May Explain Why Dario Amodei Looks So Terrified All the Time
items.summary: Pull up any random photo of billionaire Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and you’re likely to land on a facial expression expressing something between horror and deep consternation. There may be a simple explanation for that: he knows the truth about his company’s finances. New reporting by the Wall Street Journal revealed the mounting costs for the AI lab, which ballooned to a net loss of $80 billion in the first six months of 2026. Anthropic’s losses for the same period a year prior were $13 billion — still an eye-watering sum, but peanuts compared to its runaway spending this year (the WSJ called it “one of the largest half-year losses ever reported.”) The bleak financial numbers come from a draft IPO prospectus viewed by the WSJ , which notes that the company’s revenue for the first half of 2026 grew by just $1.1 billion over the same period to $16.3 billion. The figures add to the anxiety around how long the AI spending bubble can sustain itself. If Anthropic’s losses continue to mount at a rate far exceeding revenue growth, there’s simply no way the lab can dig itself out of the hole it’s burrowed for itself. That would be bad news for the US economy as a whole, which now hinges almost entirely on circular AI investments and data center development . Beyond the immediate losses, the WSJ notes that the AI lab is also footing a $450 billion bill for cloud computing infrastructure over the next seven to ten years — meaning the clock is ticking on what is surely the costliest game of “kick-the-can” the world has ever seen. More on Anthropic: Anthropic Secretly Lobbying Government to Only Shut Down an AI Model If It’s Poised to Kill More Than 50 People

items.summary: There’s the PHP signal: Two pre-auth RCEs, swathes of the internet possibly exposed. (Get the official advisory here and a high-fidelity, free scanner here * for detecting exposure from Shubham Shah and team.) Amazon says attacks may have started from October 17, check logs. There’s the PHP noise: Did Chainguard break the embargo? (Yes, and the PHP Foundation is not happy .) Did OpenAI fail to properly credit Ryan Austin at Calif.io for finding the vulnerability first? Or was it Wiz? Then there’s the evergreen context: Frontier models are going to keep making it easier to find vulnerabilities and exploit them. There are going to be a lot more celebrity bugs, sometimes amplified by Big Marketing. Akamai Scale AI with confidence on the infrastructure built for it. Akamai Cloud delivers high-performance cloud computing with enterprise-grade security, core to edge. Learn more. Meanwhile organisations will continue to get hacked because they are using “Password1” or, like OVHcloud , failing to notice a developer’s MacBook had an infostealer on it for a year and letting said developer link personal GitHub accounts to the corporate organisation without GitHub's "immutable releases" feature enabled; enabling a supply chain attack . It's Plus ça change, plus c'est la même chose , but now on steroids. We refer readers to Cloudflare CSO Grant Bourzikas’ sensible comments earlier this year after pointing Mythos at the company’s stack. “The loudest reaction [from] security leaders has been about speed - scan faster, patch faster, compress the response cycle. More than one team we have spoken with is now operating under a two-hour SLA from CVE release to patch in production. The instinct is understandable: when the attacker timeline shortens, the defender timeline has to shorten with it. “Faster is not going to be enough, and we think a lot of teams are about to spend a lot of time, effort, and money learning that the hard way.” Let's get together Honest conversations tend to happen best among a small cohort of people in which nobody is trying to sell a solution. (Perhaps the Shirky Principle holds: “Institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution.”) We're big fans of convening our community to break bread for sanity checks, information-sharing and relationship-building. That is one of the principles of our biannual The Stack Summit . We love enterprise technology’s big Jamborees like Web Summit or re:Invent, but it’s the intimate, Chatham House rule gatherings where meaningful knowledge is often shared, connections forged, and intel disseminated. We ran our first in New York in April. There were just 50 people in the room. Together, they held over $25 billion in annual technology budget. We’re back in London on November 4th . I’ll be hosting a fireside conversation with the Group COO of the UK’s biggest bank and the Group CTO of the UK’s biggest pharmaceutical company to kick things off. Both Ron van Kemenade and Shobie Ramakrishnan are deeply insightful and very candid leaders. We’ll be getting real about their views on evolving architectures, operational models, and the maturity or otherwise of their teams’ agentic efforts as well as more broadly how they are harnessing AI, data, and process changes to drive organisational growth. We also have sessions with one of Europe’s largest digital banks about how it built its award-winning customer service agent for 20 million customers on a mix of LLMs and SLMs without, well, breaking the bank. We're getting technical about running AI behind an airgap and optimising smaller models for edge environments and more. items.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
items.summary: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.”

items.title: eMudhra to Exit Global SSL/TLS Certificate Business
items.summary: Bengaluru-based eMudhra will exit its global SSL/TLS certificate business after a security incident prompted Google, Mozilla, and Apple to block affected certificates. The company said on Thursday that its board decided to exit the business, which contributes around 1% of its global revenue, and focus on enterprise software and other digital trust services. The decision follows the discovery of eight eMudhra certificate authorities with weak private keys that could potentially have allowed attackers to create fake website certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. The eight compromised private keys were the numbers—-4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. A typical P-384 cryptographic private key is a randomly generated 384-bit number, offering roughly 2384, or 10115, possible values, which are nearly impossible to guess. The eMudhra keys, on the other hand, were recoverable in less than a second. eMudhra said the problem originated in an error during a key-generation process in April 2025. The company said its infrastructure had not been compromised, no data had been breached, and the affected authorities had not issued certificates to end users. It revoked the affected authorities after discovering the issue and is investigating the root cause. Google blocked the affected certificates in Chrome and extended protections to supported Android devices. Mozilla blocked them in Firefox, while Apple also introduced safeguards. India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued an advisory, while the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology said it had formed a special team to investigate the incident. The authorities have distinguished the affected international website-certificate business from eMudhra's domestic digital signature and eSign services, which remain operational. eMudhra said it would provide replacement certificates to affected customers free of charge through partners. Its certificate-status and revocation services will continue until existing certificates expire or are replaced. The company said rising compliance costs, competition from providers offering certificates free of charge and the scrutiny following the incident had contributed to its decision to exit the business. Bengaluru-based eMudhra will exit its global SSL/TLS certificate business after a security incident prompted Google, Mozilla, and Apple to block affected certificates.

The company said on Thursday that its board decided to exit the business, which contributes around 1% of its global revenue, and focus on enterprise software and other digital trust services.

The decision follows the discovery of eight eMudhra certificate authorities with weak private keys that could potentially have allowed attackers to create fake website certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. 

The eight compromised private keys were the numbers—-4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. 

A typical P-384 cryptographic private key is a randomly generated 384-bit number, offering roughly 2384, or 10115, possible values, which are nearly impossible to guess. 

The eMudhra keys, on the other hand, were recoverable in less than a second.

eMudhra said the problem originated in an error during a key-generation process in April 2025. The company said its infrastructure had not been compromised, no data had been breached, and the affected authorities had not issued certificates to end users. 

It revoked the affected authorities after discovering the issue and is investigating the root cause.

Google blocked the affected certificates in Chrome and extended protections to supported Android devices. Mozilla blocked them in Firefox, while Apple also introduced safeguards. 

India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued an advisory, while the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology said it had formed a special team to investigate the incident. 

The authorities have distinguished the affected international website-certificate business from eMudhra's domestic digital signature and eSign services, which remain operational.

eMudhra said it would provide replacement certificates to affected customers free of charge through partners. Its certificate-status and revocation services will continue until existing certificates expire or are replaced.

The company said rising compliance costs, competition from providers offering certificates free of charge and the scrutiny following the incident had contributed to its decision to exit the business. 

Its other operations, including enterprise identity management, electronic signatures and public key infrastructure products, are unaffected, it said.

items.title: When an AI Video Edit Changes More Than You Asked
items.summary: Getting the new words right is only part of changing a sign in a video. You also want to keep the shot you chose. Suppose an AI editor replaces the lettering, and the preview looks convincing. Before accepting it, you still need to establish what happened to the rest of the footage. That review extends beyond spelling. As the sign turns, the words have to stay with its surface, while the scene around it remains as you intended. A good still frame tells you very little about the transition…

Every gotcha below follows the same shape. First the symptom: what you actually see when it bites you, in the form you will recognize at 2 a.m. Then why it happens: the root cause, usually a reasonable-looking decision with a hidden cost. Then the fix: the concrete change, stated plainly enough to apply today. Work through them with your own server in mind. At least one of them is already in your code. The client’s log shows a framing error like unexpected token or invalid JSON-RPC message, and every retry fails the same way. Restarting changes nothing. The server process is alive and healthy; the conversation between the two ends is not. Why it happens: On the stdio transport, stdout is not a logging channel. It is the wire. MCP messages travel as newline-delimited JSON-RPC over the server’s standard output, so a single stray line, one print(“debug”), a library that logs its banner on import, a warning from a dependency, is enough to corrupt the message framing. The client reads your debug line where it expected a JSON-RPC envelope, fails to parse it, and the session is over before it began. Hand-testing hides the problem because your terminal happily shows both the stray output and the real messages side by side. The client cannot do that. It is parsing a stream, not reading a screen. The fix: Log to stderr, never stdout. Make this a rule with no exceptions, enforced in code review and in your starter template. In Python, configure your logging handlers to write to sys.stderr; in Node, write to process.stderr. Audit your dependencies too: some libraries print on import, and those prints are just as fatal. If a dependency will not stay quiet, wrap it, redirect its output, or replace it. Then add a test that runs your server’s initialization sequence and asserts that stdout contains only valid JSON-RPC messages, one per line. That test is cheap, and it catches the one debug print that slips in three months from now. The entire logging setup is three lines: import logging, sys logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.INFO) # every handler points at stderr; stdout stays pristine Figure 11.1 One stray line on stdout corrupts JSON-RPC framing, fails the handshake, and cascades into every tool on the server appearing unavailable. The chatty tool Symptom: Your tools work, but every call feels expensive. Responses come back slowly, the model’s answers get vaguer as the session continues, and eventually context fills up with material the model never asked for. Your http-status server’s lookup_http_status is the classic small-scale version: one call returns every category, every code, and a paragraph of history for each, when the caller wanted the meaning of 429. Why it happens: Tool results land directly in the model’s context, and context is a budget, not a hard drive. Returning everything is the easiest code to write, so it is the first code everyone writes: fetch the rows, serialize them all, hand them back. The cost is invisible in testing, where a single call looks fine, and brutal in production, where the model pays for every token on every turn, and the relevant fact drowns in fifty irrelevant ones. A tool that returns megabytes to answer a one-line question is not being thorough. It is being wasteful with the most expensive resource in the system. The fix: Return references and pages, not dumps. Give the caller a page of results and a cursor for the next page, the way any well-designed API does. Prefer summaries with drill-down over full detail: ten category names with a count each, then a tool that expands one category on demand. For the http-status server, that means lookup_http_status returns the code, the name, and one line of meaning, and a separate parameter asks for the extended history only when the caller opts in. As a rule of thumb, if a tool’s typical response is longer than a few hundred lines, it needs pagination, filtering, or a narrower shape. Measure response sizes in your tests, the way Chapter 9 measured latency, and fail the build when a tool’s default response crosses your budget. Figure 11.2 A tool that returns everything crowds the model’s context; the same tool returning one page plus a cursor leaves room for the actual work. Errors that say nothing Symptom: A tool call fails, and the model does the worst possible thing: it guesses. It retries the same bad call with slightly different arguments, tries a different tool at random, or confidently reports success to the user while nothing happened. Your logs show the tool returned {“error”: “failed”} or a raw stack trace, and the model had no better information than you gave it. Why it happens: Error strings are written for the developer who wrote the code, not for the agent that has to recover from the failure. “failed” names nothing. A stack trace names everything except what matters: it tells the model about your file layout while hiding the one fact it needs, which is what to do differently. The model is a reasonable reader of error messages, but it can only reason from what you put in front of it. Vague errors produce vague retries, and vague retries produce incidents. The fix: Every error names three things: the value that was wrong, the rule it broke, and the remedy. Chapter 4 introduced this pattern, and production is where it earns its keep: {"error": "invalid input"} {"error": "code 'abc' is not a three-digit HTTP status (100-599); retry with a numeric code, e.g. 404."} The second one tells the model exactly what failed, what the constraint is, and what a correct retry looks like. Build a small error helper in your server so every tool raises errors in the same shape, and review error messages the way you review tool descriptions: they are part of the interface the model reads. Secrets in the schema Symptom: Everything works in your test environment, and then a security review, or worse, a curious user, notices that your tool descriptions contain live API keys, internal hostnames, or credential formats. The keys are visible in the client’s tool listing, which means they are visible to the model, which means they can end up in conversation history, logs, or a response to an unrelated question. Why it happens: Schemas and descriptions feel like documentation, and developers treat them that way, pasting example requests that happen to contain real tokens, or describing an argument as “the API key for the billing service, format sk-live-…”. But a tool schema is not documentation. It is data the host hands to the model on every session. Anything you write in a description or an example value is something you have disclosed to every model that ever lists your tools. Secrets do not belong in the contract; they belong behind it. The fix: Keep every credential server-side and reference it by name, never by value. Your server holds the keys in its own configuration or secret store; the tool schema refers to accounts, environments, or profiles by opaque identifier, and the server resolves those identifiers to credentials at call time. If an argument genuinely needs a user-supplied token, the host collects it through its own secure channel, not through a string you pasted into a description. Then grep your schemas and descriptions for anything that looks like a key, a token, or an internal hostname, and add that grep to your release checklist. Chapter 6 covers the full auth story; this is its cheapest rule. Remote servers with no auth Symptom: Your server runs on Streamable HTTP, reachable from the network, and anyone who finds the URL can call your tools. There is no incident yet, which is exactly the problem: the absence of an incident is not evidence of safety. Roughly 40% of public MCP servers expose tools with no authentication at all (Fudan University active scan of 7,973 servers, May 2026; OWASP reports a similar figure). Why it happens: Local servers over stdio inherit the security of the machine they run on; the transport itself is the boundary, and Chapter 7 leaned on that fact. Remote servers inherit nothing. The moment your server answers over HTTP, the network is the boundary, and an open endpoint is an open proxy to everything your tools can touch. Teams skip auth because the demo works without it, the OAuth dance from Chapter 6 feels heavy for an internal tool, and “we will add it before launch” quietly becomes “it has been in production for six months.” The fix: Put OAuth with scopes in front of every remote server before it serves its first real request, exactly as Chapter 6 describes. Scopes matter as much as the login: a token that can call any tool is barely better than no token, because a compromised or over-eager client can reach the destructive tools too. Scope tokens to the tools each client actually needs, and keep the read-only tools on narrower scopes than the mutating ones. If the OAuth setup feels heavy for an internal prototype, treat that feeling as a signal, not a veto: the prototype is about to become production, and production without auth is the gotcha this section is named after. The god server Symptom: One server exposes forty tools across six domains: files, databases, email, calendar, deployment, and billing. Tool choice gets unreliable; the model picks the email tool when it wanted the notification tool, or calls a destructive deployment tool when a read would have done. Reviews get harder because every change touches the same sprawling surface. And when the server needs different permissions for different tools, you discover you cannot scope it: it is all or nothing. Why it happens: Consolidation is tempting. One server means one deployment, one auth configuration, one thing to monitor. But a server is a trust boundary as well as a deployment unit, and Chapter 2’s rule stands: never give every server broad visibility. Each tool a server exposes is a capability every client of that server can see and, subject to the host’s policy, invoke. Packing unrelated capabilities into one server forces every client to be trusted with all of them, which means your least-trusted client sets the security posture of your most dangerous tool. The fix: Split by domain and by trust level, the way Chapter 10’s coordination story assumed: small, focused servers, one isolated client per server, each with the minimum tools and the minimum scopes it needs. The billing tools live on the billing server with the billing credentials; the file tools live on the file server with file credentials. Yes, this means more deployments. That is the trade, and it is worth it: a compromised or confused client can only reach the tools on the servers it was connected to. When you feel the pull to add “just one more tool” to a server that has nothing to do with it, that feeling is this gotcha knocking. Treating annotations as enforcement Symptom: You marked your dangerous tool with the annotation that says it is not read-only, or you set a hint that the tool should require approval, and then you watched a host call it freely with no approval step. Or the reverse: you marked a tool read-only and assumed the model could never change state through it, until someone found the tool that “reads” a configuration by rewriting it. Why it happens: Annotations in MCP are advisory. They are hints the server offers about a tool’s behavior, readOnlyHint, destructive hints, and the like, and a well-behaved host uses them to make better decisions about approvals and presentation. But the protocol does not enforce them, and not every host honors them the same way. Treating an annotation as a security control is like treating a “please knock” sign as a lock. The server asserted a property; nothing in the wire guarantees the client acted on it. The fix: Enforce policy on your side of the boundary. If a tool must not run without human approval, the host owns that decision, per the architecture in Chapter 2: the host owns orchestration, policy, approval, and UX. Your server’s job is to make the host’s job easy: accurate annotations, clear descriptions of consequences, and, for the truly dangerous operations, its own confirmation step or a separate privileged tool with tighter scopes. And never trust a read-only annotation on a tool you did not audit. If the tool can change state, say so in the annotation and the description, and scope it accordingly. Defense in depth means the annotation, the host policy, and the server-side check all agree, and none of them is load-bearing alone. Assuming a sticky session Symptom: Your server works over stdio, where the process lives as long as the session. You move it to Streamable HTTP, and suddenly multi-step workflows break: the second call in a sequence cannot see what the first call stored, progress vanishes between requests, and resuming a session after a network hiccup starts from zero. Why it happens: MCP servers are stateless by default. The stdio transport hid that from you because the process itself was the session: in-memory state survived from one message to the next, and it felt like the protocol was keeping state for you. Over Streamable HTTP, each request may reach a fresh process, a different replica, or the same process after a restart. Anything you kept in a global variable was never part of the contract. It was an accident of the transport, and the new transport does not repeat the accident. The fix: Design every tool call as if it is the first one the server has ever seen. Pass the state the call needs in its arguments or in a resource the client can read back; persist anything durable in a real store, not in process memory. Chapter 7’s rule is the bright line: when the work itself is long-lived, hand it to Tasks, the protocol’s mechanism for durable work, rather than simulating a session out of globals and hope. Then test it the honest way: run two sequential tool calls against a server process you restart in between. If the second call behaves differently than it did in one long-lived process, you were depending on the accident. Polling a long job instead of using tasks Symptom: A tool kicks off work that takes minutes: an export, a scan, a batch job. The model, having no way to wait, calls a status tool in a tight loop: are we done yet, are we done yet, are we done yet. Each poll burns context and a request, the transcript fills with dozens of identical status checks, and if the session ends, nobody ever learns the result. Why it happens: The request-response shape of a tool call suggests a synchronous world, so developers build long jobs behind a synchronous-looking tool and leave the waiting to the caller. But the caller is a language model with a context budget, and every poll is a full round trip that says nothing new. Polling is the model doing with tokens what an event or a durable handle should do with almost none. The fix: Use Tasks for durable work, as Chapter 7 prescribes. The tool starts the job and returns a task handle immediately; the client checks the task’s status with backoff or subscribes to its completion instead of hammering a status endpoint. Design the status check to be cheap and the completion payload to carry the actual result, so the dozens of polls become a handful of quiet checks and one useful answer. As a rule, if your status tool gets called more than a few times per job in testing, the polling interval is wrong or the mechanism is: reach for Tasks before you reach for a longer sleep. Flying blind in production Symptom: Something is slow, or wrong, or both, and you cannot say which call, which tool, or which session is responsible. Your logs show a flat stream of messages with no way to connect a tool call to the request that triggered it. The host team blames your server, you blame the host, and neither of you has evidence. Why it happens: Observability was deferred. The server logs to wherever was convenient, with no request identifiers, no timing, and no structured fields, because during development there was exactly one developer and one session. In production there are many of both, and a log line without a correlation ID is a fact without an address. Chapter 8 built the case for tracing the full path from host to client to server; this gotcha is what that path looks like when you skip it. The fix: Give every request a correlation ID at the edge and propagate it through every log line your server emits, structured, to stderr, with timings. Log the tool name, the session or task identifier, the duration, and the outcome on every call; log nothing that belongs in the schema, per the secrets rule above. Then make sure you can answer three questions from your logs alone: which tool is slowest, which tool fails most, and what a single session did from start to finish. If you cannot answer all three in under five minutes, your observability is not done. It is the difference between debugging with evidence and debugging with opinions. Pre-production checklist Run this list against your own server before it serves real traffic. Every item traces back to a gotcha in this chapter or a rule from an earlier one. If an item fails, fix it now; production is an expensive place to learn. Stdout carries only JSON-RPC messages. Run the initialization sequence and assert that every line on stdout parses as a JSON-RPC envelope. All logging goes to stderr. Dependencies are quiet. No library prints, banners, or warnings to stdout on import or during calls. Tool responses are budgeted. The default response of every tool is measured, paginated where it can grow, and small enough that a session of normal use stays well inside context limits. Errors name the value, the rule, and the remedy. Read every error path and confirm a model could retry correctly from the message alone. No secrets in schemas. Grep tool names, descriptions, examples, and defaults for keys, tokens, internal hostnames, and credential formats. None found. Remote servers require auth. Every Streamable HTTP deployment sits behind OAuth with scopes, and tokens are scoped to the tools each client needs. Servers are focused. No server exposes tools across unrelated domains, and no client is connected to capabilities it does not need. Annotations are accurate and unenforced assumptions are gone. Nothing destructive relies on an annotation alone; the host policy and server-side checks agree. State is explicit. Two sequential calls with a server restart in between behave the same as two calls in one long-lived process. Durable work uses Tasks. Long jobs do not invite polling. Status checks are cheap, backed off, and few; completion carries the result. Every request is traceable. Correlation IDs flow through structured logs, and you can answer: slowest tool, most-failing tool, full session history. Wire schemas are pinned by tests. Tool input and output shapes are asserted in automated tests, so a drifted schema fails the build instead of failing a session. Destructive tools have a second gate. Deletion, money movement, publishing, and external messages require host approval or a server-side confirmation, never a bare call. Timeouts and retries are set. Every outbound call your server makes has a timeout, and retries are bounded with backoff, so one slow dependency cannot wedge your server. The rollback plan exists. You know which version is running, how to revert to the previous one, and how to tell clients to reconnect. Fifteen checks, most of them automatable, all of them cheaper than the incident they prevent. Keep this list next to your deployment pipeline and run it on every release, not just the first one. Gotchas do not retire; they wait for the release where you stopped checking. Chapter checkpoint You now have the field guide to the failures this book promised to help you avoid: Stdout is the wire on stdio: log to stderr, and test that stdout carries only JSON-RPC. Chatty tools waste the model’s context budget: return pages, summaries, and references. Errors must name the value, the rule, and the remedy, or the model will guess. Secrets live server-side: schemas and descriptions are visible to the model. Remote servers need OAuth with scopes: no-auth endpoints are borrowed trouble. Focused servers beat god servers: one isolated client per server, minimum tools, minimum scopes. Annotations are advisory: enforce policy in the host and verify server-side. Servers are stateless by default: make state explicit and hand durable work to Tasks. Polling burns context: use Tasks with backoff and cheap status checks. Observability is the difference between debugging with evidence and debugging with opinions. Design exercise Take the server you have been building through this book, or the http-status server from the running example and run the pre-production checklist against it honestly. Pick three checklist items you are least sure about and write down the evidence for each: passing or failing. For each failing item, write the smallest fix that would make it pass, and the test that would keep it passing. Find one tool whose default response is larger than it needs to be, and sketch its paginated shape: page size, cursor, and what the first page contains. Find one error message your server can produce today, and rewrite it to name the value, the rule, and the remedy. Identify the most destructive tool your server exposes, and confirm it has a second gate: host approval, server-side confirmation, or tighter scopes. Bring the results to Chapter 12, where we look at where the protocol is going and how you can help shape it. The servers that survive contact with production are not the clever ones. They are the checked ones. Key terms Anti-pattern: a recurring approach that looks reasonable and reliably causes harm. Cascade: a failure that spreads from one component to others through a shared dependency. Chatty tool: a tool whose responses are large enough to waste context or crowd out other work. Correlation ID: an identifier attached to a request as it crosses component boundaries, so logs from each side can be joined. References and further reading Model Context Protocol, “What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/getting-started/intro Model Context Protocol, “Specification.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/index Model Context Protocol, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture Martin Kleppmann, “Designing Data-Intensive Applications,” Chapter 8 (fault tolerance) and Chapter 11 (stream processing). O’Reilly Media, 2017. Google Site Reliability Engineering, “Monitoring Distributed Systems.” https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ Fudan University active scan of 7,973 public MCP servers (May 2026) — 40.55% exposed tools with no authentication; similar figures in the official registry audit (41%) and OWASP (38%). https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ Next: Chapter 12 — The Road Ahead: where MCP goes from here. Follow to get it when it drops. Gotchas and Anti-Patterns was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
