It retries the same bad call with slightly different arguments, tries a different tool at random, or confidently reports success to the user while nothing happened. Your logs show the tool returned {“error”: “failed”} or a raw stack trace, and the model had no better information than you gave it.

Why it happens: Error strings are written for the developer who wrote the code, not for the agent that has to recover from the failure. “failed” names nothing. A stack trace names everything except what matters: it tells the model about your file layout while hiding the one fact it needs, which is what to do differently. The model is a reasonable reader of error messages, but it can only reason from what you put in front of it. Vague errors produce vague retries, and vague retries produce incidents.

The fix: Every error names three things: the value that was wrong, the rule it broke, and the remedy. Chapter 4 introduced this pattern, and production is where it earns its keep:

{"error": "invalid input"}
{"error": "code 'abc' is not a three-digit HTTP status (100-599); retry with a numeric code, e.g. 404."}

The second one tells the model exactly what failed, what the constraint is, and what a correct retry looks like. Build a small error helper in your server so every tool raises errors in the same shape, and review error messages the way you review tool descriptions: they are part of the interface the model reads.

Secrets in the schema

Symptom: Everything works in your test environment, and then a security review, or worse, a curious user, notices that your tool descriptions contain live API keys, internal hostnames, or credential formats. The keys are visible in the client’s tool listing, which means they are visible to the model, which means they can end up in conversation history, logs, or a response to an unrelated question.

Why it happens: Schemas and descriptions feel like documentation, and developers treat them that way, pasting example requests that happen to contain real tokens, or describing an argument as “the API key for the billing service, format sk-live-…”. But a tool schema is not documentation. It is data the host hands to the model on every session. Anything you write in a description or an example value is something you have disclosed to every model that ever lists your tools. Secrets do not belong in the contract; they belong behind it.

The fix: Keep every credential server-side and reference it by name, never by value. Your server holds the keys in its own configuration or secret store; the tool schema refers to accounts, environments, or profiles by opaque identifier, and the server resolves those identifiers to credentials at call time. If an argument genuinely needs a user-supplied token, the host collects it through its own secure channel, not through a string you pasted into a description. Then grep your schemas and descriptions for anything that looks like a key, a token, or an internal hostname, and add that grep to your release checklist. Chapter 6 covers the full auth story; this is its cheapest rule.

Remote servers with no auth

Symptom: Your server runs on Streamable HTTP, reachable from the network, and anyone who finds the URL can call your tools. There is no incident yet, which is exactly the problem: the absence of an incident is not evidence of safety. Roughly 40% of public MCP servers expose tools with no authentication at all (Fudan University active scan of 7,973 servers, May 2026; OWASP reports a similar figure).

Why it happens: Local servers over stdio inherit the security of the machine they run on; the transport itself is the boundary, and Chapter 7 leaned on that fact. Remote servers inherit nothing. The moment your server answers over HTTP, the network is the boundary, and an open endpoint is an open proxy to everything your tools can touch. Teams skip auth because the demo works without it, the OAuth dance from Chapter 6 feels heavy for an internal tool, and “we will add it before launch” quietly becomes “it has been in production for six months.”

The fix: Put OAuth with scopes in front of every remote server before it serves its first real request, exactly as Chapter 6 describes. Scopes matter as much as the login: a token that can call any tool is barely better than no token, because a compromised or over-eager client can reach the destructive tools too. Scope tokens to the tools each client actually needs, and keep the read-only tools on narrower scopes than the mutating ones. If the OAuth setup feels heavy for an internal prototype, treat that feeling as a signal, not a veto: the prototype is about to become production, and production without auth is the gotcha this section is named after.

The god server

Symptom: One server exposes forty tools across six domains: files, databases, email, calendar, deployment, and billing. Tool choice gets unreliable; the model picks the email tool when it wanted the notification tool, or calls a destructive deployment tool when a read would have done. Reviews get harder because every change touches the same sprawling surface. And when the server needs different permissions for different tools, you discover you cannot scope it: it is all or nothing.

Why it happens: Consolidation is tempting. One server means one deployment, one auth configuration, one thing to monitor. But a server is a trust boundary as well as a deployment unit, and Chapter 2’s rule stands: never give every server broad visibility. Each tool a server exposes is a capability every client of that server can see and, subject to the host’s policy, invoke. Packing unrelated capabilities into one server forces every client to be trusted with all of them, which means your least-trusted client sets the security posture of your most dangerous tool.

The fix: Split by domain and by trust level, the way Chapter 10’s coordination story assumed: small, focused servers, one isolated client per server, each with the minimum tools and the minimum scopes it needs. The billing tools live on the billing server with the billing credentials; the file tools live on the file server with file credentials. Yes, this means more deployments. That is the trade, and it is worth it: a compromised or confused client can only reach the tools on the servers it was connected to. When you feel the pull to add “just one more tool” to a server that has nothing to do with it, that feeling is this gotcha knocking.

Treating annotations as enforcement

Symptom: You marked your dangerous tool with the annotation that says it is not read-only, or you set a hint that the tool should require approval, and then you watched a host call it freely with no approval step. Or the reverse: you marked a tool read-only and assumed the model could never change state through it, until someone found the tool that “reads” a configuration by rewriting it.

Why it happens: Annotations in MCP are advisory. They are hints the server offers about a tool’s behavior, readOnlyHint, destructive hints, and the like, and a well-behaved host uses them to make better decisions about approvals and presentation. But the protocol does not enforce them, and not every host honors them the same way. Treating an annotation as a security control is like treating a “please knock” sign as a lock. The server asserted a property; nothing in the wire guarantees the client acted on it.

The fix: Enforce policy on your side of the boundary. If a tool must not run without human approval, the host owns that decision, per the architecture in Chapter 2: the host owns orchestration, policy, approval, and UX. Your server’s job is to make the host’s job easy: accurate annotations, clear descriptions of consequences, and, for the truly dangerous operations, its own confirmation step or a separate privileged tool with tighter scopes. And never trust a read-only annotation on a tool you did not audit. If the tool can change state, say so in the annotation and the description, and scope it accordingly. Defense in depth means the annotation, the host policy, and the server-side check all agree, and none of them is load-bearing alone.

Assuming a sticky session

Symptom: Your server works over stdio, where the process lives as long as the session. You move it to Streamable HTTP, and suddenly multi-step workflows break: the second call in a sequence cannot see what the first call stored, progress vanishes between requests, and resuming a session after a network hiccup starts from zero.

Why it happens: MCP servers are stateless by default. The stdio transport hid that from you because the process itself was the session: in-memory state survived from one message to the next, and it felt like the protocol was keeping state for you. Over Streamable HTTP, each request may reach a fresh process, a different replica, or the same process after a restart. Anything you kept in a global variable was never part of the contract. It was an accident of the transport, and the new transport does not repeat the accident.

The fix: Design every tool call as if it is the first one the server has ever seen. Pass the state the call needs in its arguments or in a resource the client can read back; persist anything durable in a real store, not in process memory. Chapter 7’s rule is the bright line: when the work itself is long-lived, hand it to Tasks, the protocol’s mechanism for durable work, rather than simulating a session out of globals and hope. Then test it the honest way: run two sequential tool calls against a server process you restart in between. If the second call behaves differently than it did in one long-lived process, you were depending on the accident.

Polling a long job instead of using tasks

Symptom: A tool kicks off work that takes minutes: an export, a scan, a batch job. The model, having no way to wait, calls a status tool in a tight loop: are we done yet, are we done yet, are we done yet. Each poll burns context and a request, the transcript fills with dozens of identical status checks, and if the session ends, nobody ever learns the result.

Why it happens: The request-response shape of a tool call suggests a synchronous world, so developers build long jobs behind a synchronous-looking tool and leave the waiting to the caller. But the caller is a language model with a context budget, and every poll is a full round trip that says nothing new. Polling is the model doing with tokens what an event or a durable handle should do with almost none.

The fix: Use Tasks for durable work, as Chapter 7 prescribes. The tool starts the job and returns a task handle immediately; the client checks the task’s status with backoff or subscribes to its completion instead of hammering a status endpoint. Design the status check to be cheap and the completion payload to carry the actual result, so the dozens of polls become a handful of quiet checks and one useful answer. As a rule, if your status tool gets called more than a few times per job in testing, the polling interval is wrong or the mechanism is: reach for Tasks before you reach for a longer sleep.

Flying blind in production

Symptom: Something is slow, or wrong, or both, and you cannot say which call, which tool, or which session is responsible. Your logs show a flat stream of messages with no way to connect a tool call to the request that triggered it. The host team blames your server, you blame the host, and neither of you has evidence.

Why it happens: Observability was deferred. The server logs to wherever was convenient, with no request identifiers, no timing, and no structured fields, because during development there was exactly one developer and one session. In production there are many of both, and a log line without a correlation ID is a fact without an address. Chapter 8 built the case for tracing the full path from host to client to server; this gotcha is what that path looks like when you skip it.

The fix: Give every request a correlation ID at the edge and propagate it through every log line your server emits, structured, to stderr, with timings. Log the tool name, the session or task identifier, the duration, and the outcome on every call; log nothing that belongs in the schema, per the secrets rule above. Then make sure you can answer three questions from your logs alone: which tool is slowest, which tool fails most, and what a single session did from start to finish. If you cannot answer all three in under five minutes, your observability is not done. It is the difference between debugging with evidence and debugging with opinions.

Pre-production checklist

Run this list against your own server before it serves real traffic. Every item traces back to a gotcha in this chapter or a rule from an earlier one. If an item fails, fix it now; production is an expensive place to learn.

  1. Stdout carries only JSON-RPC messages. Run the initialization sequence and assert that every line on stdout parses as a JSON-RPC envelope. All logging goes to stderr.
  2. Dependencies are quiet. No library prints, banners, or warnings to stdout on import or during calls.
  3. Tool responses are budgeted. The default response of every tool is measured, paginated where it can grow, and small enough that a session of normal use stays well inside context limits.
  4. Errors name the value, the rule, and the remedy. Read every error path and confirm a model could retry correctly from the message alone.
  5. No secrets in schemas. Grep tool names, descriptions, examples, and defaults for keys, tokens, internal hostnames, and credential formats. None found.
  6. Remote servers require auth. Every Streamable HTTP deployment sits behind OAuth with scopes, and tokens are scoped to the tools each client needs.
  7. Servers are focused. No server exposes tools across unrelated domains, and no client is connected to capabilities it does not need.
  8. Annotations are accurate and unenforced assumptions are gone. Nothing destructive relies on an annotation alone; the host policy and server-side checks agree.
  9. State is explicit. Two sequential calls with a server restart in between behave the same as two calls in one long-lived process. Durable work uses Tasks.
  10. Long jobs do not invite polling. Status checks are cheap, backed off, and few; completion carries the result.
  11. Every request is traceable. Correlation IDs flow through structured logs, and you can answer: slowest tool, most-failing tool, full session history.
  12. Wire schemas are pinned by tests. Tool input and output shapes are asserted in automated tests, so a drifted schema fails the build instead of failing a session.
  13. Destructive tools have a second gate. Deletion, money movement, publishing, and external messages require host approval or a server-side confirmation, never a bare call.
  14. Timeouts and retries are set. Every outbound call your server makes has a timeout, and retries are bounded with backoff, so one slow dependency cannot wedge your server.
  15. The rollback plan exists. You know which version is running, how to revert to the previous one, and how to tell clients to reconnect.

Fifteen checks, most of them automatable, all of them cheaper than the incident they prevent. Keep this list next to your deployment pipeline and run it on every release, not just the first one. Gotchas do not retire; they wait for the release where you stopped checking.

Chapter checkpoint

You now have the field guide to the failures this book promised to help you avoid:

  • Stdout is the wire on stdio: log to stderr, and test that stdout carries only JSON-RPC.
  • Chatty tools waste the model’s context budget: return pages, summaries, and references.
  • Errors must name the value, the rule, and the remedy, or the model will guess.
  • Secrets live server-side: schemas and descriptions are visible to the model.
  • Remote servers need OAuth with scopes: no-auth endpoints are borrowed trouble.
  • Focused servers beat god servers: one isolated client per server, minimum tools, minimum scopes.
  • Annotations are advisory: enforce policy in the host and verify server-side.
  • Servers are stateless by default: make state explicit and hand durable work to Tasks.
  • Polling burns context: use Tasks with backoff and cheap status checks.
  • Observability is the difference between debugging with evidence and debugging with opinions.
Design exercise

Take the server you have been building through this book, or the http-status server from the running example and run the pre-production checklist against it honestly.

  1. Pick three checklist items you are least sure about and write down the evidence for each: passing or failing.
  2. For each failing item, write the smallest fix that would make it pass, and the test that would keep it passing.
  3. Find one tool whose default response is larger than it needs to be, and sketch its paginated shape: page size, cursor, and what the first page contains.
  4. Find one error message your server can produce today, and rewrite it to name the value, the rule, and the remedy.
  5. Identify the most destructive tool your server exposes, and confirm it has a second gate: host approval, server-side confirmation, or tighter scopes.

Bring the results to Chapter 12, where we look at where the protocol is going and how you can help shape it. The servers that survive contact with production are not the clever ones. They are the checked ones.

Key terms

Anti-pattern: a recurring approach that looks reasonable and reliably causes harm.

Cascade: a failure that spreads from one component to others through a shared dependency.

Chatty tool: a tool whose responses are large enough to waste context or crowd out other work.

Correlation ID: an identifier attached to a request as it crosses component boundaries, so logs from each side can be joined.

References and further reading
  1. Model Context Protocol, “What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/getting-started/intro
  2. Model Context Protocol, “Specification.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/index
  3. Model Context Protocol, “Architecture overview.” https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture
  4. Martin Kleppmann, “Designing Data-Intensive Applications,” Chapter 8 (fault tolerance) and Chapter 11 (stream processing). O’Reilly Media, 2017.
  5. Google Site Reliability Engineering, “Monitoring Distributed Systems.” https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
  6. Fudan University active scan of 7,973 public MCP servers (May 2026) — 40.55% exposed tools with no authentication; similar figures in the official registry audit (41%) and OWASP (38%). https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/

Next: Chapter 12 — The Road Ahead: where MCP goes from here. Follow to get it when it drops.

items.title: Unicorn India Ventures Launches US Operations To Back Indian Deep-Tech Startups
items.summary: Deep-tech venture capital firm Unicorn India Ventures (UIV) has launched operations in the US, appointing former Google executive Kishore Kanakamedala as Venture Partner to lead the expansion. The move aims to help Indian deep-tech startups access US markets, investors and technology ecosystems. The announcement comes shortly after UIV announced the first close of the IITM Unicorn Frontier Fund I at ₹450 crore, within three months of receiving SEBI approval. The firm said it saw significant interest from US investors in Indian deep-tech startups while raising its third fund, which closed at ₹1,200 crore earlier this year. Bhaskar Majumdar, Founder and Managing Partner of Unicorn India Ventures, said launching US operations was the natural next step after closing its ₹1,200 crore third fund, driven by strong interest from US investors in Indian deep-tech startups. UIV plans to build a team of mid-to-senior-level operator-investors in the US. They will develop local ecosystems to help portfolio companies establish a presence in the country, while building a broader investor base for Indian deep-tech businesses. The US operations will also focus on promoting India's deep-tech growth story and creating an active co-investment ecosystem. UIV said the expansion would help founders accelerate their scale-up and technology readiness level (TRL) journeys, while keeping its India-based investment team informed about developments in global technology markets. Kanakamedala said the opportunity to work with UIV came as India emerged as a deep-tech hub, supported by product-based companies, government policies, and increasing access to risk capital. Kanakamedala outlined his mandate as Venture Partner: to back creators solving high-impact deep-tech challenges, assist portfolio startups in expanding into the US market, grow the investor base, and stay ahead of global technology developments to support the India-based investment team. Founded in 2016, Mumbai-based UIV invests in early-stage Indian deep-tech companies developing products based on strong intellectual property, with typical cheque sizes of ₹10 crore to ₹25 crore. The firm manages about $350 million across its funds and has backed 54 companies in semiconductors, space, defence, healthcare, robotics, and agritech. Its portfolio includes TakeMe2Space, Netrasemi , Genrobotics, EyeROV and Satleo Labs. In 2026, UIV launched the ₹1,000-crore IITM Unicorn Frontier Fund I in strategic partnership with IIT Madras and IIT Madras Research Park.

items.title: Ukraine's new armored assaults show the tank isn't dead, but the rules have changed
items.summary: Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it carried out successful mechanized assaults behind Russian lines in its Operation Vivaldi. Yevhen Kotenko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images Mechanized assaults have been rare in Ukraine, but amid a major offensive, its forces pulled off two. The Ukrainian commander behind the operation doubted the assaults would succeed. He said using armored vehicles now needs extensive planning and support, much like a special operation. A massive Ukrainian operation retaking territory from Russian forces has shown that assaults with tanks and armored vehicles are still possible in a drone-heavy war, but far more support and planning are now necessary to execute them. Tanks and other armored vehicles have faced serious challenges on battlefields dominated by drones, mines, and artillery, prompting both sides to move away, tactically speaking, from large-scale mechanized assaults. Those decisions have led observers to question whether tanks still have a role in modern warfare. Those discussions have taken a new turn in the wake of recent Ukrainian combat operations. Ukrainian forces involved in Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive that has so far taken back 277 square kilometers of territory, carried out two successful mechanized assaults behind Russian lines this week, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, the unit conducting the operation, told the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. George Barros, the director of innovation at the Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank, told Business Insider that this appears to be "the first successful mechanized tactical level breakthrough in a drone-dominated battlefield." Sharing details of the operation, Biletskyi said he had been skeptical it could be done, remaining unsure until the last minute whether armored vehicles could be used successfully, but he decided to allow brigade commanders to try. The assaults required extensive preparation and coordination. "Today, the use of armored vehicles is effectively a special operation. It requires extremely detailed planning and the coordination of a huge number of assets," Biletskyi told Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news site. Tanks have struggled in Ukraine, leading to their reduced role in large assaults and reassessments about how they can be used in modern warfare. SERGEI CHUZAVKOV/AFP via Getty Images Barros said that while the assault's territorial gains were limited, he believes it is the most consequential and meaningful offensive in theater and in military science observed so far. "It's a really big deal," he said. "It decisively proves that it is possible to achieve mechanized maneuver at the tactical level in a drone-dominated battlefield." The mission planning involved separate training for vehicle crews and infantry, fitting vehicles with additional equipment, and extensive support to shield the advance. Biletskyi did not specify the equipment used, but electronic warfare, additional armor, and supporting drones and robots are among the kinds of tools that can help protect assault forces. "The big lesson here is that the tank isn't dead, and the tank isn't obsolete," Barros said, "but rather the prerequisites to make the tank useful have become lengthy and extensive and very difficult to achieve, but all the same important and critical for success on the battlefield." The challenge is replicating that success. Such assaults require more resources and preparation time than some units can reasonably dedicate to the mission. Barros noted that very few Ukrainian units are as well trained and well equipped as the Third Army Corps, Vivaldi's lead unit. The Third Army Corps, shown here using an armored vehicle in training, showed how mechanized warfare can be done under new conditions. Third Army Corps But if Ukraine is successful in proliferating these lessons and tactics into other elements of its armed forces, "then we will have a Ukrainian military that is extremely capable and able to roll back the Russians, whereas the Russians still lag potentially years behind the Ukrainians in terms of being able to conduct these kinds of maneuvers," he said. The recent Vivaldi assaults build on a broader effort to bring armored vehicles back into bigger offensive breakthrough operations. ISW observed in May that Ukraine, for the first time since 2023, was beginning to carry out more frequent mechanized counterattacks, including using armored vehicles in front-line attacks. In August, ISW assessed that Ukraine had been able to reintroduce limited mechanized maneuver through improved planning, suppression of Russian air defenses, and an emerging drone advantage. And by October, the think tank had detected an edge for Ukraine in these kinds of renewed operations. Biletskyi said this week that the mechanized assault allowed his forces to achieve the partial encircling of the settlement of Nove and the deployment of infantry behind Russian lines to attack drone operators concealed in wooded areas. He said the attacks degraded Russia's ability to conduct drone operations and gather battlefield intelligence, setting conditions for a tactical breakthrough. Eliminating drone operators is key, Barros said, because it allows Ukrainian forces to push forward. It's something he said Ukraine has become better at over the course of the year, which was why Ukrainian vehicles were able to advance further. Vivaldi's leaders have emphasized the importance of shaping the battlefield by weakening the enemy first, including through the use of artillery, drones, and robots. The war's dense networks of drones, land mines, and artillery have made large armored assaults difficult and dangerous. Inexpensive drones, in particular, make it hard to concentrate forces and complicate maneuvers. Both sides have added protective armor while decreasing tank activity, often keeping them farther from the front. Vivaldi shows they're not out of the fight, though. Western partners are still betting on tanks and buying new ones, but they foresee changes in how they are supported and deployed. Officials say tanks still have a place, but their role may shift. They will need to work alongside assets like drones. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said in May that "legacy platforms are not obsolete" but "the decisive question is the force mix: how can we combine ships, aircraft, tanks and high-end systems with robotics, drones, sensors, software and new effectors to increase lethality and better protect our soldiers?" Read the original article on Business Insider

Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it carried out successful mechanized assaults behind Russian lines in its Operation Vivaldi.

Yevhen Kotenko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images

  • Mechanized assaults have been rare in Ukraine, but amid a major offensive, its forces pulled off two.
  • The Ukrainian commander behind the operation doubted the assaults would succeed.
  • He said using armored vehicles now needs extensive planning and support, much like a special operation.

A massive Ukrainian operation retaking territory from Russian forces has shown that assaults with tanks and armored vehicles are still possible in a drone-heavy war, but far more support and planning are now necessary to execute them.

Tanks and other armored vehicles have faced serious challenges on battlefields dominated by drones, mines, and artillery, prompting both sides to move away, tactically speaking, from large-scale mechanized assaults. Those decisions have led observers to question whether tanks still have a role in modern warfare.

Those discussions have taken a new turn in the wake of recent Ukrainian combat operations.

Ukrainian forces involved in Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive that has so far taken back 277 square kilometers of territory, carried out two successful mechanized assaults behind Russian lines this week, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, the commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, the unit conducting the operation, told the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi.

George Barros, the director of innovation at the Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank, told Business Insider that this appears to be "the first successful mechanized tactical level breakthrough in a drone-dominated battlefield."

Sharing details of the operation, Biletskyi said he had been skeptical it could be done, remaining unsure until the last minute whether armored vehicles could be used successfully, but he decided to allow brigade commanders to try.

The assaults required extensive preparation and coordination. "Today, the use of armored vehicles is effectively a special operation. It requires extremely detailed planning and the coordination of a huge number of assets," Biletskyi told Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news site.

Tanks have struggled in Ukraine, leading to their reduced role in large assaults and reassessments about how they can be used in modern warfare.

SERGEI CHUZAVKOV/AFP via Getty Images

Barros said that while the assault's territorial gains were limited, he believes it is the most consequential and meaningful offensive in theater and in military science observed so far.

"It's a really big deal," he said. "It decisively proves that it is possible to achieve mechanized maneuver at the tactical level in a drone-dominated battlefield."

The mission planning involved separate training for vehicle crews and infantry, fitting vehicles with additional equipment, and extensive support to shield the advance. Biletskyi did not specify the equipment used, but electronic warfare, additional armor, and supporting drones and robots are among the kinds of tools that can help protect assault forces.

"The big lesson here is that the tank isn't dead, and the tank isn't obsolete," Barros said, "but rather the prerequisites to make the tank useful have become lengthy and extensive and very difficult to achieve, but all the same important and critical for success on the battlefield."

The challenge is replicating that success. Such assaults require more resources and preparation time than some units can reasonably dedicate to the mission. Barros noted that very few Ukrainian units are as well trained and well equipped as the Third Army Corps, Vivaldi's lead unit.

The Third Army Corps, shown here using an armored vehicle in training, showed how mechanized warfare can be done under new conditions.

Third Army Corps

But if Ukraine is successful in proliferating these lessons and tactics into other elements of its armed forces, "then we will have a Ukrainian military that is extremely capable and able to roll back the Russians, whereas the Russians still lag potentially years behind the Ukrainians in terms of being able to conduct these kinds of maneuvers," he said.

The recent Vivaldi assaults build on a broader effort to bring armored vehicles back into bigger offensive breakthrough operations.

ISW observed in May that Ukraine, for the first time since 2023, was beginning to carry out more frequent mechanized counterattacks, including using armored vehicles in front-line attacks.

In August, ISW assessed that Ukraine had been able to reintroduce limited mechanized maneuver through improved planning, suppression of Russian air defenses, and an emerging drone advantage. And by October, the think tank had detected an edge for Ukraine in these kinds of renewed operations.

Biletskyi said this week that the mechanized assault allowed his forces to achieve the partial encircling of the settlement of Nove and the deployment of infantry behind Russian lines to attack drone operators concealed in wooded areas.

He said the attacks degraded Russia's ability to conduct drone operations and gather battlefield intelligence, setting conditions for a tactical breakthrough.

Eliminating drone operators is key, Barros said, because it allows Ukrainian forces to push forward. It's something he said Ukraine has become better at over the course of the year, which was why Ukrainian vehicles were able to advance further. Vivaldi's leaders have emphasized the importance of shaping the battlefield by weakening the enemy first, including through the use of artillery, drones, and robots.

The war's dense networks of drones, land mines, and artillery have made large armored assaults difficult and dangerous. Inexpensive drones, in particular, make it hard to concentrate forces and complicate maneuvers. Both sides have added protective armor while decreasing tank activity, often keeping them farther from the front.

Vivaldi shows they're not out of the fight, though.

Western partners are still betting on tanks and buying new ones, but they foresee changes in how they are supported and deployed. Officials say tanks still have a place, but their role may shift. They will need to work alongside assets like drones.

Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said in May that "legacy platforms are not obsolete" but "the decisive question is the force mix: how can we combine ships, aircraft, tanks and high-end systems with robotics, drones, sensors, software and new effectors to increase lethality and better protect our soldiers?"

items.title: An AI agent in "Skynet mode" hijacks unprotected language models to launch self-sustaining cyberattacks
items.summary: Security researchers at Symantec have found an offensive AI agent that hijacks unprotected language models on the web and uses them to attack servers, steal databases, and install cryptominers on its own. It runs up to 100,000 steps without human input. The owner of the hijacked model gets stuck with the bill. items.title: Nutanix announces AI infrastructure tie-ups with NVIDIA, Supermicro and Netris
items.summary: Nutanix announced on 22nd October its collaboration with NVIDIA, Supermicro and Netris on infrastructure for production AI. All three arrangements are described as plans, and the company's own disclaimer says some features will be offered "on a when-and-if-available basis." The American cloud software company said it plans to work toward "Day Zero" support for NVIDIA's Vera CPUs, starting with Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP) on bare metal, with planned expansion to virtualised Nutanix environments. The company said demand for production AI is growing, and organisations are under pressure to deploy increasingly complex infrastructure faster and turn AI investments into business value. It says capacity constraints and operational complexity can slow progress. The stated aim of the partnerships is to reduce deployment complexity, speed up time to value and cut AI costs. Nutanix argues that agentic AI workloads combine inference with tool calls, code execution and retrieval, so CPU performance is expected to become essential between GPU operations. It will pair Vera with NVIDIA OpenShell to create private runtime environments for agents. "AI agents need fast CPUs to execute code, use tools and process data between model calls," Hannah Coutand, Director of Product Marketing for Vera CPU at NVIDIA, said. Nutanix and Supermicro announced plans for a jointly engineered system combining Supermicro servers, NVIDIA GPUs, Nutanix Agentic AI (NAI) and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. The companies say it aims to cut custom configuration and integration delays and lower token costs for enterprises running inference on-premises. Nutanix would supply the AI cloud control plane and AI storage. Nutanix Cloud Platform will be integrated with Netris's network automation and multitenancy platform. Netris would handle the physical network fabric, enforcing tenant isolation on networking hardware . The target customers are AI cloud providers that rent out GPU infrastructure. Thomas Cornely, Nutanix's Executive Vice President of Product Management, said the collaborations mean "we plan to help customers accelerate deployments of agents and AI services on a unified platform with built-in security, performance, and governance." Nutanix's forward-looking statements notice says the information "should not be used when making a purchasing decision." It adds that the company does not commit to delivering any described functionality, and that the collaborations remain subject to development work and commercial arrangements among the parties. No pricing, release dates or performance figures were given.

items.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
items.summary: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.

items.title: Competing in RoboCup@Home and winning the 2026 best paper award: an interview with Raphael Memmesheimer
items.summary: Team NimbRo’s robot in action during the RoboCup@Home competition at RoboCup 2026. Raphael leads the team. Raphael Memmesheimer has been successfully competing in the RoboCup@Home league winning the RoboCup@Home competition five times. He and his colleagues won the best paper award at RoboCup 2026 for their work “Efficient Image Annotation via Semi-Supervised Object Segmentation with Label Propagation” . We caught up with Raphael to find out more about this research, his history with RoboCup, and the challenges of the @Home competition. Could you start by telling us how you got involved with RoboCup@Home? I’ve actually been involved in the @Home league since I was a student, and my first time going to a World Cup for @Home was in 2013. That competition motivated me to do a PhD and infected me in a way that meant I basically aligned my academic career to it. I always return to robot competitions because this is one of the rare places where you can benchmark robots in a real environment and have a real competition. Commonly in research you tune your approaches on data sets and show that they perform in a one-shot video. In robot competitions, you basically have to roll out your robot, it enters the arena, and then it operates autonomously on its own. It is always interesting to see how new developments make the robots perform better. You and your co-authors won the best paper award at the RoboCup symposium this year. Congratulations! Could you give us a quick introduction to the paper? The motivation for this work is that we only have two preparation days at the RoboCup competitions. So we arrive there, we have to assemble our robots, and the robots need to get used to the new environment [a model apartment] that we haven’t seen before. Also, the robots don’t have a clue about anything in this apartment. And within the two preparation days, the robots need to learn the objects they are interacting with. For example, they have to recognise what a spoon is, or a specific drink. Our paper basically supports us in very efficiently generating this data such that the robots can more quickly learn models for the objects that are involved in this competition. And the interesting thing is it’s not just a few objects that we can distinguish between; there can be up to 50 different objects that we haven’t seen before. Our approach basically optimizes the process so that we can quickly get a good vision model for the robot. We are aware of open-vocabulary approaches but found them to have issues distinguishing between objects of a category like drinks. Is it possible to do some pre-training to anticipate objects that might be used in the competition? Partially that’s possible, but most objects cannot really be anticipated. We know that there are drinks, there are snacks, that there are cutlery items in the apartment. But what cannot be anticipated is the details because objects come from different areas in the world. The organisers will usually go to a shopping mall and just get local groceries there. Those objects are then distributed in the apartment. Part of the object set comes from the publicly available YCB Dataset , for those we can gather data beforehand, and of course pre-training with large general object sets. Could you talk about your methodology? We use a multi-stage approach. Firstly, we segment, such that we learn what an object actually is on a segmentation level. We look at all the objects that robots saw in the past editions of these competitions, and we train one model that just says, “oh, there is something which might be an object” . And then we get reference images of the actual objects and we semi-supervised or semi-automatically label those objects. The idea is that we combine identifying something as an object with a reference of what could actually be there. That allows us to simplify the labeling approach. Around 60% of the data is automatically labeled based on our approach. That would take a lot of hours by human annotation. Labeled example images from different competition venues. Figure from “Efficient Image Annotation via Semi-Supervised Object Segmentation with Label Propagation” . Have you been able to use the method already in RoboCup competitions? Yes, we used it in Brazil for RoboCup 2025 and at RoboCup GermanOpen for the local RoboCup competitions. The method is continuously evolving. Now that we have this very good vision model, it means that we save a lot of time during the two preparation days and we can concentrate more on testing and achieving the actual tasks instead of just focusing on the vision element. One side note: nowadays there are promptable object detection or segmentation methods, but we found that they don’t scale yet to the number of classes that are involved in this competition. They work fine with 5 to 10 different classes, but we had issues distinguishing all 50 classes just by prompting them. In this year’s World Cup (in Korea) we used an evolved approach where we used videos to generate even more data. Team NimbRo’s robot picking laundry from the washing machine. How did your team get on in the competition this time? It went well. We had issues, as always during competitions, but we ended up in 3rd place. There was a new “Doing Laundry” task introduced this year. The robot had to carry a laundry basket from a washing machine to a folding table and open the washing machine. It had to detect the washing machine door, then find the specific point to grasp the handle to open the machine door. Then it had to pull out t-shirts and fold them. Our robot performed the best in this task. It was able to open the washing machine and start folding the laundry. And this was possible because we used these semi-automatic labeling approaches. What were the other tasks that teams needed to carry out? The first big hurdle at the competition is to make the robot pass the initial inspection. Robots must satisfy certain safety and interactive capabilities and if they fail they are not allowed to take part in the competition. In the competition itself there are five main tasks. One is human-robot interaction. The robots have to open the door for party guests and greet them. Here, the robot has to go to the door, find the handle, align the end-effector to the handle, open the door, let the human enter, speak with the guest while holding eye-contact, guide them to the living room, find them a free seat, and introduce this guest to any other guests. This process continues on repeat as long as there are new guests arriving. Team NimbRo’s robot opening the door. Another task is a pick and place task, and this time we had to clear a table after breakfast. So the robot had to bring the cutlery to the dishwasher, put a dishwasher tablet into the dishwasher, close the dishwasher, and then prepare the table ready for the next meal. That’s a very manipulation intensive task. There is also a general-purpose service robot task. This task is undefined because the robot has to deal with a random natural language command that can incorporate all elements of the apartment. For example it might be asked to go and fetch a particular drink or snack and hand it to someone. In the past there were people from the audience called into the arena and asked to give a command. It’s interesting to see how good these robots are at interacting with a new person and not someone they are used to receiving commands from. Another interesting task is the restaurant task. Here, the robots are not in the known environment that we trained them in for two days, instead they are taken to an unknown restaurant location. The robot is placed there and needs to serve naturally. Only the menu is known to the teams in advance. The robots need to scan the restaurant to autonomously operate and find waving customers. The order is then given by voice, and usually these restaurant environments are very noisy. This is a very interesting task for the audience because it’s in the wild and people gather around it to watch it. Then, of course, there’s the new laundry task that I described above. To add to what I said before, this is a very hard task because the robot cannot see into the washing machine. So it has to feel if it has a T-shirt in its hand and take the t-shirt out of the machine. Then the robot has to go to a table and start folding other t-shirts. Team NimbRo Interesting. I was at RoboCup in Eindhoven and I found the @Home competition fascinating. We actually won the competition that year! The league was more divided then, with three different leagues: two standard platforms and an open platform league. It was the open platform league that we won. Now, all of those leagues have been merged. This year there were 24 teams from all over the world participating in just one league, which is amazing. It also drives competition a lot. How much of an improvement have you seen over the years that you’ve been doing RoboCup@Home? There are always phases of improvement, as I would describe them. I started pre-deep learning, and there were no vision robust models for seeing objects in unknown environments. What was working well was mapping and navigation. When I started in the league, the robots were already talking, but often, instead of talking to a human like they were supposed to, they might talk to a potted plant or a coat hanger because they had a shape similar to a human. This is no longer the case – nowadays we perceive humans quite well. We can also recognize speech quite well. Task planning is still a challenge, but it has improved. Then there are things that appear and push the boundaries, such as large language models, open vocabulary approaches and, most recently, agentic systems. But every now and then there’s stagnation because teams are just overwhelmed by the wide amount of different challenges that this competition throws at you. Basically your robot has to do everything. It needs to navigate in an apartment, it needs to be able to interact with humans, it has to manipulate items, and it has to do task planning. And all of those are very intensive research areas that are challenging in themselves. In addition the implementations must be very robust, as there are only a few trials. How are you and the team planning to improve the robot for the next competition? We are working on improving manipulation capabilities so that the robot can more quickly pick various objects. We are also continuously testing our robots’ performance to make our robots more human-like, and using two arms for manipulation is something we want to improve. About Raphael Raphael Memmesheimer’s long-term research goal is to develop autonomous service robots that assist people in everyday environments: robots that perceive, understand, and learn from human behavior using multi-modal sensory information and that prove themselves outside the lab. He is currently a postdoctoral researcher with the Autonomous Intelligent Systems (AIS) group at the University of Bonn, where he re-established and leads the domestic service robot team NimbRo@Home. He is also a founding member of the Center for Robotics at the University of Bonn. Raphael Memmesheimer has extensive experience in benchmark robotics competitions, having led teams at two universities to multiple international titles. Notably, he has won the RoboCup@Home World Championship five times (including three consecutive titles), along with multiple victories at the RoboCup German Open and top placements in the European Robotics League and the World Robot Summit.

The league was more divided then, with three different leagues: two standard platforms and an open platform league. It was the open platform league that we won.

Now, all of those leagues have been merged. This year there were 24 teams from all over the world participating in just one league, which is amazing. It also drives competition a lot.

How much of an improvement have you seen over the years that you’ve been doing RoboCup@Home?

There are always phases of improvement, as I would describe them. I started pre-deep learning, and there were no vision robust models for seeing objects in unknown environments. What was working well was mapping and navigation. When I started in the league, the robots were already talking, but often, instead of talking to a human like they were supposed to, they might talk to a potted plant or a coat hanger because they had a shape similar to a human. This is no longer the case – nowadays we perceive humans quite well. We can also recognize speech quite well. Task planning is still a challenge, but it has improved. Then there are things that appear and push the boundaries, such as large language models, open vocabulary approaches and, most recently, agentic systems. But every now and then there’s stagnation because teams are just overwhelmed by the wide amount of different challenges that this competition throws at you. Basically your robot has to do everything. It needs to navigate in an apartment, it needs to be able to interact with humans, it has to manipulate items, and it has to do task planning. And all of those are very intensive research areas that are challenging in themselves. In addition the implementations must be very robust, as there are only a few trials.

How are you and the team planning to improve the robot for the next competition?

We are working on improving manipulation capabilities so that the robot can more quickly pick various objects. We are also continuously testing our robots’ performance to make our robots more human-like, and using two arms for manipulation is something we want to improve.

About Raphael

Raphael Memmesheimer’s long-term research goal is to develop autonomous service robots that assist people in everyday environments: robots that perceive, understand, and learn from human behavior using multi-modal sensory information and that prove themselves outside the lab. He is currently a postdoctoral researcher with the Autonomous Intelligent Systems (AIS) group at the University of Bonn, where he re-established and leads the domestic service robot team NimbRo@Home. He is also a founding member of the Center for Robotics at the University of Bonn.

Raphael Memmesheimer has extensive experience in benchmark robotics competitions, having led teams at two universities to multiple international titles. Notably, he has won the RoboCup@Home World Championship five times (including three consecutive titles), along with multiple victories at the RoboCup German Open and top placements in the European Robotics League and the World Robot Summit.

items.title: JanAI Partners With Four Universities To Expand AI Access In Rural India
items.summary: JanAI has partnered with four universities to expand access to artificial intelligence (AI) education in rural India and create opportunities for rural youth and entrepreneurs. The company has collaborated with Presidency University, Manipal Academy of Higher Education (MAHE), Bengaluru, RV College of Engineering and the University of Liverpool’s Bengaluru campus to establish a research hub, a rural incubator, an entrepreneurship hackathon and learning programmes for rural ambassadors. The initiatives aim to connect academic research and student-led innovation with local needs and help rural communities explore AI-driven businesses and livelihood opportunities. “Rural India is full of people with the aspiration and ingenuity to solve the challenges around them. These partnerships bring that potential into direct conversation with the research, knowledge and resources of our universities,” said Madan Padaki, founder of JanAI. “We want young people’s learning to lead to greater capability, the confidence to build, and economic opportunity in their own community. That is how AI becomes meaningful in people’s lives.” The facilities will support rural innovation and entrepreneurship by helping turn ideas addressing village-level challenges into practical solutions and viable businesses. JanAI has also launched the Tech4Bharat mass entrepreneurship hackathon in partnership with RV College of Engineering and GAVS (Global Accelerator Vision Summit). The programme invites students to develop solutions to challenges faced by micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), encouraging them to identify business opportunities through practical problem-solving. The University of Liverpool’s Bengaluru campus will provide structured learning programmes for 100 rural JanAI Ambassadors, with a particular focus on the Kalyana Karnataka region. University students will also be encouraged to develop AI solutions for village-level challenges, drawing on rural communities' experiences and needs. Alongside the university partnerships , JanAI has opened its tenth AI Café in Wardha, Maharashtra. The cafés serve as community spaces where people can learn about AI and explore its applications in everyday life.

items.title: HCLTech Launches NVIDIA-Powered Validation Offering for Software-Defined Vehicles
items.summary: HCLTech has launched an AI-powered verification and validation (V&V) offering for automotive software, built on NVIDIA’s simulation technologies and AI models. The offering targets vehicle manufacturers and tier-1 suppliers developing software-defined vehicles . The offering links requirements, test creation and execution, failure analysis, and compliance reporting across the validation process. The company identified fragmented toolchains, manual testing workflows and labour-intensive compliance processes as challenges in validating increasingly complex vehicle software, particularly as automakers roll out over-the-air updates. According to HCLTech, the system uses NVIDIA Omniverse, Cosmos, Alpamayo, Omniverse NuRec and Isaac Sim to generate and test scenarios in virtual environments, including rare and safety-critical conditions. The company said this could reduce reliance on physical testing and expand scenario coverage. The offering also uses NVIDIA’s Agent Toolkit to coordinate multiple AI agents, with reasoning powered by NVIDIA Nemotron open models. HCLTech said the agents are designed to support different stages of validation while maintaining links between requirements, test results and compliance records. The announcement did not disclose customer deployments or quantified reductions in testing time and costs. “Automotive software is evolving faster than traditional validation processes were designed to handle,” said Pankaj Tagra, Chief Growth Officer and Global Head, Mobility at HCLTech. He pointed to frequent software updates, complex vehicle systems and changing configurations as factors that make validation difficult to scale. NVIDIA’s Sebastian Scheurle, EMEA Industry Lead Automotive Enterprise, said simulation could help automakers test safety-critical scenarios earlier in development. “Validation now sets the pace for software-defined vehicles,” Scheurle said. On October 12, HCLTech announced a global partnership with Anthropic to integrate Claude and Claude Code into its engineering workflows and selected enterprise software products.

items.title: The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. Anthropic’s Delay Just Proved It.
items.summary: By Anurag Gurtu When a company delays its IPO to show investors better numbers, that’s a strategy. When the NYC pension fund publicly asks you to delay it over AI safety concerns, your chief rival’s CEO calls his own IPO “ill-advised” and postpones it until at least next year, tech stocks are sliding on open-weight model fears, and your own prospectus warns of “existential risks to humanity” from the product you’re selling, that’s not a strategy. That’s a market sending you a message. Anthropic ‘s numbers are extraordinary. Its third-quarter 2026 revenue was reportedly $16.8 billion — up 45% quarter on quarter. That means the company’s annualized revenue run rate is roughly $67 billion. What the S-1 actually says Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived. Here are the numbers from Anthropic’s leaked prospectus : $4.6 billion: Anthropic’s full-year 2025 revenue. $7.33 billion : What Anthropic spent on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone — more than its total revenue. $42 billion: Anthropic’s net loss in 2025. The roadshow will immediately explain that $34 billion of it was a noncash accounting charge — an adjustment to the estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into shares. $518 billion: How much Anthropic expects to spend, at least, over the course of a decade on AI infrastructure with six partners, including Google , Microsoft and Amazon , according to the confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters . About 80% of the total is noncancelable or payable regardless of usage. $2 trillion: That’s the IPO valuation Anthropic is still targeting for November, a figure representing 435x its 2025 revenue. One more number from the S-1 that the roadshow will bury: A quarter of Anthropic’s 2025 revenue came from two unnamed customers. Three signals the market is sending The IPO delay is the headline. It isn’t the only signal worth reading. Signal one: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine. Last week, the supervisor of New York City’s pension funds — which reportedly hold roughly $7 million in Anthropic exposure today, but could hold dramatically more if Anthropic enters the Russell 3000 post-IPO — sent a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging the company to pause the IPO entirely. The risks he cited are the same ones Anthropic’s own prospectus flags: increasingly autonomous AI systems that could behave in unexpected ways, create security problems, and in the document’s own language, pose “existential risks to humanity.” Signal two: Sam Altman delays OpenAI ’s IPO. OpenAI has said it will not go public in 2026. CEO Altman called an IPO at this moment “ill-advised” given AI safety concerns, and while that framing is partly strategic — positioning OpenAI as the more responsible actor — it’s also a real signal when the CEO of the second-most valuable AI company in the world looks at current conditions and decides to wait. Signal three: The chip selloff. Last week’s $2 trillion chip-stock selloff was driven partly by concern over AI-buildout costs. Gartner ’s forecast helps explain the concern: Through 2030, it sees at most $3.6 trillion in revenue attributable to AI data centers, versus $8.5 trillion needed to cover planned investment, financing costs and a 12% return. The open-weight problem Here is the structural argument that no amount of Q3 revenue growth resolves: Anthropic’s $2 trillion valuation requires closed-model AI to maintain a durable pricing premium over open-weight alternatives. That premium is being systematically dismantled. Open-weight AI is challenging the economics behind closed-model valuations. Enterprise adoption rose from 23% to 67% in 2026, with companies reporting 70%–90% cost savings. DeepSeek R1 offers frontier-level performance on most enterprise benchmarks at 7 cents per million input tokens; independent analysis puts Anthropic’s comparable input and output pricing at roughly 18x and 23x higher, respectively. DeepSeek’s weights are free to download, allowing enterprises to self-host without a model-provider API contract or per-token billing, while the capability gap with closed models reportedly closes within six months of a frontier release. Against that backdrop, New Constructs — the research firm that called Anthropic’s proposed offering “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility” — calculated that justifying a $2 trillion valuation would require an immediate 10% after-tax operating margin sustained for a decade, extraordinary revenue growth, and $358 billion in annual after-tax operating profit by 2035. Why this is worse than 1999 The dot-com bubble had a genuine excuse. Nobody knew what the internet would become. The AI IPO wave of 2026 does not have that excuse. Worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.59 trillion in 2026 , up 47% year over year, according to Gartner. Yet a July 2025 MIT NANDA report estimated that 95% of the organizations it examined were getting no return from generative AI. Meanwhile, KPMG said in its own report earlier this year that just 7% of surveyed leaders say they’ve established ROI from AI. This is the context in which Anthropic is asking investors to pay 435x 2025 revenue for a company with $518 billion in locked infrastructure commitments, 25% revenue concentration in two unnamed clients, and a pricing moat that open-weight models are closing in six-month cycles. The delay from October to November doesn’t change any of those numbers. It adds one quarter of revenue data. What actually survives this correction Here is what no AI IPO roadshow will say out loud: The biggest enterprise AI winners will not necessarily own the most expensive model. They will own the architecture that turns any model into governed, auditable, measurable outcomes — through proprietary enterprise data, domain-specific fine-tuning, multiagent orchestration and controls that make autonomous execution trustworthy. That value does not depend on keeping model capabilities scarce or securing a $2 trillion valuation. It compounds in production, where customers understand that the model is not the product. The deployment is. The dot-com crash did not happen because the internet was bad. It happened because the price was wrong. AI investors face the same distinction: Real technology does not automatically justify its valuation. A strong quarter and a one-month delay do not close that gap. November simply gives Anthropic more time to explain the math. Anurag Gurtu , the co-founder and CEO of Airrived , is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk , Tripwire and Sun Microsystems , and a public company, FireEye . He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification. By Anurag Gurtu

When a company delays its IPO to show investors better numbers, that’s a strategy. When the NYC pension fund publicly asks you to delay it over AI safety concerns, your chief rival’s CEO calls his own IPO “ill-advised” and postpones it until at least next year, tech stocks are sliding on open-weight model fears, and your own prospectus warns of “existential risks to humanity” from the product you’re selling, that’s not a strategy.

That’s a market sending you a message.

Anthropic‘s numbers are extraordinary. Its third-quarter 2026 revenue was reportedly $16.8 billion — up 45% quarter on quarter. That means the company’s annualized revenue run rate is roughly $67 billion.

What the S-1 actually says Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived.

Here are the numbers from Anthropic’s leaked prospectus:

  • $4.6 billion: Anthropic’s full-year 2025 revenue.
  • $7.33 billion: What Anthropic spent on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone — more than its total revenue.
  • $42 billion: Anthropic’s net loss in 2025. The roadshow will immediately explain that $34 billion of it was a noncash accounting charge — an adjustment to the estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into shares.
  • $518 billion: How much Anthropic expects to spend, at least, over the course of a decade on AI infrastructure with six partners, including Google, Microsoft and Amazon, according to the confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters. About 80% of the total is noncancelable or payable regardless of usage.
  • $2 trillion: That’s the IPO valuation Anthropic is still targeting for November, a figure representing 435x its 2025 revenue.

One more number from the S-1 that the roadshow will bury: A quarter of Anthropic’s 2025 revenue came from two unnamed customers.

Three signals the market is sending

The IPO delay is the headline. It isn’t the only signal worth reading.

Signal one: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine. Last week, the supervisor of New York City’s pension funds — which reportedly hold roughly $7 million in Anthropic exposure today, but could hold dramatically more if Anthropic enters the Russell 3000 post-IPO — sent a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging the company to pause the IPO entirely.

The risks he cited are the same ones Anthropic’s own prospectus flags: increasingly autonomous AI systems that could behave in unexpected ways, create security problems, and in the document’s own language, pose “existential risks to humanity.”

Signal two: Sam Altman delays OpenAI’s IPO. OpenAI has said it will not go public in 2026. CEO Altman called an IPO at this moment “ill-advised” given AI safety concerns, and while that framing is partly strategic — positioning OpenAI as the more responsible actor — it’s also a real signal when the CEO of the second-most valuable AI company in the world looks at current conditions and decides to wait.

Signal three: The chip selloff. Last week’s $2 trillion chip-stock selloff was driven partly by concern over AI-buildout costs. Gartner’s forecast helps explain the concern: Through 2030, it sees at most $3.6 trillion in revenue attributable to AI data centers, versus $8.5 trillion needed to cover planned investment, financing costs and a 12% return.

The open-weight problem

Here is the structural argument that no amount of Q3 revenue growth resolves: Anthropic’s $2 trillion valuation requires closed-model AI to maintain a durable pricing premium over open-weight alternatives. That premium is being systematically dismantled.

Open-weight AI is challenging the economics behind closed-model valuations. Enterprise adoption rose from 23% to 67% in 2026, with companies reporting 70%–90% cost savings. DeepSeek R1 offers frontier-level performance on most enterprise benchmarks at 7 cents per million input tokens; independent analysis puts Anthropic’s comparable input and output pricing at roughly 18x and 23x higher, respectively.

DeepSeek’s weights are free to download, allowing enterprises to self-host without a model-provider API contract or per-token billing, while the capability gap with closed models reportedly closes within six months of a frontier release.

Against that backdrop, New Constructs — the research firm that called Anthropic’s proposed offering “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility” — calculated that justifying a $2 trillion valuation would require an immediate 10% after-tax operating margin sustained for a decade, extraordinary revenue growth, and $358 billion in annual after-tax operating profit by 2035.

Why this is worse than 1999

The dot-com bubble had a genuine excuse. Nobody knew what the internet would become. The AI IPO wave of 2026 does not have that excuse.

Worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.59 trillion in 2026, up 47% year over year, according to Gartner. Yet a July 2025 MIT NANDA report estimated that 95% of the organizations it examined were getting no return from generative AI. Meanwhile, KPMG said in its own report earlier this year that just 7% of surveyed leaders say they’ve established ROI from AI.

This is the context in which Anthropic is asking investors to pay 435x 2025 revenue for a company with $518 billion in locked infrastructure commitments, 25% revenue concentration in two unnamed clients, and a pricing moat that open-weight models are closing in six-month cycles.

The delay from October to November doesn’t change any of those numbers. It adds one quarter of revenue data.

What actually survives this correction

Here is what no AI IPO roadshow will say out loud: The biggest enterprise AI winners will not necessarily own the most expensive model. They will own the architecture that turns any model into governed, auditable, measurable outcomes — through proprietary enterprise data, domain-specific fine-tuning, multiagent orchestration and controls that make autonomous execution trustworthy.

That value does not depend on keeping model capabilities scarce or securing a $2 trillion valuation. It compounds in production, where customers understand that the model is not the product. The deployment is.

The dot-com crash did not happen because the internet was bad. It happened because the price was wrong. AI investors face the same distinction: Real technology does not automatically justify its valuation. A strong quarter and a one-month delay do not close that gap. November simply gives Anthropic more time to explain the math.

Anurag Gurtu, the co-founder and CEO of Airrived, is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk, Tripwire and Sun Microsystems, and a public company, FireEye. He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification.

items.title: Acquirers Are Snapping Up Boom-Era Startups That Haven’t Raised Funding In Years
items.summary: When a venture-backed startup goes a few years without raising a new round, it’s common to presume its odds of a sizable exit have gone down as well. But that’s often not the case, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. This year, a number of larger acquisitions of private companies involved startups that haven’t disclosed a new investment for more than four years. Several of these acquisitions are quite recent — and in some cases, quite large. The standout is Uber ’s purchase earlier this month of ezCater , a platform for catering and workplace meals, for $2.3 billion in cash. The deal comes nearly five years after Boston-based ezCater raised its last reported venture funding round. That’s not the only one. A number of companies whose names might feature on a playlist of 2021 boom-era unicorns have sold to acquirers in recent months, including one-time highfliers like Airtable , Headspace and Miro . In many cases, companies are selling at valuations which, while not puny, are still far below their former peaks. Who’s getting acquired To illustrate the extent to which these aging startups are finding acquirers, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of 15 deals involving well-funded companies that haven’t raised equity funding for four or more years. Post-peak runway One big issue for older and middle-aged startups is that valuations hit a cyclical peak in 2021 and early 2022. Many companies that raised during that time had difficulty attracting fresh capital or were reluctant to close new rounds at reduced valuations. Even with the more recent AI boom, little went to this cohort. Moreover, since the 2021 boom-era rounds were quite large, funded startups commonly had the option to cut operating costs and extend their runways with existing capital. As a result, quite a few companies that haven’t raised rounds in years are still chugging along, managing to survive and even grow without more venture funding. EzCater is a case in point. In the year prior to its acquisition, the business generated more than $2.5 billion in gross bookings. It had an annual growth rate in the high teens, with average order sizes over $400. That said, even that revenue and growth rate didn’t secure ezCater much of an acquisition premium from its last funding round. At $2.3 billion, Uber’s purchase price is 53% above the $1.5 billion pre-money valuation the catering startup secured in its last funding round in late 2021. Acquisitions below peak venture valuation In many cases, even good-sized acquisitions of well-funded startups are occurring at valuations far below former peaks. Take Miro, a provider of online collaboration tools that agreed to sell to Bending Spoons last month in a deal valued around $1.36 billion. That’s a huge step down from early 2022, when San Francisco-based Miro closed its last round at a $17.5 billion post-money valuation. Or consider Bending Spoons’ prior purchase of data and workflow platform Airtable , for $1.28 billion in August. That’s barely over one-tenth the $11 billion valuation Airtable secured in its December 2021 Series F. Fashion startup Everlane is another that lost its shimmer after securing a 2020 valuation in the hundreds of millions. It sold to fast-fashion leader Shein this spring for $100 million. In the health and wellness sector, meanwhile, Headspace also saw its valuation plunge. The meditation and mental health app sold to Sword Health in a deal reportedly valued around $300 million. That’s well below its peak post-money valuation of around $2.6 billion. A good thing? While startup investors aren’t celebrating acquisitions made far under peak private valuations, they’re not the worst outcome. And for startups themselves, they’re also far from a catastrophic scenario. Of course, every unicorn investor hopes for high-multiple returns. But for startups that go years without funding, the market seems to be telling us that’s not likely in the cards. Fashion startup Everlane is another that lost its shimmer after securing a 2020 valuation in the hundreds of millions. It sold to fast-fashion leader Shein this spring for $100 million.

In the health and wellness sector, meanwhile, Headspace also saw its valuation plunge. The meditation and mental health app sold to Sword Health in a deal reportedly valued around $300 million. That’s well below its peak post-money valuation of around $2.6 billion.

A good thing?

While startup investors aren’t celebrating acquisitions made far under peak private valuations, they’re not the worst outcome. And for startups themselves, they’re also far from a catastrophic scenario.

Of course, every unicorn investor hopes for high-multiple returns. But for startups that go years without funding, the market seems to be telling us that’s not likely in the cards.
