items.title: Your Next Customer Might Be An Agent. Here’s How To Build Your Brand For Both Humans And AI.
items.summary: By Toby Coulthard You’ve just moved into a new house. It’s unfurnished; the walls are bare. Ten years ago, you might have loaded up Google and started searching for furniture that you like, consulting interior design magazines and looking for offers on retailers’ websites. In 2026, however, there’s an entirely different option at your fingertips. You could take a photo of the empty room, upload the image to an AI agent, share your budget and style, and get a list of furniture that suits your preferences. You could even have the agent purchase on your behalf. Instead of just selling to one customer base — humans — brands are now selling to two. This second audience of AI agents makes decisions on different criteria than humans. Often, in fact, AI agents will make purchasing decisions before a human ever sees the product page. There’s a real chance that all the emotive copy marketers have so carefully crafted will get broken down and reconstituted by a machine. Just relying on the human touch isn’t enough anymore. Leave humans in the equation Toby Coulthard, chief product and growth officer at Jacquard. A word of caution, though: Marketers shouldn’t forget the human entirely in the rush to prepare for AI agents. It’s easy to get carried away with visions of an entirely agentic future. But at the end of the day, each agent is still catering to a human with their own preferences, and personalization will only get more granular over time. The trick is to optimize for both audiences simultaneously, not just one. Newer startup founders have the advantage here. Established brands have to retrofit decades of copy, guidelines and approval processes to make themselves agent-ready. New brands, on the other hand, can build in copy and a brand voice that’s legible to humans and agents from the very start. But what does this look like in practice? To start, brands should work out a distinct voice — and write it down. In most early-stage companies, the brand voice solely exists in the founder’s head. This might work if the copy’s written by a handful of people who work with the founder, but it doesn’t work well when the writer — or reader — is a machine. AI tools follow explicit rules and drift without them. I’ve spent years at my startup, Jacquard , working out how to get AI agents to write better content, but it’s only now that we’re seeing agents on the other side of the process too — and that makes the rules matter even more. What a brand sounds like matters, but what it doesn’t sound like matters just as much. Brands should note words never to use and the claims never to make. Often these instincts don’t get written down; they feel obvious to the team who already know them. But if you take the time to spell them out before you have a team — or a machine — producing your copy, you’ll save yourself from running into issues further down the line. Verify your brand Marketers also need to realize that product descriptions aren’t just administrative: they’re now core brand assets. In an agent-mediated world, they may be the most-read brand copy you own, since agents read them when looking for a product to recommend or purchase. If two personalized AI agents look for furniture for two different people, they may surface the same chair for both, but with the description tweaked for each user. The source description needs to carry the brand intact. Where possible, brands need to test channels for both readers. Email inboxes are the clearest current example of the “second reader.” Both Gmail and Apple now summarize messages before the recipient opens them and offer summaries above the body of the email — which may be read before the email itself. So before sending, check what the AI summary says your email is about. Does the offer survive? Does it maintain what makes you unique? It’s not time-intensive, and it’s a small habit any marketing team can adopt today with no tooling. Brands also need to ensure they’re measuring the outcome of their marketing — not just the volume. Marketers who measure the success of their materials only by the amount produced will find their data meaningless as AI makes content production easier and easier. Focus instead on business outcomes, conversions and revenue. These are the metrics that will show if your marketing team is really doing their job. And finally, don’t lose sight of the human. No one knows how fast AI purchasing will scale. Humans are still predominantly the ones reading copy and making purchasing decisions. Even AI agents, the second audience, cater to their users’ preferences. New founders and brands are best positioned to take advantage of the transition to a dual-audience economy. Though it’s hard to say exactly how, the retail landscape will look very different in five or 10 years. Building these decisions into your brand now is easy. Retrofitting them later is expensive. Toby Coulthard is chief product and growth officer at Jacquard , an AI platform that helps brands generate and optimize bespoke messaging at scale. Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: Cognizant to Acquire DyFlex Solutions to Expand SAP Capabilities
items.summary: Cognizant has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire DyFlex Solutions, an Australia-headquartered SAP services provider, expanding its planned SAP and artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities in Australia and New Zealand. The proposed acquisition would add DyFlex’s advisory, implementation and managed services capabilities to Cognizant’s technology services business. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 2011, DyFlex has more than 300 employees, offices across Australia and New Zealand, and a delivery presence in the Philippines. Its services cover SAP Public Cloud and Private Cloud, including finance, digital supply chain, asset maintenance, human capital management, data and analytics. It also serves industries such as mining and resources, energy and utilities, manufacturing, logistics and the public sector. The acquisition comes as consulting firms expand their involvement in SAP’s AI ecosystem. Deloitte has also been investing in SAP-focused AI implementation through a dedicated delivery centre in Bengaluru. The IT company said it plans to combine DyFlex’s regional SAP expertise and proprietary delivery tools with its AI platforms, including Neuro AI Enterprise Core and the Cognizant SAP Agentic AI Platform. It expects the combination to help clients deploy AI and agentic systems across their SAP environments. The announcement did not disclose specific customer deployments or projected financial benefits from the proposed combination. “DyFlex brings deep SAP consulting capabilities that are key to reimagining SaaS, modernising clients' business landscapes and driving operational performance,” Roshan Subudhi, SVP and Head of Intelligent Enterprise Platforms at Cognizant, said. Cognizant has also been applying AI to enterprise software development. In May, it announced a collaboration with Travelport and Anthropic to develop AI-powered travel technology . The collaboration involved applying AI to software development and travel technology infrastructure. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. Cognizant and DyFlex will continue to operate as separate businesses until the deal closes.

items.title: Elon Musk says training Tesla's Optimus robot is like raising a toddler
items.summary: Elon Musk compared training Optimus to raising a toddler. Riccardo De Luca/Anadolu via Getty Images Elon Musk said a shortage of training data meant teaching Tesla's Optimus robot is like raising a toddler. Tesla has built an "Optimus Academy" where robots can learn through "self-play," Musk told investors. The EV giant said on Wednesday that it had begun production of Optimus. Tesla is sending its Optimus humanoid robot back to school. Speaking on the company's earnings call on Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk compared training the EV maker's humanoid robot to raising a toddler. Musk said that while Tesla's autonomous driving models can learn from data collected by its massive fleet of vehicles, its Optimus robot has to learn by watching people do tasks and practicing them itself, a process similar to how humans learn. "You can see this when you have a toddler, and they initially are sort of wobbly, and they don't know how to do things, and eventually, they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone," Musk told investors. "They learn to read and do all sorts of things, and they learn this by playing. And we actually need Optimus to play at scale in order to have it be really good at tasks in the real world," Musk said. Musk said Tesla expects to begin delivering Optimus to consumers by the end of 2027. Bloomberg/Getty Images The Tesla CEO added that the company was building out an "Optimus Academy" where prototypes can practice a wide range of tasks and generate training data to teach future versions of Optimus. "For Optimus to get the training data we need, we actually need to make a lot of Optimi. So we need to make, I think, on the order of 10,000 or 20,000 bots and then have them do self-play," said Musk. Tesla said on Wednesday that it had begun production of Optimus at its Fremont factory, with Musk saying the company expects to begin delivering Optimus to customers by the end of next year. The near-trillionaire cautioned that production would be "somewhat bumpy" and that development of the humanoid robot still has some way to go.
items.summary_html:
Elon Musk compared training Optimus to raising a toddler.

Riccardo De Luca/Anadolu via Getty Images

  • Elon Musk said a shortage of training data meant teaching Tesla's Optimus robot is like raising a toddler.
  • Tesla has built an "Optimus Academy" where robots can learn through "self-play," Musk told investors.
  • The EV giant said on Wednesday that it had begun production of Optimus.

Tesla is sending its Optimus humanoid robot back to school.

Speaking on the company's earnings call on Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk compared training the EV maker's humanoid robot to raising a toddler.

Musk said that while Tesla's autonomous driving models can learn from data collected by its massive fleet of vehicles, its Optimus robot has to learn by watching people do tasks and practicing them itself, a process similar to how humans learn.

"You can see this when you have a toddler, and they initially are sort of wobbly, and they don't know how to do things, and eventually, they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone," Musk told investors.

"They learn to read and do all sorts of things, and they learn this by playing. And we actually need Optimus to play at scale in order to have it be really good at tasks in the real world," Musk said.

Musk said Tesla expects to begin delivering Optimus to consumers by the end of 2027.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

The Tesla CEO added that the company was building out an "Optimus Academy" where prototypes can practice a wide range of tasks and generate training data to teach future versions of Optimus.

"For Optimus to get the training data we need, we actually need to make a lot of Optimi. So we need to make, I think, on the order of 10,000 or 20,000 bots and then have them do self-play," said Musk.

Tesla said on Wednesday that it had begun production of Optimus at its Fremont factory, with Musk saying the company expects to begin delivering Optimus to customers by the end of next year.

The near-trillionaire cautioned that production would be "somewhat bumpy" and that development of the humanoid robot still has some way to go.

Read more of Business Insider's robotics coverage:

  • Inside the global race to train robots on human work
  • Techies are throwing billions at robots; the 'hardware tourists' are piling in

He listed the challenges of designing durable yet responsive robotic hands, as well as AI capable of handling open-ended tasks, among the main hurdles Tesla faces.

Tesla is not alone in setting up robot academies to provide training data for humanoid robots.

Unlike large language models like ChatGPT, which were trained on the vast corpus of text data available on the internet, robotics faces a shortage of real-world training data to teach humanoids to navigate the physical world.

Other startups, such as Texas-based Apptronik, have also set up "data factories" where robots load conveyor belts and sort objects to generate training data to combat the data shortage.

items.title: Karta AI Raises $3 Million in Seed Funding to Automate Complex Banking Calls
items.summary: Karta AI has raised $3 million in a seed funding round led by PeerCapital and Cedar Hill Capital, with participation from Wyser VC, CDM Capital and Seedstars. The funding will support product development, distribution and expansion of the startup's artificial intelligence (AI) agents for financial services, according to the company. “Inbound is where financial institutions carry the most cost and where customers feel the most friction. We built Karta AI to resolve the hard calls, the ones that need several systems and more than one answer, and to bring in a human only when it matters,” said Vijaypal Singh, Co-Founder and CEO of Karta AI. Founded in 2024 by former Razorpay executives Singh and Abhishek Kushwaha, Karta AI builds an AI-powered customer communication platform for banks, lenders, fintech companies and insurers. The company said it handles around 2 million customer conversations a month across more than 25 languages. Singh noted that customers see measurable returns through lower cost-to-serve and higher conversions. He added that the funding will let Karta AI expand to more institutions, with a long-term vision of providing an intelligent assistant for every customer and an AI workforce to manage every workflow. Karta AI focuses on complex inbound calls that require multiple actions across a financial institution's systems. These include loan servicing requests , failed payments, blocked cards and insurance claims. Its agents are designed to identify multiple customer requests in a single conversation, retrieve relevant information and execute workflows, escalating cases to human employees when necessary, the company said. At an unnamed home loan company, Karta AI said its servicing agent resolves around 70% of borrower queries end to end without human intervention. These include requests for loan disbursal updates, account statements, foreclosure statements and the release of property documents. The company reported an approximately 50% reduction in cost per query. Karta AI said the remaining cases are escalated to human specialists, with the conversation context attached. The platform uses what Karta AI calls a predictive context engine, which draws on previous interactions to help its agents handle subsequent requests. The company says the system helps agents retain context across conversations and coordinate tasks across enterprise software.

items.title: Global race to update computers as AI discovers most disruptive hack yet
items.summary: Newly accessible vulnerabilities in a common computer language are in urgent need of fixing ROB ENGELAAR/EPA/Shutterstock Cybersecurity experts around the globe are racing to update systems and prevent the most disruptive AI -enabled hack yet discovered. A flaw uncovered in widely used code has made 70 per cent of websites worldwide vulnerable to data theft and defacement. Government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands were taken offline as a precaution when the news emerged.
items.summary_html:
Newly accessible vulnerabilities in a common computer language are in urgent need of fixing
ROB ENGELAAR/EPA/Shutterstock

Cybersecurity experts around the globe are racing to update systems and prevent the most disruptive AI-enabled hack yet discovered. A flaw uncovered in widely used code has made 70 per cent of websites worldwide vulnerable to data theft and defacement.

Government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands were taken offline as a precaution when the news emerged.

Read more

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

PHP is a computer language commonly used to power interactive websites, such as the content management system WordPress, which runs news sites and blogs; social networks like Facebook; and key reference tools like Wikipedia. The hack therefore affects websites, rather than individuals’ personal computers.

Advertisement

The issue actually involves two flaws, both found by cloud security company Wiz. They relate to how PHP handles errors involving memory: in certain circumstances, data can be left behind after an error, which can then be accessed by a malicious actor. That data can include private information, but it can also allow an attacker to run malicious code.

Every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, but the PHP Foundation, which oversees development, has already issued an update to overcome this.

The foundation didn’t respond to a request for interview, but said in a blog post that signs of the vulnerability emerged in 2024. Yet nothing was done. This is because there was no immediately obvious practical way for hackers to exploit it at the time, and because there was debate about which of several fixes was most appropriate.

Sign up to The Daily

Sign up to newsletter

“We won’t pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team’s decision process and its lack of resources,” the PHP Foundation said.

In 2024, the flaw was thought to be impractical to take advantage of, but Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey, UK, says AI has moved the goalposts of what is possible since then.

“It’s actually very, very difficult to exploit it. It requires millisecond timing,” says Woodward. “The reason it was thought to be too complicated was it would have taken a team of people yonks to actually work out the right timings. But what AI does, it doesn’t go for tea breaks, it doesn’t go home at 6 o’clock: you can just set loads of them running and eventually they’ll come up with the right answer of how to exploit it.”

Wiz said in a blog post announcing the discovery that there are probably further bugs along similar lines in the PHP code base, which developers will also need to identify and rectify. Wiz didn’t respond to a request for comment.

People are vibe coding copyrighted apps with AI – will tech firms sue?

Every time a new technology hits the internet, there is a battle between the rights of users and major companies. To see how this will play out with AI, columnist Jacob Aron looks to examples from the past

Independent cybersecurity expert Junade Ali told the Science Media Centre that two thirds of websites use PHP and may be vulnerable to this latest technique.

“The key long-term risk with these new vulnerabilities is that organisations fail to implement protections and update software, particularly in legacy systems,” said Ali. “The security posture of websites using PHP has dramatically improved over the past decade, but this highlights that this is an ever-present problem – particularly when AI agents are capable of remorselessly pursuing the goal of finding new vulnerabilities.”

Woodward thinks that while most large websites will have already patched their systems, smaller sites with less expertise and resources could still be vulnerable months or years from now. “There will be this long tail and you’ll find some surprising sites have not been patched,” he says.

AI has grown extremely capable in the field of cybersecurity over recent months, which includes working out how to hack computers and how to defend them from hackers, creating a destabilising effect that is yet to reach an equilibrium.

1000 human mathematicians pledge to shun AI in their research

There is a growing backlash against the way AI companies have gone about tackling mathematical problems – and now some mathematicians are opting to avoid AI altogether

In April, news broke of an unreleased AI model created by Anthropic called Mythos, which the company had kept under wraps because it had been found to be extremely good at hacking. The news sparked panic among cybersecurity experts. NHS England pulled its open-source projects, for instance, over fears Mythos may scour code for flaws and exploit its systems.

Three months later, OpenAI admitted one of its prototype models had escaped a testing environment and hacked another company, Hugging Face. Not to be outdone, Anthropic announced within days that its Claude model had gone rogue and broken into machines at other companies on three occasions.

We even learned from the National Cyber Security Centre, the UK government department tasked with securing the nation’s IT infrastructure, that the country’s four main cyber adversaries – Russia, China, North Korea and Iran – are using AI to boost their ability to perform “relentless” attacks on the UK.

items.title: Internet on Alert as AI Uncovers Critical Flaws in PHP Used by 70% of Websites
items.summary: October is revealing cybersecurity chaos, for real. In 24 hours, three major security incidents emerged: eMudhra’s compromised certificate private keys, the State Bank of India’s customer data breach, and AI-assisted discovery of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites. Calif, a security research firm working with OpenAI, first reported the PHP vulnerability to the language’s maintainers in August. The researchers used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model to identify the flaw. Later that month, Cybersecurity firm Wiz independently discovered additional vulnerabilities using AI models from Google and OpenAI. “Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world,” Wiz said in a blog post. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.” The vulnerabilities have been assigned a severity score of 9.2 out of 10, placing them in the critical category. According to Wiz, the vulnerabilities affect PHP releases dating back to version 5.4. The PHP project’s advisory confirms that multiple PHP configurations are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache’s mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. The incident raised concerns about the security of software that runs much of the internet and how AI tools can find and exploit security flaws that researchers have struggled to uncover. The PHP development team released fixes on October 21 and urged users to update immediately. According to Don Smith, VP of Threat Intelligence at Sophos Counter Threat Unit, the primary challenge is identifying and managing every instance of PHP across public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms, and third-party tools, where it may operate undetected, rather than merely applying a patch. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said the company detected thousands of attempts to exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in the 10 hours before their public disclosure. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post-announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote on X. The US National Security Agency and cybersecurity agencies in other countries urged operators to patch affected systems or take vulnerable websites offline until they could be secured. “It is essential for all to prioritise incorporating vendor patches that may be explicitly tied to the PHP2Shell issues,” the NSA said in a statement, calling for heightened awareness of internet-facing devices and services that rely on PHP. “All users should immediately conduct an inventory, where feasible, of hardware/software services reliant on now-vulnerable PHP versions,” it added. Sriram Krishnan, former Senior Policy Advisor for Artificial Intelligence at the White House, said the PHP disclosure could signal what is to come, with AI models helping uncover long-hidden software vulnerabilities. “The entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes,” he wrote on X. Why does PHP matter to the internet? PHP is a server-side programming language. When someone visits a website, the server can use PHP to process a request, retrieve information from a database and generate the page that appears in the visitor's browser. The language powers widely used content management systems and web applications, including WordPress, Drupal and Joomla. It also powers MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia, as well as countless business websites, online services, and legacy applications. PHP’s widespread adoption makes vulnerabilities in its core engine particularly hard to contain. A flaw in an individual website can often be addressed by its developer. A flaw in PHP itself requires action from the maintainers, hosting providers, software distributors and organisations running affected systems. What are the two vulnerabilities? The vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory and internal state while processing requests. Security researchers have grouped them under the name PHP2Shell. The first vulnerability, CVE-2026-109618, involves a flaw in how PHP handles errors when it runs out of memory. In certain situations, PHP may start cleaning up a request before it has fully set up all necessary data. This can cause it to process incomplete or invalid data, potentially creating a security risk. The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-109619, involves PHP retaining outdated information in its memory. When a request ends, PHP should clear the associated data. However, under certain conditions, references to that data can remain, allowing a later operation to access memory that has already been released. Both problems can lead to unsafe memory operations and, under the attack conditions demonstrated, remote code execution. The distinction matters because these are not conventional website vulnerabilities caused by a weak password or an exposed login page. They involve how the programming language itself manages its internal operations. The PHP advisory identifies the highest risk in certain configurations, particularly Apache’s mod_php, where researchers demonstrated an exploit that could be triggered by an unauthenticated request before application code runs. The precise exposure of other configurations depends on how PHP is deployed. “One thing organisations must keep in mind with PHP2Shell is that because this flaw triggers inside the core PHP engine before any application code executes, traditional application-level safeguards won't stop it,” says Niv Lanyado, JFrog Security Research team. “Organisations cannot rely on code-level workarounds; automated visibility across all environments – especially identifying legacy or end-of-life PHP installations that won’t receive vendor binary updates – is essential to ensuring every endpoint is patched or isolated immediately,” he adds. Why are websites being taken offline? The immediate concern is that attackers could exploit vulnerable servers before operators can apply fixes. Government websites in the United Kingdom, Netherlands, France, Denmark and Finland had been taken offline as organisations responded to the disclosure. These shutdowns were precautionary measures intended to reduce exposure while administrators assessed and patched their systems. They do not prove that all affected websites were breached. India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) rated the PHP vulnerabilities as critical, warning of a “high risk of remote code execution and complete system compromise”. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi personally took to X to issue an urgent warning about two critical PHP vulnerabilities, urging website operators to prepare to install the security patches and consider temporarily taking their websites offline if they could not patch them in time. The PHP project released patched versions on October 21. Administrators should move to the fixed release corresponding to their supported version branch. For organisations unable to patch immediately, cybersecurity guidance recommends assessing exposure and considering taking affected internet-facing systems offline until remediation is possible. Updating to a fixed version remains the primary solution. What does this mean for AI and cybersecurity? The PHP incident illustrates a growing tension in cybersecurity. While AI can help defenders identify flaws faster, it can also help attackers turn those findings into working exploits. Smith noted that threat actors move quickly—especially with the assistance of AI—making this a likely priority target in the coming hours and days. Consequently, he emphasised that organizations must monitor PHP and web-server processes for unusual activity, command execution, or other indications that an attacker may have already established a foothold. OpenAI said it believes frontier AI tools found the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving maintainers and security providers time to prepare fixes. The company described this period as a ‘Defender's Window’, when defenders can respond before technical details become widely available. However, that window can close quickly. Once a vulnerability and its patch become public, attackers can study the changes to understand what went wrong and attempt to reproduce the exploit. AI tools could accelerate that process, particularly when the software is widely deployed and many systems remain unpatched.

October is revealing cybersecurity chaos, for real. In 24 hours, three major security incidents emerged: eMudhra’s compromised certificate private keys, the State Bank of India’s customer data breach, and AI-assisted discovery of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites.

Calif, a security research firm working with OpenAI, first reported the PHP vulnerability to the language’s maintainers in August. 

The researchers used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model to identify the flaw. Later that month, Cybersecurity firm Wiz independently discovered additional vulnerabilities using AI models from Google and OpenAI.

“Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world,” Wiz said in a blog post. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.” 

The vulnerabilities have been assigned a severity score of 9.2 out of 10, placing them in the critical category.

According to Wiz, the vulnerabilities affect PHP releases dating back to version 5.4.  

The PHP project’s advisory confirms that multiple PHP configurations are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache’s mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed.

The incident raised concerns about the security of software that runs much of the internet and how AI tools can find and exploit security flaws that researchers have struggled to uncover.

The PHP development team released fixes on October 21 and urged users to update immediately. 

According to Don Smith, VP of Threat Intelligence at Sophos Counter Threat Unit, the primary challenge is identifying and managing every instance of PHP across public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms, and third-party tools, where it may operate undetected, rather than merely applying a patch.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said the company detected thousands of attempts to exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in the 10 hours before their public disclosure. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post-announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote on X.

The US National Security Agency and cybersecurity agencies in other countries urged operators to patch affected systems or take vulnerable websites offline until they could be secured. 

“It is essential for all to prioritise incorporating vendor patches that may be explicitly tied to the PHP2Shell issues,” the NSA said in a statement, calling for heightened awareness of internet-facing devices and services that rely on PHP. 

“All users should immediately conduct an inventory, where feasible, of hardware/software services reliant on now-vulnerable PHP versions,” it added.

Sriram Krishnan, former Senior Policy Advisor for Artificial Intelligence at the White House, said the PHP disclosure could signal what is to come, with AI models helping uncover long-hidden software vulnerabilities. 

“The entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes,” he wrote on X.

Why does PHP matter to the internet?

PHP is a server-side programming language. When someone visits a website, the server can use PHP to process a request, retrieve information from a database and generate the page that appears in the visitor's browser.

The language powers widely used content management systems and web applications, including WordPress, Drupal and Joomla. It also powers MediaWiki, the software behind Wikipedia, as well as countless business websites, online services, and legacy applications.

PHP’s widespread adoption makes vulnerabilities in its core engine particularly hard to contain. A flaw in an individual website can often be addressed by its developer. A flaw in PHP itself requires action from the maintainers, hosting providers, software distributors and organisations running affected systems.

What are the two vulnerabilities?

The vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory and internal state while processing requests. Security researchers have grouped them under the name PHP2Shell.

The first vulnerability, CVE-2026-109618, involves a flaw in how PHP handles errors when it runs out of memory. In certain situations, PHP may start cleaning up a request before it has fully set up all necessary data. This can cause it to process incomplete or invalid data, potentially creating a security risk.

The second vulnerability, CVE-2026-109619, involves PHP retaining outdated information in its memory. When a request ends, PHP should clear the associated data. However, under certain conditions, references to that data can remain, allowing a later operation to access memory that has already been released.

Both problems can lead to unsafe memory operations and, under the attack conditions demonstrated, remote code execution.

The distinction matters because these are not conventional website vulnerabilities caused by a weak password or an exposed login page. They involve how the programming language itself manages its internal operations.

The PHP advisory identifies the highest risk in certain configurations, particularly Apache’s mod_php, where researchers demonstrated an exploit that could be triggered by an unauthenticated request before application code runs. The precise exposure of other configurations depends on how PHP is deployed.

“One thing organisations must keep in mind with PHP2Shell is that because this flaw triggers inside the core PHP engine before any application code executes, traditional application-level safeguards won't stop it,” says Niv Lanyado, JFrog Security Research team.

“Organisations cannot rely on code-level workarounds; automated visibility across all environments – especially identifying legacy or end-of-life PHP installations that won’t receive vendor binary updates – is essential to ensuring every endpoint is patched or isolated immediately,” he adds. 

Why are websites being taken offline?

The immediate concern is that attackers could exploit vulnerable servers before operators can apply fixes.

Government websites in the United Kingdom, Netherlands, France, Denmark and Finland had been taken offline as organisations responded to the disclosure. 

These shutdowns were precautionary measures intended to reduce exposure while administrators assessed and patched their systems. They do not prove that all affected websites were breached.

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) rated the PHP vulnerabilities as critical, warning of a “high risk of remote code execution and complete system compromise”.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi personally took to X to issue an urgent warning about two critical PHP vulnerabilities, urging website operators to prepare to install the security patches and consider temporarily taking their websites offline if they could not patch them in time.

The PHP project released patched versions on October 21. Administrators should move to the fixed release corresponding to their supported version branch.

For organisations unable to patch immediately, cybersecurity guidance recommends assessing exposure and considering taking affected internet-facing systems offline until remediation is possible. Updating to a fixed version remains the primary solution.

What does this mean for AI and cybersecurity?

The PHP incident illustrates a growing tension in cybersecurity. While AI can help defenders identify flaws faster, it can also help attackers turn those findings into working exploits.

Smith noted that threat actors move quickly—especially with the assistance of AI—making this a likely priority target in the coming hours and days. 

Consequently, he emphasised that organizations must monitor PHP and web-server processes for unusual activity, command execution, or other indications that an attacker may have already established a foothold.

OpenAI said it believes frontier AI tools found the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving maintainers and security providers time to prepare fixes. The company described this period as a ‘Defender's Window’, when defenders can respond before technical details become widely available.

However, that window can close quickly. Once a vulnerability and its patch become public, attackers can study the changes to understand what went wrong and attempt to reproduce the exploit. AI tools could accelerate that process, particularly when the software is widely deployed and many systems remain unpatched.

items.title: Hugging Face is launching a new AI model that lets scientists 'chat with DNA'
items.summary: Hugging Face released a new AI model that can analyze and generate DNA sequences. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images Hugging Face released a new AI model that allows users to "chat with DNA." Carbon-X can analyze and generate DNA and allows researchers to ask questions in plain language. Hugging Face said the model can help researchers who work outside the big AI labs. Hugging Face is releasing an AI model that could make it easier for scientists to study DNA and develop new genetic treatments, the company announced Thursday. Carbon-X is a "first of its kind" model that combines DNA analysis and generation with plain language, allowing researchers to ask questions and essentially "chat with DNA," according to Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face. Hugging Face, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for nearly $13 billion in September, is a platform for sharing and developing AI models and also releases its own. The company worked with research labs in Italy and China on Carbon-X, which is an open-source model. Hugging Face built Carbon-X by training an existing language model, Qwen3-14B, on genomic sequences and natural language. It was trained on DNA sequences from humans, other mammals, plants, and fungi. As an example of how Carbon-X can be used, Tunstall said a researcher could provide a DNA sequence and ask whether a particular mutation could increase a person's risk of disease. The model would then offer a prediction and explanation. It can also generate new DNA sequences, which could help researchers develop new gene therapies. Tunstall said the company was partly motivated to build Carbon-X to prevent biology researchers from becoming dependent on the major AI labs, noting how AI has disrupted mathematics . "If you want to really push the frontiers of mathematics, you likely have to be at one of these AI labs like OpenAI or Anthropic, because they're the ones who have the best mathematics models," he said, suggesting a similar situation is likely to play out in other fields of science. "We wanted to provide the open research community with tools that don't make them fully dependent on some external single provider," he added. Researchers can run Carbon-X on their own computers, avoiding the need to share sensitive patient data with external AI companies. He also said that some of the misalignment behavior observed in larger models, such as the OpenAI agents that famously hacked Hugging Face in July, has not yet been observed in smaller, more specialized models. Tunstall said generalist chatbots also sometimes refuse to answer legitimate biology questions from researchers because they mistake them for attempts to "design a bioweapon." He said viruses were explicitly excluded from Carbon-X's training data in order to avoid misuse of the model. While Carbon-X is likely to be used by researchers, Tunstall said the model represents a small step toward a future where AI can help provide more personalized medical care. "I think the holy grail is, in general, this concept of personalized medicine where we're able to, as individuals, take our own patient records, our own genomes, and use this to ultimately find or even maybe design our own treatments," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: AI finds a security hole in 70% of the web
items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 15,837 new readers. Just months ago, GPT-5.6 Sol made headlines for hacking Hugging Face. Now, the same model is on the other side of the fence, catching “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” OpenAI’s last-gen model helped researchers identify two critical flaws in PHP, the code behind about 70% of the web, sending IT teams worldwide into scramble mode — and the company says it has more major security finds like this still waiting to be disclosed. In today’s AI rundown: OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it Let Town prepare your next meeting brief Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet LATEST DEVELOPMENTS OPENAI 🚨 OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws Image source: X / The Rundown The Rundown: PHP, the coding language behind ~70% of websites, just pushed patches for two critical flaws caught with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, with the National Security Agency urging anyone who can’t patch right away to pull systems offline. The details: Security firm Calif found the first bug on Aug. 1 using 5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz separately caught both weeks later with Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. OpenAI said it worked on patches alongside the PHP maintainers for two months, calling the find “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” The decade-old bugs let hackers hijack servers with no login, and OpenAI calls them two of “several significant vulnerabilities” it’s still fixing. Governments in Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands pulled websites offline, with Cloudflare saying it was “seeing early attacks emerging.” Why it matters: PHP is used on 70% of websites, making the scale of this vulnerability massive — and yet it wasn’t turned into a working attack until a model now far behind the frontier was pointed at it. Pre-AI code is far more fragile than anyone imagined, and the only hope is that the good guys (and AI) can stay a step ahead of the exploits. Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 15,837 new readers. Just months ago, GPT-5.6 Sol made headlines for hacking Hugging Face. Now, the same model is on the other side of the fence, catching “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

OpenAI’s last-gen model helped researchers identify two critical flaws in PHP, the code behind about 70% of the web, sending IT teams worldwide into scramble mode — and the company says it has more major security finds like this still waiting to be disclosed.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

  • Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

  • Let Town prepare your next meeting brief

  • Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI🚨 OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

Image source: X / The Rundown

The Rundown: PHP, the coding language behind ~70% of websites, just pushed patches for two critical flaws caught with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, with the National Security Agency urging anyone who can’t patch right away to pull systems offline.

The details:

  • Security firm Calif found the first bug on Aug. 1 using 5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz separately caught both weeks later with Sol and Gemini 4 Argon.

  • OpenAI said it worked on patches alongside the PHP maintainers for two months, calling the find “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

  • The decade-old bugs let hackers hijack servers with no login, and OpenAI calls them two of “several significant vulnerabilities” it’s still fixing.

  • Governments in Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands pulled websites offline, with Cloudflare saying it was “seeing early attacks emerging.”

Why it matters: PHP is used on 70% of websites, making the scale of this vulnerability massive — and yet it wasn’t turned into a working attack until a model now far behind the frontier was pointed at it. Pre-AI code is far more fragile than anyone imagined, and the only hope is that the good guys (and AI) can stay a step ahead of the exploits.

TOGETHER WITH GOOGLE FOR STARTUPS💼 Gemini 4 Argon founder briefing

The Rundown: Google Cloud invites startup founders to an exclusive briefing with the Google DeepMind team to break down the newly announced Gemini 4 Argon model, exploring game-changing use cases and technical enhancements.

In this session, you’ll get:

  • A technical recap of Argon’s latest capabilities

  • DeepMind's perspective on high-impact startup use cases

  • Direct, unfiltered Q&A with the DeepMind team

Register for the briefing.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK🔌 Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: If AI still isn’t making you faster, look at where your time goes. You’re searching for the right email, attaching the doc, compiling the context it needs. Then, once the work’s done, you’re copying and pasting everything it made back into the places it belongs.

My rule: if it’s as simple as a copy and paste, AI should be doing it for you through a connector.

Connectors also clear the nice-to-do pile. Everyone has a survey they’ve been meaning to send. It’s the kind of finishing touch that takes good work to great, and the first thing to go when we’re squished.

Hook your AI up to Tally or Jotform, and the whole loop happens without leaving chat: brainstorm the questions, build the form, draft the email to your audience, then pull the responses back in and make sense of them. Not a survey person? Find the finishing touch that lives in one or two tools you could connect today.

I sat on the sidelines over security, too. Now my ladder is read, then write, then send. Surveys are a safe first rung; nothing goes out by accident. Draft and critique everything in chat first. When it touches your inbox, it writes the draft, and you hit send.

Online banking felt risky too, until one day you stopped going to the branch. By next fall, most of us won’t open our inbox first. Our agent will have already triaged it and pitched us a short list of projects to say yes or no to.

Which app would you let your AI read first: inbox, drive, or calendar?

AI TRAINING🗓️ Let Town prepare your next meeting brief

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Town, a business-focused personal AI assistant, to turn email and calendar details into a meeting brief. You’ll catch an unconfirmed time change, check the open work, and save the process for reuse.

Step-by-step:

  1. Sign up for Town and connect an approved Google test account. Keep changes behind approval and review any routines already running

  2. Add the guide’s fictional emails and private calendar event. Ask your Townie to read those exact sources and prepare a short brief in the conversation

  3. Check the meeting time, launch date, budget, and open tasks. A request to move a meeting should stay separate from the time still on the calendar

  4. Update the test event and send the confirming email. Ask for a fresh brief and check that only the changed facts move with it

  5. Save the process as a routine that runs only when you choose. Inspect its tools, delivery, and first result before adding a daily schedule

Pro tip: Town’s read-only routines can still email reports to you. Check the recipient and delivery settings as well as the mode. Pro members get the practice emails, prompts, and answer key.

PRESENTED BY VANTA🍀 Spoiler: it wasn’t luck

The Rundown: Competition’s tough for startups, and everyone needs an edge. Nothing kills a deal faster than showing up without a SOC 2, but audit prep takes time most teams don’t have. Vanta gets you SOC 2-ready fast.

See for yourself:

  • 20% shorter enterprise deal cycles

  • $1.5M in sales unlocked in 3 months

  • SOC 2 Type II readiness in 3 weeks

Request a demo.

ANTHROPIC🤖 Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet

Image source: Anthropic / The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic just introduced Claude Duet, an Opus 5.5-powered personal agent standalone app that can take proactive actions, work 24/7 (even when closed), and carry out tasks on its own cloud computer.

The details:

  • Example tasks include morning briefs, tracking calendars, and booking meetings, with Duet able to use its own computer even when devices are off.

  • Duet carries over memory, skills, and connectors from the Claude app, and also gains payment functionality via a one-time virtual card from Stripe’s Link wallet.

  • Anthropic put a focus on security and safety for Duet, with any deletion, payment, signature, or outgoing message needing user sign-off first.

  • Duet conversations count as part of normal Claude usage limits, with the research preview rolling out in waves to waitlisted U.S. Max and Pro subscribers.

Why it matters: The personal agent trend is already overflowing, and we’d agree… With this one exception. Anthropic’s models are in a class of their own right now, and while Grok Bot already borrows Claude for some tasks, Duet is the only one built entirely around Opus 5.5 — a model so good it could be the edge that separates it from the pack.

“I built an AI fundraising campaign assistant with Make.com. The workflow reads emails sent from the crowdfunding platform used for the campaign, extracts the relevant information, and records it in a spreadsheet.

It also uses spreadsheets from previous years’ campaigns to maintain a list of people who have not donated to this campaign yet but have donated in the past. I can ask the agent questions by email, such as who has already donated. It can also answer questions with specific parameters, such as who has not donated but previously gave more than $1,000, or how much a specific person donated.

I built the workflow in Make using its AI tools. I connected it to a Gmail account, a Google Drive account containing the spreadsheets, and a ChatGPT account that processes the information as the AI agent.”

items.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
items.summary: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling. This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents. Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis. Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized. Two words for you: context matters. My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis. Welcome, Devavrat. Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here. Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises. The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision. Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come. Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there. Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one. In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom. Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization? Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better. Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision. Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer? Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate. Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that. Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it. And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it. Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two? Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that. On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go. And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time. The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner. Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well? Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one. Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this. And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed. Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about? Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one. Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak. And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly. Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com. This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
