After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.

Two words for you: context matters.

My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.

Welcome, Devavrat.

Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here.

Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale?

Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises.

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision.

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come.

Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?

Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there.

Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one.

In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom.

Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization?

Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better.

Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision.

Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer?

Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate.

Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that.

Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it.

And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it.

Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two?

Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that.

On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go.

And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time.

The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner.

Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well?

Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one.

Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this.

And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed.

Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about?

Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one.

Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak.

And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.

Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.

That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com.

This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye.

items.title: SpaceX-Tesla merger could create a Frankenstein's monster Wall Street can't value
items.summary: Win McNamee/Getty Images This post appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Some pairings feel inevitable. "Friends" had Ross and Rachel. "The Office" had Jim and Pam. Elon Musk has SpaceX and Tesla. But a deal between Musk's two giant companies could end up looking more like Frankenstein's monster than a Hollywood love story. And investors might struggle to understand and value it. The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up isn't a shoo-in, but both sides are officially considering it . That raises questions about what's gained from a merger. Combining the companies turns Musk's two jobs into one. Their somewhat overlapping AI plans could create significant efficiencies in areas like compute and talent. Joe Ciolli, author of the First Trade newsletter , broke down the pros and cons for SpaceX and Tesla investors . These companies have A LOT under their hoods, though. Here are just some of the businesses or long-term bets that SpaceX and Tesla are pursuing: Space-mission services (Falcon 9, Dragon, Starship) Internet service (Starlink broadband) Mobile carrier (Starlink Mobile) Electric vehicles (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Roadster) Government satellite systems (Starshield) Autonomous vehicles (Robotaxi) Humanoid robots (Optimus) Energy storage (Powerwall, Megapack) Frontier AI models (Grok) Social media (X) Payments app (X Money) AI infrastructure (Colossus) AI coding tools (Cursor) And don't forget Musk's grandest ambition: colonizing Mars. A conglomerate with such a diverse set of businesses can become a headache to value. Let's start simple: How would you describe a SpaceX-Tesla entity? A space company? An AI company? A robotics company? Saying it's "a little bit of everything" might not sit well with investors. When a company plays in a bunch of industries, the market doesn't always give it the benefit of the doubt. There's a term for this phenomenon: conglomerate discount . It means a company's stock is valued lower than the sum of its individual parts. Some investors fear the company will be too complex to manage, or too expensive to run. Others worry its combined financials will make it hard to understand its true health, or stronger parts of the business will subsidize weaker ones. A widely cited 1995 paper on the topic found the discount to be between 13% and 15% among a sample of diversified companies from 1986 to 1991. Some academics and economists have argued the conglomerate discount is a relic of the past. A 2024 McKinsey report said the discount wasn't necessarily automatic. Instead, heavily diversified companies often had weak performance or lacked financial transparency , which made it harder to assess their true value. Either way, these types of companies require investors with a broad appetite. (Or a tough stomach.) Imagine you're excited about Starlink's potential , but not as keen on humanoid robots . Expensive robotics projects could suck up the budget you were hoping would go to Starlink. Or the money generated by Starlink could subsidize the losses accrued in an underperforming division. It's why giant, sprawling companies are often less appetizing than a pure-play stock. Ultimately, a deal is often about selling a vision to investors. And there's arguably no one better at doing that than Elon Musk. Now he just needs to prove SpaceX and Tesla were always meant to be together. Read the original article on Business Insider

And don't forget Musk's grandest ambition: colonizing Mars.

A conglomerate with such a diverse set of businesses can become a headache to value.

Let's start simple: How would you describe a SpaceX-Tesla entity?

A space company? An AI company? A robotics company? Saying it's "a little bit of everything" might not sit well with investors.

When a company plays in a bunch of industries, the market doesn't always give it the benefit of the doubt. There's a term for this phenomenon: conglomerate discount.

It means a company's stock is valued lower than the sum of its individual parts. Some investors fear the company will be too complex to manage, or too expensive to run. Others worry its combined financials will make it hard to understand its true health, or stronger parts of the business will subsidize weaker ones.

A widely cited 1995 paper on the topic found the discount to be between 13% and 15% among a sample of diversified companies from 1986 to 1991.

Some academics and economists have argued the conglomerate discount is a relic of the past. A 2024 McKinsey report said the discount wasn't necessarily automatic. Instead, heavily diversified companies often had weak performance or lacked financial transparency, which made it harder to assess their true value.

Either way, these types of companies require investors with a broad appetite. (Or a tough stomach.)

Imagine you're excited about Starlink's potential, but not as keen on humanoid robots. Expensive robotics projects could suck up the budget you were hoping would go to Starlink. Or the money generated by Starlink could subsidize the losses accrued in an underperforming division.

It's why giant, sprawling companies are often less appetizing than a pure-play stock.

Ultimately, a deal is often about selling a vision to investors. And there's arguably no one better at doing that than Elon Musk.

Now he just needs to prove SpaceX and Tesla were always meant to be together.

items.title: AI Agents are Making Human Customer Service a Specialist Job
items.summary: AI agents are taking over routine customer service tasks, pushing human contact centre workers towards more complex problems that require judgement, specialised knowledge, and human intervention. In an exclusive interview with AIM, Thomas Wyatt, COO of communications-platform-as-a-service provider Twilio , says enterprises should not look at AI as a wholesale replacement for their contact centres. Instead, companies can route routine level-one and level-two queries to AI while reserving human agents for more complicated cases. A large share of customer service queries do not require a highly skilled human agent. AI agents can be trained on a company’s knowledge base, FAQs, policies, and other information to resolve routine requests. Wyatt says this can reduce the amount of human capital required for cases that are relatively straightforward. But AI will not necessarily be able to resolve every customer problem. “AI agents can only take it so far. There’s usually a reason why a certain percentage of those cases need to be escalated to a human,” Wyatt says. But handing the conversation to a human comes with its own requirement: context cannot be lost. Wyatt says customers should not have to repeat their entire problem after an AI agent hands the conversation to a human. Wyatt explains that Twilio Conversation Memory helps preserve the context of a conversation, allowing a human specialist to understand what has happened and continue resolving the issue without asking the customer to repeat themselves. AI or Human Support Wyatt believes customers will increasingly choose between AI and human support based on the complexity of their needs. He points to Philippine Airlines, which gave customers the choice of interacting with an AI or waiting for a human. A simple request, such as increasing baggage allowance, could be handled by AI. A more complicated situation involving an elderly passenger, wheelchair assistance, or special food requirements could be directed to a human. “People are actually pretty smart to self-serve,” Wyatt says. He expects this choice to become a bigger part of customer service as AI agents become more capable. Voice AI a Major Growth Driver Messaging remains Twilio’s largest business, followed by voice, while WhatsApp is the fastest-growing channel, albeit from a smaller base. Voice AI has become particularly important. Wyatt says Twilio’s voice business is growing faster than it has in years, driven by building applications around voice agents. Per Wyatt, customers want Twilio to provide capabilities such as voice recording, transcription, sentiment analysis, real-time connections to large language models (LLMs), and customer memory. “They want to focus their energy on building the workflows and the verticalisation of those use cases to meet the customer need in a very specialised way,” Wyatt says. Twilio is also extending these software capabilities across channels. A customer using the platform for voice can add messaging without having to build a separate software stack. Twilio’s Moat Wyatt says that while AI has made it relatively easier to generate software, Twilio’s underlying communications infrastructure is much harder to replicate. Twilio has around 4,800 carrier relationships across 180 countries, built over more than a decade. Whether a company sends an SMS through a carrier, uses RCS through Google or communicates through WhatsApp, the interaction ultimately depends on physical communications infrastructure and relationships with carriers and platforms. “You could vibe-code a wrapper around our communication infrastructure, but you can’t vibe-code the communication infrastructure,” Wyatt says. The company wants to move beyond connectivity and provide the software layer that sits on top of that infrastructure. Wyatt sees value in vibe coding for simple applications, prototypes, and proof-of-concept work. But he cautions against using it as the primary way to build production-grade enterprise software. The problem is maintainability. If developers do not understand how an application was built, debugging and modifying it can become difficult. He expects enterprises to increasingly use tools such as Claude and Codex as coding assistants, rather than handing over entire software projects to AI. However, without human judgement, companies risk creating technical debt and what he describes as “slop” that will have to be fixed later. From APIs to AI-Native Communications Twilio historically provided APIs for individual communication use cases such as SMS, voice calls, and email. Wyatt says the company is now bringing these interactions together into a single, continuous conversation. He gave the example of a customer applying for a mortgage. The process could begin with a phone call, continue through a text message confirming information, and later involve an email updating the customer on the progress of the application. “It really is a unified conversation that happens over the course of a relationship between a brand and a consumer,” Wyatt says. AI is now being added on top of this infrastructure. Twilio wants AI agents to be able to access its communication capabilities directly, allowing them to communicate with customers across different channels. The company sees an opportunity in the expected growth of enterprise AI agents. According to Gartner, more than 80% of enterprises will deploy industry-specific AI agents by 2030. Many of those agents will eventually need to communicate with humans through voice, messaging, or email. India Market India is an important market for Twilio within the Asia-Pacific and Japan region, which Wyatt describes as one of the company’s fastest-growing regions globally. According to Deloitte, India's enterprise AI market is expanding rapidly, valued between $7.6 billion and $9.5 billion as of 2024–2025 and projected to surpass $130 billion by 2032 at a 39–42% CAGR. The company does not disclose specific revenue figures for India, but Wyatt identifies Reliance as one of Twilio’s flagship customers in the country. “It’s a market where we have a lot of R&D as well and customer care capabilities in terms of Twilio's investment in the region,” he says. Wyatt also points to the growing number of AI-native companies in India and the wider APJ region using Twilio, although he said the Indian market remains in its early stages for the company.

Wyatt believes customers will increasingly choose between AI and human support based on the complexity of their needs.

He points to Philippine Airlines, which gave customers the choice of interacting with an AI or waiting for a human.

A simple request, such as increasing baggage allowance, could be handled by AI. A more complicated situation involving an elderly passenger, wheelchair assistance, or special food requirements could be directed to a human.

“People are actually pretty smart to self-serve,” Wyatt says. He expects this choice to become a bigger part of customer service as AI agents become more capable.

Voice AI a Major Growth Driver

Messaging remains Twilio’s largest business, followed by voice, while WhatsApp is the fastest-growing channel, albeit from a smaller base.

Voice AI has become particularly important. Wyatt says Twilio’s voice business is growing faster than it has in years, driven by building applications around voice agents.

Per Wyatt, customers want Twilio to provide capabilities such as voice recording, transcription, sentiment analysis, real-time connections to large language models (LLMs), and customer memory.

“They want to focus their energy on building the workflows and the verticalisation of those use cases to meet the customer need in a very specialised way,” Wyatt says.

Twilio is also extending these software capabilities across channels. A customer using the platform for voice can add messaging without having to build a separate software stack.

Twilio’s Moat 

Wyatt says that while AI has made it relatively easier to generate software, Twilio’s underlying communications infrastructure is much harder to replicate.

Twilio has around 4,800 carrier relationships across 180 countries, built over more than a decade.

Whether a company sends an SMS through a carrier, uses RCS through Google or communicates through WhatsApp, the interaction ultimately depends on physical communications infrastructure and relationships with carriers and platforms.

“You could vibe-code a wrapper around our communication infrastructure, but you can’t vibe-code the communication infrastructure,” Wyatt says.

The company wants to move beyond connectivity and provide the software layer that sits on top of that infrastructure.

Wyatt sees value in vibe coding for simple applications, prototypes, and proof-of-concept work. But he cautions against using it as the primary way to build production-grade enterprise software.

The problem is maintainability. If developers do not understand how an application was built, debugging and modifying it can become difficult.

He expects enterprises to increasingly use tools such as Claude and Codex as coding assistants, rather than handing over entire software projects to AI.

However, without human judgement, companies risk creating technical debt and what he describes as “slop” that will have to be fixed later.

From APIs to AI-Native Communications

Twilio historically provided APIs for individual communication use cases such as SMS, voice calls, and email. Wyatt says the company is now bringing these interactions together into a single, continuous conversation.

He gave the example of a customer applying for a mortgage. The process could begin with a phone call, continue through a text message confirming information, and later involve an email updating the customer on the progress of the application.

“It really is a unified conversation that happens over the course of a relationship between a brand and a consumer,” Wyatt says.

AI is now being added on top of this infrastructure. Twilio wants AI agents to be able to access its communication capabilities directly, allowing them to communicate with customers across different channels.

The company sees an opportunity in the expected growth of enterprise AI agents. According to Gartner, more than 80% of enterprises will deploy industry-specific AI agents by 2030. Many of those agents will eventually need to communicate with humans through voice, messaging, or email.

India Market 

India is an important market for Twilio within the Asia-Pacific and Japan region, which Wyatt describes as one of the company’s fastest-growing regions globally.

According to Deloitte, India's enterprise AI market is expanding rapidly, valued between $7.6 billion and $9.5 billion as of 2024–2025 and projected to surpass $130 billion by 2032 at a 39–42% CAGR.

The company does not disclose specific revenue figures for India, but Wyatt identifies Reliance as one of Twilio’s flagship customers in the country.

“It’s a market where we have a lot of R&D as well and customer care capabilities in terms of Twilio's investment in the region,” he says.

Wyatt also points to the growing number of AI-native companies in India and the wider APJ region using Twilio, although he said the Indian market remains in its early stages for the company.

items.title: Walmart’s chief people officer shares 3 green flags in a job interview
items.summary: Donna Morris oversees 2.1 million employees. Ethan Miller/Getty Images Walmart chief people officer Donna Morris oversees more than 2 million workers globally. She shared three green flags that make her lean in during a job interview. Morris said she likes to see a track record of grit in a candidate. Donna Morris oversees over 2 million employees , so she knows a strong candidate when she sees one. Walmart's chief people officer identified three green flags that make her lean in during a job interview — regardless of the role they're applying for. First, she told Business Insider that she looks for a genuine alignment with the company's purpose and values. Second, she wants to see an ability to take on multiple responsibilities and make things work. "They demonstrate a track record of grit," Morris said, defining those individuals as people who have overcome adversity. In an ideal world, she said that means they've worked on the frontline, since so many of Walmart employees have customer-facing roles. She said the company looks for candidates with a focus on service. Morris, who started working at 13 at a dry cleaner's and then worked at a drugstore for eight years, said that if a candidate has never experienced what it's like to be a frontline hourly worker, it may be challenging for them to lead. Morris said those jobs gave her purpose, and she found it hard to resign. Now, when she interviews candidates, Morris said her go-to question is "If I was to ask people who've worked for you before, what will they tell me?" She said the open-ended question generates a genuine response and helps her gauge whether the person is focused on servant leadership, which is a "big green flag." Asking this question allows her to hear more about a candidate's first job or a work experience. She said that while graduating from an Ivy League school is valuable, she's more focused on hearing about what they've learned from work experience. "What was the grit they had to persevere through?" Morris asked. The chief people officer, who worked at Adobe for more than 17 years before joining Walmart, said that her third green flag is candidates who are passionate about making a difference. "That, to us, would be really, really key," Morris said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I'm the 25-year-old CEO of Lean In. I love my 2-minute cleaning hack, talking to myself on walks, and beach weekends — here's my routine.
items.summary: Bridget Griswold, the CEO of Lean In. Gabriela Hasbun for BI This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bridget Griswold, the 25-year-old CEO of Lean In, who lives in San Francisco. It's been edited for length and clarity. I fell in love with technology at Brown University, where I studied computer science and business. I worked with two female professors to build a robot. I interned at a semiconductor manufacturing company and also loved design and art. Product management felt like a really wonderful combination of all those interests, and that was my role at Meta a year after graduating from college. My team and I redesigned the Instagram search grid, so now when you search for large Instagram accounts, you're routed to the search results page rather than directly to those accounts. I'm very proud of that. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. While at Meta, an incredible female mentor connected me to Sheryl Sandberg . Meeting her felt so surreal and is what led me to start my role as CEO at Lean In in March. It feels like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to do mission-driven work. Griswold started working at Meta two years after Sheryl Sandberg stepped down as COO. Gabriela Hasbun for BI I was a swimmer as a kid, and as my swim coach used to say: "You get out of swimming what you put into it." I think that applies to many things in life: The more you put in, the more you get out. Here's a day in my life. I wake up to my needy, angelic cat around 7:30 a.m. The second I wake up, I pet my crying and whining cat. She's an angel but very needy. I'm not a breakfast person, but I need coffee immediately. I have many cups of coffee throughout the day. One of the first things I do is make some at home. I always tidy up my apartment while brushing my teeth The most productive two minutes of my day are when I brush my teeth. I clean and tidy my apartment at the same time. I'm probably not super focused on brushing my teeth, which is maybe a problem, but I'm also making my bed, emptying the dishwasher, feeding my cat, or starting the coffee maker. I always move really quickly; I don't like to sit still. Brushing my teeth and standing still would make me antsy, so I like to get something else done at the same time. I'm still adjusting to West Coast hours I moved from New York City to San Francisco in August. In New York, I went to Solidcore classes before work every day. Working on the West Coast, the workday starts earlier than on the East Coast, so I'm still learning whether I like to work out in the morning or after work. When I take the bus to the office three days a week, I often use that time to catch up on personal housekeeping tasks like scheduling appointments or texting back my friends who live on the East Coast . I come to the office around 8 a.m. or 8:30 a.m. A majority of my in-person time is spent in meetings. As CEO, I enjoy being involved in all aspects of the team. I'll meet with our content and research team — we spend a lot of time digging into data, such as some really exciting new research on trad wives in the manosphere. I also often meet with our product and tech team, as well as many of our partners, to help grow our programs. We have lunch in the office — my favorite is a salad-plus-smoothie combo — and it's a really wonderful time to connect with the team. Most of Griswold's workday consists of meetings. Gabriela Hasbun for BI I also love connecting with our Lean In community. One thing we're focused on is closing early gender gaps in AI usage. Our flagship program, Circles, consists of groups of 8 to 12 women who meet regularly to support each other in their careers — we have over 170,000 members. It's a perfect forum to hold each other accountable for upskilling in AI . Every week, I send AI tips to our network leaders. A recent one encouraged the use of AI notetakers , as women are more likely to take notes during meetings and miss out on participating. Lean In is in over 180 countries, and it's really heartwarming to see that our commitment to our mission has a positive impact on women's careers. Getting to speak with them is really energizing and rewarding. I rehearse for meetings by talking to myself on walks Another habit of mine I've been told is weird is how I prepare for big meetings . If I have a presentation or interview coming up, I'll set up a Zoom and practice speaking to myself. Talking for a long time is sort of an unnatural act, and the first time you do it is probably not going to be your best. Sometimes, I'll even go on a walk and wear headphones, pretending like I'm in a meeting or on a phone call, but I'm actually talking to myself and practicing. When there's a bug, I usually fix the code myself Because of my background in computer science, I spend a lot of my time finding bugs or things I believe we should change on our platform. I'll code and fix those on my own. Thankfully, with AI , it's so much faster to code now than it was a few years ago. Our team is busy, and my goal is to enable everyone to have as much impact and move as quickly as possible. If I can help unblock the tech team or resolve an issue rather than add it to their plate, I'm always more than happy to do so. I leave work around 6 p.m. I continue to work until I go to bed pretty much every night. It's nice to have that time at home , when I'm not running around between meetings, to focus, give feedback on documents the team has sent, write, respond to emails, and brainstorm my own ideas. I take breaks to tidy up my apartment and make dinner. Living in New York got me out of the habit of cooking, so I'm taking the initiative to cook more meals, like rice bowls. I would say about half the time I order takeout, like pho, and the other half I cook, which is progress for me. Griswold continues working when she gets home, catching up on more deep work when she doesn't have meetings. Gabriela Hasbun for BI If my work doesn't require intense focus, I'll do it from the couch and put a happy TV show on, which right now is "Schitt's Creek." I think it's a nice balance between relaxation and getting things done. I usually get in bed around 10:30 p.m. I've been trying to make a habit of reading every night instead of going on my phone , which has been a really positive change. I like anything I read to be a distraction. I'm currently reading "Big Little Lies" and enjoying it. It's nice to spend 30 minutes reading something like fantasy that's completely different from what I think about at work. That way, I'm not spinning on all the things I need to do or coming up with new ideas that can't get done in my sleep anyway. Weekends are for the beach and farmers market My boyfriend works in Los Angeles and flies up to San Francisco every weekend. We've made a tradition of going to the Fort Mason Farmers Market on Sundays for fresh produce to cook an at-home meal that night. I also enjoy seeing friends over the weekend. My preference is to go on a long walk or go to the beach. I also enjoy fitting in some work — emails, deep-focus work, or reading — throughout the weekend. items.title: Top Anthropic engineer says Claude now writes 'literally all' her team's code
items.summary: Katelyn Lesse, head of platform engineering at Anthropic. Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic platform engineering head Katelyn Lesse said that Claude now writes all her team's code. Lesse shared ways that Claude Code has helped the company become more efficient. Anthropic nears an initial public offering at a potential $2 trillion valuation. A top Anthropic engineer says that Claude Code has already wiped out all human coding at one of the AI lab's central teams. Katelyn Lesse leads the AI startup's platform engineering group, which handles the company's core services, developer tools, and product infrastructure — it's essentially the engine room of Anthropic. Lesse said at Grafana Labs ' ObservabilityCON event on Tuesday that among her staff, which tallied 200 as of this summer, the era of human-written code is fully over. "When it comes to our team and how we're actually building and maintaining our systems, all of our code is written by Claude," Lesse said. "Like, literally all of it." Anthropic's heavy reliance on Claude Code has helped it remain relatively small, as it approaches an initial public offering that could value it at nearly $2 trillion. The company's revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of this year. Maintaining its lofty valuation may depend on selling more companies on the AI-first approach espoused by Lesse and other Anthropic leaders. Lesse said that people on her teams are still designing systems and verifications, and then offloading the actual coding to Claude. She said that when the company changed the programming language of a major codebase from Python to Rust, workers developed a way to verify the final product. "But the grunt work of building the pieces and actually monitoring the pieces and actually making sure that we felt good about it, that was agents all the way down," Lesse said. Lesse said Anthropic already lets agents fix tests autonomously, with no human interaction, and it's thinking about how staff can get comfortable with agents autonomously making changes to the actual codebase, given the improvements in AI models over the last year. "As engineering leaders, we're like terrified, and we're like, let's be really careful about this, but I think the line is starting to push," Lesse said. Anthropic has also embraced Claude Code companywide. It released a report last week saying that as AI agents have worked more inside the company, it has hired for a smaller share of junior technical positions. And in May, Anthropic said that Claude then wrote more than 80% of the entire company's production code. Have a tip? items.title: Anthropic Opens Claude Duet AI Agent Preview for US Pro and Max Subscribers
items.summary: Anthropic opened a research preview of Claude Duet on October 21, introducing an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that monitors work, prioritises tasks and carries out business activities in the background. Access is initially limited to subscribers in the US on Claude Pro and Max plans through a waitlist, the company said. “We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track,” Anthropic said in its announcement. Available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, as well as through claude.ai, Claude Duet is built around the company’s Claude Opus 5.5 model . According to Anthropic, it prepares a morning briefing based on connected applications and sends notifications when it identifies something requiring attention. The agent can schedule meetings, draft emails, build dashboards, prepare financial and sales forecasts, develop prototypes and create web applications. It can also connect with more than 6,000 tools through the Claude Marketplace, including Gmail, Slack, QuickBooks and HubSpot, the company said. Claude Duet uses a virtual machine with its own browser so it can keep working when users step away from their devices. It checks connected accounts every few hours and sends updates when tasks are complete or require review. The agent also carries over existing memory, skills and connected apps from a user's Claude account. Anthropic said Claude Duet prepares work independently but requires approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents or deleting information. Securities trading and transfers between accounts remain prohibited, even with user approval. The company said Duet does not directly access users’ passwords or sign-in tokens. It also uses safeguards designed to detect prompt injection, in which malicious instructions embedded in content attempt to manipulate an AI system. The AI company said a dedicated classifier and safety prompt are designed to block requests to share highly sensitive information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Users can share health and personal financial information when they explicitly instruct the agent to send it. These are the company’s stated safeguards, and Anthropic said it continues to develop them. Anthropic said early testers have used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support and marketing. Amin Ebrahimi, owner of Shahs of Kabob, a South Florida restaurant business with about 110 employees, used the agent to work through invoices across stores. “It brings it all together,” Ebrahimi said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.” The research preview shares usage limits with the rest of Claude, with background checks and complex tasks counting towards those limits. Anthropic acknowledged that Duet may misread conversations or misjudge urgency, while its capabilities for personal errands such as booking tickets remain less developed.

Anthropic opened a research preview of Claude Duet on October 21, introducing an artificial intelligence (AI) agent that monitors work, prioritises tasks and carries out business activities in the background. Access is initially limited to subscribers in the US on Claude Pro and Max plans through a waitlist, the company said.

“We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track,” Anthropic said in its announcement.

Available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, as well as through claude.ai, Claude Duet is built around the company’s Claude Opus 5.5 model. According to Anthropic, it prepares a morning briefing based on connected applications and sends notifications when it identifies something requiring attention.

The agent can schedule meetings, draft emails, build dashboards, prepare financial and sales forecasts, develop prototypes and create web applications. It can also connect with more than 6,000 tools through the Claude Marketplace, including Gmail, Slack, QuickBooks and HubSpot, the company said.

Claude Duet uses a virtual machine with its own browser so it can keep working when users step away from their devices. It checks connected accounts every few hours and sends updates when tasks are complete or require review. The agent also carries over existing memory, skills and connected apps from a user's Claude account.

Anthropic said Claude Duet prepares work independently but requires approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents or deleting information. Securities trading and transfers between accounts remain prohibited, even with user approval.

The company said Duet does not directly access users’ passwords or sign-in tokens. It also uses safeguards designed to detect prompt injection, in which malicious instructions embedded in content attempt to manipulate an AI system.

The AI company said a dedicated classifier and safety prompt are designed to block requests to share highly sensitive information, including credit card numbers and government identification. 

Users can share health and personal financial information when they explicitly instruct the agent to send it. These are the company’s stated safeguards, and Anthropic said it continues to develop them.

Anthropic said early testers have used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support and marketing. Amin Ebrahimi, owner of Shahs of Kabob, a South Florida restaurant business with about 110 employees, used the agent to work through invoices across stores.

“It brings it all together,” Ebrahimi said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”

The research preview shares usage limits with the rest of Claude, with background checks and complex tasks counting towards those limits. 

Anthropic acknowledged that Duet may misread conversations or misjudge urgency, while its capabilities for personal errands such as booking tickets remain less developed.

items.title: Mistral boss and Yann LeCun back Swiss robotics startup Enact in $30M pre-seed round
items.summary: Swiss robotics startup Enact Intelligence has today emerged out of stealth, with a $30m pre-seed round and backing from two heavyweights from the French AI ecosystem, Mistral boss Arthur Mensch and Meta's former AI chief scientist Yann LeCun. The $30m funding is high for a pre-seed funding round and comes as investors continue to invest heavily in robotics. Enact is building the underlying technology for general purpose robots. It says it’s developing tech that enables robots to manipulate objects with greater accuracy by sensing force and touch, as it looks to make robots carry out work in industrial settings and in the real world. Its approach is different to those robotics companies which rely on cameras and visuals. Manuel Yves Galliker, its CEO and co-founder, who previously worked at the hot US robotics startup Physical Intelligence, said: “In particular, our robots sense force and touch through their own actuators, so they feel what’s happening in real time, and learn more data-efficiently while simultaneously pushing reliability and performance. A technology that works across every form factor, built for real-world deployment from day one." Investors in the round include Redalpine, Notion Capital and Firstminute Capital, with angel investors including Mensch, LeCun and Hugging Face’s Thomas Wolf. The startup is using the funds to expand the team and accelerate its hardware and R&D development. The CEO added: “We’re rethinking the full stack, from model architectures enabling multi-frequency and multi-scale intelligence, to the data pipelines all the way down to the actuators and sensors that feed the model.”

items.title: Premji Invest, Norwest and Lok Capital Plan Up to ₹1,000 Crore Investment in Vegafin: Report
items.summary: Azim Premji’s investment firm Premji Invest, along with Norwest and Lok Capital, plans to invest up to ₹1,000 crore in Vegafin Capital to build an artificial intelligence-led lending platform for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), according to a Bloomberg report published on October 21. Vegafin, founded by former ICICI Bank executive Bijith Bhaskar, has signed definitive agreements to acquire a majority stake in Gurugram-based non-banking financial company (NBFC) Bizloan. The acquisition remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. Vegafin plans to use AI-driven underwriting, digital workflows and data-based credit assessments to evaluate borrowers. The company says the platform aims to improve lending decisions , reduce processing times and operating costs, and expand access to credit for underserved MSMEs. Bizloan operates across five states through more than 35 branches and manages over ₹ 235 crore in assets under management (AUM). Founded in 2018 by Rahul Jain, Abhishek Mishra and Vikram Diwan, the NBFC focuses on secured lending to small businesses. Bhaskar said in the company announcement, “Our ambition is to leverage AI and harness data from multiple sources to develop deeper insights into MSME businesses, enabling faster, granular and accurate assessment of credit risk.” Bizloan’s existing investors include the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, Mohan Enterprises and BLinC Invest. Mohan Enterprises and the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation will exit following the transaction, while BLinC Invest will remain invested. EY Investment Banking acted as the exclusive financial adviser on the transaction.

items.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
items.summary: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip. And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade. A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more. “You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention. Matching storage to the AI data life cycle Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer. This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage What this means for how AI gets budgeted For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators. Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished. A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand. Building for economically scalable capacity Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it. What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives. Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales. There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget: What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it? Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing? If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse? Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after. This content was produced by WD. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

items.title: Cloudflare Deployed php2shell Protection Hours Before Disclosure. Here’s What the Head Start Doesn’t Cover
items.summary: Two flaws in PHP can hand an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution, and PHP says a demonstrated attack on Apache with mod_php fires before the website’s own code runs. Cloudflare switched on default protection against both at 03:02 UTC on October 21, about nine hours before public disclosure by its own count. The head start mattered, and it still leaves gaps that no firewall rule can close. What php2shell Is php2shell is the name for two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale by PHP’s security team. In the first, PHP runs out of memory partway through a request and leaves some internal data uninitialized, and request cleanup may then treat that data as valid. In the second, internal state from one request can outlive the memory behind it, and a later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before PHP resets it. Cloudflare says the flaws may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution and data exposure. PHP says all installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, and it considers the risk highest for mod_php. The advisory for the first flaw adds that no complete exploit has been demonstrated against PHP-FPM, and its CVSS vector rates attack complexity as high. The PHP Foundation said its security team did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release, although proof-of-concept code had begun to circulate. Cloudflare says Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed the flaws. Wiz says it reported its findings to PHP on August 24, that PHP acknowledged them on September 21, and that AI models helped throughout the research. PHP shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Cloudflare says the flaws affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. W3Techs puts PHP at 69.3 percent of the websites whose server-side language it can identify, as of October 22, and Cloudflare names WordPress and Magento among the platforms that depend on it. Why a WAF Has to Read the Response An application cannot defend itself against these flaws. Datadog’s reproduction used an unauthenticated POST request that never reached application code, so application-level authentication does not block it. A firewall in front of the server is one of the few places to intervene before patching, but request inspection has limits. PHP’s advisories list multipart techniques among the known ways to trigger the out-of-memory condition and name session upload progress, which is enabled by default, as a trigger for the second flaw. Cloudflare says request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. Cloudflare’s answer is full transaction detection, which it described in a companion post the same day. The capability evaluates a request together with the origin’s response, and when a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections Cloudflare has released with it. The companion post’s example is a path traversal request for a database configuration file: request inspection can recognize the attempt, but the request alone cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. The response is where that answer shows up. The design has a limit that Cloudflare states itself. A response rule cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The implication is that response inspection protects data leaving the server better than it protects the server. Imperva describes one php2shell technique that returns about 67 KB of server memory in a Set-Cookie header carrying the session ID, the kind of leak response-side detection targets. Code that has already run on the origin is another matter. Cloudflare has not published what its php2shell signatures look for, so any link between them and that leak is inference. What Each Plan Gets Cloudflare says free and paid WAF customers were protected by default from 03:02 UTC on October 21. Free customers need to do nothing, because the rules sit in the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset. Professional, Business and Enterprise customers get seven rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, and Cloudflare asks them to review the deployment and confirm it runs in block mode. Every plan, free included, also gets a response-side rule in the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset that blocks high-confidence signatures by default. The labels are generic. The rules read “Anomalous Execution” followed by a number from one to seven, with no mention of PHP or the CVEs. Cloudflare’s post says the rule descriptions will be updated soon and lists the rule IDs so teams can filter matches under Security Analytics. Until the labels change, a security team scanning its dashboard cannot tell from the names which rules cover php2shell. The Clock Started Before Disclosure The sequence matters. CVE identifiers began circulating online around 15:00 UTC on October 20 with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0, according to the PHP Foundation, which says no technical details had leaked. PHP posted an advance notice at 19:33 UTC and moved its release up from October 22 to 14:00 UTC on October 21. The foundation adds that Calif then accidentally published a video of its proof of concept, which helped others develop their own proof-of-concept code faster. Cloudflare’s rules went live at 03:02 UTC on October 21. Cloudflare counts its lead as about nine hours, but PHP’s release landed at 14:00 UTC, which makes the gap closer to eleven. Cloudflare says it had been developing protections since early October, working with the PHP Foundation, OpenAI, Wiz and others. It was not the only vendor with early notice. PHP says Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, and Imperva says the researchers briefed it confidentially before disclosure and that its Cloud WAF customers are protected out of the box. Attackers did not wait for the leak. Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that its MadPot honeypot logged an exploitation attempt dated October 17, four days before disclosure, and said it remains unclear how the actor obtained exploit information. Cloudflare says it observed attack traffic against its customers and saw attackers mutating payloads to get around its rules, though it published no counts. Vendors describe attempts more than successes. watchTowr said on October 21 that it was observing active exploitation attempts against both flaws and did not say any succeeded. Amazon says php2shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild, while also saying it is unclear whether the attempts it saw would succeed on real systems. The Hacker News reported that no source had confirmed a successful break-in of a specific server as of its October 21 update. For an unpatched server outside Cloudflare’s protection, the earliest known attack attempt predates disclosure by four days, and Amazon’s guidance reflects that: start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. Patching Is Still the Only Complete Fix Cloudflare says plainly that customers should patch PHP even with the WAF in place, and it describes its rules as an additional layer of defense in depth. The flaws sit in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or plugins does not fix them, and customers on managed hosting should ask their provider to apply the security update. PHP’s release notes say there are no complete mitigations and that updating is the only safe choice. A WAF also inspects only the traffic routed through it, so an origin server reachable by another route gets no cover. Patching carries its own friction. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the project, and 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, the security team provided minimal source backports for people building from source or without an LTS vendor. Laravel Forge warned customers that its automatic security updates do not patch PHP, because Forge installs PHP from a dedicated package repository outside Ubuntu’s own security channel. Long-running processes such as queue workers keep the old PHP until someone restarts them. What Operators Should Take From It The signal worth watching is the response side. Cloudflare says it will expand coverage over time to include detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals, which suggests its managed rules are moving from judging requests toward judging what servers send back. php2shell fits that pattern, because on the memory-disclosure path the evidence shows up in the reply. The implication for operators is straightforward. Inventory every PHP version in production, patch the supported branches, plan a move off 8.1 and earlier, and restart long-running workers after the update. Amazon also advises searching form-upload POST requests for the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and checking servers for unexpected process execution or file changes. The WAF lowers the odds while that work happens, and Cloudflare itself says attackers are already reshaping their payloads against it. Any similar runtime flaw will test the same arrangement: vendors with advance notice, a leak that shrinks the window, and customers who still have to do the patching. Clearer rule names and published attack counts would let those customers judge how much time a head start bought them.
items.summary_html:
Two flaws in PHP can hand an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution, and PHP says a demonstrated attack on Apache with mod_php fires before the website’s own code runs. Cloudflare switched on default protection against both at 03:02 UTC on October 21, about nine hours before public disclosure by its own count. The head start mattered, and it still leaves gaps that no firewall rule can close.

What php2shell Is

php2shell is the name for two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale by PHP’s security team. In the first, PHP runs out of memory partway through a request and leaves some internal data uninitialized, and request cleanup may then treat that data as valid. In the second, internal state from one request can outlive the memory behind it, and a later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before PHP resets it. Cloudflare says the flaws may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution and data exposure.

PHP says all installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, and it considers the risk highest for mod_php. The advisory for the first flaw adds that no complete exploit has been demonstrated against PHP-FPM, and its CVSS vector rates attack complexity as high. The PHP Foundation said its security team did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release, although proof-of-concept code had begun to circulate.

Cloudflare says Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed the flaws. Wiz says it reported its findings to PHP on August 24, that PHP acknowledged them on September 21, and that AI models helped throughout the research. PHP shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Cloudflare says the flaws affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. W3Techs puts PHP at 69.3 percent of the websites whose server-side language it can identify, as of October 22, and Cloudflare names WordPress and Magento among the platforms that depend on it.

Why a WAF Has to Read the Response

An application cannot defend itself against these flaws. Datadog’s reproduction used an unauthenticated POST request that never reached application code, so application-level authentication does not block it. A firewall in front of the server is one of the few places to intervene before patching, but request inspection has limits. PHP’s advisories list multipart techniques among the known ways to trigger the out-of-memory condition and name session upload progress, which is enabled by default, as a trigger for the second flaw. Cloudflare says request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic.

Cloudflare’s answer is full transaction detection, which it described in a companion post the same day. The capability evaluates a request together with the origin’s response, and when a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections Cloudflare has released with it. The companion post’s example is a path traversal request for a database configuration file: request inspection can recognize the attempt, but the request alone cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. The response is where that answer shows up.

The design has a limit that Cloudflare states itself. A response rule cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The implication is that response inspection protects data leaving the server better than it protects the server. Imperva describes one php2shell technique that returns about 67 KB of server memory in a Set-Cookie header carrying the session ID, the kind of leak response-side detection targets. Code that has already run on the origin is another matter. Cloudflare has not published what its php2shell signatures look for, so any link between them and that leak is inference.

What Each Plan Gets

Cloudflare says free and paid WAF customers were protected by default from 03:02 UTC on October 21. Free customers need to do nothing, because the rules sit in the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset. Professional, Business and Enterprise customers get seven rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, and Cloudflare asks them to review the deployment and confirm it runs in block mode. Every plan, free included, also gets a response-side rule in the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset that blocks high-confidence signatures by default.

The labels are generic. The rules read “Anomalous Execution” followed by a number from one to seven, with no mention of PHP or the CVEs. Cloudflare’s post says the rule descriptions will be updated soon and lists the rule IDs so teams can filter matches under Security Analytics. Until the labels change, a security team scanning its dashboard cannot tell from the names which rules cover php2shell.

The Clock Started Before Disclosure

The sequence matters. CVE identifiers began circulating online around 15:00 UTC on October 20 with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0, according to the PHP Foundation, which says no technical details had leaked. PHP posted an advance notice at 19:33 UTC and moved its release up from October 22 to 14:00 UTC on October 21. The foundation adds that Calif then accidentally published a video of its proof of concept, which helped others develop their own proof-of-concept code faster.

Cloudflare’s rules went live at 03:02 UTC on October 21. Cloudflare counts its lead as about nine hours, but PHP’s release landed at 14:00 UTC, which makes the gap closer to eleven. Cloudflare says it had been developing protections since early October, working with the PHP Foundation, OpenAI, Wiz and others. It was not the only vendor with early notice. PHP says Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, and Imperva says the researchers briefed it confidentially before disclosure and that its Cloud WAF customers are protected out of the box.

Attackers did not wait for the leak. Amazon Threat Intelligence reported that its MadPot honeypot logged an exploitation attempt dated October 17, four days before disclosure, and said it remains unclear how the actor obtained exploit information. Cloudflare says it observed attack traffic against its customers and saw attackers mutating payloads to get around its rules, though it published no counts.

Vendors describe attempts more than successes. watchTowr said on October 21 that it was observing active exploitation attempts against both flaws and did not say any succeeded. Amazon says php2shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild, while also saying it is unclear whether the attempts it saw would succeed on real systems. The Hacker News reported that no source had confirmed a successful break-in of a specific server as of its October 21 update. For an unpatched server outside Cloudflare’s protection, the earliest known attack attempt predates disclosure by four days, and Amazon’s guidance reflects that: start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date.

Patching Is Still the Only Complete Fix

Cloudflare says plainly that customers should patch PHP even with the WAF in place, and it describes its rules as an additional layer of defense in depth. The flaws sit in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or plugins does not fix them, and customers on managed hosting should ask their provider to apply the security update. PHP’s release notes say there are no complete mitigations and that updating is the only safe choice. A WAF also inspects only the traffic routed through it, so an origin server reachable by another route gets no cover.

Patching carries its own friction. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the project, and 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, the security team provided minimal source backports for people building from source or without an LTS vendor.

Laravel Forge warned customers that its automatic security updates do not patch PHP, because Forge installs PHP from a dedicated package repository outside Ubuntu’s own security channel. Long-running processes such as queue workers keep the old PHP until someone restarts them.

What Operators Should Take From It

The signal worth watching is the response side. Cloudflare says it will expand coverage over time to include detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals, which suggests its managed rules are moving from judging requests toward judging what servers send back. php2shell fits that pattern, because on the memory-disclosure path the evidence shows up in the reply.

The implication for operators is straightforward. Inventory every PHP version in production, patch the supported branches, plan a move off 8.1 and earlier, and restart long-running workers after the update. Amazon also advises searching form-upload POST requests for the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and checking servers for unexpected process execution or file changes. The WAF lowers the odds while that work happens, and Cloudflare itself says attackers are already reshaping their payloads against it.

Any similar runtime flaw will test the same arrangement: vendors with advance notice, a leak that shrinks the window, and customers who still have to do the patching. Clearer rule names and published attack counts would let those customers judge how much time a head start bought them.
