items.title: IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation
items.summary: IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes. Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended). Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER. Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean. Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work? The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B? Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms. Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets. Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks? On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. & How does it compare with other open ASR models? items.summary_html:
IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B, a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models: the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts.

TL;DR
  • Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes.
  • Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended).
  • Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER.
  • Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean.
  • Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set.
How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work?

The model has 3 parts, per the model card. A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks.

A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz.

The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base. IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters.

Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs.

What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B?
  • Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription.
  • Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms.
  • Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets.
  • Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones.
How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks?

On the Open ASR Leaderboard, IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%.

Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only.

Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set.

On the noisy FFASR leaderboard, it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there.

Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%.

For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated.

Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8.

&

How does it compare with other open ASR models? FeatureGranite Speech 5.0 2BQwen3-ASR-1.7BCohere Transcribe 03-2026Canary-Qwen-2.5BSize2B2.35B (Hub count)2.07B (Hub count)2.5BLicenseApache 2.0Apache 2.0Apache 2.0 (gated)CC-BY-4.0ASR languages630 + 22 Chinese dialects14English onlySpeech translationYesNot disclosedNot disclosedNoOpen ASR avg WER (Oct 21, 2026)*5.68%5.40%5.77%5.94%FFASR avg WER (Oct 18, 2026)*14.80%13.41%15.03%Not disclosedKeyword biasingUp to 2,000 termsNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedLong audio~2 min segmentsLong audio supportedNot disclosed40 s max in training

*Leaderboard averages as charted in IBM’s model card from the Open ASR and FFASR leaderboards.

What changed in Turbo CTC and 4.1 2B Plus?

Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC keeps its 470M footprint. It now transcribes 7 languages with native punctuation and capitalization. IBM compiled one Conformer block and reused its graph across the stack. That lifted throughput to 19,870 RTFx, up from about 12,600 at launch.

The updated Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus is a drop-in weight update. Average timestamp shift falls from 210.86 to 98.54. Long-form WER drops from 13.53 to 10.22. Biased-keyword WER falls from 11.79 to 6.48.

How can developers deploy it?

Granite Speech 5.0 2B runs in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp and mlx-audio. For GGUF, IBM recommends Q8_0. Lower-bit quantizations lose accuracy on audio longer than about 1 minute.

Key Takeaways
  • #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard at 5.68% WER.
  • 2B parameters, Apache 2.0, runs on GPU, Mac and local CPU.
  • 2,000-term keyword biasing across all supported languages.
  • Turbo CTC reaches 19,870 RTFx and now covers 7 languages.
  • Qwen3-ASR-1.7B still leads on accuracy and noisy audio.

Check out the model card, IBM blog and Granite Speech paper. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: The "Green AI" Crisis & Sustainable Infrastructure
items.summary: AI got far more efficient per query while its total footprint hit records. Google measured a 33x drop in energy per prompt, down to 0.24 Wh for a median text prompt, then reported an 18% rise in emissions and a 34% rise in water use. Both are true, because "energy per prompt" is the wrong unit: it is a text-only median, it says nothing about volume, and it mostly misses the hardware manufacturing behind new data centres. Globally AI is still a small share of electricity, around 0.5%, but it is growing very fast and landing on specific grids and watersheds, which is where the real crisis is. The most convincing engineering response is running less model: small, purpose-built models by default, with a large model only when the task needs it. That helps only if the savings are not immediately spent on more usage, which is what has happened so far. Read All

items.title: Cart recovery by voice: suppress purchased carts and measure incremental orders
items.summary: Originally published as a Fonix.AI practical guide by AntEngage. This republication uses the same guide content. Recover the unanswered question behind checkout AI abandoned cart recovery calls can help a D2C team understand why an eligible shopper left checkout and offer an approved next step. The aim is to resolve a question or obstacle, then verify whether an order followed. A promise to purchase, a sent link and a paid order are different outcomes. Cart recovery happens before a completed order. COD confirmation verifies an existing order before dispatch; NDR calling addresses a shipment after failed delivery. Keeping those states separate prevents the wrong call from reaching a customer. Fonix.AI provides business voice conversations in Indian languages. Use this guide to evaluate a cart workflow against your store and contact policies. Store events, checkout links and product lookups require confirmed deployment connections; this page does not imply a native ecommerce plugin. Recheck the cart immediately before contact An abandoned-checkout event records what was true at a particular time. By the time a queued call runs, the shopper may have purchased on another device, changed the cart or contacted your support team. Preserve the checkout reference, event time, store, contact preference and allowed outreach window. Read the latest checkout and related order state before calling. Suppress completed purchases, superseded checkouts and records that are no longer eligible under your policy. Do not treat an identical telephone number as sufficient proof that two carts belong to the same person. Decide how your store resolves checkout identity and avoid revealing another shopper's items. Keep only the context needed for the assistance task. If the store cannot provide a current result, hold the call or route the record for review. Repeating a stale discount or asking someone to buy an order they already paid for creates avoidable confusion. Figure 01. Keep event history. Suppress outreach when the order is complete. Find the blocker before offering a remedy Start with permission to discuss the unfinished checkout. Ask whether help would be useful. The shopper might be comparing products, checking delivery coverage, looking for a payment option or simply choosing not to buy. Shopper's question Source needed Appropriate next step Is this size available? Current variant inventory Explain the available choice without reserving unheld stock Does delivery reach my postcode? Approved serviceability lookup Confirm current coverage or route uncertainty Can I pay on delivery? Store's payment and cart rules Explain the applicable option Is the offer still valid? Current offer conditions Quote the approved terms, not a remembered campaign Can I change the item? Current catalogue and checkout capability Help with an allowed change or send the request to support I do not want to order No sales inference required End the recovery flow and honour the preference Avoid inventing scarcity, delivery dates or discounts to secure a commitment. When a question needs expertise or a store decision, hand it to the right person with the exact product and question attached. Regional language tests should include sizes, colours, quantities, prices and corrections. “One blue, not two black” changes the order. Review the final checkout state against the conversation rather than scoring fluency alone. Keep link delivery and order completion separate A checkout link should point to the store's approved destination and current cart. Define who can create or retrieve it, how long it remains usable and what happens if the contents change. Never ask the caller to disclose payment credentials to complete a purchase. If a message is configured, record whether it was requested, sent and delivered using the evidence your messaging system supplies. Do not announce delivery simply because a send request was accepted. Recheck the order state before scheduling another follow-up. Once an order exists, move to its appropriate post-order workflow instead of continuing cart recovery. A retried event should not create another recovery sequence for the same checkout. Agree on the attribution window before the pilot. A shopper who purchases several days later through another channel may be relevant to the cohort, but the call cannot automatically take credit for every subsequent order. An illustrative recovery conversation Assume a fictional store has confirmed that the checkout is still open and the requested payment option is currently available. Assistant: Hello, this is the automated assistant for Willow Store. Would you like help with the checkout you started? Shopper: Payment nahi hua. I was checking if COD is available for this address. Assistant: I can check the approved delivery and payment options. Which postcode should I use for this checkout? Shopper: The saved address is correct. Also one medium, not large. Assistant: I have noted medium as your requested size. I will check its availability and the payment option before sending a checkout link. The record should keep the payment question and size correction distinct. A link should not preserve the old size. If changing the cart requires staff action, record the request for review rather than say it was updated. Suggested outcome fields include checkout reference, current cart version, eligibility result, blocker, approved answer source, change request, link status, follow-up preference and verified order reference. Originally published as a Fonix.AI practical guide by AntEngage. This republication uses the same guide content.

Recover the unanswered question behind checkout

AI abandoned cart recovery calls can help a D2C team understand why an eligible shopper left checkout and offer an approved next step. The aim is to resolve a question or obstacle, then verify whether an order followed. A promise to purchase, a sent link and a paid order are different outcomes.

Cart recovery happens before a completed order. COD confirmation verifies an existing order before dispatch; NDR calling addresses a shipment after failed delivery. Keeping those states separate prevents the wrong call from reaching a customer.

Fonix.AI provides business voice conversations in Indian languages. Use this guide to evaluate a cart workflow against your store and contact policies. Store events, checkout links and product lookups require confirmed deployment connections; this page does not imply a native ecommerce plugin.

Recheck the cart immediately before contact

An abandoned-checkout event records what was true at a particular time. By the time a queued call runs, the shopper may have purchased on another device, changed the cart or contacted your support team.

Preserve the checkout reference, event time, store, contact preference and allowed outreach window. Read the latest checkout and related order state before calling. Suppress completed purchases, superseded checkouts and records that are no longer eligible under your policy.

Do not treat an identical telephone number as sufficient proof that two carts belong to the same person. Decide how your store resolves checkout identity and avoid revealing another shopper's items. Keep only the context needed for the assistance task.

If the store cannot provide a current result, hold the call or route the record for review. Repeating a stale discount or asking someone to buy an order they already paid for creates avoidable confusion.

Figure 01. Keep event history. Suppress outreach when the order is complete.

Find the blocker before offering a remedy

Start with permission to discuss the unfinished checkout. Ask whether help would be useful. The shopper might be comparing products, checking delivery coverage, looking for a payment option or simply choosing not to buy.

Shopper's question Source needed Appropriate next step Is this size available? Current variant inventory Explain the available choice without reserving unheld stock Does delivery reach my postcode? Approved serviceability lookup Confirm current coverage or route uncertainty Can I pay on delivery? Store's payment and cart rules Explain the applicable option Is the offer still valid? Current offer conditions Quote the approved terms, not a remembered campaign Can I change the item? Current catalogue and checkout capability Help with an allowed change or send the request to support I do not want to order No sales inference required End the recovery flow and honour the preference

Avoid inventing scarcity, delivery dates or discounts to secure a commitment. When a question needs expertise or a store decision, hand it to the right person with the exact product and question attached.

Regional language tests should include sizes, colours, quantities, prices and corrections. “One blue, not two black” changes the order. Review the final checkout state against the conversation rather than scoring fluency alone.

Keep link delivery and order completion separate

A checkout link should point to the store's approved destination and current cart. Define who can create or retrieve it, how long it remains usable and what happens if the contents change. Never ask the caller to disclose payment credentials to complete a purchase.

If a message is configured, record whether it was requested, sent and delivered using the evidence your messaging system supplies. Do not announce delivery simply because a send request was accepted.

Recheck the order state before scheduling another follow-up. Once an order exists, move to its appropriate post-order workflow instead of continuing cart recovery. A retried event should not create another recovery sequence for the same checkout.

Agree on the attribution window before the pilot. A shopper who purchases several days later through another channel may be relevant to the cohort, but the call cannot automatically take credit for every subsequent order.

An illustrative recovery conversation

Assume a fictional store has confirmed that the checkout is still open and the requested payment option is currently available.

Assistant: Hello, this is the automated assistant for Willow Store. Would you like help with the checkout you started?

Shopper: Payment nahi hua. I was checking if COD is available for this address.

Assistant: I can check the approved delivery and payment options. Which postcode should I use for this checkout?

Shopper: The saved address is correct. Also one medium, not large.

Assistant: I have noted medium as your requested size. I will check its availability and the payment option before sending a checkout link.

The record should keep the payment question and size correction distinct. A link should not preserve the old size. If changing the cart requires staff action, record the request for review rather than say it was updated.

Include calling, platform and follow-up costs in the evaluation. A recovered gross order value is not contribution margin. Review discounts, shipping, cancellations and returns using your own business data.

items.title: Agentic AI in Action, Part 31: Hands On with Temporary, Secure, and Personal Agents in Cortex
items.summary: A Hands On Guide to Temporary, Secure, and Personal Database Agents in Cortex What temporary, secure, and personal database agents actually do, plus the smaller COPY GRANTS change that rides along with them. Snowflake recently rolled out a set of Cortex Agents object enhancements, and they solve a set of small but real friction points that anyone building agents day to day will recognize. Three new capabilities matter most for practitioners. Temporary agents let you spin up a session scoped agent without touching the schema. Secure agents hide the specification from anyone who doesn’t own the object. Personal database agents give every user a private sandbox to build in, without needing a shared dev database and its grants. Worth walking through each one with a working example, all pointed at the same small semantic view, with a DESCRIBE AGENT after every creation so you can actually see what got built, not just take my word for it. Getting there takes a few short, separate steps, a database and warehouse, a table of sample data, a semantic view on top of it, then each of the four agent types in turn. Nothing here needs more than a couple of statements at a time. Step 1. Create the database, schema, and warehouse Everything in this post lives in one database and schema, my_db.my_schema, so there’s a single consistent name to follow rather than a different placeholder per section. Alongside it, create a small warehouse. If you would rather point at a warehouse you already have, skip the CREATE WAREHOUSE statement and swap my_wh for your own warehouse's name everywhere it appears further down. Step 2. Create the table and load sample data A dozen rows across three regions, four quarters, and two products, enough for an agent to answer a real aggregation question rather than an empty one. Step 3. Create the semantic view A native Snowflake semantic view on top of SALES_FACT, with a region and quarter dimension and a TOTAL_REVENUE metric. This is what every tool bearing agent below actually queries against. Note: Every example below that uses a tool points at this same object, my_db.my_schema.sales_semantic_view. The unqualified agent names in the next two steps, my_temp_agent and my_secure_agent, assume the session is still sitting in my_db.my_schema from the USE statements in Step 1. Run each step’s statements in order in the same worksheet, or qualify the names yourself if you’re picking up a step on its own, the way the COPY GRANTS and Personal Database steps already do. Let us perform a sanity check. Note: We will ask the agent below “which region has the highest total revenue”, so the above check gives us this known-correct number, “503000" to compare against. Step 4. Temporary agents. Testing without object sprawl Most Cortex Agent development starts with a handful of experimental iterations. You are tweaking a semantic view binding, trying a different orchestration instruction, or testing whether a tool responds the way you expect. Before this release, each of those iterations created a permanent schema level object that someone eventually had to clean up. Temporary agents fix that. They exist only for the current session, are visible only to the creating user and role, and disappear automatically when the session ends. Creating one does not require the CREATE AGENT privilege on the schema. Let us go ahead and create one. Confirm the object exists and the semantic view binding is correct. DESCRIBE AGENT my_temp_agent; Close the session and the agent is gone anyway, nothing to drop, nothing left behind for someone else to find later and wonder whether it’s safe to delete. For a practice like ours, where developers are constantly prototyping agent configurations against client semantic models before anything goes to a shared dev environment, this removes a real source of clutter. I’d expect this to become the default mode for anything exploratory, with CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT reserved for what’s actually going into a demo or a client environment. Step 5. Run the temporary agent Creating the object is one step, actually asking it something is a separate one. DATA_AGENT_RUN’s raw output is a single JSON payload holding the entire orchestration trace, the tool call into Cortex Analyst, the semantic model context it was handed, the SQL it generated, the query result, the model’s internal reasoning, the final answer, and a list of suggested follow up questions, all as elements of a content array. The query above flattens content and pulls out the one element whose type is text, which is the agent’s actual answer. Running it against this sample data returns a single row. That figure checks out against the sample data, North America’s four rows sum to 125000 + 138000 + 98000 + 142000 = 503000, so the semantic view’s total_revenue metric is aggregating correctly. We had also verified this earlier when we ran a sanity check on the semantic view. If you want to see the SQL Cortex Analyst actually generated rather than just the answer, the same payload carries it a few levels deeper, in the tool_result element for system_execute_sql, under its sql field. No DROP AGENT needed. The object disappears automatically when the session ends, and it was never visible to any other user or role. Step 6. Secure agents. Hiding the specification, not the answer The second enhancement addresses a governance gap that shows up as soon as an agent’s configuration becomes something you don’t want every consumer to see. An agent specification can include orchestration instructions, tool bindings, and sometimes proprietary prompt engineering that took real effort to get right. Under the old model, anyone with USAGE on the agent could run DESCRIBE AGENT or GET_DDL and read the whole thing. Secure agents close that off, following the same model Snowflake already uses for secure views and secure functions. Run that DESCRIBE AGENT as the owner and you’ll see all eight columns filled in, including the full JSON in agent_spec. This is the one I'd flag hardest for client engagements. When we hand an agent over to a client's business users, we often don't want them accessing the orchestration instructions or the exact tool wiring, either because it's genuinely proprietary or because exposing it invites people to try to reverse engineer prompt behavior. SECURE gives us that separation without a second layer of custom access control. DESCRIBE AGENT my_secure_agent; Notice the agent_spec coulmn that provides the agent specific orchestration details. This is the one we will subsequently hide from other roles. Step 7. Grant to another role and confirm the specification is hidden Create a role (“test_role”, in this example) that has nothing to do with the agent’s ownership, grant it USAGE, and run DESCRIBE AGENT from there. By default this still comes back with the full agent_spec, because it defaults to USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL. If ACCOUNTADMIN is the role you’ve used throughout, turning secondary roles off removes ACCOUNTADMIN from that set and leaves test_role on its own, which is what actually triggers the redaction. Notice now that the agent_spec column returns empty, hiding all the configuration and orchestration instructions. That’s the whole behavior change, nothing else about how the agent runs or answers is different. GET_DDL omits the specification the same way, Snowsight’s agent_spec field returns NULL in its resource view, and stage reads through GET or LS now require OWNERSHIP rather than USAGE alone. Execution itself is untouched, the agent:run endpoint, DATA_AGENT_RUN, and any task invoking the agent still load the full specification internally, so end users see no change in how the agent answers. Let us now restore the role before proceeding to the next section. Step 8. Agents in Personal Databases. A sandbox that’s already yours Every Snowflake user already has a Personal Database, mostly used for scratch tables and one-off notebooks. This release extends that to agents. You can now create and run an agent directly in the PUBLIC schema of your own Personal Database, using nothing more than your own default privileges. Personal Database names follow the USER$ format, and the name needs to be in double quotes because of the special character. This example lives in its own location, and for simplicity we will point at sales_semantic_view, the same semantic view every other agent in this post uses, so it answers from the same sample data. Swap in your own username before running this. The DESCRIBE AGENT output (below) confirms it, database_name comes back USER$KRISHNAN, schema_name comes back PUBLIC, and owner also reads USER$KRISHNAN, the database and the owning role share the same name, since a Personal Database is owned by the user it belongs to. The object sits there, even though the semantic view it queries lives in my_db.my_schema. The practical benefit here is that it it removes a specific piece of setup friction. A developer who wants to try something persistent, something they intend to keep around past one session but don’t yet want to put in a shared schema, no longer needs someone to grant CREATE AGENT on a dev database first. Their Personal Database is already theirs. Step 9. Run the Personal Database agent Let us now run this. Same fully qualified agent name, and the same FLATTEN extraction pattern, with the same QUALIFY narrowing it to the last text element. The answer comes back grounded in Widget A and Widget B from SALES_FACT, as the agent, sitting in your own Personal Database, is querying the exact same semantic view as the temporary and secure agents above. Step 10. COPY GRANTS, worth a mention A smaller fourth change rides along with these three. CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT now supports COPY GRANTS, which preserves explicit privileges, other than OWNERSHIP, when an agent is replaced. To actually see this in action, create the agent, grant a second role USAGE on it, then replace it with COPY GRANTS. Let us first create an agent to grant, so there’s something to replace. We will grant usage to the test_role which we had previously created. Step 11. Replace the agent with COPY GRANTS Now replace it. Without COPY GRANTS, the GRANT above would need to be reissued, the replaced object starts with a clean grant slate otherwise. Anyone who has had to re-run a batch of GRANT statements after every CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT during iterative development will appreciate this one. Step 12. Confirm the replaced agent kept its grant Confirm that the granted role can call the agent. test_role gets back the same North America answer as Step 5. USAGE survived the replace without a single GRANT statement re-run. Where this fits Put together, these four changes describe a fairly clear intent from Snowflake. Temporary agents and Personal Database agents lower the friction of building and iterating. Secure agents and COPY GRANTS tighten up what happens once an agent is ready for production and needs to be shared, governed, and maintained without losing its access history. For our Cortex practice, the workflow this suggests is straightforward. Prototype with a temporary agent in a session, or a persistent one in your Personal Database if you want to come back to it. Once the configuration is solid, promote it into the shared schema as a secure agent, with COPY GRANTS, as required, carrying the access controls forward on every subsequent replace. It closes a real gap between prototyping and production that we would mostly been working around by hand until now. The code files for this blog can be accessed here. I share hands-on, implementation-focused perspectives on Generative & Agentic AI, LLMs, Snowflake and Cortex AI, translating advanced capabilities into practical, real-world analytics use cases. Do follow me on LinkedIn and Medium for more such insights. items.summary: The Hidden Treasure in Your Factory: (How to rescue “Dark Data” without investing thousands with local AI) Image created by GPT 5.6 luna. Manufacturing plants live in a constant duality. On one hand, they operate with latest state-of-the-art equipment seamlessly integrated into IoT ecosystems; on the other, they rely on very robust legacy machinery that has been running for years. However, this machinery remains isolated from the rest of the company’s systems. When improvement, automation, or monitoring plans are designed, these veteran machines are often left out of the budget. Why? Usually, because upgrading their proprietary software through the original manufacturer is expensive and can cost thousands of dollars. However, despite their low technological visibility, their impact on production remains incredibly high. These machines constantly generate reports and data. Understanding the trends and drifts of this data is highly useful for quality control, production, and maintenance tasks. The “Dark Data” Problem Technology consultancies refer to this as “Dark Data”. It is estimated that between 60% and 73% of enterprise data is never analyzed or is so unstructured that it provides no value. A 2020 IDC survey of 1,500 business leaders stated that 68% of available enterprise data goes unutilized (1) . The Hidden Treasure in Your Factory: (How to rescue “Dark Data” without investing thousands with local AI)Image created by GPT 5.6 luna.

Manufacturing plants live in a constant duality. On one hand, they operate with latest state-of-the-art equipment seamlessly integrated into IoT ecosystems; on the other, they rely on very robust legacy machinery that has been running for years. However, this machinery remains isolated from the rest of the company’s systems.

When improvement, automation, or monitoring plans are designed, these veteran machines are often left out of the budget. Why? Usually, because upgrading their proprietary software through the original manufacturer is expensive and can cost thousands of dollars. However, despite their low technological visibility, their impact on production remains incredibly high.

These machines constantly generate reports and data. Understanding the trends and drifts of this data is highly useful for quality control, production, and maintenance tasks.

The “Dark Data” Problem

Technology consultancies refer to this as “Dark Data”. It is estimated that between 60% and 73% of enterprise data is never analyzed or is so unstructured that it provides no value. A 2020 IDC survey of 1,500 business leaders stated that 68% of available enterprise data goes unutilized (1).

Reliable sources such as Seagate, Forrester, or Forbes have spoken openly on the subject, and numerous companies offer solutions that are technologically advanced and reliable, but also expensive to implement.

All this data remains on local servers or gets trapped in PDF reports that nobody has the time to structure and study.

These reports contain critical information for maintenance, production and quality teams:

  • Average batch values: Critical for tracking product quality over time.
  • Working parameters: Trends indicating component wear and tear.
  • Processing times, alarms, and stops: Fundamental for calculating real productivity.
The Challenge of Connectivity and Structuring

Veteran equipment runs on reliable software inside its closed environment. However, the cost of updating the software and connectivity with the rest of the plant’s tools, together with the hours of downtime that it implies, means that it remains isolated.

If you’re lucky, your proprietary software will allow you to export (or read) data to a CSV file before printing the PDF report, allowing a Python script to process the data at almost no cost.

Unfortunately, the standard output is a PDF report that gets reviewed by production and quality teams, before being archived in a folder. These PDFs contain the fundamental data about product quality, working variables, alarms, and process times.

Depending on the batch duration, the number of alarms, or operator modifications, the structure of these PDFs varies wildly. Extracting reliable data from them using traditional software (like standard OCR) is a nightmare. A slightly shifted table, an unexpected page break, different text length, or an unforeseen value will change the format and generate extraction problems.

The result is known: thousands of reports stored on local servers and computers. Companies do not usually have the resources to save and analize all this data manually.

The Solution: Local Artificial Intelligence

Generative AI has changed the rules of the industrial game and provides the “low-cost” solution. A Python script backed by an open-source Large Language Model (LLM) can run 100% locally and privately on a standard computer, recovering all data and exporting it to an updated Excel sheet daily.

The AI can understands the technical context. It can differentiate between values measured in the same units, understand abbreviations, and avoid confusing concepts.

Fig. 1: Examples of fictional unstructured reports. Some of the challenges posed to the extraction system are highlighted.How It Works Under the Hood (The Python Implementation)

To prove this isn’t just theory, I generated 20 fake, unstructured PDF reports featuring different layouts, abbreviations, semantic traps (like confusing “compression pressure” with “pre-compression pressure”), and mixed units. All with the intention of confusing the AI and generating the worst-case scenario (fig. 1).

I built a Python script that uses Llama 3.1 (8B) running entirely locally via Ollama, meaning no factory data ever leaves the plant. All PDF reports should be exported to a folder or computer outside the equipment to prevent failures that affect production. Here are the four technical pillars that make this extraction possible:

  1. Connecting to the Local AI. Instead of paying for cloud APIs, I decide to use the standard OpenAI Python library to connect to our local Ollama server, avoiding costs and exposing our data to the cloud. Ollama can run without GPU, if you use lightweight models, running perfectly on a standard CPU. All tests were run in a standard personal computer (my own laptop).
from openai import OpenAI
# Pointing to the local Ollama instance
client = OpenAI(
    api_key="local", 
    base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1" 
)

2. Extracting text while preserving spatial relationship. Traditional PDF extractors scramble columns of text. Tests performed with pypdf2 work very well on reports that contain only text, but they generate extraction problems if the reports contain tables. Using pdfplumber with the layout=True parameter provides the solution. It preserves the physical spacing of the document, ensuring the AI can understand the structure of the report.

import pdfplumber

def extract_text_pdf(route_to_your_pdf):
    text = ""
    with pdfplumber.open(route_to_your_pdf) as pdf:
        for page in pdf.pages:
            # layout=True is key: it respects spacing between columns
            text_page = page.extract_text(layout=True)
            if text_page:
                text += text_page + "\n"
    return text

3. Forcing Strict JSON Output from the LLM. We need to avoid any kind of hallucination or made-up data. We don’t want a chat with an AI. We need the raw structured data as is found in the source. By setting the temperature=0.0 (eliminating hallucination) we reduce fabricated data data, and forcing a json_object response format, helps ensure the result follows the required structure.

import json

def process_text_with_ai(text):
    prompt = f"""
    Read the following pharmaceutical tablet compression report and extract:
    - Batch
    - Start Date / Time
    - End Date / Time
    -Etc
    
	Return ONLY a valid JSON object with these exact keys. If data is missing, output "Not found".
    Text: {text[:4000]}
    """
		
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama3.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        response_format={ "type": "json_object" },
        temperature=0.0  # Low temperature for precision
    )
    
    return json.loads(respuesta.choices[0].message.content)

4. Very Clear prompt to avoid errors. The model provides the information we ask for, just it is found in the reports. For example, it might return the same value but in a different format (250000 vs 250.000) or sometimes include a units, which can cause problems when writing the data to a file. Defining every detail in the prompt after testing is the only way to ensure a perfect output.

prompt = f"""
         Read the following pharmaceutical tablet compression report and extract:
    …..
    - Average weight (numeric value in mg, no units)  
    - Compression pressure (numeric value in kN, no units) 
    - Conforming units (format: 1958600) 
    - Alarms (literal text)
    
    Return ONLY a valid JSON object with these exact keys. If data is missing, output "Not found".
    Text: {texto[:4000]}
The Results: Revealing the Dark Data

The script processed the 20 unstructured PDFs with a 99.6% recovery rate. The 0.4% failure occurred when I intentionally omitted an end date, forcing the AI to estimate it. The recovery rate of the data inside the reports was 100% (fig. 2).

Fig. 2: ‘Raw’ data from the 20 fictional reports exported to Excel (Headers in Spanish from local test). 100% of the data contained in the reports was retrieved. The value in green does not appear in the report and was incorrectly inferred by the AI. The alarm list is complete, although the Excel spread sheet’s output format does not make this apparent.

By automating this reading process and generating structured formats (like Excel or SQL) (fig.3), factories instantly unlock three pillars of Industry 4.0 with virtually zero (or very little) hardware investment:

  • Real OEE Visibility: Extracting exact batch durations, real machine speeds and stops, and conforming units directly from the reports eliminates the bias of manual data entry. OEE can be analyzed at the end of the bath or day on machines that usually don’t have real-time OEE. Making it a metric instead of an estimation.
  • Long-Term Quality Control: Monitoring the trend of critical values across hundreds of batches reveals long-term trend deviations and prevents process drift.
  • Data-Driven Preventive Maintenance: The real treasure lies in the trend of working parameters. A slight increase in motor workload or pressure reveals component wear, allowing maintenance teams to intervene before a catastrophic stop in production.
Fig. 3: Structured data in an Excel spreadsheet for the 20 process reports. (Headers in Spanish from local test). Calculation of batch averages, parameters, and OEE based on process time and the number of conforming units. The positive and negative trends in the charts are due to deliberately generated data used to test the system.

Digitizing and extracting plant data does not always require replacing heavy machinery or high software and hardware update budgets. Sometimes, true innovation consists of using cutting-edge technology to finally listen to what our oldest machines have been trying to tell us in PDF format for years.

What Should Be the Next Step?

I asked myself what should be the next phase to improve this idea.

Firstly, automation: creating a script to automatically update the PDF reading of a file.

Secondly, I was thinking about using AI to generate a brief report of the extracted data, saving time on the everyday task of studying the data. I was on a break talking about the topic of Dark Data, when somebody said, “If nobody has time to recover the data, nobody will have time to study it.” As I heard that, it was clear that I had a new goal: the complete automation of the extraction, including an AI in charge of generating a brief report about the data.

Automation:

Most factory equipment runs on Windows. To create the automation process on Windows, we need to create a .bat file to automatically run our .py file.

Because it is necessary to run the Ollama server first on Windows, you have to include the instructions in the .bat file. Waiting a few seconds for it to fully load into RAM is necessary, and closing Ollama later avoids a waste of computer resources.

@echo off
echo Starting Ollama Server...
start /b ollama serve
echo Waiting to load AI...
timeout /t 5 /nobreak > nul

python "C:\path\to\your_file.py" :: Run your Python file here

echo Closing Ollama...
taskkill /F /IM ollama.exe /T > nul
echo task end

Later, you have to open the Task Scheduler from the Start menu. There, you can click “Create Basic Task”, name it as you wish, and choose “Daily” at your preferred time. In the “Action” step, select “Start a program” and point to your .bat file. Done.

To avoid processing the same files every day, the processed reports should be tracked in some way. I use a .txt file to store their names. Inside our .py file, we should include a function to check if the report has already been processed.

for file in stored_pdfs: 
    if file not in processed_files:
        # Process the file
Reporting the Data After Extraction

Before generating a report that summarizes the data, we need to pass it to our AI for analysis. But the data we write to Excel and keep in our program’s “memory” is raw data. In my original idea, the means, sums, and other calculations were done by the Excel file. However, the Excel file does not perform any calculations if it is not open.

It is possible to run these files without a graphical interface, but depending on the program you use on your computer (Microsoft Office, LibreOffice, OpenOffice) to open the .xlsx file, the instructions are very different. This makes it difficult to use the same script or method on different computers, complicating the deployment. I decided to do the math with Python as well, using the Numpy library.

I created a statistics.py file to handle the calculations. This file takes the raw data extracted by our Llama 3.1 stored in our .xlsx file's raw data sheet. It calculates the values that we will need (averages, means, OEE, others). Once it is done, it is sent back to our .xlsx file.

# sending data to the .xlsx file example

try:
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(excel_file)
    ws = wb["Statistical_Summary"]

    # Map values to specific cells 
    # Row 2: Total batches (B2)
    ws["B2"] = total_batches
    ws["C2"] = len(latest_10)

    # Row 3: Theoretical weight

    # Row 4: Average weight (mg)
    ws["B4"] = round(historical["weight"], 2)
    ws["C4"] = round(recent["weight"], 2)

No matter which program you choose to check your data, it will be avalaible there. Excel, or similar tool, can create charts and organize the data in a way that’s easy to understand. The file also sends a summary to our AI model, which uses it to generate the report.

# Return a text summary for DeepSeek to process
summary_for_ai = f”””
Comparison (historical: {total_batches} batches vs. the latest 10 batches):
- Average weight (mg): Historical={historical[‘weight’]:.2f} | Latest 10={recent[‘weight’]:.2f}
- Time loss (%): Historical={historical[‘time_loss’]:.2f} | Latest 10={recent[‘time_loss’]:.2f}
- Overall OEE: Historical={historical[‘oee’]:.2f}% | Latest 10={recent[‘oee’]:.2f}%
“””
return summary_for_ai

To generate the report, I decided to use a more “capable” model in reasoning: deepseek-r1:8b. We could use the same model for data extraction and report generation, but, honestly, I wanted to test switching between models on my computer for future projects.

We need generation, but the temperature must be low I use temperature=0.3. I added the new model and prompt to my .py script as a new function:

try:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-r1:8b", 
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.3
    )
except Exception as e: print(f"Error generating report: {e}")

The report will have only four points with trends and OEE compared with the historical data. One minute of reading time leaves no excuse for not knowing your data. The report is printed in the terminal as part of the execution, but it is stored as a .txt file to be read later. I decided not to create a new .txt report every day and store hundreds of reports again, because the data is already stored and can be managed inside the Excel file. When there is a new report, it overwrites the last one.

Fig. 4: Final report generated by Deepseek-r1 as show in the .txt report.Final Thoughts

AI technology is evolving very quickly. Today, it is possible to use agents to analyze different types of reports and data, prepare the data as you need, create a presentation, and email you a summary. It may not be a perfect solution, but I hope you find it useful.

items.title: I Fine-Tuned a Local Model to Match a Hosted Model.
items.summary: I Fine-Tuned a Local Model to Match a Hosted Model. Then My Experiment Stopped Replicating. (Laya Experiment Part 2) Fine-tuned on the same 11,010 human-reviewed pairs my production auditors learned from, a self-hosted Laya model reached the hosted model’s precision band on a second client’s real pipeline output. What it still missed was a family of rule-shaped matches, so I pre-registered a retrain to teach it six rules aimed at them. At one training seed, the rule text cost 21.9 points of recall on the frozen out-of-sample pool. A second seed of the same recipe gained 4.9 on the same pool. The experiment stopped replicating. Fine-tuning is real on this client’s data. The rules did not land. Part 1 The result that didn’t survive the next training run The best checkpoint on the second client’s data was sft_enhanced: Laya fine-tuned on the 11,010 reviewed pairs with the 980-token rubric. It reached the precision band of Jev, the hosted model Part 1 compared against. What it could not close was a family of misses shaped like named rules: color, brand, pack count, unit equivalence. The pre-registered next step was to retrain from the base checkpoint with six rules in the training question, and score on a frozen out-of-sample pool, labeled blind after the rules were frozen. At one training seed, the retrained checkpoint lost 21.9 points of recall on that pool, with the label-bootstrap 95% interval entirely below zero (−0.219 [−0.268, −0.167]). The retrain report’s own caveats recommended a seed replicate before making any general claim, so I separately pre-registered and ran one. Same recipe, same data, seed 20261017 instead of 20261012, and the sign flipped: +4.9 points, with the interval entirely above zero (+0.049 [+0.010, +0.087]). A different seed is not a shuffle of the same model. In Laya, the training seed sets the RL exploration noise, the option-order shuffle, and the batch order; two runs of the same recipe are two different exploration trajectories. And the intervals above are the wrong kind of uncertainty for that question. They resample the labeled evaluation pairs, conditional on the particular checkpoints I trained. They describe how a score would change across a different sample of labels, not by retraining the recipe. Two seeds are enough to overturn a claim. It is not enough to characterize the recipe’s variability. Every interval in this report is of the first kind: label resampling at fixed checkpoints, and I treat it that way throughout. Why a local standalone decision model mattered Part 1 established the ensemble’s observed trade-off on the evaluated pipeline output: three local models voting, with splits sent to an analyst, made about as many wrong automatic calls as the hosted model at a similar review load, and far fewer missed matches at the stage where my workflow can’t recover them. The two error types are not symmetric here. A wrong merge can surface downstream during anomaly checks on the merged record. A missed match upstream has no second discovery path; the two descriptions are never seen together again. That is why recall is the side I plan around. What Part 1 left open was a smaller question: can the local model itself , not the ensemble around it, be pushed to the bar? This is a report about one model, Laya, fine-tuned on my own reviewed pairs. The auditors and Jev stay in the tables as the reference points they were in Part 1. Everything below is from my data and my runs, and where the evidence doesn’t close a question, I say so. Fine-tuning Laya on the same reviewed pairs Laya is the open-source, self-hosted implementation of the typed decision format used in Part 1: one multiple-choice question per pair (MATCH, NONMATCH, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE), with a probability distribution back. The target is task-defined product equivalence, not exact orderable-SKU identity: the rubric determines which attributes are identity-critical and which can be normalized away. The base rubric asks for a MATCH only for the same item and specification, allowing for naming, formatting, and equivalent unit representations, and says missing information is not evidence of a non-match. The six expanding rules (below) extend that with named incidental differences: color, brand, pack quantity, unit-equivalent size, value-in-range, and calendar edition. So a MATCH means the same item and specification after those normalizations; a NONMATCH means different items or incompatible specifications; INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE means the pair doesn’t carry enough to say. The versioned rubric decides which differences count as incidental, and every rule carries an exception. Three real pairs make that concrete. `TRASH CAN 45–60 GAL` and ` 45 TO 60 GALLON GREY TRASH CAN` differ only in color, which the color rule calls incidental, so under the rules, this is a match while the rule-free checkpoint treats it as a nonmatch; it is one of the 13 pairs the operator relabeled. `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.65 MSF` and `275B 32.2500 X 36.0000 122.18 MSF` differ only in the last number, which is the purchased quantity in thousand square feet, not the specification, so they match. `4X6 1 MIL CLEAR` and `4X6 4 MIL CLEAR` (poly bag) differ by one number, but that number is the thickness, which is the specification, so this is a nonmatch: a seemingly incidental difference that is the identity-critical one. I ran four fine-tuned checkpoints from the same base checkpoint at the same 2,048/2,048 operating point, in two arms: Arm A : the same 11,010 human-reviewed pairs that the SFT auditor LLMs (Qwen2.5, SmolLM3, phi4) were trained on. This is the “train Laya on the same reviewed pairs” the Part 1 teaser promised. Arm B : the pipeline’s own training pool, 348,106 rows, with gold pairs and gold descriptions excluded. Each arm got two rubric variants: vanilla (the 149-token base rubric, `match_rubric_v1`) and enhanced (the full 980-token rule ladder, `match_rubric_v007`). Four checkpoints, two knobs. The recipe All four checkpoints share one training config, verified byte-identical across the arms by diffing the run specs: the `rlcd` loss (which fits the full probability distribution, not just the argmax), choice-order shuffling, 4 epochs, seed 20261012, and the 2,048/2,048 operating point written into each checkpoint so eval refuses a mismatch. All four start from the same reviewed base checkpoint on the RTX 5090 (the full hyperparameters are in Appendix A0). Wall time is about 12 to 27 minutes for an Arm A run and 6 to 15 hours for a pool run. The seed will come back. What the data actually was Arm A . 16,033 candidate rows went in. Normalization, duplicate dropping, conflict-key dropping, and a gold-exclusion step left 11,010 rows, one per distinct pair key, 26.24% MATCH, every row human-reviewed, and none of them gold. The stage arithmetic closes both ways, on rows and on keys (appendix A0). Arm B. The pipeline’s own labeled pool: 613,509 rows, 41.27% positive, close to gold’s 41.3%. Excluding gold pairs and descriptions that leak into gold, then carving an entity-disjoint 20,000-row validation set, left 348,106 training rows. The exclusions did not preserve the prevalence: the leaked-description rows were mostly negative, so the final training split is 55.25% MATCH (192,328 of 348,106). The pool’s labels also come from the same 2026–10–07 fit run that produced gold, whose 20,000 pairs were drawn from exactly this pool, so gold is in-sample for Arm B by construction. The arms differ in prevalence, source, scale, and label provenance at once, and nothing here can isolate which of those matters. The evaluation set is the second client’s output from Part 1: 37,392 candidate pairs and 1,000 labeled (398 matches), using the same holdouts as Part 1’s second-client audit. None contains MSF, so gold comparisons use gold’s non-MSF slice. https://medium.com/media/c471f37109b0db2a9785faab6173d997/href The remaining reference points (the other base and Jev rubric rows, the three auditors, the unanimous ensemble, and the pipeline’s accept stratum) are in Appendix A1, on the same set. Fine-tuning makes Laya competitive. Both Arm A checkpoints gain 25 to 27 points of precision over the base Laya (0.79 to 0.82 against 0.54) with the same or slightly higher recall, and their decisive accuracy rises from 0.65 to 0.77. They are now in Jev’s band: sft_enhanced scores 0.791 / 0.554 against Jev rv007’s 0.788 / 0.549. sft_vanilla carries the highest point-estimate precision here (0.816), though its interval overlaps Jev’s. Precision and decisive accuracy count decisive calls only, while recall counts an undecided true match as a miss. Jev leaves about 750 pairs (2% of the set) undecided, mostly INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE; every fine-tuned Laya decides every pair. On the same data, Laya and the LLM auditors make different trade-offs. Arm A shares its training data with the qwen25 / smollm3 auditors. Laya is 8 to 17 points more precise than those two (0.79 to 0.82 against 0.65 to 0.71) but has 19 to 31 points less recall (0.53 to 0.55 against 0.74 to 0.83). Laya sits where Jev and the unanimous ensemble sit, with high precision and low recall, not where the majority votes. That’s the gap the ensemble was closing, and a single fine-tuned Laya doesn’t close it. Reaching Jev’s precision band at a fixed operating point is also not a routing win: the majority vote still recovers far more true matches (0.827 recall against 0.554), and review-normalized outcomes for the fine-tuned Laya are not yet measured. On the gold slices, the rubric axis came out a computed fail: vanilla (149 tokens) beat enhanced (980 tokens) per subset on 5 of 6 comparisons, so the richer rubric added no value on this arm. On the second client’s data, vanilla is again more precise, while enhanced trades about 2.5 points of precision for about 3 points of recall. Both are one seed per checkpoint, and the seed study below is the yardstick for how far a gap like that is from being established. The pool arm doesn’t transfer On my in-pool gold (the non-MSF slice), the pool checkpoints scored about 0.95 / 0.95, far above Arm A’s 0.81 to 0.86 / 0.69. On this client’s real output, their precision falls to about 0.76, and their recall collapses to 0.34 to 0.37, 16 to 21 points below Arm A, with both recall intervals clear of Arm A’s. They also call MATCH on about a third fewer pairs (6 to 7K against 9.5 to 10.5K). Training-data leakage is an unlikely explanation for the gap between the arms: less than 1% of this client’s pairs or descriptions appear in either arm’s training split. The gold score is in-sample for Arm B by design, so it measures fit to that distribution rather than transfer. On genuinely new data, the pool checkpoints fall back to NONMATCH. Because the arms differ in several ways at once, the result is descriptive rather than causal. The takeaway for the campaign: the Arm B report had chosen pool_vanilla as the best operating point on gold, and this result doesn’t support carrying that choice forward. When in-pool and out-of-sample disagree, the out-of-sample number is the one a production decision should lean on. Replication on fresh labels One labeled partition is one draw of labels, so I repeated the whole comparison on two more partitions of the same March 2026 link run, set1 and set2, whose 1,000-pair holdouts were labeled fresh and blind after every checkpoint was frozen. set1 holds 17,099 pairs (estimated 49.5% matches), set2 17,686 (42.4%); the pooled intervals are about ±0.04 to 0.05. One scope note: these labels were a frozen holdout for the initial pre-registered rule test. The seed and epoch studies, the paired Laya-Jev comparison, and the choice of which checkpoint to retrain all reused them afterward, so for those later analyses, set1/set2 is not an independent confirmation; they become confirmatory only after a new holdout or an independent replication. The main conclusions replicate: The majority ensemble again has the best balance of precision and recall (0.764 / 0.791, highest decisive accuracy at 0.792); The Arm A fine-tuned Laya checkpoints sit in Jev’s precision band; Arm B and base Laya trail; The pipeline’s own automatic-accept stratum is again far less precise than any decision model (0.561) while recalling only 4% of matches; it is the narrow slice of pairs the pipeline accepted on its own, and the estimate rests on 41 to 44 labeled rows per set. https://medium.com/media/00c2652ae5fa63d2f67b0522cefbc028/href sft_enhanced is the best of the evaluated Laya checkpoints on this partition, and it edges past Jev. It scores 0.827 / 0.567 against Jev rv007’s 0.788 / 0.507. Overlapping marginal intervals don’t test the difference, so I paired the two on the shared 1,000 labels. That computation ran after the reports and was not pre-registered. Because Part 1’s intervals are resampled by query item, I ran two designs with the analyzer’s stratified method and seed: pair-level resampling, as in the marginal tables, and query-clustered resampling of whole query clusters within each stratum (method detail in Appendix A7). Both give the same point estimates: sft_enhanced leads by +0.039 on precision and +0.060 on recall. The paired bootstrap places the fixed-checkpoint recall difference above zero under both resampling designs ([+0.006, +0.113] pair-level, [+0.033, +0.140] clustered). The precision difference is not robust to the resampling unit: the [−0.006, +0.088] pair-level straddles zero, and the [+0.013, +0.095] clustered sits just above it. These are statements about two frozen checkpoints on this holdout, not about retraining the recipe or another client’s data. Pooled across all four sets (2,000 labels), the two Arm A checkpoints level out on precision (sft_vanilla 0.819 [0.780, 0.851] against sft_enhanced 0.810 [0.779, 0.841]), sft_enhanced carries more recall (0.561 [0.526, 0.594] against 0.500 [0.467, 0.535]), and Jev rv007 sits at 0.788 / 0.527. The auditors are more precise here, and that’s the sets, not the models. Auditor precision is 3.6 to 6.3 points higher than on set0/set3, with recall 1 to 7 points lower. Set 1 is simply the easier set for every decision model: precision runs 9.7 to 16.7 points higher there than on set 2, and its estimated match base rate is 7 points higher. The error mix shifted, too, and it separates two problems that are easy to conflate. On set1/set2, “one side missing an attribute” is the largest false-positive reason for the majority vote (48%), the unanimous vote (46%), phi4 (46%), and Jev rv007 (55%); on set0/set3, different modifiers or dimensions led. Those are overconfident false merges: one side omits an identity-critical attribute, and the model merges anyway. That calls for an abstention rule (INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE when an identity-critical attribute is missing, and no stronger identifier establishes the match), which I have yet to test with the LLM auditors, who can actually abstain. The six rules I describe next are aimed at the opposite failure: true matches the checkpoints miss because an incidental difference looked decisive. I’m keeping those two interventions separate. Six rules, added at inference The missed matches I wanted to recover were not random-looking: several belonged to recurring, rule-shaped families, such as color differences that don’t matter, vendor or brand labels that don’t matter, and pack counts that don’t matter. So I wrote six “expanding” rules, each naming a difference that does not make two items different, and tested whether appending them to the rubric at inference time recovers matches the checkpoints miss, and what precision it costs. https://medium.com/media/2cde0ac6abe876cfbff755739998679e/href Every rule carries a guard: the product type and the other stated specs must agree. Before freezing, the rules were scanned against every labeled non-match on set0/set3, and four were narrowed down to those that would have flipped one. The discipline is what makes the verdict mean anything. The rule files and rubrics were committed and git-tagged before any set1/set2 label existed , and I pre-registered the decision criteria per checkpoint: Helps: recall gain with its 95% interval above zero, and the precision drop’s lower bound ≥ −3 points. Hurts: a precision loss beyond −3 points with the interval below zero, or a gold non-MSF precision drop beyond 2 points. No effect: anything else. The verdict, from the two out-of-sample sets labeled after the tag: https://medium.com/media/3cb5dc8d22f571811264ee9d48658043/href Verdict: all four checkpoints receive the formal NO EFFECT label, under pre-registered criteria that failed to anticipate a recall loss. Both Arm A checkpoints move in the intended direction (about +2 to +3 points of recall for about 2 points of precision), and neither recall gain clears its 95% interval. For the two Arm A checkpoints, the observed precision cost was small (at most −1.2 points on gold non-MSF, inside the 2-point limit), but the recall gain was not established. pool_vanilla goes the wrong way: it loses 5.8 points of recall with the interval well below zero and cuts its MATCH calls by about 27%. The pre-registered “hurts” rule only tests a precision loss, so pool_vanilla is graded “no effect”. I’m stating that gap rather than re-grading after the fact. The likeliest explanation, untested, is that pool_vanilla trained on a 149-token rule-free question, so the 978-token expanding rubric is far outside anything it saw. pool_enhanced is already trained on a rules block and barely moves (+0.6 points). And the finding that sets up the next leg: the rules didn’t reliably land. Appending them changed decisions, but neither Arm A checkpoint met the pre-specified improvement criterion. The matches they miss carry p_MATCH around 0.02 to 0.05, and the MATCH-volume lift (+7 to +10%) appears only partially as recovered matches on the labeled holdout. One caveat the design can’t settle: the change also made the question much longer (149 to 978 tokens on vanilla, 980 to 1,793 on enhanced), so I can’t tell whether the checkpoints ignored the rule semantics or reacted to a longer, unfamiliar question; a length-matched placebo rubric would separate those. What the data do show is that an inference-time rubric change didn’t reliably teach these checkpoints a rule. It nudged them. Retraining sft_enhanced with the expanding rubric If a rule can’t be taught at inference time, can it be taught in training? The cleanest test uses the checkpoint already doing the best work and already trained on a rules-bearing rubric, sft_enhanced , and retrains its recipe from the base checkpoint: the same 11,010 Arm A rows, the same config, but with the expanding rubric `match_rubric_v008` (the v007 ladder plus the six rules, a 1,793-token head). The rendered question differed by exactly the six rules, and nothing else moved. A second arm, `sft_expanding_aug`, added 1,193 generated rule-consistent rows and 13 relabels of existing training rows, to test whether rule-consistent data does what rule text didn’t. Both runs were pre-registered by a git tag before scoring, with the verdict criteria pinned. The single-seed headline On the frozen set1/set2 test pool (1,000 labels, 471 matches), at a single seed: https://medium.com/media/2abad17b4988d07fc8caa5c7f1ef520a/href At seed 1, the checkpoint trained with the rule text found fewer matches, not more. sft_expanding’s recall fell from 0.567 to 0.348 (−25.4 on set1, −17.9 on set2), and it called MATCH about 35% less often. All three pre-registered comparisons graded “hurts” at this seed: the rule text lost 21.9 points of recall; the rule-consistent data recovered 13.7 of those, but still graded “hurts” because gold non-MSF precision fell 8.0 points; and the two together finished 8.2 points of recall below sft_enhanced. Of these runs, the inference-only rules had the highest observed recall (0.589), without retraining. Truncation is ruled out: at a 1,793-token head, 254 tokens remain for the pair state, and no pair was clipped. The second seed flips the sign https://medium.com/media/1bc2a62cacc4a17b7285e2146366d13a/href Changing only the seed moved out-of-sample recall by 9 points for the v007 recipe and 18 points for the v008 recipe, and the retrain report’s correction note withdraws the 22-point loss as a single-seed result. The two-seed means still lean about 8.5 points negative (sft_expanding 0.438 against sft_enhanced 0.523), but each recipe’s two seeds overlap the other’s (0.348 to 0.527 against 0.478 to 0.567). The decision changes: the rule-text effect is unresolved, consistent with no effect, a moderate negative effect, or an effect that depends on the seed. What the seed actually moves This finding changes how the whole campaign should be read. On held-out data from the training distribution, the seeded checkpoints look nearly identical: 95 to 96% precision and 93 to 95% recall on the SFT test split, which moves at most 2 points with the seed. Gold non-MSF recall moves up to 5. The second client’s test pool moves 9 to 18. That pattern suggests a transfer-stability problem, but two seeds do not establish its general size or cause. So every other single-seed training comparison in this report is untested by replication: the rubric axis, Arm A against Arm B, and the augmentation arm. Their gaps (8 to 24 points of recall) sit inside or near the seed difference. The closest to holding is the pool arm, whose recall (0.32 to 0.34) sits below both sft_enhanced seeds (0.478 and 0.567), but the pool runs’ own seed variation is unobserved. The inference-time rubric comparisons are the exception: they compare the same checkpoint under two questions, so the training seed doesn’t enter the comparison, though the size of that effect still depends on which checkpoint it is applied to. The read None of the pre-committed readings fired as written: the loss was recall, not precision, and it didn’t replicate across the seed. The recommendation the criteria actually support is the conservative one: keep the original 4-epoch sft_enhanced checkpoint as a provisional Arm A baseline. The expanding rules at inference are cheap to reverse and showed no clear harm for that checkpoint, but they did not meet the pre-registered benefit criterion, and the same change cost pool_vanilla 5.8 points of recall. I would not promote them as an improvement yet. The augmented arm isn’t a clean test of rule-consistent data either. On the development sets, it is on par with sft_enhanced (recall 0.553 vs. 0.554); on the test sets, it isn’t. It differs from sft_expanding in three ways at once with no ablation, and the generated rows carry defects: about 5% are malformed outright (the inch regex reads `1 1/2"` as `2"`), and many of the rest are stereotyped or labeled the wrong way. The 13 relabels were applied only to training rows, while four of those pairs retained their original labels in the validation and test splits. It's fitted temperature also hit Laya’s 5.0 cap. The full accounting is in Appendix A7. And the deeper read: in the tested runs, changing the training question coincided with an out-of-sample recall shift comparable to the shift observed across seeds, and the recipe effect itself did not replicate. Until recipes are compared with a seed budget and judged on the out-of-sample mean with the spread reported, the training side of this campaign is telling me about the noise, not the rules. Ways this work could have misled me A single labeler, no adjudication. Every holdout here (1,000 pairs on set0/set3 and 1,000 on set1/set2) was labeled blind by a single person (the operator), with no second review. A systematic labeling bias would show up in every model at once, and I can’t separate it from a real model difference. The labels are blind (descriptions only, no model verdicts), and the rules were frozen before the test labels existed, but the human-in-the-loop is one. 500 labels per set. Pooled intervals are about ±0.04 to 0.05. An effect of about 2 points, exactly the size of the Arm A recall gains from the expanding rules, sits right at what this sample can detect. “No effect” can mean “not enough labels to see a 2-point effect.” Set difficulty as a confound. sft_enhanced’s edge over Jev was measured on the partition that contains the easier set. The pooled four-set number (2,000 labels) is the more defensible one, and there the two Arm A checkpoints are level in precision. No abstention, no calibrated uncertainty. INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE was never a training label in any arm, so no checkpoint learned to abstain. Deciding every pair says nothing about whether the class probabilities the checkpoints emit are calibrated, so routing on them is not yet justified. Reproducibility rests on a preserved working tree, not on the tags alone. The git tags pin the pre-registrations and the rule files, and each run’s `run_info.json` records the rendered rubric’s content hash. But the scoring path imports modules still untracked in the repo: the metric definitions, the v006/v007 rule and rubric files, and the renderer. A fresh checkout of the tagged commits cannot reproduce these numbers on its own; they depend on the untracked working-tree files they ran from, which are preserved intact. A leading-zero ID bug was caught and fixed. The set2 reference IDs were read as integers, and 1,677 lost a leading zero, breaking a join and surfacing as a summarize refusal. It’s fixed (IDs read as text, with a test), and the affected Jev run was re-run from scratch. It affected a side statistic, not any number in this report. Retained candidates only. The fine-tuned Laya was scored on the candidates the pipeline retained. This says nothing about matches lost earlier, in blocking or below the review line. What it cost, and what’s next Jev’s API charges for the set1/set2 replication runs are billed to the account and not itemized here. Everything else ran locally on the RTX 5090: Arm A fine-tuning about 12 to 27 minutes per run, the pool arm 6 to 15 hours per run, the two retrain runs 78 to about 106 minutes, the seed and epoch study about 2.6 hours across four runs, and inference about 45 seconds (vanilla) to about 195 seconds (enhanced) per set. The human cost is the labeling: 1,000 blind-labeled pairs for Part 1 and 1,000 fresh ones here. The next legs, in order: A seed budget before any other claim. Re-run the single-seed comparisons (the rubric axis, Arm A against Arm B, the rule text) with at least two to three seeds per arm and judge on the out-of-sample mean with the spread reported. That includes a clean augmentation retest: fix the identified defects, use real brand-vs-brand swaps, and apply the 13 relabels to the validation and test copies as well. Calibrate, then route. Check the fine-tuned Laya’s class probabilities for calibration on the labeled holdouts, and only then build the routing comparison Part 1 promised: wrong merges and missed matches per unit of analyst review, for a single fine-tuned Laya against the ensemble and Jev. A routing policy tuned to one checkpoint is tuned to a score whose out-of-sample ranking may not survive retraining, which is why the seed budget comes first. The missing-attribute rule for the auditors. Test INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE when an identity-critical attribute is missing, and no stronger identifier establishes the match, on the LLM auditors, where it can actually abstain. The caveats are the differences between a field report and a benchmark: one-second client, one labeler, single runs per checkpoint except for the two-seed study, and scoring on retained candidates only.
