items.summary_html:
Every developer, designer, and solo founder experimenting with "vibe coding" hits the exact same wall within thirty minutes of rapid progress.

The initial velocity feels magical. You open Cursor, Claude Code, or Google Antigravity, type a casual description of a web application, and watch three hundred lines of functional React or Python materialize in seconds. But as soon as you give the model critical feedback, request an architectural adjustment, or ask for a refined user interface, the system begins to degrade.

Instead of researching how top-tier engineering teams solve the problem, the model invents makeshift patches directly from stale training memory. When you suggest an intuitive but flawed workaround, the model enthusiastically agrees with you, compounding technical debt. When you ask it to write landing page copy, it floods the screen with robotic clichés and passive hedging. When you ask it to style a dashboard, it peppers the layout with neon borders, fake telemetry codes, and nested box clutter.

This failure mode is not a flaw in your intelligence or your prompt wording. It is an architectural failure of unconstrained generation. Large language models operate on probabilistic text completion. Without deterministic operational boundaries, they default to lowest-common-denominator habits.

To solve this systematically, Longwave AI Lab engineered the Anti-Slop AI Harness: a production-hardened, four-module constitution distributed across Cursor Rules (.cursor/rules/*.mdc), Claude Code Skills (CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills/), and Google Antigravity (GEMINI.md and .agents/skills/).

Here is the exact breakdown of why default models decay, how the four invariant modules eliminate that decay, and how you can drop this harness into your project in thirty seconds.

1. The Four Fatal Flaws of Unharnessed AI

When you run an autonomous coding agent or an interactive coding assistant without a governing harness, the model reliably falls into four cognitive traps:

Flaw 1: Static-Memory Guessing (Zero Live Benchmarking)

When you point out that an interface feels awkward or a database query runs slowly, the model does not verify modern standards. It generates a patch based on patterns memorized during pre-training. This produces obsolete patterns: old library APIs that were deprecated two years ago, generic bootstrap-like CSS hacks, and invented utility functions.

Flaw 2: Sycophancy Bias (The Yes-Man Trap)

Standard language models are alignment-tuned to please the human operator. If a non-coder says, "Let's put an alert banner and three nested cards here to make it obvious," the assistant replies, "Great idea! Let me do that right away." It treats human prescriptions as gospel, even when those prescriptions violate visual hierarchy, create accessibility failures, or break database normalization.

Flaw 3: Memory-Only Apologies and Error Loops

When an agent introduces a build failure or breaks an existing test, it apologizes profusely: "I apologize for that oversight. Let me fix that immediately." It makes a slight modification, runs the build, fails again on the same underlying premise, and burns your context window in a loop. Prose promises do not prevent recurrent errors.

Flaw 4: Stylistic Degradation and Sci-Fi Greebling

When generating visual components, unharnessed models fill empty space with artificial complexity. In 3D modeling and physical prop design, this is called "greebling" (gluing tiny plastic parts onto a surface to make it look mechanical). In AI-generated code, greebling takes the form of meaningless slashes (//, ///), fake telemetry tags (#REF-01, SECTOR_A), middle-dot chains (A · B · C), nested borders, and tiny ten-pixel text that no human can read. In prose, it takes the form of generic filler phrases, passive sentences, and overused transition words.

2. The 4-Module Invariant Architecture

The Anti-Slop AI Harness replaces probabilistic guesswork with four structural invariants. These rules do not suggest; they dictate hard operational boundaries.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        ANTI-SLOP AI HARNESS                             |
|                                                                         |
|  +-----------------------------+     +-------------------------------+  |
|  | Module 01: Benchmark-First  |     | Module 02: Pushback Firewall  |  |
|  | - Ban static-memory patches |     | - 3 Operating modes           |  |
|  | - Live multi-archetype scan |     | - Option B formulation        |  |
|  | - Transparent audit record  |     | - 3x Linter graduation law    |  |
|  +-----------------------------+     +-------------------------------+  |
|                 |                                    |                  |
|  +-----------------------------+     +-------------------------------+  |
|  | Module 03: Editorial Voice  |     | Module 04: Quiet Luxury UI    |  |
|  | - Topic-Comment syntax      |     | - >= 70% open canvas          |  |
|  | - Zero translationese       |     | - Zero box-in-box nesting     |  |
|  | - 15-28 word sentence cap   |     | - Punctuation-free cards      |  |
|  +-----------------------------+     +-------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
Module 01: Multi-Archetype Live Benchmark Protocol (RULE-BENCHMARK-FIRST)

Free Starter Pack & Pro Full Harness

This protocol establishes a zero-tolerance invariant against memory-only patching:

  1. Mandatory Live Inspection: Whenever a critique or new feature request arrives, the AI must trigger live web inspection tools across at least two to three distinct industry archetypes:
    • For UI and visual design: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Stripe Press, Linear, Raycast, and Vercel.
    • For typography and editorial clarity: Pentagram, Kinfolk, The New York Times Visual Investigations, and Monocle.
    • For motion and visual narrative: Ordinary Folk, Vox, Johnny Harris, Kurzgesagt, and Cleo Abram.
    • For engineering and system design: Stripe API Architecture, Cloudflare Architecture, AWS Well-Architected Framework, and Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
  2. Self-Critique vs. Global Standard: Before touching the code, the model must explicitly document why the previous attempt failed and how top-tier teams handle the problem structurally.
  3. Execution with Verifiable Attribution: The model implements the extracted mechanism and logs the reference source, URL, access date, and applied change directly in its verification log.
Module 02: 3-Mode Pushback Firewall and 3x Graduation Law (RULE-PUSHBACK-FIREWALL)

Pro Full Harness

This module turns your AI assistant from a sycophantic yes-man into a principal architect and co-founder firewall:

  1. Three Operating Modes:
    • [AUTO-EXECUTE]: Applied to clear, architecturally sound tasks. Executed immediately with zero friction.
    • [CLARIFY-FIRST]: Applied when an instruction has multiple valid interpretations that alter system architecture. The AI asks at most one or two crisp multiple-choice questions with a recommended default.
    • [HARD-STOP PUSHBACK]: Applied when the user proposes a change that violates visual hierarchy, crowds the canvas, creates technical debt, or solves a real symptom with the wrong medicine.
  2. The 4-Step Pushback Protocol:
    • Step 1: Validate the underlying symptom (separate what you saw from how you proposed fixing it).
    • Step 2: State the structural risk plainly in non-jargon language.
    • Step 3: Propose Option B (a world-class alternative that solves the root problem without side effects).
    • Step 4: Respect explicit human overrides while isolating the change for easy reversion.
  3. The 3x Graduation Law: If the AI makes the same error pattern three times during a project, it is strictly forbidden from apologizing. It must halt and author an automated verification script (Node.js, AST parser, or bash linter returning exit code 1) that programmatically bars that mistake from occurring again.
Module 03: 5-Layer Natural Editorial Voice Engine (RULE-ANTI-SLOP-VOICE)

Pro Full Harness

This engine strips out corporate filler, passive hedging, and translationese:

  • Layer 1: Direct Verb Architecture: Banned nominalization. Replaces heavy noun phrases ("The execution of the script causes a reduction in runtime") with active verbs ("Running the script cuts runtime").
  • Layer 2: Cliché Blacklist: Eliminates words like delve, tapestry, beacon, landscape, paradigm shift, synergy, elevate, and foster. Every abstract claim must include either a sensory anchor or a numerical comparison.
  • Layer 3: Plain-Spoken Headings: Banned trademarked self-help labels ("The 3-Step Framework", "The Art of..."). Headings must express one complete thought centered on a verb.
  • Layer 4: Clean Punctuation Hygiene: Bans the overuse of em-dashes and semicolons as crutches to stitch weak thoughts together. Prose relies on clean periods, commas, and natural rhythm.
  • Layer 5: Sentence Length Ceiling: Sentences are strictly capped at 28 words on average, with a hard ceiling at 45 words.
Module 04: Quiet Luxury UI and Anti-Greebling Minimalism (RULE-QUIET-LUXURY-UI)

Pro Full Harness

This module guarantees that visual interfaces maintain breathing room and editorial elegance:

  • The >= 70% Open Canvas Law: At least 70% of any viewport, modal, or slide canvas must remain uncluttered background. Whitespace is treated as a first-class structural component.
  • Zero Box-in-Box Nesting: Never nest a bordered card inside another bordered card. Visual grouping must use vertical whitespace (16px to 28px), typographic contrast, or a single hairline border (1px at 15% opacity).
  • Punctuation-Free Glass Cards: Visual badges use rounded corners, clean padding, and a single 3px bottom accent bar. Status dots (•), colons inside labels (Type:), and trailing ellipses (...) are strictly eliminated.
  • Readable Type Hierarchy: Minimum 14px for metadata, 16px to 18px for body prose, and 28px to 48px for headings. Microscopic 10px text is banned.
3. Comprehensive 5-Dimension Comparison Table

Here is how unharnessed models compare directly against an agent governed by the Anti-Slop AI Harness:

Operational Dimension ❌ Standard Unharnessed AI ✅ With Anti-Slop AI Harness Response to User Critique Guesses from static pre-training weights; slaps on makeshift labels or generic CSS fixes. Mandatory Live Multi-Archetype Benchmark: Surveys 2 to 3 live industry references (Apple HIG, Stripe, Linear, Pentagram) before touching code. When Given Flawed Prescriptions Sycophantic Yes-Man: Compliments your idea ("Great point!") and implements the destructive patch, degrading the product. 3-Mode Pushback Firewall: Validates your symptom, explains the structural side effect, and delivers a superior Option B. Recurring Error Handling Apologizes repeatedly ("I apologize for the confusion!") and repeats the same bug ten minutes later. 3x Graduation Law: On the 3rd recurrence of any bug pattern, writes an automated linter (exit code 1) to eliminate the bug permanently. Writing & Documentation Robotic AI Slop: Floods text with delve, tapestry, testament, passive hedging, and endless em-dashes. 5-Layer Editorial Engine: Active verbs, Topic-Comment syntax, 15 to 28 word sentence ceiling, zero em-dashes, and strict cliché bans. UI & Visual Layout Sci-Fi Greebling: Clutters views with //, #REF-01, nested bordered boxes, neon glows, and unreadable 10px fonts. Quiet Luxury Minimalism: Enforces >= 70% Open Canvas, generous whitespace, clean glass badges, and zero fake technical symbols.
4. Real-World Code Examples: Before vs. After

To understand the difference this harness makes in practice, examine three concrete transformations across UI styling, behavioral pushback, and technical copy.

Example 1: UI Component Refactor (From Greebled Clutter to Quiet Luxury) ❌ Before (Default AI Output with Sci-Fi Greebling) 
// Typical unharnessed AI response when asked for a "modern telemetry card"
export function MetricCard({ title, value, status }: MetricProps) {
  return (
    <div className="border border-cyan-500/40 bg-slate-950 p-4 rounded-lg shadow-cyan-500/20 shadow-lg">
      <div className="flex justify-between items-center text-[10px] text-cyan-400 font-mono tracking-widest border-b border-cyan-800 pb-1 mb-2">
        <span>// SYS.REF-049 //span>
        <span>• STATUS: {status.toUpperCase()} •span>
      div>
      <div className="border border-slate-800 bg-slate-900/60 p-3 rounded mb-2">
        <span className="text-xs text-slate-400 uppercase tracking-wider">{title}:span>
        <h3 className="text-2xl font-bold text-white font-mono">{value}h3>
      div>
      <p className="text-[11px] text-slate-500 italic">CALIBRATION · OK · 2026p>
    div>
  );
}
✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 04 Applied) 
// Governed by Module 04: >= 70% Open Canvas, Zero Greebling, Clean Glass Card
export function MetricCard({ title, value, status }: MetricProps) {
  return (
    <div className="relative rounded-xl border-b-[3px] border-amber-500/80 bg-zinc-900/40 p-6 backdrop-blur-md transition-all hover:bg-zinc-900/60">
      <div className="flex items-baseline justify-between mb-3">
        <span className="text-sm font-medium text-zinc-400">{title}span>
        <span className="text-xs font-medium text-amber-400/90">{status}span>
      div>
      <div className="text-3xl font-semibold tracking-tight text-zinc-100">
        {value}
      div>
    div>
  );
}

Notice the immediate difference: the fake slashes, nested boxes, status dots, and illegible ten-pixel font sizes vanish. In their place is a single-layer container with generous padding, clear typographic contrast, and a quiet three-pixel accent bar.

Example 2: Behavioral Pushback (From Sycophancy to Principal Architect)

Suppose you tell your AI: "The landing page hero looks empty. Add three bordered highlight boxes and a bright red countdown timer in the header."

❌ Before (Unharnessed AI Response)

"Great idea! Adding three highlight boxes and a bright red countdown timer will create urgency and make the hero section look much more engaging. I've updated the code with animated red borders and badge components."

✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 02 Pushback Protocol)

[HARD-STOP PUSHBACK]

1. Validating the Symptom: You noticed that the top of the page lacks visual tension and doesn't immediately pull the reader into the value proposition. That observation is accurate.

2. Structural Risk: Adding three bordered boxes and a bright red timer will crowd the viewport below the 70% open canvas threshold. On mobile screens, it pushes the primary call-to-action completely below the fold and introduces visual anxiety that cheapens the brand.

3. Option B (World-Class Alternative): Instead of adding bordered containers and timer clutter, we can:

  • Increase the primary headline font weight from 500 to 700 and tighten line height to 1.05.
  • Introduce an understated editorial kicker badge in muted amber.
  • Add 32px of vertical whitespace above the primary action button.

This creates crisp visual punch while keeping the canvas open and calm. If you still want the three boxes, reply override and I will implement them cleanly in an isolated component.

Example 3: Technical Product Copy (From AI Buzzwords to Direct Human Prose) ❌ Before (Default AI Slop Copywriting)

"In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, our cutting-edge platform allows teams to delve into advanced workflows. It stands as a testament to seamless synergy, empowering builders to unlock their full potential while navigating the complexities of modern software development."

✅ After (Anti-Slop Harness: Module 03 Applied)

"Most developer tools force you to trade speed for control. We built our pipeline around two commands that run in under five seconds, leaving your existing repository untouched."

5. 30-Second Quickstart Guide (Zero Coding Required)

The harness is engineered to install into any modern AI environment without configuration overhead.

items.title: Perplexity and NVIDIA Researchers Introduce JOLT: a Joint Teacher-Student Reinforcement Learning Method
items.summary: Perplexity , along with NVIDIA team, has introduced JOLT, a new post-training method for language models. JOLT stands for Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching . It trains a single model in 2 roles. The teacher sees privileged information; the student does not. The key change is that the teacher is trained too, so its feedback stays usable. On MATH, JOLT matched GRPO’s accuracy with 6.5x fewer processed training tokens. For teams running RL post-training, that is a direct compute question. TL;DR What it is: a post-training method. Size: tested on Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Runs on: 1 shared model plays both roles, so no separate teacher model. Training hardware: Not disclosed. Performance: JOLT+ posts the highest mean score in every setting tested against GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill. Best: AppWorld state-test pass rate of 72.09% with JOLT+, vs 62.20% for GRPO (+9.9 points). Worst: JOLT without student reward scores 51.92% on AppWorld, below GRPO. What is Perplexity JOLT? JOLT is a self-distillation method from Perplexity and NVIDIA that trains one model as teacher and student. It builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) . Why does RL post-training need a better teacher? Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO , gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow. On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution. The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training. How does JOLT work? JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time: Teacher: gets privileged information. It learns from outcome rewards, plus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the student. Student: sees only the task. It learns from the teacher’s token-level distillation signal on its own attempts. On-policy: each role learns from trajectories generated under its own context. JOLT+: adds the student’s own outcome reward to the student update. The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy. && How does JOLT perform on benchmarks? The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information: GSM8K: DeepSeek-V2-Lite; teacher gets the verified answer. MATH: Qwen3-0.6B; teacher gets worked reference solutions. LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen3-8B on 131 problems; teacher gets a passing sibling solution or execution feedback. AppWorld: Qwen3-4B-Instruct; teacher gets summaries of past attempts. Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct trained on TMax ; teacher gets private verifier files. JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 , JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%. Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%. How much training compute does JOLT save? On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens. JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD. How does JOLT compare with GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill? All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper , with hyperparameters tuned per method. Method descriptions link to each method’s own paper. Feature JOLT JOLT+ GRPO OPSD π-Distill Separate teacher model No No No teacher No (self-teacher) No (shared model) Teacher is trained Yes (reward + KL to student) Yes (reward + KL to student) Not applicable No Yes (KL-regularized) Student signal Dense distillation, on-policy Distillation + outcome reward Group-relative outcome reward Dense distillation, on-policy Off-policy, teacher trajectories MATH, Qwen3-0.6B (%) 72.14 ± 0.90 72.59 ± 1.17 68.36 ± 3.73 61.20 ± 2.10 42.25 ± 1.10 LCBv6, Qwen3-8B (%) 47.64 ± 1.10 49.08 ± 0.41 46.13 ± 1.83 45.34 ± 1.50 38.23 ± 1.72 AppWorld, Qwen3-4B (%) 51.92 ± 5.30 72.09 ± 6.01 62.20 ± 2.83 29.49 ± 2.48 59.85 ± 2.97 Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 (%) 6.56 10.96 8.25 2.82 4.99 Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@32 (%) 25.69 34.83 30.34 16.90 22.31 Code Not yet released Not yet released Not disclosed GitHub Not disclosed Terminal-Bench base model: 5.18% pass@1, 22.81% pass@32. Key Takeaways 1 model plays teacher and student, and the teacher is trained too. 6.5x fewer processed tokens than GRPO at matched MATH accuracy. JOLT+ beats GRPO by 9.9 points on AppWorld. Plain JOLT still trails GRPO on AppWorld and Terminal-Bench. Check out the paper on arXiv and the Perplexity research blog post . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? Connect with us

Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO, gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow.

On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution.

The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training.

How does JOLT work?

JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time:

  • Teacher: gets privileged information. It learns from outcome rewards, plus a KL penalty that keeps it close to the student.
  • Student: sees only the task. It learns from the teacher’s token-level distillation signal on its own attempts.
  • On-policy: each role learns from trajectories generated under its own context.
  • JOLT+: adds the student’s own outcome reward to the student update.

The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy.

&&

How does JOLT perform on benchmarks?

The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information:

  • GSM8K: DeepSeek-V2-Lite; teacher gets the verified answer.
  • MATH: Qwen3-0.6B; teacher gets worked reference solutions.
  • LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen3-8B on 131 problems; teacher gets a passing sibling solution or execution feedback.
  • AppWorld: Qwen3-4B-Instruct; teacher gets summaries of past attempts.
  • Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct trained on TMax; teacher gets private verifier files.

JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%.

Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%.

How much training compute does JOLT save?

On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens.

JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD.

How does JOLT compare with GRPO, OPSD and π-Distill?

All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper, with hyperparameters tuned per method. Method descriptions link to each method’s own paper.

FeatureJOLTJOLT+GRPOOPSDπ-DistillSeparate teacher modelNoNoNo teacherNo (self-teacher)No (shared model)Teacher is trainedYes (reward + KL to student)Yes (reward + KL to student)Not applicableNoYes (KL-regularized)Student signalDense distillation, on-policyDistillation + outcome rewardGroup-relative outcome rewardDense distillation, on-policyOff-policy, teacher trajectoriesMATH, Qwen3-0.6B (%)72.14 ± 0.9072.59 ± 1.1768.36 ± 3.7361.20 ± 2.1042.25 ± 1.10LCBv6, Qwen3-8B (%)47.64 ± 1.1049.08 ± 0.4146.13 ± 1.8345.34 ± 1.5038.23 ± 1.72AppWorld, Qwen3-4B (%)51.92 ± 5.3072.09 ± 6.0162.20 ± 2.8329.49 ± 2.4859.85 ± 2.97Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@1 (%)6.5610.968.252.824.99Terminal-Bench 2.1 pass@32 (%)25.6934.8330.3416.9022.31CodeNot yet releasedNot yet releasedNot disclosedGitHubNot disclosed

Terminal-Bench base model: 5.18% pass@1, 22.81% pass@32.

Key Takeaways
  • 1 model plays teacher and student, and the teacher is trained too.
  • 6.5x fewer processed tokens than GRPO at matched MATH accuracy.
  • JOLT+ beats GRPO by 9.9 points on AppWorld.
  • Plain JOLT still trails GRPO on AppWorld and Terminal-Bench.

Check out the paper on arXiv and the Perplexity research blog post. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: PHP2Shell: How AI Found a 14-Year-Old Bug in PHP, and Why the Patch Race Is On
items.summary: Two critical flaws in the engine behind a huge share of the web, an early leak, and a preview of how AI changes security work for both defenders and attackers. The short version On October 21, PHP shipped emergency updates for two critical flaws, CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and let an attacker with no account run code on a web server. OpenAI says the underlying bug had been sitting in PHP for 14 years. What makes this story different is who found it: AI-assisted researchers, before attackers did, as far as anyone knows. thehackernews Fortune How AI found it Security firm Calif found the first flaw in August with help from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Calif had been invited to OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which proactively hunts for flaws in digital infrastructure. Google-owned Wiz found the flaws independently, weeks later. Wiz says it used its own Wiz Atlas tool plus Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to adapt exploits across PHP versions and setups. PHP rushes out emergency patches for two critical bugs AI found first +3 Note what “AI found it” means here. Humans steered, and the models did heavy lifting on discovery and exploit development. Calif itself cautions that no model can unearth all bugs from simple prompts. The Hacker News also reports that knowing the target’s history still mattered. cyberkendra thehackernews OpenAI says frontier AI found these flaws before attackers did, giving maintainers a “Defender’s Window” to prepare fixes and protections. The result was a two-month effort between OpenAI, PHP maintainers, researchers and security providers. cyberscoopcyberscoop How attackers can abuse it Here is the concept in plain terms, at the level the public advisories describe it. Both flaws are use-after-free bugs. A fatal error mid-request, typically running out of memory, interrupts PHP before it cleans up, and a later request or reused worker then treats the freed memory as live data. Every known trigger is a multipart/form-data request, the format used for file uploads, and PHP parses it before your application code runs. That is why no login is needed and why your own code quality doesn’t matter. sansecsansec Two outcomes matter. One flaw can leak memory on its own, similar to Heartbleed, exposing passwords, session tokens, API keys and TLS private keys from other requests. The other leads to remote code execution, and an exploit tool credited to Calif combines both bugs into one attack that needs no login. Calif demonstrated it against WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel and other popular PHP apps. After a break-in, defenders are told to look for web shells, new files in the web root, cron jobs, scheduled tasks and new accounts. PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (CVE-2026–109618, CVE-2026–109619) +3 How it unfolded The disclosure was meant to be orderly. Details leaked on October 20, PHP pulled its release forward a day, and Calif had mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept. Chainguard also published patched images about six hours before the official fix. thehackernews Is it being exploited? Attempts, yes. Confirmed breaches, not yet reported. Cloudflare saw attack traffic and watched attackers change payloads to get around its firewall rules, and watchTowr confirmed active exploitation attempts against both flaws. No source had reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server at the time of the update. Some organizations went offline as a precaution, including BambooHR and several Dutch government sites. Sansec expects mass exploitation now that the patch and write-ups are public. PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge +2 What to do Update the PHP runtime, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM and long-running workers. Fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. thehackernews Updating WordPress or Laravel does not update PHP. It comes from your server package, host or container image. thehackernews Config workarounds only reduce specific attack paths. Updating is the only complete fix. thehackernews PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates, though source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. thehackernews The bigger picture Wiz compares PHP2Shell to Heartbleed, and coverage puts its potential reach at around 70% of the internet. Treat that as a headline estimate, not a measured figure. The lasting lesson is the economics. Wiz says AI turned a long-standing flaw into a practical exploit. OpenAI expects similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Old bugs that were “too hard to exploit” are getting cheaper to prove, for defenders and attackers alike. The advantage goes to whoever patches fastest. items.summary_html:
Two critical flaws in the engine behind a huge share of the web, an early leak, and a preview of how AI changes security work for both defenders and attackers.

The short version

On October 21, PHP shipped emergency updates for two critical flaws, CVE-2026–109618 and CVE-2026–109619, nicknamed PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and let an attacker with no account run code on a web server. OpenAI says the underlying bug had been sitting in PHP for 14 years. What makes this story different is who found it: AI-assisted researchers, before attackers did, as far as anyone knows. thehackernewsFortune

How AI found it

Security firm Calif found the first flaw in August with help from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Calif had been invited to OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, which proactively hunts for flaws in digital infrastructure. Google-owned Wiz found the flaws independently, weeks later. Wiz says it used its own Wiz Atlas tool plus Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol to adapt exploits across PHP versions and setups. PHP rushes out emergency patches for two critical bugs AI found first +3

Note what “AI found it” means here. Humans steered, and the models did heavy lifting on discovery and exploit development. Calif itself cautions that no model can unearth all bugs from simple prompts. The Hacker News also reports that knowing the target’s history still mattered. cyberkendrathehackernews

OpenAI says frontier AI found these flaws before attackers did, giving maintainers a “Defender’s Window” to prepare fixes and protections. The result was a two-month effort between OpenAI, PHP maintainers, researchers and security providers. cyberscoopcyberscoop

How attackers can abuse it

Here is the concept in plain terms, at the level the public advisories describe it. Both flaws are use-after-free bugs. A fatal error mid-request, typically running out of memory, interrupts PHP before it cleans up, and a later request or reused worker then treats the freed memory as live data. Every known trigger is a multipart/form-data request, the format used for file uploads, and PHP parses it before your application code runs. That is why no login is needed and why your own code quality doesn’t matter. sansecsansec

Two outcomes matter. One flaw can leak memory on its own, similar to Heartbleed, exposing passwords, session tokens, API keys and TLS private keys from other requests. The other leads to remote code execution, and an exploit tool credited to Calif combines both bugs into one attack that needs no login. Calif demonstrated it against WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, Laravel and other popular PHP apps. After a break-in, defenders are told to look for web shells, new files in the web root, cron jobs, scheduled tasks and new accounts. PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (CVE-2026–109618, CVE-2026–109619) +3

How it unfolded

The disclosure was meant to be orderly. Details leaked on October 20, PHP pulled its release forward a day, and Calif had mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept. Chainguard also published patched images about six hours before the official fix. thehackernews

Is it being exploited?

Attempts, yes. Confirmed breaches, not yet reported. Cloudflare saw attack traffic and watched attackers change payloads to get around its firewall rules, and watchTowr confirmed active exploitation attempts against both flaws. No source had reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server at the time of the update. Some organizations went offline as a precaution, including BambooHR and several Dutch government sites. Sansec expects mass exploitation now that the patch and write-ups are public. PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as Exploit Attempts Emerge +2

What to do

  • Update the PHP runtime, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM and long-running workers. Fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. thehackernews
  • Updating WordPress or Laravel does not update PHP. It comes from your server package, host or container image. thehackernews
  • Config workarounds only reduce specific attack paths. Updating is the only complete fix. thehackernews
  • PHP 8.1 and older no longer get updates, though source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. thehackernews

The bigger picture

Wiz compares PHP2Shell to Heartbleed, and coverage puts its potential reach at around 70% of the internet. Treat that as a headline estimate, not a measured figure. The lasting lesson is the economics. Wiz says AI turned a long-standing flaw into a practical exploit. OpenAI expects similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Old bugs that were “too hard to exploit” are getting cheaper to prove, for defenders and attackers alike. The advantage goes to whoever patches fastest.

items.title: Deploying Vision GGUF Models to Amazon SageMaker with llama.cpp
items.summary: Cost-Effective Multimodal AI- Deploy Vision GGUF Models with Llama.cpp on SageMaker The “Local LLM” revolution has given us incredible tools like llama.cpp and the GGUF format, allowing us to run high-performance Vision models on modest hardware. But there is a massive leap between running an OCR model in a local terminal and serving it as a production-grade, auto-scaling API on the cloud. When you need to move beyond “it works on my machine,” Amazon SageMaker is the gold standard. However, SageMaker’s pre-built environments don’t always support the cutting-edge efficiency of quantized GGUF vision models. To bridge this gap, we must go BYOC (Bring Your Own Container) . By wrapping the raw speed of llama.cpp inside the modern, asynchronous architecture of FastAPI , we can create a custom inference engine that SageMaker treats like any other managed endpoint. This approach gives you the best of both worlds: the extreme memory efficiency of 4-bit quantization and the industrial-strength reliability of AWS. In this end-to-end guide, we will build a custom OCR solution that handles complex visual reasoning without the “GPU tax” of unquantized models. We’ll cover: Building a SageMaker-compatible Docker container from scratch. Architecting a FastAPI wrapper to handle the /invocations and /ping lifecycle. Optimizing Vision-Language GGUF models for high-speed text extraction. Deploying the final stack to a live SageMaker Endpoint . Prerequisites and Setup First, verify Docker is running and install the Hugging Face Hub library to pull our model weights. !docker version !pip install huggingface-hub We’ll dynamically pull your AWS account details to ensure this script is portable across regions. Note: Ensure you replace "your-bucket-name"with an actual S3 bucket in your account. import subprocess S3_BUCKET_NAME = "bucket_name" # Please change the Bucketname when you running this cell ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME = "ecr_repo_name" AWS_ACCOUNT_ID = subprocess.check_output("aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text", shell=True).decode().strip() AWS_REGION = subprocess.check_output("aws configure get region", shell=True).decode().strip() ECR_URI=f"{AWS_ACCOUNT_ID}.dkr.ecr.{AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com" ECR_REPOSITORY_URI=f"{ECR_URI}/{ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME}" IMAGE_TAG="latest" MODEL_NAME="Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf" 2. Downloading GGUF Model Files We need two files: the quantized weights and the multimodal projector (the “eyes” of the model). We’ll use the Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF, which is highly efficient for document text extraction. from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download import os GGUF_NAME = "Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf" MM_PROJ_NAME = "mmproj-F16.gguf" MODEL_PATH = hf_hub_download( repo_id="unsloth/Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF", filename=GGUF_NAME, local_dir="~/SageMaker/workspace/", local_dir_use_symlinks=False ) MMPROJ_PATH = hf_hub_download( repo_id="unsloth/Nanonets-OCR-s-GGUF", filename=MMPROJ_NAME, local_dir=r"/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/workspace", local_dir_use_symlinks=False, ) print("✅ Model:", MODEL_PATH) print("📦 Size:", round(os.path.getsize(MODEL_PATH)/1024/1024, 2), "MB") 3. Implementing the FastAPI Inference Server Our main.py handles the SageMaker lifecycle. We use Lazy Loading for the model to ensure the container starts quickly, though the very first request will bear the "Cold Start" load time. %%writefile main.py import os, base64, io, logging from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response from PIL import Image, ImageOps, ImageEnhance from llama_cpp import Llama from llama_cpp.llama_chat_format import MiniCPMv26ChatHandler # Setup logging to see output in SageMaker/Docker logs logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) app = FastAPI() # --- DIAGNOSTIC LOGGING BLOCK --- MODEL_DIR = "/opt/ml/model" logger.info(f"Checking directory: {MODEL_DIR}") if os.path.exists(MODEL_DIR): # List all files and subdirectories found in the model path contents = [] for root, dirs, files in os.walk(MODEL_DIR): for name in files: contents.append(os.path.join(root, name)) if contents: logger.info(f"✅ FOUND {len(contents)} files in {MODEL_DIR}:") for f in contents: # Print file size to ensure it's not a 0-byte corrupted download size_mb = os.path.getsize(f) / (1024 * 1024) logger.info(f" - {f} ({size_mb:.2f} MB)") else: logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} exists but is EMPTY.") else: logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} directory DOES NOT EXIST.") # SageMaker unpacks S3 model.tar.gz into /opt/ml/model MODEL_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf" MMPROJ_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/mmproj-F16.gguf" # Global model variable for lazy loading llm = None def load_model(): global llm if llm is None: chat_handler = MiniCPMv26ChatHandler(clip_model_path=MMPROJ_PATH, verbose=False) llm = Llama( model_path=MODEL_PATH, chat_handler=chat_handler, n_ctx=2096, #max for t4 is 128000 (128k) , we have limited to 2096 (2k context) n_gpu_layers=-1, verbose=False ) @app.get("/ping") async def ping(): return Response(status_code=200) @app.post("/invocations") async def invocations(request: Request): load_model() payload = await request.json() # 1. Standardize input to a list of tasks # This supports {"image": "..."} OR {"images": ["...", "..."]} raw_images = payload.get("images", []) if not raw_images and "image" in payload: raw_images = [payload["image"]] prompt = payload.get("prompt", "Extract all text from this image") max_tokens = int(payload.get("max_tokens", 512)) temperature = float(payload.get("temperature", 0.0)) if not raw_images: return Response(content="Missing 'image' or 'images' in payload", status_code=400) results = [] # 2. Process the batch sequentially for i, image_b64 in enumerate(raw_images): try: out = llm.create_chat_completion( messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{image_b64}"}}, {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, ], }], max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=temperature, ) results.append({ "index": i, "text": out["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip(), "finish_reason": out["choices"][0].get("finish_reason"), "usage": out.get("usage") }) except Exception as e: results.append({"index": i, "error": str(e)}) # 3. Return the batch result return {"results": results} 4. Building the Docker Image (BYOC) We use a multi-stage build to keep the runtime image lean. We pull a pre-compiled llama-cpp-python wheel for CUDA 12.4 to avoid lengthy compilation times during the build. %%writefile Dockerfile FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 AS builder ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3-pip python3-dev RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip RUN pip install llama-cpp-python --extra-index-url https://abetlen.github.io/llama-cpp-python/whl/cu124 RUN pip install --no-cache-dir fastapi uvicorn pillow FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04 RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages COPY --from=builder /usr/local/bin /usr/local/bin COPY main.py . RUN mkdir -p /opt/ml/model EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"] 5. Packaging and Pushing Crucial Step: When creating the model.tar.gz, ensure the files are at the root of the archive so SageMaker finds them at /opt/ml/model/. # Package artifacts !tar -cvzf model.tar.gz Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf mmproj-F16.gguf # Upload to S3 !aws s3 cp model.tar.gz s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz # Build and Push Container !aws ecr get-login-password --region {AWS_REGION} | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin {ECR_URI} !docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" . !docker tag "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG" !docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"Upload to S3 bucket Building and pushing image to ECR !docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG" . !docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG" 6. Deployment to SageMaker Endpoint We deploy to an ml.g4dn.xlarge instance. Even though GGUF is efficient on CPUs, using the NVIDIA T4 GPU ensures low-latency OCR performance. import sagemaker from sagemaker.model import Model role = sagemaker.get_execution_role() container_uri = f"{ECR_REPOSITORY_URI}:{IMAGE_TAG}" model_s3_url = f"s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz" ocr_model = Model( image_uri=container_uri, model_data=model_s3_url, role=role, name="nanonets-ocr-gguf-model" ) predictor = ocr_model.deploy( initial_instance_count=1, instance_type="ml.g4dn.xlarge", endpoint_name="vision-ocr-endpoint", container_startup_health_check_timeout=600 ) 7. Conclusion By combining llama.cpp and SageMaker BYOC , you’ve built a production-grade OCR pipeline that is both high-performance and cost-aware. You are no longer restricted by pre-built cloud containers and can leverage the latest quantized multimodal models as soon as they drop on Hugging Face. Don’t forget to clean up: sagemaker_c = boto3.client('sagemaker') sagemaker_c.delete_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name) sagemaker_c.get_waiter('endpoint_deleted').wait(EndpointName=endpoint_name) print("Endpoint + model deleted!") Deploying Vision GGUF Models to Amazon SageMaker with llama.cpp was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Cost-Effective Multimodal AI- Deploy Vision GGUF Models with Llama.cpp on SageMaker

The “Local LLM” revolution has given us incredible tools like llama.cpp and the GGUF format, allowing us to run high-performance Vision models on modest hardware. But there is a massive leap between running an OCR model in a local terminal and serving it as a production-grade, auto-scaling API on the cloud.

When you need to move beyond “it works on my machine,” Amazon SageMaker is the gold standard. However, SageMaker’s pre-built environments don’t always support the cutting-edge efficiency of quantized GGUF vision models.

To bridge this gap, we must go BYOC (Bring Your Own Container).

In this end-to-end guide, we will build a custom OCR solution that handles complex visual reasoning without the “GPU tax” of unquantized models. We’ll cover:

  • Building a SageMaker-compatible Docker container from scratch.
  • Architecting a FastAPI wrapper to handle the /invocations and /ping lifecycle.

  • Deploying the final stack to a live SageMaker Endpoint.
  1. Prerequisites and Setup

First, verify Docker is running and install the Hugging Face Hub library to pull our model weights.

!docker version
!pip install huggingface-hub

We’ll dynamically pull your AWS account details to ensure this script is portable across regions.

Note: Ensure you replace "your-bucket-name"with an actual S3 bucket in your account.
import subprocess
S3_BUCKET_NAME = "bucket_name" # Please change the Bucketname when you running this cell

)

)

Our main.py handles the SageMaker lifecycle. We use Lazy Loading for the model to ensure the container starts quickly, though the very first request will bear the "Cold Start" load time.

from PIL import Image, ImageOps, ImageEnhance
from llama_cpp import Llama
from llama_cpp.llama_chat_format import MiniCPMv26ChatHandler

# Setup logging to see output in SageMaker/Docker logs
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

app = FastAPI()

# --- DIAGNOSTIC LOGGING BLOCK ---
MODEL_DIR = "/opt/ml/model"
logger.info(f"Checking directory: {MODEL_DIR}")

if os.path.exists(MODEL_DIR):
    # List all files and subdirectories found in the model path
    contents = []
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(MODEL_DIR):
        for name in files:
            contents.append(os.path.join(root, name))
    
    if contents:
        logger.info(f"✅ FOUND {len(contents)} files in {MODEL_DIR}:")
        for f in contents:
            # Print file size to ensure it's not a 0-byte corrupted download
            size_mb = os.path.getsize(f) / (1024 * 1024)
            logger.info(f" - {f} ({size_mb:.2f} MB)")
    else:
        logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} exists but is EMPTY.")
else:
    logger.error(f"❌ {MODEL_DIR} directory DOES NOT EXIST.")

# SageMaker unpacks S3 model.tar.gz into /opt/ml/model
MODEL_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf"
MMPROJ_PATH = "/opt/ml/model/mmproj-F16.gguf"

# Global model variable for lazy loading
llm = None

def load_model():
    global llm
    if llm is None:
        chat_handler = MiniCPMv26ChatHandler(clip_model_path=MMPROJ_PATH, verbose=False)
        llm = Llama(
            model_path=MODEL_PATH,
            chat_handler=chat_handler,
            n_ctx=2096, #max for t4 is 128000 (128k) , we have limited to 2096 (2k context)
            n_gpu_layers=-1, 
            verbose=False
        )

@app.get("/ping")
async def ping():
    return Response(status_code=200)

@app.post("/invocations")
async def invocations(request: Request):
    load_model() 
    
    payload = await request.json()
    
    # 1. Standardize input to a list of tasks
    # This supports {"image": "..."} OR {"images": ["...", "..."]}
    raw_images = payload.get("images", [])
    if not raw_images and "image" in payload:
        raw_images = [payload["image"]]
        
    prompt = payload.get("prompt", "Extract all text from this image")
    max_tokens = int(payload.get("max_tokens", 512))
    temperature = float(payload.get("temperature", 0.0))
    
    if not raw_images:
        return Response(content="Missing 'image' or 'images' in payload", status_code=400)

    results = []

    # 2. Process the batch sequentially
    for i, image_b64 in enumerate(raw_images):
        try:
            out = llm.create_chat_completion(
                messages=[{
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": [
                        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{image_b64}"}},
                        {"type": "text", "text": prompt},
                    ],
                }],
                max_tokens=max_tokens,
                temperature=temperature,
            )
            
            results.append({
                "index": i,
                "text": out["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip(),
                "finish_reason": out["choices"][0].get("finish_reason"),
                "usage": out.get("usage")
            })
        except Exception as e:
            results.append({"index": i, "error": str(e)})
    
    # 3. Return the batch result
    return {"results": results}

4. Building the Docker Image (BYOC)

We use a multi-stage build to keep the runtime image lean. We pull a pre-compiled llama-cpp-python wheel for CUDA 12.4 to avoid lengthy compilation times during the build.

%%writefile Dockerfile
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 AS builder
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3-pip python3-dev
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip
RUN pip install llama-cpp-python --extra-index-url https://abetlen.github.io/llama-cpp-python/whl/cu124
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir fastapi uvicorn pillow

FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3 python3-pip && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/bin /usr/local/bin
COPY main.py .
RUN mkdir -p /opt/ml/model
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

5. Packaging and Pushing

Crucial Step: When creating the model.tar.gz, ensure the files are at the root of the archive so SageMaker finds them at /opt/ml/model/.

# Package artifacts
!tar -cvzf model.tar.gz Nanonets-OCR-s-Q4_K_M.gguf mmproj-F16.gguf

# Upload to S3
!aws s3 cp model.tar.gz s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz

# Build and Push Container
!aws ecr get-login-password --region {AWS_REGION} | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin {ECR_URI}
!docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" .
!docker tag "$ECR_REPOSITORY_NAME" "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"
!docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"Upload to S3 bucket

Building and pushing image to ECR

!docker build -t "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG" .
!docker push "$ECR_REPOSITORY_URI":"$IMAGE_TAG"

6. Deployment to SageMaker Endpoint

We deploy to an ml.g4dn.xlarge instance. Even though GGUF is efficient on CPUs, using the NVIDIA T4 GPU ensures low-latency OCR performance.

import sagemaker
from sagemaker.model import Model

role = sagemaker.get_execution_role()
container_uri = f"{ECR_REPOSITORY_URI}:{IMAGE_TAG}"
model_s3_url = f"s3://{S3_BUCKET_NAME}/nanonets-ocr/model.tar.gz"

ocr_model = Model(
    image_uri=container_uri,
    model_data=model_s3_url,
    role=role,
    name="nanonets-ocr-gguf-model"
)

predictor = ocr_model.deploy(
    initial_instance_count=1,
    instance_type="ml.g4dn.xlarge",
    endpoint_name="vision-ocr-endpoint",
    container_startup_health_check_timeout=600
)

7. Conclusion

By combining llama.cpp and SageMaker BYOC, you’ve built a production-grade OCR pipeline that is both high-performance and cost-aware. You are no longer restricted by pre-built cloud containers and can leverage the latest quantized multimodal models as soon as they drop on Hugging Face.

Don’t forget to clean up:

sagemaker_c = boto3.client('sagemaker')
sagemaker_c.delete_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name)
sagemaker_c.get_waiter('endpoint_deleted').wait(EndpointName=endpoint_name)
print("Endpoint + model deleted!")

items.title: Is Cursor Becoming a Grok-First Editor?
items.summary: Models from different labs are part of Cursor’s appeal. Its new plans change which of them your subscription actually pays for. Illustration generated with AI. What appeals to me about Cursor is the ability to use models from different labs in one editor. You can choose the model that works best for a particular task, rather than expect one model to be the best at everything. Cursor’s supported models That choice matters over time, too. A month later, a new release may change which model you prefer. I want to be able to use it without having to rethink my whole setup. Committing my workflow to one lab would mean giving up part of the reason for using a multi-model tool. That is what interests me about Cursor’s new plans. How much of that flexibility are you still paying for? What changes if you use models from several labs? The useful comparison is with what a Cursor subscriber already gets. Legacy Pro, Pro+ and Ultra plans include an allowance for third-party models through an “Other Models” pool. Switching to The X Subscription removes that allowance. Existing subscribers can keep their old plan, price and features, so this is a decision to evaluate before switching. Cursor’s legacy-plan comparison The new bundle was announced on October 12 and includes Cursor, Grok and X benefits. The X Subscription announcement On the new individual Premium plan, $30 a month before tax includes usage for Grok and Composer. If you directly select Claude, GPT or Gemini, you pay for that usage separately at API list price using prepaid credit. Super and Ultra work the same way for direct third-party model selection. The $8 Plus plan does not offer third-party models. Current individual plans The included model pool lists both Grok and Composer. Source: Cursor documentation , captured October 19, 2026. If you mostly want Grok, the new bundle may suit you. If you use Cursor to work with Claude or Gemini, the editor’s features have to justify the subscription while you pay for those models on top. That is a different proposition from a plan that already includes some of their usage. To me, that is a move toward a Grok-first product, with Composer alongside it. Cursor keeps other models available, but the new package gives you a reason to spend more of your time with its own models. The decision is different for existing and new users For an existing Pro subscriber, there is a concrete comparison to make. Legacy Pro costs $20 a month and includes some third-party model usage. The new Premium tier costs $30 a month and charges separately when you directly choose those models. Premium adds other benefits, so these are different packages, not a like-for-like price increase. But someone who mainly wants Claude or Gemini should notice what happens to that part of the subscription. Cursor’s plan comparison Cursor identifies Premium as the nearest new tier to Pro, not an identical package. Sources: Legacy plans , new plans . Checked October 20, 2026. There is also a reason not to rush the decision. Cursor says moving from a legacy plan is optional and permanent. Existing customers can keep their plan, price and features. Keeping Pro may be a better fit for a particular user than moving to a bundle whose included usage favors different models. Switching terms New customers start on The X Subscription. They do not have that legacy-plan option. For them, the question is whether Cursor’s editor and agent features are worth paying for alongside the models they actually want to use. The answer may be yes, but the subscription price alone will not tell them their total cost. Is it worth looking beyond Cursor? For someone who wants Grok and will use the rest of the bundle, the new plans have an obvious appeal. My hesitation is about choosing Cursor specifically to work across labs, then paying for a subscription whose included models do not match that reason for choosing it. That is where alternatives become relevant. GitHub Copilot offers models from several labs within its catalog, subject to plan, client and organization rules. OpenCode supports configurable providers and local models, with setup and usage costs to account for. They are worth comparing if keeping access to different labs is the main attraction. Copilot models , OpenCode providers I read Cursor’s new pricing as a shift toward a Grok-first product, with Composer alongside it. That may be a good direction for developers who want those models. It makes Cursor a harder choice to justify for someone who values the freedom to follow a better option from another lab. The reason I would choose a multi-model editor is to keep that choice open. I would want the subscription to make it easier to use the models I prefer, including the next one that comes along. Is Cursor Becoming a Grok-First Editor? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Models from different labs are part of Cursor’s appeal. Its new plans change which of them your subscription actually pays for.

Illustration generated with AI.

What appeals to me about Cursor is the ability to use models from different labs in one editor. You can choose the model that works best for a particular task, rather than expect one model to be the best at everything. Cursor’s supported models

That choice matters over time, too. A month later, a new release may change which model you prefer. I want to be able to use it without having to rethink my whole setup. Committing my workflow to one lab would mean giving up part of the reason for using a multi-model tool.

That is what interests me about Cursor’s new plans. How much of that flexibility are you still paying for?

What changes if you use models from several labs?

The useful comparison is with what a Cursor subscriber already gets. Legacy Pro, Pro+ and Ultra plans include an allowance for third-party models through an “Other Models” pool. Switching to The X Subscription removes that allowance. Existing subscribers can keep their old plan, price and features, so this is a decision to evaluate before switching. Cursor’s legacy-plan comparison

The new bundle was announced on October 12 and includes Cursor, Grok and X benefits. The X Subscription announcement

On the new individual Premium plan, $30 a month before tax includes usage for Grok and Composer. If you directly select Claude, GPT or Gemini, you pay for that usage separately at API list price using prepaid credit. Super and Ultra work the same way for direct third-party model selection. The $8 Plus plan does not offer third-party models. Current individual plans

The included model pool lists both Grok and Composer. Source: Cursor documentation, captured October 19, 2026.

If you mostly want Grok, the new bundle may suit you. If you use Cursor to work with Claude or Gemini, the editor’s features have to justify the subscription while you pay for those models on top. That is a different proposition from a plan that already includes some of their usage.

To me, that is a move toward a Grok-first product, with Composer alongside it. Cursor keeps other models available, but the new package gives you a reason to spend more of your time with its own models.

The decision is different for existing and new users

For an existing Pro subscriber, there is a concrete comparison to make. Legacy Pro costs $20 a month and includes some third-party model usage. The new Premium tier costs $30 a month and charges separately when you directly choose those models. Premium adds other benefits, so these are different packages, not a like-for-like price increase. But someone who mainly wants Claude or Gemini should notice what happens to that part of the subscription. Cursor’s plan comparison

Cursor identifies Premium as the nearest new tier to Pro, not an identical package. Sources: Legacy plans, new plans. Checked October 20, 2026.

There is also a reason not to rush the decision. Cursor says moving from a legacy plan is optional and permanent. Existing customers can keep their plan, price and features. Keeping Pro may be a better fit for a particular user than moving to a bundle whose included usage favors different models. Switching terms

New customers start on The X Subscription. They do not have that legacy-plan option. For them, the question is whether Cursor’s editor and agent features are worth paying for alongside the models they actually want to use. The answer may be yes, but the subscription price alone will not tell them their total cost.

Is it worth looking beyond Cursor?

For someone who wants Grok and will use the rest of the bundle, the new plans have an obvious appeal. My hesitation is about choosing Cursor specifically to work across labs, then paying for a subscription whose included models do not match that reason for choosing it.

That is where alternatives become relevant. GitHub Copilot offers models from several labs within its catalog, subject to plan, client and organization rules. OpenCode supports configurable providers and local models, with setup and usage costs to account for. They are worth comparing if keeping access to different labs is the main attraction. Copilot models, OpenCode providers

I read Cursor’s new pricing as a shift toward a Grok-first product, with Composer alongside it. That may be a good direction for developers who want those models. It makes Cursor a harder choice to justify for someone who values the freedom to follow a better option from another lab.

The reason I would choose a multi-model editor is to keep that choice open. I would want the subscription to make it easier to use the models I prefer, including the next one that comes along.

items.title: Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story
items.summary: For two decades, data centres were relatively safe, lucrative real estate investments. They attracted investors because they served as digital infrastructure — the essential plumbing that keeps the internet running. The growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and its increased demands on computing power has meant data centre builders are in a race to build out sufficient supply. But in the past two weeks, investors have started to have genuine concerns about the long-term viability of these businesses. On Wednesday, shares in NextDC, one of Australia’s largest data centre builders, collapsed by 40% after it said delays at its flagship Melbourne site meant its revenue forecasts would fall short of forecasts. These delays have come about after the local community raised significant concerns about the impact of NextDC’s M3 data centre expansion. Electricity distributor Jemena paused the construction of the giant concrete power poles that had been snaking their way along Footscray streets, after local councils raised concerns about the impact on residential neighbourhoods. These 22-metre power poles are crucial to NextDC’s operations in Footscray. Data centre operators make their profits from selling access to the massive amounts of power that AI chips need. Without that power, these facilities cannot remain viable. NextDC is not alone in facing significant headwinds. Data centre company Firmus abruptly cancelled its multi-billion dollar listing on the Australian stock exchange, due to a lack of investor demand. Similarly, London-based data centre developer Nscale is struggling to attract buyers for a stock market listing on Wall Street. Shares in CoreWeave, which claims to operate the world’s most powerful AI supercomputer , dropped 15% in one day last week on concerns about its financial strength. These jitters reflect the harsh reality of AI: while the hype is strong, the business models are coming under increasing scrutiny. Rising costs for massive investments Hundreds of billions of dollars have been spent globally on training models and building the data centres to house the infrastructure that powers AI. The pipeline of investments is expected to reach some US$10 trillion (A$14.25 trillion) by 2032. Until recently, much of the capital expenditure was funded internally by the AI companies or by raising money directly from investors; more recently, they have been borrowing vast sums in the corporate bond market. And while those investing in AI are patient, they still expect to see significant financial returns. Community campaigners demonstrating against a planned data centre in Kilmarnock, Scotland. Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images Sticky inflation and rising interest rates complicate this further. Data centre developers now face higher borrowing costs, plus higher construction costs. And rising interest rates can make other investments more attractive. Analysts estimate that giants like OpenAI and Anthropic will need to increase revenues by 80% a year for the next six years to meet investors’ revenue expectations. Yet, indicators suggest that consumer and corporate spending on paid AI models is slowing down . Racing for chips To make things worse, the hardware that AI depends upon is driving real investor concern. Historically, data centres could operate for decades with minimal maintenance, guaranteeing rents and returns. But AI chips have a shelf life of only a few years. Each new generation requires upgrades to power delivery and cooling, trapping data centres on a treadmill of multibillion-dollar expenses to pay for these upgrades. Even if AI revenues stabilise enough to support these expenses, there’s no guarantee that data centre companies will be able to access the chips they need to fill data centres, and to support AI demand. Amazon recently admitted it is hoarding billions of AI chips, even though it doesn’t have any capacity for installing them . This massive over-investment is driven by anxieties around long-term supplies. This gold rush for chips is why American chip manufacturer Nvidia is one of the few companies in the AI space to actually be making money. Nvidia also invests in the companies that buy its chips — its own customers — raising concerns about circular financing . The social licence Beyond the balance sheet, investors are also concerned about the loss of social licence for data centres amid local community protests. Community concerns around data centres are already high , driven by persistent noise (from energy transmission), visual impact, localised heating, and environmental concerns . And these concerns will only grow if data centres start to impact the cost of living by pushing up electricity or water prices. Forecasts suggest that New South Wales data centres could consume up to 25% of Sydney’s daily water demand within a decade. In Victoria, transmission company AusNet is reviewing requests from data centres for more than 10 gigawatts of connections, which could exceed the state’s entire supply capacity . In both cases, this level of demand will inevitably affect consumer prices. When will communities benefit? The AI age depends on the physical infrastructure of data centres. But the current path we are on demands ever-increasing capital from investors to fund a relentless upgrade cycle. It demands huge volumes of power and water from local utilities. And it places a significant burden on the communities that host these data centres. These factors mean the era of data centres being a safe stock market investment are over. And if investors become unwilling to fund these risks blindly, and communities become resistant to hosting these centres, this month’s stock market jitters may turn into a steeper market sell-off. To shore up investor confidence, it’s important that investments in AI do not just focus on building better models, but also models that are more efficient — in terms of their costs, energy demands and spatial requirements. And if they can be designed to support the electricity grid by adding, rather than displacing, renewables capacity, then communities may begin to feel the benefits of investments into AI.

items.title: A Coding Guide to Cactus Whistle: Does a 16.9 MB Speech Model Hold Up Against Whisper Base? Word Error Rate, Speed, Streaming, Timestamps, Keywords, and Speech-to-Tool Calls on a CPU
items.summary:
In this tutorial, we use Whistle , Cactus Compute’s speech-to-text model, a 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU, transcribes seven languages, and returns word timestamps and probabilities. The model card claims it beats Whisper base on LibriSpeech; we test it on seeded test-clean and test-other samples, comparing Whistle with Whisper tiny and base on identical clips, judged by paired speaker-cluster intervals with Holm correction. We find a lead over greedy Whisper base on test-other, no significant gap against beam search, and a speed advantage that narrows as clips grow. Beyond the headline, we probe a 30-second window where the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, plus streaming latency, timestamps, keyword biasing, other languages, noise, embeddings, and speech-to-tool calls. Our figures are one-run samples from an Apple M4, and published full-split numbers are quoted, not measured. " + "=" * 78) print(title) print("=" * 78) def section(name): def wrap(fn): def run(*a, **kw): banner(name) t0 = time.time() try: out = fn(*a, **kw) RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok" return out except Exception as e: RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}" print(f"

[{time.time() - t0:.0f} s]") json.dump({"results": RESULTS, "verdicts": VERDICTS}, open("results.json", "w"), indent=1) return run return wrap banner("1. items.summary_html:
In this tutorial, we use Whistle, Cactus Compute’s speech-to-text model, a 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU, transcribes seven languages, and returns word timestamps and probabilities. The model card claims it beats Whisper base on LibriSpeech; we test it on seeded test-clean and test-other samples, comparing Whistle with Whisper tiny and base on identical clips, judged by paired speaker-cluster intervals with Holm correction. We find a lead over greedy Whisper base on test-other, no significant gap against beam search, and a speed advantage that narrows as clips grow. Beyond the headline, we probe a 30-second window where the pinned engine silently drops the middle of longer audio, plus streaming latency, timestamps, keyword biasing, other languages, noise, embeddings, and speech-to-tool calls. Our figures are one-run samples from an Apple M4, and published full-split numbers are quoted, not measured.

def section(name):
    def wrap(fn):
        def run(*a, **kw):
            banner(name)
            t0 = time.time()
            try:
                out = fn(*a, **kw)
                RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok"
                return out
            except Exception as e:
                RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
                print(f"\n[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                traceback.print_exc(limit=3)
                return None
            finally:
                print(f"\n[{time.time() - t0:.0f} s]")
                json.dump({"results": RESULTS, "verdicts": VERDICTS}, open("results.json", "w"), indent=1)
        return run
    return wrap

def fetch(url, tries=7):
    """GET with retries. The datasets-server rate-limits anonymous callers (HTTP 429): honour Retry-After when it is
    sent, otherwise back off 5, 10, 20, 40 ... seconds, and never give up on the first refusal."""
    for k in range(tries):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as r:
                return r.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            if k == tries - 1:
                raise
            wait = int(e.headers.get("Retry-After", 0) or 0) if e.code == 429 else 0
            time.sleep(max(wait, 5 * 2 ** k) if e.code in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) else 2)
        except Exception:
            if k == tries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(3 * (k + 1))
 
 
def page(dataset, config, split, offset, length=100):
    """One page of a Hub dataset through the datasets-server rows API: metadata plus signed audio URLs."""
    url = (f"https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/rows?dataset={dataset}&config={config}"
           f"&split={split}&offset={offset}&length={length}")
    time.sleep(0.25)                                  # stay under the anonymous rate limit when paging a whole split
    return json.loads(fetch(url))
 
 
def load_audio(row):
    """Download one row's clip; return 16 kHz mono float32 samples and the sha256 of the original file."""
    data = fetch(row["audio"][0]["src"])

    if sr != SR:

def all_rows(dataset, config, split):
    out, offset = [], 0
    while True:
        rows = page(dataset, config, split, offset)["rows"]
        out += [r["row"] for r in rows]
        offset += 100
        if len(rows) < 100:

def dataset_sha(dataset):
    return json.loads(fetch(f"https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/{dataset}"))["sha"][:12]
 
 
def wer_counts(ref, hyp):
    """Errors (S+D+I) and reference words for one normalised pair; an empty hypothesis is all deletions."""
    n = len(ref.split())
    if not hyp.strip():
        return n, n
    o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp)
    return o.substitutions + o.deletions + o.insertions, n
 
 
def sdi(ref, hyp):
    if not hyp.strip():
        return 0, len(ref.split()), 0
    o = jiwer.process_words(ref, hyp)
    return o.substitutions, o.deletions, o.insertions
 
 
def corpus_wer(errs, words):
    return 100.0 * sum(errs) / max(sum(words), 1)
 
 
def _by_cluster(clusters, *arrays):
    tot = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0.0] * len(arrays))
    for i, c in enumerate(clusters):
        for j, a in enumerate(arrays):
            tot[c][j] += a[i]
    return tot
 
 
def wer_ci(clusters, errs, words, B=2000, seed=0):
    """95% percentile interval of a corpus WER, resampling clusters (speakers) with replacement."""
    tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs, words)
    keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(B):
        d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys))
        boots.append(100 * sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) / max(sum(tot[c][1] for c in d), 1))
    return np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
 
 
def paired_contrast(clusters, errs_a, words, errs_b, label_a, label_b, B=2000, seed=0):
    """WER(a) - WER(b) with a paired speaker-cluster bootstrap: the same resampled speakers for both systems."""
    tot = _by_cluster(clusters, errs_a, errs_b, words)
    keys, rng = sorted(tot), random.Random(seed)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(B):
        d = rng.choices(keys, k=len(keys))
        w = max(sum(tot[c][2] for c in d), 1)
        boots.append(100 * (sum(tot[c][0] for c in d) - sum(tot[c][1] for c in d)) / w)
    boots = np.array(boots)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    p = 2 * min((boots <= 0).mean(), (boots >= 0).mean())
    return {"a": label_a, "b": label_b, "diff": corpus_wer(errs_a, words) - corpus_wer(errs_b, words),
            "lo": lo, "hi": hi, "p": max(p, 1 / B), "clusters": len(keys)}
 
 
def holm(ps, alpha=0.05):
    order, keep = np.argsort(ps), [False] * len(ps)
    for rank, i in enumerate(order):
        if ps[i] <= alpha / (len(ps) - rank):
            keep[i] = True
        else:
            break
    return keep
 
 
def verdict(c, significant):
    """Verdict rule: diff = WER(other system) - WER(Whistle). CI entirely > 0 and Holm-significant -> Whistle ahead;
    entirely < 0 and significant -> Whistle behind; otherwise no significant difference at this sample size."""
    if c["lo"] > 0 and significant:
        return "Whistle ahead"
    if c["hi"] < 0 and significant:
        return "Whistle behind"
    return "no significant difference at this n"
 
 
def fmt_contrast(c):
    return f"{c['diff']:+.2f} pts (95% CI {c['lo']:+.2f}..{c['hi']:+.2f}, {c['clusters']} speakers)"

def whisper_model(size):
    if size not in WHISPER:
        WHISPER[size] = whisper.load_model(size, device="cpu")
    return WHISPER[size]
 
 
def run_whisper(size, audio, language="en", **kw):
    """openai-whisper with its defaults (greedy with temperature fallback) unless kw says otherwise. Seeded per call,
    because the fallback samples. Returns text, whether any segment needed the fallback, and the wall time."""
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    WHISPER_SECONDS[size] += len(audio) / SR
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    r = whisper_model(size).transcribe(audio, language=language, fp16=False, **kw)
    fell_back = any(s.get("temperature", 0) > 0 for s in r["segments"])
    return r["text"], fell_back, time.perf_counter() - t0

def audio_seconds(clips, seconds):
    """Exactly `seconds` of speech: clips concatenated in sample order, then trimmed."""
    out, total = [], 0
    for c in clips:
        out.append(c["audio"])
        total += c["dur"]
        if total >= seconds:
            break
    return np.concatenate(out)[:int(seconds * SR)]
